### Defining j on elliptic curves makes modular transformations preserve it

**Remember:** j sees only the lattice, not its basis or its size.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F03 (Modular and automorphic functions), 14H52. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Define j on lattices, the integer spans of two real-linearly independent complex numbers, by j = 1728g₂³/(g₂³ − 27g₃²). Here g₂ = 60∑λ⁻⁴ and g₃ = 140∑λ⁻⁶ over the nonzero lattice points λ. So j depends only on the set of lattice points and does not change when the lattice is scaled.

**Problem.** Let j(τ) be the j-invariant of ℂ/(ℤ + ℤτ), where Im τ &gt; 0. Then j((aτ + b)/(cτ + d)) = j(τ) for integers a, b, c and d with ad − bc = 1.

**How the definition helps.** A substitution of determinant one only changes the basis and scales the lattice, and neither changes j. For τ′ = (aτ + b)/(cτ + d), multiplying ℤ + ℤτ′ by cτ + d gives the span of aτ + b and cτ + d, which is ℤ + ℤτ since ad − bc = 1. Under scaling by α, the numerator and denominator of j both scale by α⁻¹² (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Modular form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_form). It says: “For example, the j-invariant j(z) of an elliptic curve, regarded as a function on the set of all elliptic curves, is a modular function.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Bounding modular forms at the cusp makes each space finite-dimensional

**Remember:** No poles at the cusp, so only finitely many forms fit.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F11 (Holomorphic modular forms of integral weight). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a subgroup G of finite index in SL₂(ℤ) and an integer k, a weight k modular form is holomorphic on the upper half-plane and satisfies f(γz) = (cz+d)ᵏf(z) for every γ in G with bottom row (c,d). It must also be bounded at every cusp. That is, (cz+d)⁻ᵏf(γz) stays bounded as Im z → ∞ for every γ in SL₂(ℤ) with bottom row (c,d).

**Problem.** For finite-index G in SL₂(ℤ), the space Mₖ(G) of weight k modular forms is finite-dimensional. For the full modular group and even k → ∞, its explicit dimension formula has leading term k/12.

**How the definition helps.** Boundedness at the cusps means no poles there, so modular forms are holomorphic sections of a line bundle on the compact modular curve, and Riemann–Roch gives finite dimension (our own). Without that condition the full group has the infinitely many independent weight-four functions E₄jⁿ for n ≥ 0 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Modular form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_form). It says: “For example, the spaces Mₖ(G) and Sₖ(G) are finite-dimensional, and their dimensions can be computed thanks to the Riemann–Roch theorem in terms of the geometry of the G-action on H”

**Sources:**

- [J.-P. Serre, A Course in Arithmetic, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 7, Springer, 1973](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4684-9884-4)
- [N. Koblitz, Introduction to Elliptic Curves and Modular Forms, 2nd ed., Springer, 1993](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4612-0909-6)

### Lattice homogeneity gives Eisenstein series their modular transformation law

**Remember:** Sum over the lattice, not the basis, and scaling gives the weight.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F11 (Holomorphic modular forms of integral weight). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In the lattice definition, a weight k modular form is a function F on lattices, the integer spans of two real-linearly independent complex numbers, with F(αΛ) = α⁻ᵏF(Λ) for every nonzero complex α. Also f(τ) = F(ℤ + ℤτ) must be holomorphic for Im τ &gt; 0 and bounded as Im τ → ∞.

**Problem.** For even k &gt; 2, let Gₖ(τ) sum (m + nτ)⁻ᵏ over all integer pairs except (0, 0), with Im τ &gt; 0. It satisfies Gₖ(−1/τ) = τᵏGₖ(τ) and Gₖ(τ + 1) = Gₖ(τ).

**How the definition helps.** Gₖ is the function F(Λ) = ∑λ⁻ᵏ over nonzero lattice points, which ignores the basis and scales by α⁻ᵏ when Λ is scaled by α. Replacing τ by τ + 1 keeps the lattice, and ℤ + ℤ(−1/τ) is the lattice scaled by 1/τ, giving the factor τᵏ (our own checks). The remaining work is absolute convergence for k &gt; 2 and holomorphy at infinity.

**Wikipedia:** [Modular form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_form). It says: “The key idea in proving the equivalence of the two definitions is that such a function F is determined, because of the second condition, by its values on lattices of the form ℤ + ℤτ, where τ ∈ H.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Newforms give a Hecke eigenbasis including primes that divide the level

**Remember:** Throw out forms inherited from lower levels, and all Hecke operators diagonalize.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F11 (Holomorphic modular forms of integral weight), 11F25. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix a weight k and a level N, with trivial character. The oldforms are the cusp forms g(dz) with g of level M properly dividing N and d dividing N/M, and the new subspace is their orthogonal complement for the Petersson inner product. On it, each system of eigenvalues for the Hecke operators prime to N occurs only once (Atkin–Lehner).

**Problem.** On this new subspace the usual Hecke operators Tₙ commute and are self-adjoint, including Tₚ for primes dividing N. Thus the space has a basis of simultaneous eigenforms for the full Hecke algebra.

**How the definition helps.** By multiplicity one, the bad-prime operators, which commute with the good ones, act on each new eigenline by scalars, and these are real for trivial character (our own). With the orthogonal eigenbasis this makes every Tₙ self-adjoint on the new subspace. On old subspaces g(z) and g(pz) share all good eigenvalues, and Tₚ for p dividing N need not be self-adjoint there (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Atkin–Lehner theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atkin%E2%80%93Lehner_theory). It says: “the algebra of operators on newforms they generate is a finite-dimensional C\*-algebra that is commutative; and by the spectral theory of such operators, there exists a basis for the space of newforms consisting of eigenforms for the full Hecke algebra.”

**Sources:**

- [A. O. L. Atkin and J. Lehner, Hecke operators on Γ₀(m), Math. Ann. 185 (1970) 134–160](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01359701)

### Vanishing at the cusps makes the Petersson inner product finite

**Remember:** Forms that die at the cusp have finite length.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F11 (Holomorphic modular forms of integral weight), 11F25. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A cusp form of weight k for the modular group is a modular form whose Fourier expansion ∑aₙqⁿ, with q = exp(2πiz), has a₀ = 0. So it vanishes at the cusp and decays like exp(−2π Im z) there.

**Problem.** The Petersson integral of f ḡ yᵏ dx dy / y² over a fundamental domain converges when f or g is a cusp form. The Hecke operators Tₙ are self-adjoint for it, so the cusp forms have a basis of common Hecke eigenforms with real Fourier coefficients.

**How the definition helps.** Exponential decay of one cusp form beats the factor yᵏ⁻² at the cusp, so the integral converges (our own). The Hecke operators commute and are self-adjoint, so the spectral theorem gives a common eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. Normalizing a₁ = 1 makes each aₙ the Tₙ eigenvalue, so the coefficients are real (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Cusp form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cusp_form), [Petersson inner product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petersson_inner_product). It says: “Cuspidality is what is required to make this integral finite.”

**Sources:**

- [E. Hecke, Über Modulfunktionen und die Dirichletschen Reihen mit Eulerscher Produktentwicklung. I, Math. Ann. 114 (1937)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01594160)
- [J.-P. Serre, A Course in Arithmetic, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 7, Springer, 1973](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4684-9884-4)

### Cusp constants become residues

**Remember:** Constant terms become residues when the cusp is filled in.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F23 (Relations with algebraic geometry and topology), 11F11. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Take a torsion-free subgroup of finite index in SL₂(ℤ). Move each cusp to infinity, assume its stabilizer consists of translations, and let the cusp width h be the least positive one. A weight two form f gives the differential f(τ)dτ, which in the coordinate q = exp(2πiτ/h) is h f dq/(2πiq) (our own).

**Problem.** At each cusp, expand the transformed form in exp(2πiτ/h). The sum of its constant coefficients, each multiplied by its own cusp width, is zero.

**How the definition helps.** So the residue of f(τ)dτ at a cusp is h times the constant coefficient, divided by 2πi (our own). The residue theorem on the compact modular curve says these residues sum to zero (our own).

**nLab:** [modular form](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/modular+form). It says: “Using the Kodaira-Spencer isomorphism one can show that the space of cusp forms of weight 2 are the differentials on the corresponding modular curve.”

### Sections add modular weights

**Remember:** Multiplying sections adds the exponents of their tensor powers.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F23 (Relations with algebraic geometry and topology), 11F11. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On the compactified complex moduli stack of elliptic curves with the chosen level structure, let ω be the extended Hodge line bundle. Its fiber at an elliptic curve is the line of translation-invariant differentials. A modular form of weight k is a global holomorphic section of ω⊗ᵏ.

**Problem.** The product of forms of weights k and ℓ at the same level has weight k + ℓ. If one factor vanishes at every cusp, the product does too.

**How the definition helps.** Tensoring the two sections adds their tensor powers and preserves vanishing at the cusps (our own). The work is identifying sections on the compactification with analytic forms that are holomorphic at the cusps (our own).

**nLab:** [modular form](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/modular+form). It says: “A modular form of weight k is a section of ω⊗ᵏ.”

### Weight two cusp forms give differentials

**Remember:** A cusp zero cancels the simple pole in the differential.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F23 (Relations with algebraic geometry and topology), 11F11. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix full level N ≥ 3 over ℂ, and let ω be the Hodge line bundle on the compact modular curve, whose fiber at an elliptic curve is its line of invariant differentials. A weight two form is a section of ω⊗², and a cusp form is one that vanishes at every cusp, the points added to compactify the curve.

**Problem.** Weight two cusp forms on the compact complex modular curve are its holomorphic one-forms.

**How the definition helps.** The Kodaira–Spencer isomorphism identifies ω⊗² with the one-forms that may have simple poles at the cusps. Vanishing at a cusp cancels that pole, leaving a holomorphic one-form (our own).

**nLab:** [modular form](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/modular+form). It says: “Using the Kodaira-Spencer isomorphism one can show that the space of cusp forms of weight 2 are the differentials on the corresponding modular curve.”

### Hecke operators at distinct primes commute

**Remember:** Translations in separate prime factors commute.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F25 (Hecke-Petersson operators, differential operators (one variable)), 11F70. arXiv math.NT, math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a prime p outside the level, put K = GL₂(ℤₚ) and choose one representative g from each coset gK in K diag(p,1) K. On right K-invariant adelic forms, the local Hecke operator sums right translations by these representatives in the p-component (our own).

**Problem.** Hecke operators at distinct primes outside the level commute on classical modular forms.

**How the definition helps.** The moves at one prime leave the other prime factor alone (our own). Their sums therefore commute term by term (our own). The work is the adelic description of classical forms and the comparison of local translations with classical Hecke operators (our own).

**nLab:** [automorphic form](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/automorphic+form). It says: “These are the adelic automorphic forms. They may be thought of as subsuming ordinary modular forms for all level structures.”

### Normalizing eigenforms by a(1) = 1 makes coefficients equal Hecke eigenvalues

**Remember:** Set the first coefficient to one, and the coefficients become eigenvalues.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F25 (Hecke-Petersson operators, differential operators (one variable)), 11F30. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A normalized Hecke eigenform of weight k for SL₂(ℤ) is a cusp form with first Fourier coefficient one and an eigenvalue for every Tₘ.

**Problem.** For a normalized Hecke eigenform, Tₘ f = a(m) f for all m, and a(m)a(n) = Σ dᵏ⁻¹ a(mn/d²) over d dividing gcd(m,n). So the coefficients are multiplicative, and the L-function of f has an Euler product.

**How the definition helps.** The first Fourier coefficient of Tₘf equals a(m), so the eigenvalue equals a(m). The level-one Hecke multiplication law gives the divisor sum, hence multiplicativity and the Euler product (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Hecke operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hecke_operator). It says: “Thus for normalized cuspidal Hecke eigenforms of integer weight, their Fourier coefficients coincide with their Hecke eigenvalues.”

### Quasimodularity preserves derivatives

**Remember:** Allow the extra chain-rule term instead of losing derivatives.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F25 (Hecke-Petersson operators, differential operators (one variable)), 11F37. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A weight k quasimodular form for SL₂(ℤ) is a holomorphic function f that transforms like a modular form up to a polynomial correction. Precisely, there is a polynomial Pτ(X) with constant term f(τ) and coefficients holomorphic on the upper half-plane and at infinity. For every γ in SL₂(ℤ) with bottom row (c,d), (cτ+d)⁻ᵏf(γτ) = Pτ(c/(cτ+d)) (our own).

**Problem.** Differentiation maps a weight k quasimodular form to a weight k + 2 quasimodular form. The ordinary modular forms are not closed under differentiation, as the derivative of E₄ shows.

**How the definition helps.** The polynomial allows exactly the extra factors that the chain rule introduces (our own). Differentiation raises the weight by two and the polynomial degree by at most one. The ordinary weight-four Eisenstein series E₄ has a nonzero extra term, so its derivative fails the ordinary modular law (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Almost holomorphic modular form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almost_holomorphic_modular_form). It says: “Ramanujan observed that the derivative of any quasimodular form is another quasimodular form.”

**Remember:** A root chooses a direction in the two old copies.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F25 (Hecke-Petersson operators, differential operators (one variable)), 11F85. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let f be a normalized cusp eigenform of weight k, level N and trivial character, and let p be a prime outside N. A refinement at p chooses a root of X² − aₚX + pᵏ⁻¹, where aₚ is the pth Fourier coefficient.

**Problem.** At level Np, Uₚ replaces each nth Fourier coefficient by the coefficient at pn. If the roots differ, the span of f(τ) and f(pτ) has two Uₚ eigenlines, and each refinement labels the line whose eigenvalue is the chosen root.

**How the definition helps.** The chosen root specifies one eigenvalue and hence one line (our own). If β is the other root, the line with eigenvalue α is generated by f(τ) − β f(pτ) (our own). The work is computing Uₚ on this span and showing that its characteristic polynomial is the original pth Hecke polynomial (our own).

### Even self-dual lattices give modular theta series

**Remember:** Even norms give translation and self-duality gives inversion.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F27 (Theta series; Weil representation; theta correspondences), 11F11. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A positive definite integral lattice L is even if every squared length is even, so τ ↦ τ + 1 fixes every term of its theta series (our own). **Problem.** An even self-dual positive definite lattice of rank 8m, for positive integral m, has a scalar theta series of weight 4m for SL₂(ℤ). The odd self-dual lattice ℤ⁸ fails the translation rule.

**How the definition helps.** Evenness fixes every summand under τ ↦ τ + 1, and Poisson summation with self-duality shows that the series at −1/τ is τ to the power 4m times the series at τ (our own). These two moves generate SL₂(ℤ), and positive definiteness gives holomorphy at infinity (our own). For the odd lattice ℤ⁸, translation flips the sign of the terms from vectors of squared length one (our own).

### Distinct indices become orthogonal

**Remember:** Averaged over an orthonormal basis, coefficient products act like a delta.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F30 (Fourier coefficients of automorphic forms), 11F72. arXiv math.NT, math.SP. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix even k ≥ 4 and positive integers q, m, n, and take a Petersson-orthonormal basis of weight k cusp forms for Γ₀(q) with trivial character, using the unscaled Petersson integral. The normalized sum is Γ(k−1)(4π√(mn))¹⁻ᵏ times the sum over the basis of the conjugate mth coefficient times the nth coefficient. This factor makes the diagonal term of the Petersson formula equal one for m = n and zero otherwise (our own).

**Problem.** As the positive integer q grows, this sum tends to one for equal indices and zero otherwise. The error is O(q to the power 1−k), with k,m,n fixed.

**How the definition helps.** The Petersson formula gives the stated diagonal and restricts every other modulus c to positive multiples of q. The trivial Kloosterman bound cancels the denominator c (our own). The Bessel factor is O(c¹⁻ᵏ), so summing gives O(q¹⁻ᵏ) (our own).

**Paper or page:** [On the Density of Low Lying Zeros of a Large Family of Automorphic L-functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.09050v2). It says: “where δ(m,n) = 1 when m=n and 0 otherwise and S denotes a Kloosterman sum.”

### Harmonic weights normalize Petersson diagonals

**Remember:** Weight each form by the reciprocal of its squared norm.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F30 (Fourier coefficients of automorphic forms), 11F72. arXiv math.NT, math.SP. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix even k ≥ 4 and positive integer q, and choose an orthogonal basis of weight k cusp forms for Γ₀(q) with trivial character. The harmonic weight of each basis vector f is Γ(k−1)(4π)¹⁻ᵏ divided by its squared Petersson norm, using unscaled hyperbolic area.

**Problem.** Divide the nth Fourier coefficient by n to the power (k−1)/2 and call the result a(n), for each positive n. In the Petersson formula, the harmonic-weighted sum of conjugate a(m) times a(n) is a diagonal term, one for m = n and zero otherwise, plus Kloosterman terms.

**How the definition helps.** The reciprocal squared norm cancels any rescaling of a basis vector, and the factor Γ(k−1)(4π)¹⁻ᵏ makes the diagonal coefficient one. In our own derivation, expanding a Poincaré series, a sum of translates of one Fourier mode, in the orthogonal basis supplies the reciprocal norms. Its other Fourier coefficients give the Kloosterman terms.

**Wikipedia:** [Petersson trace formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petersson_trace_formula). It says: “a kind of orthogonality relation between coefficients of a holomorphic modular form.”

**Paper or page:** [Trace formula and functional equation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.16921v2). It says: “δ(m=n) + 2π i⁻ᵏ ∑₍c&gt;0, c≡0 (D)₎ Sχ(m,n;c)/c J₍k−1₎(4π√(mn)/c).”

### Poincaré series extract coefficients

**Remember:** Average one mode to recover one coefficient.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F30 (Fourier coefficients of automorphic forms), 11F11. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For even k &gt; 2 and integer n ≥ 1, the nth Poincaré series sums the weight k transforms of exp(2πinτ). Take one transform per left coset of the stabilizer of infinity in SL₂(ℤ).

**Problem.** Pair a cusp form with this series using the Petersson integral, linear in the cusp form, without dividing by the domain’s area. The result is its nth Fourier coefficient times Γ(k − 1) divided by (4πn) to the power k − 1. These series span the space of cusp forms.

**How the definition helps.** Unfolding the average of one mode turns the integral over a fundamental domain into an integral over a vertical strip against exp(2πinτ), justified by absolute convergence for k &gt; 2 (our own). Integrating over x picks out the nth coefficient, and the y-integral gives Γ(k−1)/(4πn) to the power k − 1 (our own). A cusp form orthogonal to every series has all coefficients zero, so the series span (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Poincaré series (modular form)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincar%C3%A9_series_%28modular_form%29). It says: “In general, the Poincaré series is, for n ≥ 1, a cusp form.”

### Dual isogenies make Fricke involutive

**Remember:** Dualize the isogeny twice to recover it.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F32 (Modular correspondences, etc.), 14G35. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Over ℂ, a point of Y₀(N) represents an elliptic curve and a quotient map φ with cyclic kernel of order N. Its dual is the reverse map whose composite with φ multiplies points by N. Define the Fricke map by sending φ to its dual.

**Problem.** The Fricke map on Y₀(N) is an involution. It extends to an involution of its smooth compactification X₀(N).

**How the definition helps.** Dualizing twice recovers φ, so the Fricke map squares to the identity (our own). The dual isogeny theorem gives this identity and shows that the dual of a cyclic isogeny of degree N is again cyclic (our own). An automorphism of a smooth curve extends to its smooth projective compactification (our own).

### Factorial powers isolate ordinary forms

**Remember:** Factorial powers keep units and kill the rest.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F33 (Congruences for modular and p-adic modular forms), 11F85. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let U be a Hecke operator on a finite free module over the p-adic integers. Its ordinary part is the largest direct summand on which U is invertible, with a complement on which the powers of U tend to zero. The ordinary projector is the limit of U to the power n!, which modulo each power of p becomes the identity on the first summand and zero on the second (our own).

**Problem.** The limit exists and is idempotent. Its image is the ordinary part, and it commutes with every operator that commutes with U.

**How the definition helps.** Modulo pʳ, U has finite order on the ordinary part and is nilpotent on its complement, so the factorial powers are eventually the identity and zero there (our own). This builds the projector without factoring a characteristic polynomial, and it is idempotent with image the ordinary part (our own). Any operator commuting with U commutes with its powers and their limit (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Twisted Triple Product p-adic L-function for Finite Slope Families of Hilbert Modular Forms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.13230v2). It says: “is the ordinary projector $e<sub>n.o</sub> = \\lim <sub>n\\to \\infty </sub> U<sup>n!</sup>$.”

The product of the two completions is modular and has degree at most the sum (our own). The work is the completion theorem, which identifies this definition with the polynomial transformation law (our own).

### Quadratic indices rule out negative terms

**Remember:** A negative direction produces arbitrarily negative traces in its orbit.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F46 (Siegel modular groups; Siegel and Hilbert-Siegel modular and automorphic forms). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A degree g Siegel Fourier index is a symmetric g-by-g matrix T with integer diagonal and half-integer off-diagonal entries, and its mode at the period matrix Z is exp(2πi tr(TZ)). For a level-one scalar form, the index changes T ↦ UᵀTU by integral invertible U keep the coefficient's absolute value (our own).

**Problem.** Take a level-one holomorphic function that obeys the Siegel modular law in degree at least two; its Fourier terms indexed by matrices with a negative direction vanish. In degree one this fails, since the modular function j has a pole at infinity.

**How the definition helps.** A negative direction gives a primitive integer vector v with negative value, and adding large multiples of v to another basis vector, which needs g ≥ 2, sends the trace of UᵀTU to minus infinity (our own). Boundedness of the form on the period cell at Im Z = I gives \|a(T)\| ≤ C exp(2π tr T) for each index in the orbit (our own). So the common absolute value is zero (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Siegel modular form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siegel_modular_form). It says: “Corollary to this theorem is the fact that Siegel modular forms of degree g &gt; 1 have Fourier expansions and are thus holomorphic at infinity.”

**Remember:** The Fourier index is the index in the translation rule.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F50 (Jacobi forms), 11F46. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A holomorphic Jacobi form of weight k and index m is a function φ(τ,z) on ℍ×ℂ with two transformation rules, where e(t) = exp(2πit). For γ in SL₂(ℤ) with bottom row (c,d), φ(γτ, z/(cτ+d)) = (cτ+d)ᵏ e(mcz²/(cτ+d)) φ(τ,z). For integers λ, μ, φ(τ, z+λτ+μ) = e(−m(λ²τ+2λz)) φ(τ,z), and its Fourier support is 4mn ≥ r² (our own).

**Problem.** A degree-two Siegel modular form depends on a symmetric two-by-two complex matrix with positive definite imaginary part. For a level-one form of weight k, expand in the last diagonal entry ω. For each integer m &gt; 0, the coefficient of exp(2πimω) is a Jacobi form of weight k and index m.

**How the definition helps.** The Jacobi definition packages exactly how one Fourier slice transforms under the subgroup preserving the expansion direction (our own). A translation contributes the exponential for that slice's index (our own). The work is restricting the Siegel transformation law to this subgroup and checking the resulting Fourier support (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Jacobi form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobi_form). It says: “Examples in two variables include Jacobi theta functions, the Weierstrass ℘ function, and Fourier–Jacobi coefficients of Siegel modular forms of genus 2.”

**Problem.** For a classical level-one Jacobi form of weight k and positive integer index m, the 2m coefficient functions are unique. Together they transform with weight k − ½ by the inverse transpose of the matrices transforming the theta series.

**Paper or page:** [Lᵖ-Norm Bounds for Automorphic Forms via Spectral Reciprocity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.05613v3). It says: “(𝓛±H)(t) ≔ ∫₀∞ 𝒥±₍t₎(x) H(x) dx/x”

- [N. V. Kuznetsov, Petersson’s conjecture for cusp forms of weight zero and Linnik’s conjecture (1981).](https://doi.org/10.1070/SM1981v039n03ABEH001518)
- [Henryk Iwaniec and Emmanuel Kowalski, Analytic Number Theory (2004), Theorem 16.5.](https://doi.org/10.1090/coll/053)

### Centralizers combine conjugate terms

**Remember:** One orbit of conjugate elements needs one quotient integral.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 58J50. arXiv math.SP, math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let Γ act freely and discretely by orientation-preserving isometries on ℍ with compact quotient X. For γ∈Γ, let C be its centralizer in Γ. Its orbital integral integrates k(d(z,γz)) over C∖ℍ with hyperbolic area, for a smooth compactly supported distance weight k.

**Problem.** The orbital integral equals the integral over X of the sum of diagonal kernel terms indexed by the conjugacy class of γ.

**How the definition helps.** Left cosets Cg label the conjugates g⁻¹γg exactly once (our own). Translating a fundamental region of Γ by those representatives gives a fundamental region of C up to null sets (our own). Changing variables gives the orbital integral (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg trace formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_trace_formula). It says: “with the first term corresponding to the identity element and the remaining terms forming a sum over the other conjugacy classes”

**Sources:**

- [Dennis A. Hejhal, The Selberg Trace Formula for PSL(2,ℝ), volume I (1976).](https://doi.org/10.1007/BFb0079608)

### Completed factors make scattering unitary

**Remember:** On the critical line the scattering quotient divides conjugates.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 11M36. arXiv math.SP, math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On the modular surface, normalize the Eisenstein eigenfunction so its horizontal average is yˢ + φ(s)y¹⁻ˢ at height y. The coefficient φ(s) measures scattering at the narrowing end. Complete the Riemann zeta function by setting Λ(w) = Γ(w/2)ζ(w) divided by π to the power w/2.

**Problem.** The scattering coefficient equals Λ(2s−1)/Λ(2s). It has absolute value one on Re(s) = ½, including its limiting value −1 at s = ½.

**How the definition helps.** The Eisenstein constant-term formula gives the quotient. On Re s = ½, the functional equation Λ(w) = Λ(1−w) and conjugation make the numerator the conjugate of the denominator, which is nonzero away from s = ½ because ζ has no zeros on Re w = 1 (our own). At s = ½ the poles of Λ at 0 and 1 have opposite residues, giving the limit −1 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_zeta_function). It says: “In this case the determinant of the scattering matrix is given by: φ(s) = π¹ᐟ² Γ(s−1/2) ζ(2s−1) / (Γ(s) ζ(2s)).”

**Sources:**

- [Henryk Iwaniec, Spectral Methods of Automorphic Forms, second edition (2002).](https://doi.org/10.1090/gsm/053)

### Congruence gives Selberg’s spectral gap

**Remember:** Congruence structure, not finite index, keeps eigenvalues above 3/16.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 58J50. arXiv math.NT, math.SP. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Call a subgroup of SL(2,ℤ) a congruence subgroup if it contains every matrix congruent to the identity modulo some positive integer. Each such subgroup acts on the upper half-plane by fractional linear transformations.

**Problem.** For congruence subgroups, every positive discrete Laplace eigenvalue on the quotient is at least 3/16. General finite-index subgroups can have arbitrarily small positive eigenvalues.

**How the definition helps.** Containing a principal congruence subgroup is exactly the hypothesis of Selberg’s 3/16 theorem. For general finite index, cut the punctured modular torus along a nonseparating curve and take n-sheeted cyclic covers (our own). A slowly varying cosine across the sheets gives mean-zero test functions with Rayleigh quotient O(1/n²), and below ¼ the variational principle gives a small discrete eigenvalue (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg's 1/4 conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg%27s_1/4_conjecture). It says: “Selberg showed that the eigenvalues are at least 3/16.”

**Sources:**

- [Atle Selberg, On the estimation of Fourier coefficients of modular forms (1965).](https://doi.org/10.1090/pspum/008/0182610)

### Cusp truncation gives finite norms

**Remember:** Cut the two power terms, not the whole cusp.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 58J50. arXiv math.SP, math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On the modular surface, the horizontal average of the Eisenstein series E(z,s) at height y is yˢ+φ(s)y¹⁻ˢ. For Y&gt;1, truncate E by subtracting this average in the standard cusp above Y and keeping E elsewhere.

**Problem.** For fixed real t ≠ 0 and s = ½+it, the truncated series is square integrable for hyperbolic area. Its squared norm equals 2 log Y + O(1) as Y grows, with the error bound depending on t.

**How the definition helps.** Only the two constant-term waves yˢ and φ(s)y¹⁻ˢ fail to be square integrable in the cusp, while the other Fourier modes decay exponentially (our own). Below height Y each wave contributes log Y since \|φ(s)\| = 1, and their cross term stays bounded for fixed t ≠ 0 (our own). The Maass–Selberg relation gives the full norm formula (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Maass–Selberg relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maass%E2%80%93Selberg_relations). It says: “However the integral defining the inner product does not converge, so the Eisenstein series first have to be truncated.”

**Sources:**

- [Henryk Iwaniec, Spectral Methods of Automorphic Forms, second edition (2002).](https://doi.org/10.1090/gsm/053)

### Free compact quotients simplify traces

**Remember:** No fixed points or cusps means only closed geodesics remain.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 58J50. arXiv math.SP, math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let Γ be a discrete group of orientation-preserving isometries of the hyperbolic plane with compact quotient and no nonidentity element of finite order.

**Problem.** In Selberg’s trace formula, the geometric sum contains only the identity and terms indexed by oriented closed geodesics.

**How the definition helps.** The conditions exclude elliptic elements, which fix interior points, and parabolic elements, which create cusps; the modular group has both, such as z ↦ −1/z and z ↦ z + 1 (our own). Every remaining nonidentity element translates along a geodesic that closes on the quotient. The trace formula gives each conjugacy class its term.

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg trace formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_trace_formula). It says: “the group Γ has no parabolic or elliptic elements (other than the identity).”

**Sources:**

- [Dennis A. Hejhal, The Selberg Trace Formula for PSL(2,ℝ), volume I (1976).](https://doi.org/10.1007/BFb0079608)

### Kuznetsov signs select odd forms

**Remember:** Subtracting the two signs cancels every even contribution.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 11F30. arXiv math.NT, math.SP. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Use the level one Kuznetsov formula, which relates Fourier coefficients on the modular surface to Kloosterman sums. For positive integers m, n, take half the difference of its identities for (m,n) and (m,−n), with the same even test function, decaying as the formula requires, in both. A form with reflection sign ε has −n coefficient equal to ε times its n coefficient (our own).

**Problem.** Only odd cusp forms, the Laplace eigenfunctions that change sign under x ↦ −x, contribute on the spectral side. Each product of normalized coefficients carries the test weight divided by L(1, ad f), the adjoint L-function of the form at one.

**How the definition helps.** The difference gives a form with reflection sign ε the weight (1−ε)/2, which is one for odd forms and zero for even forms. The continuous integrals in the two identities agree and cancel. This uses the signed coefficient formulas proved by Kuznetsov summation (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Lᵖ-Norm Bounds for Automorphic Forms via Spectral Reciprocity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.05613v3). It says: “ε₍f₎⁽¹ ∓ ¹⁾⁄² λ₍f₎(m) λ₍f₎(n)/L(1, ad f)”

**Sources:**

- [N. V. Kuznetsov, Petersson’s conjecture for cusp forms of weight zero and Linnik’s conjecture (1981).](https://doi.org/10.1070/SM1981v039n03ABEH001518)
- [Peter Humphries and Rizwanur Khan, Lᵖ-Norm Bounds for Automorphic Forms via Spectral Reciprocity.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.05613v3)

### Length weights recover primitive counts

**Remember:** Subtract the shorter repeats before counting the new geodesics.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 58J50. arXiv math.SP, math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On a closed oriented surface of curvature −1, call an oriented closed geodesic primitive if it traverses its path only once. For each primitive length ℓ, counting multiplicity, place mass ℓ/(2 sinh(mℓ/2)) at mℓ for each positive integer m. Add masses at equal lengths.

**Problem.** The Laplace eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity, determine how many primitive oriented geodesics have each length.

**How the definition helps.** Selberg’s trace formula recovers the total mass at each length from the spectrum, with the area from Weyl’s law (our own). At length ℓ, subtract the masses from repeats of shorter primitive geodesics and divide by ℓ/(2 sinh(ℓ/2)) to get the primitive count (our own). Only finitely many geodesics lie below each length, so the recursion runs in order (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg trace formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_trace_formula). It says: “so the lengths of primitive closed geodesics are spectral invariants.”

**Sources:**

- [Dennis A. Hejhal, The Selberg Trace Formula for PSL(2,ℝ), volume I (1976).](https://doi.org/10.1007/BFb0079608)

### Mean zero gives heat decay

**Remember:** Remove constants before asking the heat flow to decay.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 58J50. arXiv math.NT, math.SP. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let Γ be a subgroup of SL(2,ℤ) containing every matrix congruent to the identity modulo some positive integer. On its upper half-plane quotient, take square integrable functions whose integral against hyperbolic area is zero.

**Problem.** At time t ≥ 0, heat flow on this space has operator norm at most exp(−3t/16).

**How the definition helps.** The zero integral removes the constants, which heat flow leaves unchanged. On the rest, Selberg’s theorem puts every discrete eigenvalue at 3/16 or above, and the continuous spectrum begins at ¼. Heat flow multiplies a spectral component at λ by exp(−tλ), giving the bound (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg's 1/4 conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg%27s_1/4_conjecture). It says: “Selberg showed that the eigenvalues are at least 3/16.”

**Sources:**

- [Atle Selberg, On the estimation of Fourier coefficients of modular forms (1965).](https://doi.org/10.1090/pspum/008/0182610)

### Odd reflection removes Eisenstein spectrum

**Remember:** Reflection makes the average at the only cusp vanish.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 58J50. arXiv math.SP, math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On the modular surface, determinant-one integer matrices identify points z = x+iy of the upper half-plane by fractional linear transformations. Call a square integrable function odd if f(−x+iy) = −f(x+iy) almost everywhere.

**Problem.** On the odd subspace the Laplacian has an orthonormal eigenbasis with finite multiplicities and no finite accumulation of eigenvalues.

**How the definition helps.** Oddness makes the horizontal average vanish at every height, since x and −x cancel over the period from −½ to ½ (our own). The surface has only one cusp, so this is the whole cuspidal condition, and it removes the Eisenstein series. The Laplacian commutes with the reflection, and its spectrum on cusp forms is discrete.

**Wikipedia:** [Maass wave form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maass_wave_form). It says: “A Maass form f is called even, if i(f)=f and odd if i(f)=−f.”

**Sources:**

- [Henryk Iwaniec, Spectral Methods of Automorphic Forms, second edition (2002).](https://doi.org/10.1090/gsm/053)

### Opposite signs remove Kuznetsov diagonals

**Remember:** Opposite nonzero frequencies cannot match on the diagonal.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 11F30. arXiv math.NT, math.SP. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On the modular surface, pair Fourier modes of frequencies m and −n for positive integers m,n. Use an even test function h analytic in the strip \|Im(t)\| ≤ ½+δ for some δ &gt; 0. Require h to decay there at least as fast as (1+\|t\|) to the power −2−δ.

**Problem.** In the Kuznetsov formula relating Fourier coefficient averages to exponential sums, these pairs have zero diagonal contribution, even when m = n.

**How the definition helps.** Opposite signs mean the frequencies m and −n are never equal. In our own derivation, the identity term is the integral of exp(2πi(m+n)x) over one period, which is zero since m + n &gt; 0. The Kuznetsov formula evaluates the remaining contributions.

**Paper or page:** [Lᵖ-Norm Bounds for Automorphic Forms via Spectral Reciprocity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.05613v3). It says: “δ(m,±n) 𝒩±h±”

**Sources:**

- [N. V. Kuznetsov, Petersson’s conjecture for cusp forms of weight zero and Linnik’s conjecture (1981).](https://doi.org/10.1070/SM1981v039n03ABEH001518)
- [Peter Humphries and Rizwanur Khan, Lᵖ-Norm Bounds for Automorphic Forms via Spectral Reciprocity.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.05613v3)

### Resolvent differences have finite traces

**Remember:** Subtract before tracing to cancel the slow spectral tail.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 11M36. arXiv math.SP, math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On a closed oriented surface of curvature −1, let Δ be the nonnegative Laplacian. For real a &gt; ½ define its shifted inverse R(a) = (Δ − ¼ + a²)⁻¹. For distinct a,b &gt; ½ take D = R(a) − R(b).

**Problem.** The singular values of D have finite sum, so D has a trace. Neither shifted inverse alone has this property. After subtracting the identity contribution in Selberg’s trace formula, the trace equals F(a) − F(b), where F(a) = Z′(½+a)/(2a Z(½+a)).

**How the definition helps.** Subtraction turns terms of size 1/λ into terms of size 1/λ², and by Weyl’s law the nth eigenvalue grows like n, so the sum converges (our own). The Fourier weight of R(a) is exp(−a\|u\|)/(2a) (our own). Selberg’s trace formula turns the geodesic sum into the stated difference of logarithmic derivatives of Selberg zeta (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg trace formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_trace_formula). It says: “The trace formula is also central to the analytic theory of the Selberg zeta function.”

**Sources:**

- [Dennis A. Hejhal, The Selberg Trace Formula for PSL(2,ℝ), volume I (1976).](https://doi.org/10.1007/BFb0079608)

### Short Fourier support removes orbit terms

**Remember:** A weight blind to every geodesic length leaves only the area.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 58J50. arXiv math.SP, math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On a closed oriented surface X of curvature −1, let L be the shortest length of a closed geodesic. Take h(r) = ∫ℝ g(u) exp(iru) du, where g is smooth, even, and zero outside a compact subset of (−L, L), so g vanishes at every closed geodesic length.

**Problem.** Write each Laplace eigenvalue as ¼ + r², with multiplicity. Then ∑ h(r) = area(X)/(4π) times ∫ℝ r h(r) tanh(πr) dr.

**How the definition helps.** In Selberg’s trace formula each closed geodesic term carries the factor g at its length, so every such term is zero (our own). Only the identity term remains. A weight positive at L would keep the shortest geodesics.

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg trace formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_trace_formula). It says: “∑ₙ₌₀∞ h(rₙ) = μ(X)/(4π) ∫₋∞∞ r h(r) tanh(πr) dr + ∑₍{T}₎ log N(T₀)/(N(T)¹ᐟ² − N(T)⁻¹ᐟ²) g(log N(T)).”

**Sources:**

- [Dennis A. Hejhal, The Selberg Trace Formula for PSL(2,ℝ), volume I (1976).](https://doi.org/10.1007/BFb0079608)

### Weighted counts control unweighted errors

**Remember:** Weigh each geodesic by its length, as Chebyshev weighs each prime.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 11M36. arXiv math.NT, math.SP. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On a closed oriented surface of curvature −1, Ψ(X) counts each oriented closed geodesic of length at most log X, with weight the length ℓ of the primitive geodesic it repeats, the one that makes one circuit. It is the analogue of Chebyshev’s function, with N(P) = exp(ℓ) playing the role of a prime.

**Problem.** Fix ½ &lt; θ &lt; 1 and suppose Ψ(X) = X + O(X raised to θ). Then the number of primitive P with N(P) ≤ X differs from ∫₂ˣ du/log u by O((X raised to θ)/log X).

**How the definition helps.** The weights let the repeated circuits be subtracted from Ψ before partial summation (our own). Double circuits contribute O(√X) and higher repeats O(X¹ᐟ³ log X), both below the error (our own). Partial summation then removes the weight log N(P) and gives the stated error (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Prime geodesic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_geodesic). It says: “weighted counting functions analogous to the Chebyshev function”

**Sources:**

- [Dennis A. Hejhal, The Selberg Trace Formula for PSL(2,ℝ), volume I (1976).](https://doi.org/10.1007/BFb0079608)

### Zero cusp averages give discrete spectra

**Remember:** Average zero on every horizontal circle, and nothing escapes up the cusp.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 58J50. arXiv math.SP, math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On the modular surface, the upper half-plane modulo SL₂(ℤ), a square-integrable function is cuspidal when its average over each horizontal circle is zero: ∫₀¹ f(x+iy) dx = 0 for almost every y &gt; 0. These circles shrink as they run into the cusp, the thin end of the surface.

**Problem.** On this subspace the nonnegative Laplacian has an orthonormal eigenbasis. Each eigenvalue has finite multiplicity, and only finitely many lie below any fixed bound.

**How the definition helps.** The zero average removes the constant mode, the only mode that can spread out along the cusp (our own). A Poincaré inequality on each circle then makes bounded-energy functions uniformly small high in the cusp (our own). Compactness on the remaining bounded region gives discrete spectrum (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Maass wave form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maass_wave_form). It says: “Then Δₖ operates on C(Γ∖ℋ,k) and has a discrete spectrum.”

**Sources:**

- [Henryk Iwaniec, Spectral Methods of Automorphic Forms, second edition (2002).](https://doi.org/10.1090/gsm/053)

### Cyclotomic determinants detect abelian quotients

**Remember:** Over ℚ, the determinant sees all roots of unity, hence everything abelian.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 11G05. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The adelic representation of an elliptic curve is the Galois action on all its points of finite order at once, with matrices over the profinite integers. Through the Weil pairing, its determinant is the Galois action on all roots of unity together (our own).

**Problem.** For an elliptic curve over ℚ, the kernel of the determinant on its adelic image equals the closed commutator subgroup of that image, the smallest closed normal subgroup with abelian quotient.

**How the definition helps.** By Kronecker–Weber the roots of unity generate the maximal abelian extension of ℚ, so the determinant kernel is the subgroup fixing that extension (our own). That subgroup is the closed commutator subgroup of the Galois group, and its image is the closed commutator subgroup of the adelic image (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Degrees of points with rational j-invariant on X₀(n) and X₁(n)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.13199v1). It says: “Let $E$ be an elliptic curve defined over $\\Q$. Then, we have $\\cG<sub>E</sub> \\cap \\SL(\\Zhat) = \[\\cG<sub>E</sub>, \\cG<sub>E</sub>\]$.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Monodromy isolates infinite inertia

**Remember:** N measures the infinite part of inertia; N zero leaves only finite.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 11F85. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an ℓ-adic representation ρ of the Galois group of a p-adic field, with ℓ ≠ p, some open subgroup of inertia acts as ρ(g) = exp(t(g)N). Here t is the tame ℓ-adic character of inertia and N is a nilpotent matrix, the monodromy operator (our own).

**Problem.** The representation has finite inertia image exactly when N is zero.

**How the definition helps.** If N = 0, an open subgroup of inertia acts trivially, so the inertia image is finite (our own). If N ≠ 0, the matrices exp(t(g)N) take infinitely many values, since t has open image in ℤℓ (our own). Grothendieck’s monodromy theorem supplies the description (our own).

**nLab:** [Weil-Deligne representation](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Weil-Deligne+representation). It says: “N is a nilpotent monodromy operator”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Residual semisimplification removes lattice dependence

**Remember:** Every stable lattice gives the same simple factors after reduction.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Reduce a Galois representation through a stable lattice, a Galois-stable free submodule over the valuation ring that spans the space, and replace the reduction by the direct sum of its irreducible factors. This semisimplified reduction depends only on reduced characteristic polynomials, which are the same for every lattice (our own).

**Problem.** For a continuous representation over a finite extension of ℚₚ, all stable lattices have isomorphic semisimplified reductions. Their reductions can differ before this step.

**How the definition helps.** Every lattice gives the same reduced characteristic polynomials, so Brauer–Nesbitt makes the semisimplifications isomorphic (our own). Before that step lattices can differ: let Galois act through an unramified ℤₚ quotient, with t ∈ ℤₚ fixing e and sending f to f + te (our own). The lattice spanned by e, f reduces to a nontrivial extension, but the one spanned by e/p, f reduces trivially (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Brauer–Nesbitt theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brauer%E2%80%93Nesbitt_theorem). It says: “the characteristic polynomials of ρ₁(g) and ρ₂(g) coincide for all g ∈ G, then ρ₁ and ρ₂ are isomorphic representations.”

**Paper or page:** [Stable free lattices in residually reducible Galois deformations and control theorem of Selmer groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.03608v2). It says: “the semi-simplification (T/ϖT)ˢˢ of the residual representation is decomposed into two distinct characters”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Semisimplification makes Frobenius traces decisive

**Remember:** Traces remember the simple pieces and forget how they fit together.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 11F11. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The semisimplification of a finite-dimensional representation V is the direct sum of the irreducible quotients in a chain of invariant subspaces from 0 to V. It keeps exactly what traces see, since a nonsplit extension and its split sum have the same traces (our own).

**Problem.** Let two continuous representations of a number field’s Galois group over a finite extension of ℚℓ be unramified, with inertia acting trivially, outside finitely many primes. If their Frobenius traces agree outside finitely many primes, their semisimplifications are isomorphic.

**How the definition helps.** Traces cannot tell an extension from its split sum, so the semisimplification is the most that traces can determine (our own). Chebotarev density and continuity extend the trace equality to the whole Galois group, and Brauer–Nesbitt in characteristic zero gives the isomorphism (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Brauer–Nesbitt theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brauer%E2%80%93Nesbitt_theorem). It says: “Then the representation is uniquely determined by the values of the traces of ρ(Frobₚ)”

**Paper or page:** [Eisenstein degeneration of Euler systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.02078v2). It says: “there are exactly three isomorphism classes of continuous Galois representations”

**Sources:**

- [Eisenstein degeneration of Euler systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.02078v2)

### The Weil pairing gives the determinant

**Remember:** The Weil pairing turns the determinant line into roots of unity.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 11G05. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The determinant character on E\[n\], the geometric n-torsion of an elliptic curve over a number field, is the Galois action on its exterior square, a free rank-one ℤ/nℤ-module. The Weil pairing identifies this exterior square with the nth roots of unity, compatibly with Galois (our own).

**Problem.** For an elliptic curve over a number field, each Galois element acts on the nth roots of unity by raising them to its determinant on E\[n\].

**How the definition helps.** The determinant is by definition the action on the exterior square, so the identification moves it to the roots of unity (our own). The Weil pairing is alternating, perfect and Galois equivariant, which makes the identification an isomorphism of Galois modules (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Weil pairing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weil_pairing). It says: “With this definition it can be shown that w is alternating and bilinear,”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Defining L-factors by ℓ-adic cohomology makes isogenous elliptic curves share them

**Remember:** Rational cohomology cannot see an isogeny, so the factors agree.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G05 (Elliptic curves over global fields), 14G10. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Define the local factor at a finite prime v from V = H¹ét(E over K̄, ℚℓ), with ℓ prime to v, as 1/det(1 − N(v)⁻ˢF acting on Vᴵ) (our own). Here Vᴵ is the part fixed by inertia, and F is geometric Frobenius, the inverse of the residue-field power map. So the factor depends only on V as a rational Galois representation (our own).

**Problem.** Elliptic curves that are isogenous over a number field have the same L-factor at every prime, good or bad.

**How the definition helps.** An isogeny induces an isomorphism on rational cohomology, because composing with its dual multiplies by its degree, which is invertible in ℚℓ (our own). An isomorphism of Galois representations preserves inertia invariants and Frobenius determinants, so the factors agree (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Hasse–Weil zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse%E2%80%93Weil_zeta_function). It says: “A more refined definition became possible with the development of étale cohomology”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre and John Tate, Good reduction of abelian varieties (1968)](https://doi.org/10.2307/1970722)

### Local-condition Selmer groups sit between rational points and Tate–Shafarevich torsion

**Remember:** Selmer keeps the torsion classes that are trivial at every place.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G05 (Elliptic curves over global fields), 11R34. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The n-Selmer group of an elliptic curve E over a number field K is the set of classes in H¹(K, E\[n\]) that become zero in H¹(Kᵥ, E) at every place v (our own). So it keeps the classes whose torsors have a point over every completion (our own).

**Problem.** There is an exact sequence 0 → E(K)/nE(K) → n-Selmer group → Ш\[n\] → 0. Here Ш, the Tate–Shafarevich group, classifies torsors of E, curves on which E acts simply transitively over K̄, that have a point over every completion.

**How the definition helps.** The Kummer sequence maps H¹(K, E\[n\]) onto H¹(K, E)\[n\] with kernel E(K)/nE(K) (our own). The Selmer condition takes the preimage of the locally trivial classes, which form Ш\[n\], so restricting gives the sequence (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Selmer group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selmer_group). It says: “More generally one can define the Selmer group of a Galois module”

**Sources:**

- [Joseph H. Silverman, The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, Chapter X, §4 (2009)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-387-09494-6)

### Quadratic twists split odd torsion

**Remember:** The original gives the plus part, the twist gives the minus part.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11G05 (Elliptic curves over global fields), 11F80. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let σ be the nonidentity automorphism of a quadratic extension L/K of number fields. The K-points of the quadratic twist correspond to the L-points P of the original curve with σP = −P, while the original curve’s K-points are those with σP = P (our own).

**Problem.** For any odd positive integer n, the points killed by n over L split as a direct sum. The two groups are the K-rational points killed by n on the original curve and on its quadratic twist.

**How the definition helps.** For odd n, P = ½(P + σP) + ½(P − σP) splits each point killed by n uniquely into a σ-fixed part and a σ-negated part (our own). For n = 2 the signs coincide: on y² = x³ − x all two-torsion is rational, so the two parts overlap (our own).

**Paper or page:** [The Effect of Quadratic Base Change on Torsion of Elliptic Curves](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.03709v2). It says: “If n is an odd positive integer we have E(K(√d))\[n\] ≃ E(K)\[n\] ⊕ Eᵈ(K)\[n\].”

### Requiring y ≠ 0 makes congruent numbers the curves of positive rank

**Remember:** A rational affine point with nonzero y gives a triangle.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11G05 (Elliptic curves over global fields), 11D25. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A positive rational A is congruent if it is the area of a right triangle with rational sides. Equivalently, y² = x³ − A²x has a rational point with y ≠ 0, which rules out the three points of order two (our own).

**Problem.** A rational point with y ≠ 0 on the curve has infinite order: no multiple of it in the group law is zero. So A is congruent exactly when the curve has positive rank, which means infinitely many rational points.

**How the definition helps.** The torsion points of this curve are exactly the point at infinity and the points with y = 0, so a point with y ≠ 0 has infinite order. Such a point exists exactly when the rank is positive (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congruent<sub>number</sub>](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/https%3A//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congruent_number). It says: “the only torsion points on this elliptic curve are those with y equal to 0, hence the existence of a rational point with y nonzero is equivalent to saying the elliptic curve has positive rank.”

**Paper or page:** [A Theorem of Fermat on Congruent Number Curves](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.09604). It says: “Equivalently, A is a congruent number if and only if the congruent number curve y²=x³−A²x has a rational point (x,y)∈ℚ² with y≠0.”

### Scheme kernels retain inseparable degrees

**Remember:** Kernel rank counts geometric points with their multiplicities.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G05 (Elliptic curves over global fields), 14K02. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The kernel of an isogeny as a group scheme is the whole fiber over zero, with multiplicities, and its rank is the dimension of its coordinate algebra over the base field. So the rank counts each kernel point as often as its multiplicity, unlike a count of geometric points (our own).

**Problem.** Over a global function field, the kernel rank of an isogeny of elliptic curves equals its degree. This includes inseparable isogenies, where some multiplicities exceed one.

**How the definition helps.** An isogeny is finite and flat, so the fiber over zero has the same total multiplicity as the generic fiber, which is the degree (our own). A count of geometric points fails: Frobenius in characteristic p has degree p but only one geometric kernel point (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Explicit surjectivity of Galois representations of products of elliptic curves over function fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.20910v3). It says: “Let H ⊆ ker(φ) be a subgroup scheme”

### Squarefree conductors exclude additive reduction

**Remember:** Smooth contributes zero, a node contributes one, and a cusp contributes more.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11G05 (Elliptic curves over global fields), 11G40. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An elliptic curve over a number field is semistable if at every finite prime its minimal model reduces to a smooth curve or to a curve with a node, never a cusp. The conductor exponent is 0 for smooth reduction, 1 for a node, and 2 plus a nonnegative wild term for a cusp (our own).

**Problem.** An elliptic curve over a number field is semistable exactly when its conductor ideal has no repeated prime factor.

**How the definition helps.** So the conductor has a repeated prime exactly at the primes with a cusp, the additive primes (our own). For example, y² = x³ + 5 has a cusp at 5 and exponent two there (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Conductor of an elliptic curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conductor_of_an_elliptic_curve). It says: “ε=0 for good reduction, ε=1 for multiplicative reduction and ε=2 for additive reduction.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The conductor of an elliptic curve is the level of its newform

**Remember:** Bad primes of the curve become the level of its modular form.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G05 (Elliptic curves over global fields), 11F11. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A normalized newform of level N is a cusp form for Γ₀(N), an eigenform of all Hecke operators with first coefficient one, that does not come from any lower level dividing N. Precisely, it is Petersson orthogonal to all forms lifted from proper divisor levels (our own).

**Problem.** Every elliptic curve over ℚ of conductor N comes from a normalized newform of weight 2 and level exactly N, with integer coefficients. For a good prime p, its coefficient aₚ is p + 1 minus the number of points of E mod p.

**How the definition helps.** Newness fixes the level exactly, removing copies of forms from lower levels (our own). The modularity theorem then identifies that level with the conductor and the coefficients with the point counts (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Modularity theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modularity_theorem). It says: “is the smallest integer for which such a parametrization can be found (which by the modularity theorem itself is now known to be a number called the conductor)”

### Torsors encode local failure

**Remember:** No rational origin means a nonzero torsor class.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G05 (Elliptic curves over global fields), 11R34. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A torsor for an elliptic curve E is a curve on which E acts simply transitively over an algebraic closure, and it is trivial exactly when it has a rational point. The Tate–Shafarevich group consists of the torsor classes with a point over every completion.

**Problem.** A smooth projective geometrically integral genus-one curve over a number field has an associated elliptic curve, its Jacobian. If the curve has points everywhere locally but none globally, it gives a nonzero Tate–Shafarevich class of its Jacobian.

**How the definition helps.** A rational point identifies the torsor with E acting on itself, so a class is zero exactly when the curve has a point (our own). Local points put the class in the Tate–Shafarevich group, and the missing global point makes it nonzero (our own). Selmer’s cubic 3x³ + 4y³ + 5z³ = 0 is an example.

**Wikipedia:** [Tate–Shafarevich group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate%E2%80%93Shafarevich_group). It says: “3x³ + 4y³ + 5z³ = 0”

**Sources:**

- [Lang and Tate, Principal Homogeneous Spaces Over Abelian Varieties](https://doi.org/10.2307/2372778)

### Weil pairings identify Galois determinants

**Remember:** Pair two basis vectors and watch the determinant act on roots of unity.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G05 (Elliptic curves over global fields), 14H52. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The ℓ-adic Tate module of an elliptic curve over a number field K is the set of compatible sequences of torsion points Pᵣ of order dividing ℓʳ, with ℓPᵣ₊₁ = Pᵣ, on which Galois acts termwise. Its Weil pairings at all levels fit together into one perfect alternating pairing with values in the compatible ℓ-power roots of unity (our own).

**Problem.** For an elliptic curve over a number field, each field automorphism fixing that field acts on the Tate module. Its determinant gives its exponent of action on the compatible roots of unity of ℓ-power order.

**How the definition helps.** Pairing two basis vectors gives a primitive root of unity, and an alternating bilinear pairing raises it to the determinant of a change of basis (our own). Galois equivariance of the pairing then makes each automorphism raise that root to its determinant.

**Wikipedia:** [Weil pairing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weil_pairing). It says: “giving rise to a non-degenerate pairing on the n-torsion.”

### Frobenius lines detect local isogenies

**Remember:** At good reduction, a Frobenius eigenline is a rational isogeny kernel.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G07 (Elliptic curves over local fields), 11F80. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A rational cyclic subgroup of order q of an elliptic curve over K is a line in its q-torsion E\[q\] that every Galois element preserves, and quotienting by it gives an isogeny of degree q over K (our own). At good reduction with q ≠ ℓ, Galois acts on E\[q\] through Frobenius alone, so the test is whether one matrix has an eigenline (our own).

**Problem.** Let an elliptic curve over ℚℓ have good reduction, staying smooth modulo ℓ, and let q ≠ ℓ be an odd prime. It has a ℚℓ-isogeny of degree q exactly when the Frobenius characteristic polynomial has square or zero discriminant modulo q.

**How the definition helps.** Isogenies of degree q correspond to rational lines, and good reduction makes the torsion action unramified, so Frobenius alone must fix a line (our own). A 2×2 matrix fixes a line exactly when its characteristic polynomial has a root modulo q, which for odd q is the discriminant test (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Local points on twists of X(p) with applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.04294v3). It says: “Then E/ℚℓ admits a ℚℓ-isogeny of degree q if and only if (Δℓ/q) ∈ {0, 1}.”

### Inertia detects good reduction

**Remember:** A prime divides the conductor exactly when inertia moves the Tate module.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G07 (Elliptic curves over local fields), 11G40. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** At a finite prime, the conductor exponent of an elliptic curve is codim(Vᴵ) + Sw(V), where V is its rational ℓ-adic Tate module for ℓ prime to the residue characteristic, Vᴵ is the part fixed by inertia, and Sw is the Swan conductor. Both terms are nonnegative, so the exponent is zero exactly when inertia acts trivially (our own).

**Problem.** For an elliptic curve over a number field, its conductor ideal contains a prime factor exactly where the curve has bad reduction.

**How the definition helps.** The Néron–Ogg–Shafarevich theorem says inertia acts trivially on V exactly at good reduction. So a prime divides the conductor exactly at bad reduction (our own).

**Paper or page:** [A proof of Néron--Ogg--Shafarevich criterion via its archimedean analogue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.13255v1). It says: “Then, A has good reduction if and only if ρ ∣ Iᴋ is trivial.”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre and John Tate, Good Reduction of Abelian Varieties (1968)](https://doi.org/10.2307/1970722)

### Tate quotients reveal triangular actions

**Remember:** Roots of unity form the invariant line in Tate curve torsion.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G07 (Elliptic curves over local fields), 14G22. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Over a local field K, the Tate curve with parameter q, a nonzero element of positive valuation, has as points over each finite extension L the group L× modulo the powers of q. Its ℓ-torsion is the classes of x with xˡ a power of q, and these contain the ℓth roots of unity as a Galois-stable line (our own).

**Problem.** Let an elliptic curve over K have split multiplicative reduction, a node with two rational branches. For each prime ℓ different from the characteristic of K, its ℓ-torsion has a basis in which every Galois element acts by an upper triangular matrix.

**How the definition helps.** Tate uniformization identifies the curve with this quotient for a suitable q. Sending the class of x, with xˡ = qᵃ, to a modulo ℓ is a Galois-invariant surjection onto ℤ/ℓℤ whose kernel is the roots of unity (our own). A basis that starts on this line gives triangular matrices (our own).

### The Tate quotient displays torsion

**Remember:** Roots of unity give the submodule, and roots of q give the quotient.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G07 (Elliptic curves over local fields), 11F80. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Over a local field K, take a nonzero q of positive valuation. The Tate curve has as geometric points the nonzero elements of an algebraic closure modulo powers of q, so a point is killed by n when a representative x has xⁿ = qᵃ for some integer a.

**Problem.** For n invertible in K, the points killed by n map onto ℤ/nℤ with kernel the nth roots of unity. The Galois action on this extension records the obstruction to taking an nth root of q over K.

**How the definition helps.** The map sending x to a modulo n has kernel the nth roots of unity, and an nth root of q maps to 1, so the map is onto (our own). The ratios of that root with its Galois conjugates give the Kummer cocycle of q (our own).

**nLab:** [Tate curve](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Tate+curve). It says: “which may be thought of as the quotient of the multiplicative group by q⁽ℤ⁾.”

### Unramified tests can miss points

**Remember:** Good reduction lets the Kummer test forget inertia.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G07 (Elliptic curves over local fields), 11S25. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** At a place of odd residue characteristic, a class in H¹ of an elliptic curve’s points killed by two passes the unramified test if it vanishes on inertia, and the Kummer test if it comes from halving a local point of the curve. At good reduction, halving a local point needs only an unramified extension (our own).

**Problem.** The two tests agree at good reduction, where the reduced curve stays smooth. They can differ at bad reduction even if inertia fixes every point killed by two.

**How the definition helps.** At good reduction, doubling is étale, so Kummer classes are unramified, and Lang’s theorem gives the reverse inclusion (our own). For a uniformizer π, the Tate curve with parameter π² has rational two-torsion (our own). Yet halving the class of π needs a square root of an element of odd valuation, so this Kummer class is ramified (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Galois module structures and the Hasse principle in twist families via the distribution of Selmer groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.14026v1). It says: “H¹ᵤᵣ(kᵥ,E\[2\]), otherwise.”

### Valuation counts Tate curve components

**Remember:** Take the valuation and reduce it modulo the valuation of q.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G07 (Elliptic curves over local fields), 14G20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Over a nonarchimedean local field K, Tate’s presentation gives the points of a split multiplicative elliptic curve as K× modulo the powers of a parameter q. Use the valuation v normalized to take all integer values, so v(q) is a positive integer.

**Problem.** The Néron model extends the elliptic curve to a smooth group over the valuation ring. The group of connected components of its special fiber is cyclic of order v(q).

**How the definition helps.** The component of a point is its valuation modulo v(q), and every residue occurs since v takes all integer values (our own). The units, of valuation zero, are exactly the points on the identity component, so the component group is cyclic of order v(q).

**Wikipedia:** [Tate curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate_curve). It says: “there is an isomorphism of groups from k⁎/qℤ to this elliptic curve”

### Drinfeld isogenies invert after localization

**Remember:** Divide the dual isogeny by the scalar in the composite.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G09 (Drinfel'd modules; higher-dimensional motives, etc.). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In the isogeny category of Drinfeld modules for A = 𝔽q\[T\], a map is a morphism, an additive polynomial respecting the A-actions, divided by a nonzero element of A. So any morphism whose composites with another morphism are the action of one nonzero a becomes invertible (our own).

**Problem.** Assume A embeds in the base field through its scalar action. Then every isogeny, a nonzero map between the modules, has an inverse in the isogeny category.

**How the definition helps.** The dual isogeny theorem gives f̂ with f ∘ f̂ and f̂ ∘ f both equal to the action of one nonzero a in A. Dividing f̂ by a gives the inverse of f.

### Good reduction preserves prime-to-characteristic torsion

**Remember:** Full degree and simple roots let every torsion point reduce uniquely.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11G09 (Drinfel'd modules; higher-dimensional motives, etc.). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A rank r Drinfeld module φ for A = 𝔽q\[T\] over a complete discretely valued field has good reduction if in some coordinate φ(T) has integral coefficients and a unit leading coefficient. Then reduction keeps the degree of each φ(a), so no torsion point is lost (our own).

**Problem.** Let a in A have nonzero image in the residue field. At good reduction, reducing coordinates gives a bijection between the points killed by a over the two algebraic closures.

**How the definition helps.** Good reduction keeps the degree of φ(a), and its derivative a is a unit, so Hensel’s lemma lifts each reduced root uniquely (our own). Over 𝔽q((T)), φ(T) = T + τ + Tτ², with τ(x) = xᑫ, fails this: φ(T+1) has q² distinct roots, but its reduction has only q (our own).

### Lattice quotients give Drinfeld torsion

**Remember:** The exponential sends fractions of periods to torsion points.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G09 (Drinfel'd modules; higher-dimensional motives, etc.). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The exponential of a Drinfeld module for A = 𝔽q\[T\] over the completed algebraic closure at infinity is a surjective additive map e with e(az) = φₐ(e(z)), where φₐ is the action of a. Its kernel Λ is the period lattice, so e(z) is killed by a exactly when az lies in Λ.

**Problem.** For nonzero a in A, the points killed by a form the quotient a⁻¹Λ/Λ. In rank r, this gives r copies of A/(a).

**How the definition helps.** Exponential coordinates turn solving φₐ(x) = 0 into checking whether az lies in Λ, and two solutions give the same point exactly when they differ by a period (our own). Drinfeld uniformization supplies the surjective exponential and a lattice free of rank r over A.

**Remember:** Invert integers, and the reverse isogeny becomes an inverse.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G10 (Abelian varieties of dimension &gt; 1), 14K15. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The rational Tate module of an abelian variety is its ℓ-adic Tate module, the compatible sequences of ℓ-power torsion points, tensored with ℚℓ, for ℓ invertible in the base field. In it every nonzero integer acts invertibly (our own).

**Problem.** Every isogeny between abelian varieties induces an isomorphism of rational Tate modules. An isogeny is a surjective group map with finite kernel.

**How the definition helps.** An isogeny has a reverse map whose composites in both orders are multiplication by one positive integer m. On rational modules m is invertible, so the reverse map divided by m is the inverse (our own).

**Remember:** Point count is a degree, and degrees cannot be negative.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G20 (Curves over finite and local fields), 14G15. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an elliptic curve over 𝔽q, the degree of an endomorphism counts its generic fiber with multiplicities, with degree zero for the zero map, and it is a nonnegative quadratic form. For q-power Frobenius F, the degree of F − 1 is the number N of rational points (our own).

**Problem.** The number N of rational points on an elliptic curve over the field with q elements satisfies \|N − q − 1\| ≤ 2√q.

**How the definition helps.** F − 1 has kernel the rational points, each simple since its differential is −1, so deg(F − 1) = N (our own). Since degree is a nonnegative quadratic form, deg(aF + b) = qa² + (q + 1 − N)ab + b² ≥ 0 for all integers a, b (our own). Scaling extends this to rationals, so the discriminant (q + 1 − N)² − 4q is at most zero (our own).
