**Problem.** For a fixed number field and modulus, each of the h ray classes contains a proportion tending to 1/h of all prime ideals. Count prime ideals by the size of their residue fields.

**How the definition helps.** Weighting the prime ideal count by this projector splits it into one sum per character (our own). Kai’s weighted prime ideal theorem gives a main term only for the trivial character, with coefficient 1/h (our own). Partial summation removes the logarithmic weights (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Notes on Mitsui's Prime Number Theorem with Siegel zeros](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.11816v2). It says: “where β is the potential Siegel zero mod 𝔮.”

**Sources:**

- [Wataru Kai, Notes on Mitsui's Prime Number Theorem with Siegel zeros](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.11816v2)

### Fixed cosets count degree-one primes

**Remember:** Fixed cosets are the cycles of length one.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R44 (Distribution of prime ideals). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Put a number field K inside a finite Galois extension L of ℚ with group G, so G permutes the cosets of the subgroup H fixing K. At an unramified prime p, the cycles of Frobenius on these cosets match the primes of K above p, and each cycle length is the residue degree.

**Problem.** The number of primes of K above p with residue field of size p equals the number of cosets fixed by Frobenius. The density of rational primes with such a factor equals the fraction of group elements fixing a coset.

**How the definition helps.** A prime of residue degree one is a Frobenius cycle of length one, which is a fixed coset. Chebotarev’s theorem then turns the fraction of group elements fixing some coset into a density of primes (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Density questions on arithmetic equivalence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.01166v1). It says: “{\\rm Trace}(\\rho <sub>K</sub>({\\rm Frob}<sub>\\ell </sub>)) =a<sub>\\ell </sub>(K).”

**Sources:**

- [Guillermo Mantilla-Soler, Density questions on arithmetic equivalence (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.01166v1)
- [N. Tschebotareff, Die Bestimmung der Dichtigkeit einer Menge von Primzahlen, welche zu einer gegebenen Substitutionsklasse gehören (1926)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01206606)

### Ideal norms isolate first-degree primes

**Remember:** An inert quadratic prime enters at its square.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R44 (Distribution of prime ideals). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The norm of a nonzero prime ideal 𝔭 above p is the size of its residue field, pᶠ with f the residue degree, so a prime of degree above one has norm at least p² (our own).

**Problem.** In a number field of degree n, at most n√x prime ideals of norm ≤ x have degree greater than one. Hence the count of degree-one prime ideals is asymptotic to x/log x.

**How the definition helps.** A prime of degree above one with norm ≤ x lies over some p ≤ √x, and each p has at most n primes above it (our own). This gives at most n√x such primes (our own). Landau’s prime ideal theorem counts all prime ideals of norm ≤ x as about x/log x, so n√x is negligible (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Landau prime ideal theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landau_prime_ideal_theorem). It says: “the prime ideal theorem is dominated by the ideals of norm a prime number.”

**Sources:**

- [Edmund Landau, Neuer Beweis des Primzahlsatzes und Beweis des Primidealsatzes (1903)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01444310)

### Principal primes have reciprocal class-number density

**Remember:** Principal means identity in the Hilbert class field.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R44 (Distribution of prime ideals). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Hilbert class field H of a number field K is its largest abelian extension unramified at every place, with no repeated prime factors and real embeddings staying real. A prime ideal of K is principal exactly when it splits completely in H.

**Problem.** Among prime ideals of K, the proportion that are principal tends to 1/h. Count primes by residue field size, and let h count ideal classes, which identify ideals differing by a field scalar.

**How the definition helps.** Class field theory identifies Gal(H/K) with the class group, of size h, and sends a prime to its class. Chebotarev’s theorem gives the identity element density 1/h (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Hilbert class field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_class_field). It says: “Its degree over K equals the class number of K”

**Sources:**

- [N. Tschebotareff, Die Bestimmung der Dichtigkeit einer Menge von Primzahlen, welche zu einer gegebenen Substitutionsklasse gehören (1926)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01206606)

### Quarter turns let prime angles equidistribute

**Remember:** Take angles modulo the rotations made by units.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R44 (Distribution of prime ideals). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The angle of a prime ideal of ℤ\[i\] is the argument of any generator, taken modulo π/2, because the four generators differ by powers of i, which are quarter turns (our own).

**Problem.** Order these prime ideals by norm, the size of their residue field. The fraction with angle in any fixed subinterval of \[0,π/2) tends to the interval length divided by π/2.

**How the definition helps.** Taking angles modulo π/2 makes exp(4in·arg a) a well-defined character on ideals for each integer n. For n ≠ 0, Hecke’s prime ideal theorem makes its average over primes tend to zero (our own). Weyl’s criterion then gives the stated proportions (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Hecke character](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hecke_character). It says: “The only units are powers of i, so the factor of 4 in the exponent ensures that the character is well defined on ideals.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Real places preserve principal-prime density

**Remember:** The ordinary class field keeps real places real.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R44 (Distribution of prime ideals). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The ordinary Hilbert class field is the largest abelian extension in which no finite prime ramifies and every real embedding stays real. The narrow class field drops the condition on real embeddings.

**Problem.** For K = ℚ(√3), all prime ideals split completely in its ordinary Hilbert class field. In its narrow class field, the proportion tends to one half when primes are ordered by residue field size.

**How the definition helps.** ℚ(√3) has class number one, so its ordinary Hilbert class field is K itself and every prime splits trivially. Its narrow class field is K(i), of degree two and ramified only at the real places. Chebotarev’s theorem gives density one half for the primes that split there (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Hilbert class field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_class_field). It says: “in the extension K(i)/K there is ramification at the archimedean places”

**Sources:**

- [N. Tschebotareff, Die Bestimmung der Dichtigkeit einer Menge von Primzahlen, welche zu einer gegebenen Substitutionsklasse gehören (1926)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01206606)

### Split primes identify normal fields

**Remember:** Complete splitting detects the normal closure.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R44 (Distribution of prime ideals). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A prime splits completely in a finite Galois extension M of K when it has \[M:K\] distinct prime factors in M. Equivalently, it is unramified and its Frobenius in Gal(M/K) is trivial.

**Problem.** Two finite Galois extensions of a number field K inside one algebraic closure are equal if their completely split prime sets differ only finitely.

**How the definition helps.** In a common Galois closure, a prime splits completely in M exactly when its Frobenius lies in the normal subgroup fixing M (our own). Chebotarev’s theorem detects any difference between two normal subgroups on infinitely many primes (our own). Without normality this fails: ℚ(∛2) and its Galois closure share their split primes outside ramification (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Chebotarev density theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chebotarev_density_theorem). It says: “is uniquely determined by the set of primes of K that split completely in it.”

**Sources:**

- [N. Tschebotareff, Die Bestimmung der Dichtigkeit einer Menge von Primzahlen, welche zu einer gegebenen Substitutionsklasse gehören (1926)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01206606)

### Split primes intersect under composita

**Remember:** Fixing both fields fixes every element they generate together.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R44 (Distribution of prime ideals). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite Galois number field K, S(K) is the set of rational primes that split completely in K, namely those unramified in K whose Frobenius is the identity.

**Problem.** For two finite Galois number fields K and L, S(KL) = S(K) ∩ S(L). In particular this intersection has natural density 1/\[KL:ℚ\].

**How the definition helps.** An automorphism fixes the compositum KL exactly when it fixes both K and L, and Frobenius in KL restricts to Frobenius in each (our own). A prime is unramified in KL exactly when it is unramified in both, so the sets intersect (our own). Chebotarev’s theorem gives the identity class density 1/\[KL:ℚ\].

**Paper or page:** [Density questions on arithmetic equivalence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.01166v1). It says: “S(K̃L̃) = S(K̃) ∩ S(L̃).”

**Sources:**

- [Guillermo Mantilla-Soler, Density questions on arithmetic equivalence (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.01166v1)
- [N. Tschebotareff, Die Bestimmung der Dichtigkeit einer Menge von Primzahlen, welche zu einer gegebenen Substitutionsklasse gehören (1926)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01206606)

### Adele rings extend by tensoring

**Remember:** An extension just tensors the adeles once more.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R56 (Adèle rings and groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Define the adele ring of a number field K as K ⊗\_ℚ 𝔸\_ℚ. A rational adele is a real number together with one p-adic number for each prime p, integral at all but finitely many p.

**Problem.** For finite extensions L/K of number fields, the adele ring of L is L tensored over K with the adele ring of K.

**How the definition helps.** With this definition, L ⊗<sub>K</sub> (K ⊗\_ℚ 𝔸\_ℚ) = L ⊗\_ℚ 𝔸\_ℚ by associativity of tensor products (our own). The real work is matching this ring with the usual restricted product of completions (our own). Tensoring at each p gives the product of the completions above p, and integral parts agree at almost all p (our own).

**nLab:** [ring of adeles](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/ring+of+adeles). It says: “and the ring of adeles over k is the tensor product 𝔸ₖ ≔ k ⊗𝒪 𝔸𝒪.”

**Wikipedia:** [Adele ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adele_ring). It says: “If L/K is a finite extension of number fields, then the adelic construction is compatible with extension of scalars.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Adeles turn two classical theorems of number theory into one compactness statement

**Remember:** Norm-one ideles modulo K× hold class group and units together.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R56 (Adèle rings and groups), 11R29, 11R27. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An idele of a number field K has a nonzero entry in each completion and a unit entry at almost every finite place; its norm multiplies all normalized local absolute values (our own). The norm-one idele class group is the ideles of norm one modulo the diagonal copy of K× (our own).

**Problem.** For a number field K, the quotient of the norm-one ideles by K× is compact. This one statement is equivalent to the finiteness of the ideal class group together with Dirichlet's unit theorem.

**How the definition helps.** Sending an idele class to its ideal gives a map onto the ideal class group, which is discrete (our own). Up to compact factors, its kernel is the logarithmic hyperplane modulo the unit lattice (our own). So the quotient is compact exactly when the class group is finite and the units have full rank, as Dirichlet’s theorem says (our own).

**nLab:** [ring of adeles](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/ring+of+adeles), [group of ideles](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/group+of+ideles), [ideal class group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/ideal+class+group). It says: “the finiteness of the ideal class group and the Dirichlet unit theorem are equivalent to a certain quotient of the ideles being compact and discrete.”

**Sources:**

- [Tom Weston, The idelic approach to number theory, lecture notes (undated)](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1PK0lPR7yq-1s1aooX4ZLr_zY4s2Ej36z/view)

### Finite ideles recover ideal classes

**Remember:** Forget the local units and keep the prime exponents.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R56 (Adèle rings and groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A finite idele picks a nonzero element of the completion at each finite prime 𝔭, a local unit at all but finitely many. Its prime exponents ord\_𝔭 therefore name a fractional ideal, the product of 𝔭 to those exponents (our own).

**Problem.** Divide the finite ideles by the tuples of local units and the nonzero field elements embedded diagonally. The result is the ordinary ideal class group, which identifies fractional ideals differing by a scalar.

**How the definition helps.** Every fractional ideal arises, because each completion has an element of exponent one (our own). The kernel of this map is the tuples of local units, and diagonal field elements give exactly the principal ideals (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Adele ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adele_ring). It says: “so the ordinary ideal class group is recovered as a quotient of the idele class group.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Ideles with almost all unit coordinates have unique normalized representatives over ℚ

**Remember:** One rational factor cancels every finite valuation and fixes the real sign.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R56 (Adèle rings and groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A rational idele has a nonzero real entry and a nonzero p-adic entry for each prime p, a unit at almost every p. Its class identifies ideles that differ by one nonzero rational in every entry (our own).

**Problem.** Each class contains exactly one idele whose p-adic entries are all units and whose real entry is positive.

**How the definition helps.** Dividing by ±∏ pᵛᵖ, with vₚ the valuations, clears every finite valuation and makes the real entry positive; only finitely many vₚ are nonzero (our own). The only positive rational with valuation zero at every prime is 1, so the representative is unique (our own).

**nLab:** [group of ideles](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/group+of+ideles). It says: “The idele class group may be expressed as ℚ× ∖ 𝔸ℚ× ≃ (0,∞) × ∏ₚ ℤₚ×.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The idele class group states Artin reciprocity as one theorem

**Remember:** Quotient all ideles by diagonal global scalars.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R56 (Adèle rings and groups), 11R37. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The idele class group of a global field K is the quotient of its idele group by the diagonal subgroup K×.

**Problem.** For a number field K, the Artin map is surjective and factors through the idele class group. It gives an isomorphism from the idele class group modulo the connected component of 1 onto Gal(Kᵃᵇ/K).

**How the definition helps.** One quotient supplies a common domain for reciprocity at every finite abelian extension (our own). Global Artin reciprocity identifies its quotient by the identity component with the full abelian Galois group for number fields.

**nLab:** [Artin reciprocity law](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Artin+reciprocity+law), [class field theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/class+field+theory), [group of ideles](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/group+of+ideles). It says: “says that this map is surjective, that it factors through the idele class group”

**Sources:**

- [Serge Lang, Algebraic Number Theory, 2nd edition, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 110, Springer (1994)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4612-0853-2)
- [Jürgen Neukirch, Alexander Schmidt, Kay Wingberg, Cohomology of Number Fields, 2nd edition, Springer (2008)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-37889-1)

### The idele topology is finer than the subspace topology from the adeles

**Remember:** Give the ideles the topology that makes x ↦ x⁻¹ continuous.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R56 (Adèle rings and groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Give the ideles, the units of the adeles 𝔸, the topology they get as pairs (x, x⁻¹) inside 𝔸 × 𝔸, so that inversion is just swapping the two coordinates. Equivalently, this is the restricted-product topology with respect to the local unit groups 𝒪ᵥ×.

**Problem.** With this topology the ideles form a topological group, in which multiplication and inversion are continuous. With the subspace topology from the adeles, inversion is not continuous.

**How the definition helps.** Inversion swaps the coordinates of (x, x⁻¹), and multiplication is continuous in each coordinate (our own). In the subspace topology, the idele equal to 1 except for a uniformizer at the k-th prime tends to 1 as k grows (our own). The inverses never enter the neighbourhood of 1 that requires integrality at every finite place (our own).

**nLab:** [group of ideles](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/group+of+ideles), [ring of adeles](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/ring+of+adeles). It says: “Note: multiplicative inversion is not continuous in the subspace topology.”

**Sources:**

- [Tom Weston, The idelic approach to number theory, lecture notes](https://web.archive.org/web/20221205214531/https://people.math.umass.edu/~weston/oldpapers/idele.pdf)
- [Pete L. Clark, Adeles and Ideles, lecture notes](https://web.archive.org/web/20240508060418/http://alpha.math.uga.edu/~pete/8410Chapter6.pdf)

### The restricted product topology makes the adele ring locally compact

**Remember:** Keep compact integer rings in all but finitely many coordinates.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R56 (Adèle rings and groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An adele of a global field K lies in some set Uₛ, the product of the completions Kᵥ for v in a finite set S containing the archimedean places and of the local integer rings Oᵥ for v outside S (our own). The restricted product topology gives each Uₛ its product topology and makes it open.

**Problem.** The adele ring of a global field is locally compact. A global field is a number field or a function field of a curve over a finite field.

**How the definition helps.** Each Uₛ is locally compact, because finitely many local fields are locally compact and the product of the compact rings Oᵥ is compact by Tychonoff’s theorem (our own). Every adele lies in an open Uₛ, so the adele ring is locally compact.

**nLab:** [ring of adeles](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/ring+of+adeles). It says: “The restricted product is a filtered colimit of a system of open inclusions between locally compact Hausdorff rings, and is therefore itself locally compact Hausdorff.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The restricted product topology makes the rationals discrete in their adeles

**Remember:** Integral at every prime and smaller than one forces zero.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R56 (Adèle rings and groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A rational adele has a real entry and one p-adic entry per prime p, integral at almost every prime. Basic open sets are products of local open sets equal to ℤₚ at all but finitely many primes, so one open set can require integrality at every prime at once (our own).

**Problem.** The rational numbers, placed diagonally in the adeles of ℚ, form a discrete subgroup.

**How the definition helps.** The open set (−1, 1) × ∏ ℤₚ contains no nonzero rational (our own). A rational in every ℤₚ has no prime in its denominator, so it is an integer, and an integer of absolute value below 1 is 0 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Adele ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adele_ring). It says: “The field K embeds diagonally in 𝔸ₖ as a discrete subring”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Trace pairings make adeles self-dual

**Remember:** The trace pairing glues the local character groups together.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R56 (Adèle rings and groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a number field K, pair two adeles x and y by multiplying ψ(Tr(xᵥyᵥ)) over all places v, where Tr is the local trace down to ℚ and ψ is the standard additive character of that completion of ℚ (our own).

**Problem.** This pairing identifies the additive adele group of a number field with its continuous character group.

**How the definition helps.** At almost every place the trace of integers is integral, so the factor is 1 and each adele gives a global character (our own). Local trace duality makes each completion self-dual, and continuity forces almost every local factor to be trivial on local integers (our own). Restricted product duality then glues the local isomorphisms (our own).

**nLab:** [ring of adeles](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/ring+of+adeles). It says: “The additive group 𝔸ₖ is Pontrjagin self-dual in the sense that the map ϕ: 𝔸ₖ → 𝔸ₖ∧ induced from the pairing ⟨−, −⟩ is an isomorphism onto the character group.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Invertible ideals give the Picard group of an order

**Remember:** At a nonmaximal order, keep only ideals with inverses.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R65 (Class groups and Picard groups of orders). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an order R in a number field K, a fractional ideal I, a nonzero finitely generated R-submodule of K, is invertible if IJ = R for some fractional ideal J. The Picard group is the invertible fractional ideals modulo the nonzero principal ones.

**Problem.** The Picard group of an order is isomorphic to the group of isomorphism classes of finitely generated modules locally free of rank one. Tensor product gives the group law.

**How the definition helps.** Invertible ideals are exactly those locally generated by one element, which are the modules locally free of rank one (our own). Without invertibility, cancellation fails: in ℤ\[2i\], the ideal I = 2ℤ\[i\] satisfies I² = 2I, yet I ≠ 2ℤ\[2i\] (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Dedekind domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedekind_domain). It says: “For an arbitrary domain one may define the Picard group Pic(R) as the group of invertible fractional ideals Inv(R) modulo the subgroup of principal fractional ideals.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Rationalization removes closed-point contributions

**Remember:** Finite residue K-groups disappear when you tensor with the rationals.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R70 (K-theory of global fields), 19D50. arXiv math.KT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The rational K-group Kₙ(R) ⊗ ℚ of a ring kills every element of finite order in its integral K-group, such as all of Kₘ(F) for a finite field F and m ≥ 1 (our own).

**Problem.** Let A be the ring of integers of a number field and S any set of rational primes. Inverting S preserves all rational K-groups in degrees n ≥ 2.

**How the definition helps.** Quillen’s localization sequence puts Kₙ and Kₙ₋₁ of the residue fields at S on either side of Kₙ(A) → Kₙ(A\[S⁻¹\]), and for n ≥ 2 these are finite (our own). Filtered colimits handle infinite S (our own). Integrally the map can fail: {−1, 3} in K₂(ℤ\[1/3\]) has nontrivial boundary modulo 3 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Algebraic K-theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_K-theory). It says: “then there is a long exact sequence”

**Sources:**

- [Daniel Quillen, Higher algebraic K-theory I (1973)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BFb0067053)
- [Daniel Quillen, On the cohomology and K-theory of the general linear groups over a finite field (1972)](https://doi.org/10.2307/1970825)

### Defining ramification index as a group index makes ramification indices multiply

**Remember:** Indices of nested groups multiply.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory), 13F30. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a discrete valuation ring B dominating A, meaning its maximal ideal contracts to that of A, the ramification index e(B/A) is the index in ℤ of the values that the normalized valuation of B takes on the fraction field of A (our own).

**Problem.** For discrete valuation rings A ⊂ B ⊂ C with each inclusion local, e(C/A) = e(C/B)e(B/A).

**How the definition helps.** Under the valuation of C, the values on A, B and C form a chain of subgroups of ℤ, and indices multiply along a chain (our own). The real work is showing that this agrees with the definition by exponents of ideals (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Lemma 15.112.3.](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0BRL). It says: “Then the ramification indices of B/A and C/B multiply to give the ramification index of C/A.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Defining unramified as finite étale makes composita of unramified extensions unramified

**Remember:** Tensor the integer rings, then select the factor for the compositum.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory), 13B40. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a discrete valuation ring A with fraction field K, call a finite separable extension L/K unramified if the integral closure of A in L is finite étale over A (our own). Finite étale algebras stay finite étale under tensor products and when passing to a factor (our own).

**Problem.** If L₁ and L₂ are finite separable unramified extensions of K inside one algebraic closure, then their compositum is unramified. The compositum is the smallest field that contains both.

**How the definition helps.** The tensor product of the two integral closures is finite étale over A, hence a product of normal domains because A is normal (our own). The compositum is a factor of the generic tensor product, and its integral closure is the matching domain factor, so it is finite étale (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Lemma 15.112.8.](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0EXR). It says: “there exists a a finite separable extension L/K which is unramified with respect to A containing L₁ and L₂.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### In upper numbering, abelian ramification jumps are integers

**Remember:** Weight lower time by the fraction of inertia still present.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory), 11S31. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Upper numbering reindexes the lower ramification groups by Herbrand’s function φ(s) = ∫₀ˢ \|Gₓ\|/\|G₀\| dx, with Gₓ the lower group at ⌈x⌉ and φ(s) = s on \[−1, 0\], so the upper group at φ(s) is Gₛ (our own). A jump is an index where the upper group changes (our own).

**Problem.** For a finite abelian extension of local fields, every jump of the upper ramification filtration is an integer.

**How the definition helps.** Local reciprocity sends the unit group Uⁿ, whose steps sit at integers, onto the upper group Gⁿ (our own). So the upper jumps of an abelian extension occur only at integers; this is the Hasse–Arf theorem.

**Wikipedia:** [Hasse–Arf theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse%E2%80%93Arf_theorem), [Ramification group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramification_group), [Conductor (class field theory)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conductor_%28class_field_theory%29). It says: “With the above set up of an abelian extension L/K, the theorem states that the jumps of the filtration {Gᵗ(L/K) : t ≥ −1} are all rational integers.”

**Sources:**

- [Cahit Arf, Untersuchungen über reinverzweigte Erweiterungen diskret bewerteter perfekter Körper, Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik 181 (1940)](https://doi.org/10.1515/crll.1940.181.1)

### Reduced poles give ramification breaks

**Remember:** Remove p-divisible poles before reading the ramification break.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory), 11S20. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Write a cyclic degree-p extension of K = k((t)), with k finite of characteristic p, as yᵖ − y = a. The parameter a is reduced when each negative power of t in it has exponent prime to p, which replacing y by y + b can always achieve, since it changes a by bᵖ − b.

**Problem.** Suppose the reduced parameter a has a pole of order m. Then m is the unique positive ramification break in both lower and upper numbering.

**How the definition helps.** Reduction makes the pole order m prime to p, so with t of valuation p and y of valuation −m, tᵘyᵛ with pu − mv = 1 is a uniformizer (our own). Each nonidentity automorphism moves y by a nonzero prime-field constant, changing this uniformizer by valuation m + 1, so the only lower break is m (our own). With a single break, upper and lower numbering agree there (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Artin–Schreier theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artin%E2%80%93Schreier_theory). It says: “is the splitting field of an Artin–Schreier polynomial”

**Paper or page:** [Newton Polygons of Sums on Curves II: Variation in p-adic Families](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.08657v1). It says: “p<sup>j-1</sup>\\max \\{  k p<sup>-v<sub>p</sub>(c<sub>k</sub>)</sup>: v<sub>p</sub>(c<sub>k</sub>) &lt; j \\}  &amp;  \\text{if } v<sub>p</sub>(c<sub>k</sub>) &lt; j \\text{ for some } k”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Swan conductors ignore tame twists

**Remember:** Tame characters act trivially on every group the Swan conductor sees.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory), 11S25. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Swan conductor of a representation V of a finite local Galois group sums, over the higher ramification groups Gᵢ with i ≥ 1 only, the codimension of the fixed space of Gᵢ in V times \|Gᵢ\|/\|G₀\| (our own). A tame character is a one-dimensional character trivial on G₁ (our own).

**Problem.** Twisting a complex representation of a finite local Galois group by a tame character leaves its Swan conductor unchanged.

**How the definition helps.** A tame character is 1 on every group in the sum, so twisting by it leaves each fixed space unchanged (our own). The Artin conductor also counts G₀, where a tame twist can change the fixed space, even for the trivial representation (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Artin conductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artin_conductor). It says: “f(χ) − (χ(1) − χ(G₀))”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Tame ramification is exactly what a projective ring of integers needs

**Remember:** No prime divides its own ramification index.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory), 11R33. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A finite Galois extension L of ℚ is tame if no prime p divides its ramification index eₚ, the common exponent of the prime ideals in pOₗ (our own).

**Problem.** For a finite Galois extension L of ℚ with group G, the ring of integers is a projective ℤ\[G\]-module exactly when L is tamely ramified. A projective module is a direct summand of a free module.

**How the definition helps.** Tameness at p is the local condition for a normal integral basis of Oₗ ⊗ ℤₚ over ℤₚ\[G\] (our own). Noether’s theorem combines these local conditions into projectivity of Oₗ over ℤ\[G\].

**Wikipedia:** [Galois representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_representation). It says: “Then Noether's theorem states that tame ramification is necessary and sufficient for OL to be a projective module over Z\[G\].”

**Sources:**

- [Emmy Noether, Normalbasis bei Körpern ohne höhere Verzweigung, Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik 167 (1932)](https://doi.org/10.1515/crll.1932.167.147)

### Tame ramification makes trace surjective

**Remember:** The trace of one is a unit across a tame totally ramified extension.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A finite extension of p-adic fields is tame when its ramification index e, the valuation in the extension of a generator of the base maximal ideal, is prime to p, so that e is a unit.

**Problem.** The trace on the rings of integers of a finite extension of p-adic fields is onto exactly when the extension is tame.

**How the definition helps.** In the totally ramified stage of degree e, the trace sends 1 to e, which is a unit exactly in the tame case (our own). The unramified stage has surjective trace, as on finite residue fields (our own). In the wild case the trace lands in the maximal ideal; for example, ℚ₂(√2) has all integral traces in 2ℤ₂ (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Ramification (mathematics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramification_%28mathematics%29). It says: “A finite generically étale extension B/A of Dedekind domains is tame if and only if the trace Tr: B → A is surjective.”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields (1979)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Tameness gives the different exponent

**Remember:** Tame means the residue characteristic does not divide the ramification index.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A finite Galois extension of non-Archimedean local fields with ramification index e is tame when the residue characteristic does not divide e. Then every higher ramification group Gᵢ with i ≥ 1 is trivial (our own).

**Problem.** For a tame finite Galois extension of non-Archimedean local fields, the different, the inverse of the trace dual of the ring of integers, has exponent e − 1.

**How the definition helps.** Hilbert’s formula gives the different exponent as ∑ (\|Gᵢ\| − 1), and tameness leaves only the inertia term e − 1 (our own). In the wild extension ℚ₂(√2), the different is generated by 2√2, of valuation three, although e − 1 is one (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Different ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Different_ideal). It says: “is equal to e − 1 if P is tamely ramified”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Trace duality makes differents multiply

**Remember:** Trace in stages to multiply the different ideals.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The inverse different of a finite separable extension L/K of local fields is the trace dual of the integers: the x in L such that Tr(xy) is integral in K for every integer y of L. The different is its inverse ideal.

**Problem.** Let M/L/K be a tower of finite separable extensions of non-Archimedean local fields. The M/K different equals the M/L different times the extension of the L/K different to M.

**How the definition helps.** Traces compose, so x is in the M/K dual exactly when Trₘ/ₗ(xOₘ) lies in the L/K dual (our own). Dividing x by a generator of that dual turns this into the M/L dual condition (our own). So the inverse differents multiply, and hence so do the differents (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Different ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Different_ideal). It says: “In a tower of fields L/K/F the relative differents are related by δ₍L/F₎ = δ₍L/K₎ δ₍K/F₎.”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields (1979)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Trace duals make differents multiply

**Remember:** Trace duals compose because traces compose.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The inverse different of a finite separable extension of local fields is the set of x such that the trace of xy is integral for every integer y of the extension. The different is its inverse fractional ideal.

**Problem.** Consider a tower L/K/F of finite separable extensions of non-Archimedean local fields. The different of L/F equals the product of the different of L/K and the extended different of K/F.

**How the definition helps.** Traces compose, so products of the two trace-dual bases form the dual basis of the product integral basis (our own). Hence the inverse different of L/F is the product of the two inverse differents, and inverting gives the formula (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Different ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Different_ideal). It says: “In a tower of fields L/K/F the relative differents are related by δ(L/F) = δ(L/K)δ(K/F).”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Upper numbering makes ramification groups pass to quotients

**Remember:** Weight lower time by the fraction of inertia still present.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory), 11S20. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Upper numbering reindexes the lower ramification groups by Herbrand’s function φ(u) = ∫₀ᵘ \|Gₓ\|/\|G₀\| dx, with Gₓ the lower group at ⌈x⌉ and φ(u) = u on \[−1, 0\] (our own). The upper group Gᵗ is the lower group at φ⁻¹(t).

**Problem.** For a normal subgroup H of G, the image of Gᵗ in G/H is (G/H)ᵗ. This is Herbrand's theorem in upper numbering.

**How the definition helps.** Herbrand’s theorem says lower groups pass to G/H after reindexing by the Herbrand function of H (our own). Herbrand functions compose, so this reindexing disappears in upper numbering (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Ramification group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramification_group). It says: “The upper numbering is defined so as to be compatible with passage to quotients:”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 67, Springer (1979)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Upper ramification indices rescale for subgroups

**Remember:** Restrict upper groups by changing their indices, not their elements.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Herbrand’s function φ turns lower ramification indices into upper ones: φ(u) = u for −1 ≤ u ≤ 0 and φ(u) = ∫₀ᵘ dt/\[G₀ : G<sub>t</sub>\] for u ≥ 0. The upper group at v is the lower group at ψ(v), where ψ is the inverse of φ.

**Problem.** Let M/K be a finite Galois extension of local fields and L/K a Galois subextension. For u ≥ −1, the upper group at u meets Gal(M/L) in the upper group for M/L at ψ₍L/K₎(u), with ψ₍L/K₎ the inverse Herbrand function of L/K.

**How the definition helps.** Lower groups restrict to subgroups unchanged, so the rule follows by translating both sides into upper numbering (our own). This uses ψ₍M/K₎ = ψ₍M/L₎ ∘ ψ₍L/K₎, which rests on Herbrand’s quotient theorem (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Ramification groups of some finite Galois extensions of maximal nilpotency class over local fields of positive characteristic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.07928v4). It says: “Then we have $G<sup>i\\cap</sup> H=H<sup>\\psi (i)</sup>$ for all $i\\geq -1$.”

**Sources:**

- [Ramification groups of some finite Galois extensions of maximal nilpotency class over local fields of positive characteristic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.07928v4)
- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields (1979)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### De Rham representations admit tensor products

**Remember:** Tensor invariant bases to get another invariant basis.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S20 (Galois theory), 14F30. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A continuous representation V of the absolute Galois group of a finite extension K of ℚₚ on a finite-dimensional ℚₚ-vector space is de Rham if V ⊗ B has a basis of Galois-fixed vectors. Here B is Fontaine’s de Rham period field, whose fixed field is K.

**Problem.** Tensor products of de Rham representations are de Rham. Their spaces of fixed vectors after extension to B tensor over K.

**How the definition helps.** Tensoring two fixed bases gives a fixed basis of the tensor product (our own). In a fixed basis, a vector is fixed exactly when its coefficients lie in K, so the fixed spaces tensor over K (our own). This agrees with the usual dimension test, because fixed vectors independent over K stay independent over B (our own).

**nLab:** [p-adic Hodge theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/p-adic+Hodge+theory). It says: “If the dimension of V is equal to the dimension of V₍dR₎, we say that V is de Rham.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Cartier duals detect missing roots

**Remember:** Keep the Galois action on the roots when taking the dual.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11S25 (Galois cohomology). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Cartier dual of a finite Galois module M over a p-adic field K is Hom(M, K̄×), with Galois acting on both sides by (σf)(m) = σ(f(σ⁻¹m)) (our own). For M = ℤ/nℤ, evaluation at 1 identifies it with the roots of unity μₙ, Galois action included (our own).

**Problem.** Let K be a p-adic field and n a positive integer. The order of H²(K, ℤ/nℤ) is the number of nth roots of unity in K.

**How the definition helps.** Tate local duality pairs H²(K, ℤ/nℤ) perfectly with H⁰(K, μₙ), the nth roots of unity in K. Perfectly paired finite groups have the same size (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Duality for the condensed Weil-étale realisation of 1-motives over p-adic fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.19910v2). It says: “Then we have a perfect cup-product pairing\\\[  \\H^ q(G<sub>F</sub>,N)\\otimes \\H^ {2-q}(G<sub>F</sub>,\\operatorname{Hom}(N,\\overline{F}<sup>\\times </sup>))\\rightarrow \\H^ 2(G<sub>F</sub>,\\overline{F}<sup>\\times </sup>)=\\mathbbm {Q}/\\mathbbm {Z}.  \\\]”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Norm-one tori count local norms

**Remember:** Restrict scalars to the base field and take the kernel of the norm.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S25 (Galois cohomology), 11S31. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite separable extension L/K, the norm-one torus T is the kernel of the norm from the restriction of scalars of the multiplicative group of L to that of K. So T(K) is the set of x ∈ L× with Nₗ/ₖ(x) = 1 (our own).

**Problem.** For a finite abelian extension L/K of non-Archimedean local fields, H¹(K, T) has order \[L:K\].

**How the definition helps.** The sequence 1 → T → R(𝔾ₘ) → 𝔾ₘ → 1, with Hilbert’s theorem 90 and Shapiro’s lemma, gives H¹(K, T) ≅ K×/Nₗ/ₖ(L×) (our own). Local reciprocity identifies this quotient with Gal(L/K), of order \[L:K\] (our own).

**nLab:** [Galois cohomology](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Galois+cohomology). It says: “Galois cohomology refers to the group cohomology of G with coefficients in a G-module naturally associated to L.”

**Wikipedia:** [Local class field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_class_field_theory). It says: “the reciprocity map induces an isomorphism of the quotient group K×/N(L×)”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Twisted duals make local Tate duality perfect

**Remember:** Dual into roots of unity, not ℚ/ℤ, for a perfect pairing.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11S25 (Galois cohomology), 11S31. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The twisted dual of a finite Galois module A over a p-adic field K is A′ = Hom(A, μ), with μ the roots of unity in K̄ and Galois acting on both sides by (σf)(a) = σ(f(σ⁻¹a)) (our own).

**Problem.** Cup product gives a perfect pairing between Hⁱ(K, A) and H²⁻ⁱ(K, A′) with values in the Brauer group ℚ/ℤ, for i = 0, 1, 2.

**How the definition helps.** Evaluation A × A′ → μ is Galois-equivariant, and Tate’s local duality theorem makes the resulting cup product perfect (our own). The untwisted dual fails over ℚ₂: the constant module ℤ/3 has three invariants (our own). Its untwisted dual is ℤ/3 again, whose second cohomology is zero because ℚ₂ has only one cube root of unity (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Local Tate duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_Tate_duality). It says: “It shows that the dual of such a Galois module is the Tate twist of usual linear dual.”

**Sources:**

- [Jürgen Neukirch, Alexander Schmidt and Kay Wingberg, Cohomology of Number Fields, Springer (2008)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-37889-1)

### Unramified classes are Frobenius quotients

**Remember:** Remove inertia, then one Frobenius operator computes the group.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S25 (Galois cohomology), 11F80. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite Galois module M over a local field with finite residue field, a first cohomology class is unramified if it comes from the Galois group of the residue field acting on the elements fixed by inertia. That group is topologically generated by Frobenius, so such a cocycle is fixed by its value at Frobenius (our own).

**Problem.** The unramified first cohomology group is A/(F − 1)A, where A is the inertia-fixed subgroup and F is Frobenius, the map raising residues to the residue field size.

**How the definition helps.** Every value in A occurs, because F acts on the finite group A through a finite cyclic quotient (our own). Changing a cocycle by a coboundary changes its value at F by an element of (F − 1)A (our own).

**nLab:** [Selmer group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Selmer+group). It says: “the unramified local condition is defined as follows:”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Cup products invert swapped symbols

**Remember:** Cup the two Kummer classes and read their local invariant as a root.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; p-adic formal groups), 11S25. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a non-Archimedean local field K containing the nth roots of unity, with n prime to its characteristic, the Hilbert symbol (a, b) is the local invariant in μₙ of the cup product of the Kummer classes of a and b (our own). Cup products of degree-one classes are anticommutative (our own).

**Problem.** For all nonzero a and b in K, the Hilbert symbols (a, b) and (b, a) multiply to one.

**How the definition helps.** Swapping a and b negates the cup product class (our own). The swap also exchanges the two μₙ factors, which acts trivially because μₙ lies in K (our own). In μₙ, negation is inversion, so (b, a) = (a, b)⁻¹ (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Hilbert symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_symbol). It says: “skew symmetric: (a,b) = (b,a)⁻¹”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Fundamental classes make norms commute

**Remember:** Reciprocity is cup product with the class of invariant 1/\[E:K\].

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; p-adic formal groups), 11S25. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite Galois extension E/K of local fields with group G, the fundamental class is the class in H²(G,E×) with Brauer invariant 1/\[E:K\]. Cup product with it defines inverse reciprocity from Gᵃᵇ to K×/N(E×) (our own). Its restriction to a subgroup is again the fundamental class.

**Problem.** For a field L between K and E, take the map Gal(E/L)ᵃᵇ → Gal(E/K)ᵃᵇ induced by inclusion. Under inverse reciprocity it is the norm map L×/N(E×) → K×/N(E×).

**How the definition helps.** Because the fundamental class restricts to the fundamental class, the projection formula for cup product gives norm compatibility (our own). Corestriction acts on the Galois side as the map of abelianizations and on the field side as the norm (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Class formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_formation). It says: “the restriction (of cohomology classes) of a fundamental class is another fundamental class.”

**Sources:**

- [John Tate, The Higher Dimensional Cohomology Groups of Class Field Theory](https://doi.org/10.2307/1969801)
- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Lubin–Tate torsion extends cyclotomy

**Remember:** Formal group torsion plays the role of roots of unity.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; p-adic formal groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a p-adic field K with integer ring O, uniformizer π and residue field of size q, a Lubin–Tate formal O-module has a π-series with linear term πX that reduces to Xᑫ modulo π (our own). Its division tower adjoins all πⁿ-torsion points for all n ≥ 1, and Galois acts on these points through O× (our own).

**Problem.** The division tower and the maximal unramified extension together generate the maximal abelian extension of K. If \[K:ℚₚ\] exceeds one, adjoining all roots of unity of p-power order to the maximal unramified extension gives a smaller field.

**How the definition helps.** Lubin–Tate reciprocity identifies the tower’s Galois group with O×, and the tower with the maximal unramified extension gives the maximal abelian extension. O× has p-adic rank \[K:ℚₚ\], but the cyclotomic character lands in ℤₚ×, of rank one (our own). So cyclotomy misses directions when \[K:ℚₚ\] exceeds one (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Théorie locale du corps de classes et (φ,Γ)-modules Lubin-Tate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.13986v1). It says: “L'extension Fⁿʳ · F∞ est l'extension abélienne maximale de F”

**Sources:**

- [Jonathan Lubin and John Tate, Formal Complex Multiplication in Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.2307/1970622)

### Lubin–Tate torsion gives abelian extensions

**Remember:** O acts on torsion, so Galois acts through units.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; p-adic formal groups), 11S15. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let O be a complete discrete valuation ring with uniformizer π and finite residue field of size q. A Lubin–Tate formal O-module for π is a one-dimensional commutative formal group with an action of O, where π acts by a series πX + ⋯ that reduces to Xᑫ modulo π (our own).

**Problem.** For n ≥ 1, adjoining all points killed by πⁿ gives a totally ramified extension, meaning its ramification index equals its degree. Its Galois group is the unit group of O modulo πⁿ, that is, (O/πⁿO)ˣ.

**How the definition helps.** Galois commutes with the O-action, so it acts on the πⁿ-torsion by O-module automorphisms (our own explanation). This torsion is free of rank one over O/πⁿO, so these automorphisms form (O/πⁿO)ˣ, and every unit occurs as a Galois action. An Eisenstein polynomial for a generating point gives the degree and total ramification (our own account).

**Wikipedia:** [Lubin–Tate formal group law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lubin%E2%80%93Tate_formal_group_law). It says: “The compositum of all fields formed by adjoining such modules to the original field gives the ramified part.”

**Sources:**

- [Jonathan Lubin and John Tate, Formal Complex Multiplication in Local Fields (1965)](https://doi.org/10.2307/1970622)

### Openness rules out false norm groups

**Remember:** Finite index is not enough; the subgroup must also be open.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; p-adic formal groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let K be a non-Archimedean local field with maximal ideal 𝔪. A subgroup H of K× is open exactly when it contains 1 + 𝔪ⁿ, the units congruent to 1 modulo 𝔪ⁿ, for some n ≥ 1 (our own).

**Problem.** Open subgroups of finite index in Kˣ are exactly the norm subgroups of finite abelian extensions. In positive characteristic, some subgroups of finite index are not open, so they are not norm subgroups.

**How the definition helps.** The local existence theorem identifies the norm groups of finite abelian extensions with the open subgroups of finite index. For K = 𝔽ₚ((t)), K×/(K×)ᵖ is an uncountable 𝔽ₚ-vector space in which the dense subgroup 𝔽ₚ(t)× has countable image (our own). A nonzero linear functional that kills this image pulls back to a dense subgroup of index p, which is not open (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Local class field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_class_field_theory). It says: “between open subgroups of finite index in the multiplicative group”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Primitive torsion polynomials are Eisenstein

**Remember:** Divide out the earlier torsion and an Eisenstein polynomial remains.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; p-adic formal groups), 11S15. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a local field with uniformizer π and residue field of size q, take f(X) = πX + Xᑫ and write fⁿ for its n-fold iterate, with f⁰(X) = X. A primitive point of level n ≥ 1 is a root of fⁿ that is not a root of fⁿ⁻¹ (our own).

**Problem.** A primitive point of level n generates a totally ramified extension of degree (q − 1)qⁿ⁻¹.

**How the definition helps.** The primitive points of level n are the roots of fⁿ/fⁿ⁻¹, which equals π + (fⁿ⁻¹)ᑫ⁻¹ (our own). This polynomial is monic of degree (q−1)qⁿ⁻¹, reduces to a power of X modulo π, and has constant term π, so it is Eisenstein (our own). Adjoining a root of an Eisenstein polynomial gives a totally ramified extension of its degree (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Lubin–Tate formal group law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lubin%E2%80%93Tate_formal_group_law). It says: “If g is an Eisenstein polynomial, f(t) = tg(t) and F the Lubin–Tate formal group”

**Sources:**

- [Jonathan Lubin and John Tate, Formal Complex Multiplication in Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.2307/1970622)

### Strict isomorphisms preserve division fields

**Remember:** Changing coordinates changes torsion points but not their fields.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; p-adic formal groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix a uniformizer π of a non-Archimedean local field with integer ring O. A strict isomorphism between Lubin–Tate formal O-modules for π is a power series over O with linear term X that carries one group law and O-action to the other. Since its coefficients lie in O, it sends each torsion point into the field that point generates (our own).

**Problem.** For fixed π, every Lubin–Tate formal module generates the same field at each division level.

**How the definition helps.** Lubin–Tate theory shows that any two Lubin–Tate modules for the same π are strictly isomorphic. The isomorphism sends πⁿ-torsion to πⁿ-torsion and converges there, so it maps one division field into the other (our own). Its inverse gives the reverse inclusion (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Lubin–Tate formal group law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lubin%E2%80%93Tate_formal_group_law). It says: “All such group laws, for different choices of e satisfying these conditions, are strictly isomorphic.”

**Sources:**

- [Jonathan Lubin and John Tate, Formal Complex Multiplication in Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.2307/1970622)

### Unit levels detect wild ramification

**Remember:** Level zero sees inertia, and level one sees wild inertia.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; p-adic formal groups), 11S15. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite abelian extension of non-Archimedean local fields, the conductor exponent is the least n such that every unit at level n is a norm. Level zero is all units, and level n ≥ 1 is the units congruent to 1 modulo the nth power of the maximal ideal.

**Problem.** The conductor exponent is zero for unramified extensions and one for ramified tame extensions. It is at least two for wild extensions.

**How the definition helps.** Local reciprocity maps level zero onto the inertia group and level one onto wild inertia, the part of inertia of order a power of the residue characteristic (our own). So level zero consists of norms exactly when the extension is unramified, and level one does exactly when it is tame (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Conductor (class field theory)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conductor_%28class_field_theory%29). It says: “Equivalently, n is the smallest integer such that the local Artin map is trivial”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Unramified norms have divisible valuations

**Remember:** Send each element to Frobenius raised to its valuation.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; p-adic formal groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an unramified extension of non-Archimedean local fields, the Artin map sends a to Frobᵛ⁽ᵃ⁾, where v is the normalized valuation and Frob raises residues to the power of the base residue field size.

**Problem.** In the unramified extension of degree n of a non-Archimedean local field, the norms are exactly the elements with valuation divisible by n.

**How the definition helps.** Frobenius has order n, so Frobᵛ⁽ᵃ⁾ is trivial exactly when n divides v(a) (our own). Local reciprocity identifies the kernel of the Artin map with the norm group (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Local class field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_class_field_theory). It says: “the reciprocity map induces an isomorphism of the quotient group K×/N(L×)”

**Sources:**

- [Helmut Hasse, Die Normenresttheorie relativ-Abelscher Zahlkörper als Klassenkörpertheorie im Kleinen](https://doi.org/10.1515/crll.1930.162.145)
- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### The Weil group makes the reciprocity map an isomorphism

**Remember:** Integer Frobenius powers match integer valuations, so K× fits exactly.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11S37 (Langlands-Weil conjectures, nonabelian class field theory), 11S31. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a non-Archimedean local field K, the Weil group consists of the absolute Galois automorphisms that act on the algebraic closure of the residue field as integer powers of Frobenius. Inertia keeps its profinite topology and is an open subgroup (our own). So the Weil group modulo inertia is ℤ, just as K× modulo units is ℤ by the valuation (our own).

**Problem.** For a non-archimedean local field K, the reciprocity map gives an isomorphism from K× to the abelianized Weil group.

**How the definition helps.** Local reciprocity matches the units with the image of inertia and a uniformizer with a Frobenius lift in the abelianization (our own). The Weil form of local class field theory gives the isomorphism.

**Wikipedia:** [Weil group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weil_group). It says: “The reciprocity map of the class formation (G,A) induces an isomorphism from Aᴳ to the abelianization of the Weil group.”

**Sources:**

- [André Weil, Sur la théorie du corps de classes, Journal of the Mathematical Society of Japan 3 (1951)](https://doi.org/10.2969/jmsj/00310001)

### Weil characters need not be periodic

**Remember:** Discrete Frobenius powers allow arbitrary nonzero complex eigenvalues.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S37 (Langlands-Weil conjectures, nonabelian class field theory), 11S20. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a local field K with residue field of size q, the Weil group consists of the absolute Galois automorphisms that act on the algebraic closure of the residue field as an integer power of the Frobenius x ↦ xᑫ. Inertia, the kernel of this action, keeps its profinite topology and is open, so the quotient is the discrete group ℤ (our own).

**Problem.** A complex character of the Weil group that is trivial on inertia can assign any nonzero complex number to Frobenius. It extends continuously to the absolute Galois group exactly when that number is a root of unity.

**How the definition helps.** An unramified Weil character factors through the discrete ℤ, so its value at Frobenius can be any nonzero complex number (our own). A continuous extension to the Galois group factors through profinite ℤ, and a continuous character of a profinite group has finite image in ℂ× (our own). Conversely, a root of unity gives a character through a finite cyclic quotient (our own).

**nLab:** [Weil group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Weil+group). It says: “defined as the inverse image of Frobenius automorphisms”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Brauer invariants equate period and index

**Remember:** Period and index are both the invariant's denominator.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11S45 (Algebras and orders, and their zeta functions), 11S25. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a non-Archimedean local field K, the local invariant is the canonical isomorphism Br(K) → ℚ/ℤ (our own). The period of a central simple algebra is the order of its class, and its index is the degree of its division algebra (our own).

**Problem.** For a central simple algebra over a non-Archimedean local field, its period equals its index.

**How the definition helps.** Both equal the denominator n of the invariant (our own). The order of the class in ℚ/ℤ is n, and the unramified extension of degree n multiplies the invariant by n, so it splits the algebra (our own). The index divides every splitting degree and the period divides the index, so both equal n (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Brauer group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brauer_group). It says: “the index of A is equal to the period of A.”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Scalar extension multiplies Brauer invariants

**Remember:** Divide the parameter’s valuation by the unramified cyclic degree, modulo integers.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S45 (Algebras and orders, and their zeta functions), 11S25. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Represent a local Brauer class by a cyclic algebra built from the unramified extension of degree n, its Frobenius, and a parameter a ∈ K× (our own). Its invariant is vₖ(a)/n modulo ℤ, with vₖ the normalized valuation (our own).

**Problem.** For any finite extension E/K of non-Archimedean local fields, the invariant of the restricted Brauer class is \[E:K\] times the original invariant.

**How the definition helps.** The invariant is the unramified character’s value at Frobenius times the valuation of a (our own). Over E, Frobenius becomes its fth power and the valuation of a is multiplied by the ramification index e (our own). So the invariant is multiplied by ef = \[E:K\] (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Hasse invariant of an algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse_invariant_of_an_algebra). It says: “The invariant map attaches the element k/n mod 1 to the class.”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Finite differences extract Mahler coefficients

**Remember:** One difference lowers the binomial index by one.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S80 (Other analytic theory (analogues of beta and gamma functions, p-adic integration, etc.)). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** By Mahler’s theorem, every continuous f: ℤₚ → ℚₚ has a uniformly convergent expansion ∑ aₙ binom(x, n). The forward difference Δf(x) = f(x + 1) − f(x) sends binom(x, n) to binom(x, n − 1) by Pascal’s identity, and sends constants to zero (our own).

**Problem.** In the Mahler expansion of f, the coefficient of binom(x, n) is the nth forward difference of f at zero.

**How the definition helps.** Apply Δ n times term by term, which uniform convergence allows, and evaluate at zero (our own). Only the term of index n survives, because binom(0, m) = 0 for m ≥ 1 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Mahler's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahler%27s_theorem). It says: “the coefficients aₙ = (Δⁿf)(0) → 0 in ℚₚ as n → ∞.”

**Sources:**

- [Kurt Mahler, An Interpolation Series for Continuous Functions of a p-adic Variable (1958)](https://doi.org/10.1515/crll.1958.199.23)

### Kummer congruences determine measures

**Remember:** Functions divisible by pᵐ get values divisible by pᵐ.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11S80 (Other analytic theory (analogues of beta and gamma functions, p-adic integration, etc.)). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let O be the valuation ring of ℂₚ, the completed algebraic closure of ℚₚ. An integral measure on ℤₚˣ is a continuous ℂₚ-linear functional on continuous functions ℤₚˣ → ℂₚ that sends every O-valued function into O. By linearity it then sends every pᵐO-valued function into pᵐO.

**Problem.** Take continuous O-valued functions on ℤₚˣ with dense ℂₚ-linear span, and assign each a value in O. A unique integral measure has these values exactly when, for every finite linear combination and every integer m, the combination of values lies in pᵐO whenever the combination of functions takes values in pᵐO.

**How the definition helps.** The test is the definition’s bound, checked on the span (our own explanation). It makes the assignment well defined and continuous on the span, and density and completeness give a unique extension (our own argument).

**Paper or page:** [On p-adic Measures for Quaternionic Modular Forms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.11822v3). It says: “is equivalent to the following Kummer congruences”

**Sources:**

- [On p-adic Measures for Quaternionic Modular Forms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.11822v3)

### Trace duals locate character conductors

**Remember:** The inverse different is the largest ideal the trace character kills.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S80 (Other analytic theory (analogues of beta and gamma functions, p-adic integration, etc.)), 11S15. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite separable extension L/K of non-Archimedean local fields with integer rings O<sub>L</sub> and O<sub>K</sub>, the inverse different is the set of x ∈ L with Tr(xy) ∈ O<sub>K</sub> for every y ∈ O<sub>L</sub>. It is the largest fractional ideal of L whose trace lies in O<sub>K</sub> (our own).

**Problem.** Let ψ be an additive character of K whose largest fractional ideal of triviality is O<sub>K</sub>. Its pullback ψ ∘ Tr is trivial on a fractional ideal of L exactly when the inverse different contains that ideal.

**How the definition helps.** ψ ∘ Tr is trivial on a fractional ideal I exactly when Tr(I) ⊆ O<sub>K</sub>, because Tr(I) is a fractional ideal of K and O<sub>K</sub> is the largest one on which ψ is trivial (our own). Since I is closed under multiplication by O<sub>L</sub>, Tr(I) ⊆ O<sub>K</sub> says that I lies in the inverse different (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Different ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Different_ideal). It says: “It plays a basic role in Pontryagin duality for p-adic fields.”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Limits of powers make the Teichmüller lift multiplicative

**Remember:** Limits preserve products, and one more power shifts the sequence.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S85 (Other nonanalytic theory), 12J25. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a prime p and x ∈ 𝔽ₚ, choose any p-adic integer a with residue x, and let ω(x) be the limit of the pⁿth powers of a as n → ∞ (our own formulation). The limit exists and does not depend on a, because a pth power turns a congruence modulo pᵏ, k ≥ 1, into one modulo pᵏ⁺¹.

**Problem.** For residues x and y modulo p, ω(xy) = ω(x)ω(y). Also, ω(x) has residue x and satisfies ω(x)ᵖ = ω(x).

**How the definition helps.** The pⁿth power of a product is the product of the pⁿth powers, so the limits multiply (our own argument). Every term has residue x, and taking pth powers shifts the sequence by one place, so ω(x)ᵖ = ω(x).

**Wikipedia:** [Teichmüller character](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teichm%C3%BCller_character). It says: “If x is an integer mod p, then ω(x) is the unique solution of ω(x)ᵖ = ω(x) that is congruent to x mod p.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Principal units have unique prime-to-p roots

**Remember:** Residue one makes every prime-to-p root simple, so Hensel applies.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11S85 (Other nonanalytic theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In a finite extension of ℚₚ, the principal units are the integers whose residue modulo the maximal ideal is one.

**Problem.** For each positive integer m prime to p, raising to the mth power is an automorphism of the principal units of a p-adic field.

**How the definition helps.** For a principal unit u, the equation xᵐ = u has the root 1 modulo the maximal ideal, and its derivative m is nonzero there. Hensel’s lemma gives exactly one root with residue one, so the mth power map is bijective. Without residue one this fails, since −1 has no square root modulo 3 (our own example).

**Paper or page:** [Duality for condensed cohomology of the Weil group of a p-adic field](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.05565v1). It says: “For m coprime to p, the continuous homomorphism (−)ᵐ: 𝒰ₖⁿ → 𝒰ₖⁿ is an isomorphism of topological groups.”

**Sources:**

- [Duality for condensed cohomology of the Weil group of a p-adic field](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.05565v1)

### Artin–Schreier sheaves encode lifted characters

**Remember:** Functions that twist by ψ under translation pick up the trace.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix a nontrivial additive character ψ: 𝔽ₚ → ℂ× and x in a finite extension k of 𝔽ₚ. Take the complex functions h on the solutions y of yᵖ − y = x in an algebraic closure of k with h(y + a) = ψ(a)h(y) for a ∈ 𝔽ₚ (our own). The solutions form one orbit under translation by 𝔽ₚ, so these functions form a space of dimension one.

**Problem.** For x in any finite extension k, geometric Frobenius has trace ψ(Tr(x)) on this space. Here Tr is the field trace from k to 𝔽ₚ.

**How the definition helps.** Geometric Frobenius acts by precomposing with the \|k\|th power map (our own argument). Summing the successive pth powers of yᵖ − y = x shows that the \|k\|th power of y is y + Tr(x). So Frobenius is translation by Tr(x) and acts by ψ(Tr(x)).

**nLab:** [Artin-Schreier sequence](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Artin-Schreier+sequence). It says: “F − id ≔ (−)ᵖ − (−) : (𝔾ₐ)ₓ → (𝔾ₐ)ₓ”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Reduced phases expose the true degree

**Remember:** Remove pth-power differences before measuring a phase.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Over a finite field k of characteristic p, two polynomial phases are equivalent if they differ by gᵖ − g for a polynomial g. A phase is reduced if no term of positive degree has exponent divisible by p. Replacing a term a·xᵖᵐ by b·xᵐ with bᵖ = a gives an equivalent phase, so every phase reduces.

**Problem.** Let ψ be a nontrivial additive character of 𝔽ₚ and S(f) = ∑ₓ ψ(Tr(f(x))) over x ∈ k, with Tr the trace to 𝔽ₚ. Equivalent phases give equal sums, and if the reduced phase has degree d ≥ 1, then \|S(f)\| ≤ (d − 1)√\|k\|.

**How the definition helps.** Tr(gᵖ) = Tr(g) at every input, so equivalent phases have equal sums (our own calculation). A reduced phase of degree d ≥ 1 has degree prime to p, so the Weil bound applies. Without reduction the bound fails, since xᵖ − x has degree p but its sum is \|k\|.

**nLab:** [Artin-Schreier sequence](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Artin-Schreier+sequence). It says: “There is a short exact sequence of abelian sheaves over the étale site”

**Sources:**

- [Iwaniec and Kowalski, Analytic Number Theory, Chapter 11](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~kowalski/ik-ant-exp-sums.pdf)

### Smooth top forms give Deligne cancellation

**Remember:** Test the highest-degree part for smoothness on projective space.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Take a polynomial f of degree d ≥ 2 in m ≥ 2 variables over 𝔽𝓆, with the characteristic not dividing d. It is smooth at infinity if its degree-d part defines a smooth hypersurface in projective space, that is, the degree-d part and its first partial derivatives have no common nonzero zero over the algebraic closure.

**Problem.** Let ψ be a nontrivial additive character and let f be smooth at infinity. Then the sum of ψ(f(x)) over all x in 𝔽𝓆ᵐ has modulus at most (d − 1)ᵐ√(qᵐ).

**How the definition helps.** Smoothness at infinity is the hypothesis of Deligne’s theorem, which gives the bound. It excludes top forms with flat directions, such as f = x₁² in odd characteristic (our own example). There each other variable multiplies the Gauss sum by q, giving modulus qᵐ/√q.

**Wikipedia:** [Exponential sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_sum). It says: “The Weil conjectures had major applications to complete sums with domain restricted by polynomial conditions”

**Sources:**

- [Deligne, La conjecture de Weil I](https://www.numdam.org/item/PMIHES_1974__43__273_0/)
- [Iwaniec and Kowalski, Analytic Number Theory, Chapter 11](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~kowalski/ik-ant-exp-sums.pdf)

### Unique shifts force Burgess cancellation

**Remember:** A shift used once gives a zero or pole of order one.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 11L40. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix a nonprincipal multiplicative character χ modulo a prime p, with χ(0) = 0. A list of 2r shifts modulo p, with r ≥ 1, is exceptional if every shift in it occurs at least twice.

**Problem.** For each x modulo p, multiply χ(x + b) over the first r shifts b and its complex conjugate over the last r. For a nonexceptional list, the sum of these products over x has modulus at most 2r√p.

**How the definition helps.** A shift that occurs once gives a simple zero or pole of the quotient of the two products of linear factors, so the quotient is not a dth power for d the order of χ (our own explanation). The character sum bound in Corollary 11.24 of Iwaniec and Kowalski then applies. If the second half repeats the first, the list is exceptional and the sum equals p minus the number of distinct shifts.

**Paper or page:** [On the correlations between character sums of division polynomials under shifts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09271). It says: “Assume that Ψ is not a non-trivial power of a function in”

**Sources:**

- [Iwaniec and Kowalski, Analytic Number Theory, Chapter 11](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~kowalski/ik-ant-exp-sums.pdf)

### Negative Gauss sums lift multiplicatively

**Remember:** Negating each Gauss sum absorbs the sign in the lifting formula.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11T24 (Other character sums and Gauss sums). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a multiplicative character χ and a nontrivial additive character ψ of a finite field, the signed Gauss sum is −∑ χ(x)ψ(x) over nonzero x. Over an extension field, the lifted characters are χ of the norm and ψ of the trace.

**Problem.** For nontrivial characters over a finite field, the signed sum over an extension of degree n equals the nth power of the signed base sum.

**How the definition helps.** The Davenport–Hasse theorem says that the ordinary lifted sum equals (−1)ⁿ⁻¹ times the nth power of the base sum. Multiplying by −1 gives the nth power of the negated base sum (our own normalization).

**Paper or page:** [Davenport and Hasse's theorems and lifts of multiplication matrices of Gaussian periods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.14872). It says: “Then, for any integer n ≥ 1, we have Gₙᵣ(ψ′) = (−1)ⁿ⁻¹Gᵣ(ψ)ⁿ”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Nonpowers give Kummer cancellation

**Remember:** A dth power keeps the character constant; anything else cancels.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11T24 (Other character sums and Gauss sums), 11T23, 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let k be a finite field and d &gt; 1. A nonzero f ∈ k(x) is a geometric dth power if f = gᵈ for a rational function g over the algebraic closure, which holds exactly when d divides the order of every zero and pole of f.

**Problem.** Let χ have order d on the multiplicative group of k, where \|k\| = q. Unless f is a geometric dth power, summing χ(f(x)) over finite k-points outside its zeros and poles gives modulus at most (s − 2)√q. Here s counts infinity and all distinct finite zeros and poles over the algebraic closure.

**How the definition helps.** If f is a geometric dth power, χ(f(x)) is constant away from the zeros and poles, so there is no cancellation, as for f(x) = xᵈ (our own explanation). Otherwise the Weil bound for multiplicative character sums gives the estimate.

**nLab:** [Kummer sequence](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Kummer+sequence). It says: “the group of nth roots of unity.”

**Sources:**

- [Iwaniec and Kowalski, Analytic Number Theory, Chapter 11](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~kowalski/ik-ant-exp-sums.pdf)

### Diophantine sets with parameters let Hilbert's tenth problem meet computability

**Remember:** A tuple belongs exactly when its equation has a witness.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11U05 (Decidability (number-theoretic aspects)), 03D25. arXiv math.NT, math.LO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A set S of tuples of natural numbers is Diophantine if there is an integer polynomial p(a, x) such that a is in S exactly when p(a, x) = 0 has a solution x in natural numbers.

**Problem.** Every computably enumerable set is Diophantine (the MRDP theorem). Hence no algorithm decides whether an integer polynomial has an integer root tuple.

**How the definition helps.** MRDP makes a computably enumerable set that no algorithm decides into a Diophantine set, so deciding solvability would decide membership. Lagrange’s four-square theorem replaces each natural-number unknown by four integer unknowns, so the same holds over the integers (our own explanation).

**Wikipedia:** [Hilbert's tenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_tenth_problem). It says: “In a Diophantine equation, there are two kinds of variables: the parameters and the unknowns.
