The Diophantine set consists of the parameter assignments for which the Diophantine equation is solvable.”

**Sources:**

- [Davis, M. (1973). Hilbert's tenth problem is unsolvable. American Mathematical Monthly 80, 233–269.](https://doi.org/10.1080/00029890.1973.11993265)

### Continued fractions with minus signs make the half-line a terminal coalgebra

**Remember:** Always round strictly up, so every number has only one expansion.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11A55 (Continued fractions), 18C40. arXiv math.NT, math.CT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For x ≥ 1, let β(x) be the least integer strictly greater than x, so β(x) ≥ 2. Define ξ(x) = (β(x), 1/(β(x) − x)), which is an order-preserving bijection from ℝ≥1 onto ℕ≥2 × ℝ≥1 with inverse (a, t) ↦ a − 1/t (our own).

**Problem.** With the lexicographic order, (ℝ≥1, ξ) is the terminal coalgebra of the functor X ↦ ℕ≥2 × X on linear orders. So a real number x ≥ 1 is the same thing as its infinite stream of digits.

**How the definition helps.** Each digit a ≥ 2 gives an increasing inverse branch t ↦ a − 1/t (our own proof). The values with a fixed n-digit prefix form a half-open interval of length at most 1/n, and an infinite tail never reaches the open end, so each stream has exactly one value. Iterating ξ on any coalgebra gives its unique map to streams.

**nLab:** [continued fraction](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/continued+fraction). It says: “It may be tempting to believe that this F-coalgebra structure makes 𝐑 the terminal coalgebra. That is unfortunately not correct because the coalgebra structure ξ: 𝐑 → F(𝐑) is not an isomorphism”

**Sources:**

- [Dusko Pavlović, Vaughan Pratt, On coalgebra of real numbers, Electron. Notes Theor. Comput. Sci. 19 (1999) 103–117](https://doi.org/10.1016/S1571-0661(05)80272-5)

### Hindman's shift theorem holds for upper Banach density but not upper density

**Remember:** Move the measuring window to see density that an initial interval misses.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11B05 (Density, gaps, topology), 37A44. arXiv math.DS, math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The upper Banach density of E ⊆ ℕ is the limit superior, as n → ∞, of the largest value of \|E ∩ I\|/n over windows I of n consecutive positive integers.

**Problem.** Let E be a set of positive integers with positive upper Banach density, and let ε &gt; 0. For some k, the union E ∪ (E − 1) ∪ ⋯ ∪ (E − k) has upper Banach density greater than 1 − ε.

**How the definition helps.** Windows can move to where E is dense, which a window starting at 1 cannot (our own explanation). The union E of intervals \[Nⱼ, 2Nⱼ\] with Nⱼ₊₁/Nⱼ → ∞ has upper Banach density one, but every finite union of its backward shifts has upper density one half. Hindman’s theorem gives the shift result for upper Banach density.

**Paper or page:** [An ergodic correspondence principle, invariant means and applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.03029v2). It says: “Curiously, this result does not hold if one replaces the upper Banach density d∗ with the upper density d̄.”

**Sources:**

- [Vitaly Bergelson, Andreu Ferré Moragues, An ergodic correspondence principle, invariant means and applications, arXiv:2003.03029 (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.03029v2)

### Intersective polynomials remove modular obstructions

**Remember:** A root modulo every q defeats every multiples-of-q obstruction.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11B05 (Density, gaps, topology), 11B30. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An integer polynomial h is intersective if it has a root modulo every positive integer q, so some value h(n) is a multiple of q.

**Problem.** Suppose a set occupies a fixed positive fraction of {1, …, N} for arbitrarily large N. For every nonconstant intersective polynomial h, two distinct members have difference h(n) for some positive integer n.

**How the definition helps.** Without a root modulo q, the multiples of q form a set of positive density with no difference h(n), since their differences are multiples of q (our own argument). For example, no two even integers differ by 2n + 1. The cited density bound shows that excluding these obstructions suffices.

**Paper or page:** [A maximal extension of the Bloom-Maynard bound for sets with no square differences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.03345v1). It says: “for any intersective polynomial h ∈ ℤ\[x\] of degree k”

**Sources:**

- [A maximal extension of the Bloom–Maynard bound for sets with no square differences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.03345v1)

### Additive energy finds structured subsets

**Remember:** Count equal sums by squaring the number of representations of each sum.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The additive energy E(A) is the number of quadruples (a, b, c, d) in A⁴ with a + b = c + d, that is, the sum over s of the square of the number of ways to write s = a + b.

**Problem.** Let A be a finite nonempty subset of an abelian group with E(A) ≥ \|A\|³/K for K ≥ 1. Some subset B has \|B\| ≥ c\|A\|/K and \|B−B\| ≤ CK⁴\|B\| for absolute constants c,C &gt; 0.

**How the definition helps.** Energy counts repeated sums, so it stays large when a structured part of A has many coincidences, even if scattered points add many new sums (our own explanation). The Balog–Szemerédi–Gowers theorem turns large energy into a large subset B with few distinct differences.

**Paper or page:** [Note on the Theorem of Balog, Szemerédi, and Gowers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.10245). It says: “Given a real K ≥ 1 every additive set A with energy E(A) ≥ \|A\|³/K has a subset A′ ⊆ A”

**Sources:**

- [Christian Reiher and Tomasz Schoen, Note on the Theorem of Balog, Szemerédi, and Gowers, arXiv:2308.10245v2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.10245)

### Circle values extend cubic phases

**Remember:** Values on the whole circle allow eighth-root phases of degree three.

*True by definition.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let ΔₕP(x) = P(x + h) − P(x) for P from a vector space over 𝔽₂ to ℝ/ℤ. P has degree at most d if every d + 1 such differences, in any directions, vanish at every point. Values in ℝ/ℤ, not only 0 and 1/2, allow phases that are not signs.

**Problem.** On the two-element group, set P(0)=0 and P(1)=1/8 modulo one. Then P has degree at most three, and exp(2πiP) is not a constant times a sign-valued phase.

**How the definition helps.** On 𝔽₂, a difference in direction 0 is zero, and with direction 1 the successive differences at 0 are 1/8, −1/4, 1/2 and 0 (our own calculation). So every fourth difference vanishes. The ratio of the phases at 1 and 0 is exp(πi/4), which is not ±1, so the phase is not a constant times a sign.

**Paper or page:** [Non-classical polynomials and the inverse theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.07495v1). It says: “Then P : V → ℝ/ℤ is a non-classical polynomial of degree at most d if and only if it can be expressed in the form”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Cut tests give sparse weights bounded models

**Remember:** Products of cut tests are cut tests, because indicators intersect.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For fixed r ≥ 2, a cut test on ℤ/Nℤ averages f(x₁ + ⋯ + xᵣ) times r indicators over independent uniform x₁, …, xᵣ, where the ith indicator is of a set that does not depend on xᵢ. The arithmetic cut norm of f is the supremum of the absolute values of these averages. The product of two cut test functions is another one, since multiplying indicators intersects sets (our own explanation).

**Problem.** For every ε &gt; 0 there is an η &gt; 0, independent of N, with this property. Suppose ν ≥ 0, the cut norm of ν − 1 is at most η, and 0 ≤ f ≤ ν. Then some function g with values in \[0,1\] makes the cut norm of f − g at most ε.

**How the definition helps.** The dense model theorem reduces finding g to bounding f − g against products of test functions, using convex separation and polynomial approximation. Such products are again cut test functions, so the small cut norm of ν − 1 controls them (our own explanation).

**Wikipedia:** [Szemerédi's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szemer%C3%A9di%27s_theorem). It says: “A more general relative Szemerédi theorem has since been given by David Conlon, Jacob Fox, and Yufei Zhao.”

**Sources:**

- [Conlon, Fox and Zhao, The Green–Tao theorem: an exposition, EMS Surveys in Mathematical Sciences 1 (2014), 249–282](https://doi.org/10.4171/emss/6)

### Entropic doubling contracts under homomorphisms

**Remember:** Measure doubling with entropy, and homomorphisms can only shrink it.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity), 11B13, 94A17. arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For independent finitely supported X,Y in an abelian group, define their entropic distance as H(X−Y) − (H(X)+H(Y))/2. Here H is Shannon entropy with natural logarithms. Entropic doubling is exp(H(X+X′)−H(X)) for an independent copy X′ (our own formulation).

**Problem.** Entropic doubling cannot increase under a group homomorphism π. For independent X,Y, their entropic distance is at least the distance between πX,πY plus the mean distance between their conditional laws on the corresponding fibres.

**How the definition helps.** Proposition 1.4 bounds the distance below by the distance of the images plus a mean of distances between the conditional laws on fibres. Each fibre distance is nonnegative, since conditioning shows that the entropy of a difference is at least each single entropy. Applying this to X and −X′ gives the contraction of doubling (our own argument).

**Paper or page:** [Sumsets and entropy revisited](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.13403), [Sumsets and entropy revisited](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.13403). It says: “it enjoys somewhat better properties; for instance, it contracts upon applying a homomorphism.”

**Sources:**

- [Ben Green, Freddie Manners, Terence Tao, Sumsets and entropy revisited, Random Struct. Alg. (2024) 1-33, arXiv:2306.13403](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.13403)

### Finite complexity separates binary prime problems

**Remember:** Complexity is finite unless two forms are parallel.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For nonconstant affine forms with integer coefficients and linear parts v₁, …, vₜ, the complexity is the least s ≥ 0 such that, for each i, the other vectors split into at most s + 1 classes whose rational spans all exclude vᵢ. It is infinite if no s works, which happens exactly when two linear parts are proportional (our own).

**Problem.** Let K ⊆ \[−N,N\]ᵈ be convex with all t fixed forms positive on K, and let Λ be the von Mangoldt function. For finite complexity, the sum of ∏ᵢ Λ(ψᵢ(n)) over lattice points n in K equals vol(K)∏ₚβₚ + o(Nᵈ), where βₚ is the fraction of residues modulo p at which no form vanishes, divided by (1−1/p)ᵗ.

**How the definition helps.** Green and Tao’s counting theorem, with the later results that prove its hypotheses, gives the asymptotic for every system of finite complexity. The forms n and n + 2 have proportional linear parts, so the theorem says nothing about twin primes (our own explanation).

**Paper or page:** [Improved quadratic Gowers uniformity for the Möbius function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.09635). It says: “Let Ψ be affine forms such that no two ψᵢ differ by a constant.”

**Sources:**

- [Green and Tao, Linear equations in primes, Annals of Mathematics 171 (2010), 1753–1850](https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2010.171.1753)
- [Green, Tao and Ziegler, An inverse theorem for the Gowers Uˢ⁺¹\[N\] norm, Annals of Mathematics 176 (2012), 1231–1372](https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2012.176.2.11)
- [Green and Tao, The Möbius function is strongly orthogonal to nilsequences, Annals of Mathematics 175 (2012), 541–566](https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2012.175.2.3)

### Linear forms tests transfer Szemerédi's theorem

**Remember:** Test the doubled patterns that appear in the counting proof.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix k ≥ 3 and a prime N, and pick two independent uniform residues for each coordinate i from 1 to k. For each j, form every sum ∑ᵢ≠ⱼ (j − i)zᵢ, with zᵢ either residue at coordinate i. A weight ν ≥ 0 satisfies the k-linear forms condition if the mean of the product of ν over any subset of these sums tends to one as N grows.

**Problem.** Suppose ν satisfies this condition, 0 ≤ f ≤ ν, and the mean of f is at least δ &gt; 0. The mean of f(x)⋯f(x+(k−1)d) over uniform x,d is at least c(k,δ)−o(1), with c(k,δ)&gt;0.

**How the definition helps.** These are the products that Cauchy–Schwarz creates when it duplicates inputs in the progression count, so ν behaves there like the constant one (our own explanation). Conlon, Fox and Zhao use this to compare f with a bounded function of similar mean. The dense form of Szemerédi’s theorem then gives the lower bound.

**Wikipedia:** [Szemerédi's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szemer%C3%A9di%27s_theorem). It says: “It is not implied by Szemerédi's theorem because the primes have density 0 in the natural numbers.”

**Sources:**

- [Conlon, Fox and Zhao, A relative Szemerédi theorem, Geometric and Functional Analysis 25 (2015), 733–762](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00039-015-0324-9)
- [Conlon, Fox and Zhao, The Green–Tao theorem: an exposition, EMS Surveys in Mathematical Sciences 1 (2014), 249–282](https://doi.org/10.4171/emss/6)

### Local factors count prime progressions

**Remember:** Separate real volume from each prime’s divisibility correction.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity), 11N13. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For fixed k ≥ 3 and a prime p, βₚ is the fraction of pairs (x, d) modulo p for which none of x, x + d, …, x + (k−1)d is divisible by p, divided by (1−1/p)ᵏ. The singular series is the product of βₚ over all primes.

**Problem.** For fixed k≥3, the count of strictly increasing k-term prime progressions at most N is asymptotic to N²∏ₚβₚ divided by 2(k−1)(log N)ᵏ.

**How the definition helps.** The Green–Tao counting theorem gives the asymptotic, with N²/(2(k−1)) the number of progressions and the singular series the local correction. For p ≤ k only d = 0 works, giving p − 1 pairs (our own calculation). For p &gt; k each nonzero d forbids k starts, giving (p − 1)(p − k + 1) pairs in total (our own calculation).

**Wikipedia:** [Green–Tao theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green%E2%80%93Tao_theorem). It says: “for the number of k tuples of primes p₁ &lt; p₂ &lt; ⋯ &lt; pₖ ≤ N in arithmetic progression.”

**Sources:**

- [Green and Tao, Linear equations in primes, Annals of Mathematics 171 (2010), 1753–1850](https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2010.171.1753)
- [Green, Tao and Ziegler, An inverse theorem for the Gowers Uˢ⁺¹\[N\] norm, Annals of Mathematics 176 (2012), 1231–1372](https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2012.176.2.11)
- [Green and Tao, The Möbius function is strongly orthogonal to nilsequences, Annals of Mathematics 175 (2012), 541–566](https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2012.175.2.3)

### Minimum quadratic rank gives uniform fibers

**Remember:** Check every combination, because two high-rank quadratics can cancel.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let Q be d quadratic polynomials on a finite vector space H over 𝔽ₚ, with p an odd prime. The rank of Q is the least matrix rank of the bilinear form q(x+y) − q(x) − q(y), where q is any combination of the quadratic parts with coefficients not all zero.

**Problem.** If Q has rank at least R, each equation Q(x)=b has \|H\|p⁻ᵈ solutions up to an error of at most \|H\|/√(pᴿ).

**How the definition helps.** The Fourier expansion of the solution count has the main term \|H\|p⁻ᵈ and one term per nonzero combination (our own explanation). Each such term is at most p⁻ᵈ\|H\|/√(pᴿ), because that combination has rank at least R, so together they are at most \|H\|/√(pᴿ). Checking single polynomials is not enough, since the pair (q, q) never takes a value with unequal coordinates, however large the rank of q.

**Paper or page:** [An inverse theorem for the Gowers U³-norm relative to quadratic level sets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.07962). It says: “be a d-tuple of quadratic polynomials on H of rank at least R.”

**Sources:**

- [Sean Prendiville, An inverse theorem for the Gowers U³-norm relative to quadratic level sets, arXiv:2409.07962v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.07962)

### Normal form exposes the counting bound

**Remember:** Each rival form misses a coordinate that the chosen form uses.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A system of nonzero linear forms over 𝔽ₚ is in s-normal form if each form has a set of at most s + 1 coordinates that it uses, such that every other form omits at least one of them.

**Problem.** Let Λ(f₁,…,fₜ) be the average, over independent uniform inputs from a finite 𝔽ₚ-vector space, of the product of the fᵢ evaluated at their forms. For \[0,1\]-valued fᵢ and gᵢ, replacing all fᵢ by gᵢ changes Λ by at most the sum of the order-(s+1) Gowers norms of fᵢ − gᵢ.

**How the definition helps.** Cauchy–Schwarz in each selected coordinate removes every other form, since each other form omits a selected coordinate (our own explanation). What remains is the order-(s+1) Gowers norm of the replaced function. Replacing one function at a time and adding the bounds gives the result.

**Paper or page:** [Quasirandomness in additive groups and hypergraphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.01463). It says: “Let Φ : Gᵏ → Gᵐ be a system of linear forms in s-normal form, and suppose that Φ is coprime.”

**Sources:**

- [Davi Castro-Silva, Quasirandomness in additive groups and hypergraphs, arXiv:2107.01463v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.01463)

### Power dependence defeats lower-order counting

**Remember:** A relation among powers makes the phases cancel in the product.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix linear forms ψ₁,…,ψₜ over 𝔽ₚ with p &gt; d ≥ 2. Their dth powers are dependent if ∑ᵢ aᵢψᵢᵈ vanishes as a polynomial for some nonzero coefficient vector over 𝔽ₚ.

**Problem.** Apply each form coordinatewise to vectors in 𝔽ₚⁿ. If the dth powers are dependent, some unit-modulus functions fᵢ have product one along the forms at every input, while some fᵢ has order-d Gowers norm tending to zero as n grows.

**How the definition helps.** Take fᵢ(x) = exp(2πi aᵢ∑ⱼ xⱼᵈ/p), so the dependence makes the product along the forms equal to one (our own example). For aᵢ ≠ 0, the d-fold difference in each coordinate is a nonconstant phase, so its mean has modulus below one. The Gowers norm calculation multiplies this mean over the n coordinates, so it tends to zero.

**Paper or page:** [On a conjecture of Gowers and Wolf](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.15437). It says: “the polynomials ψ₁ˢ⁺¹, …, ψₜˢ⁺¹ are linearly independent.”

**Sources:**

- [Daniel Altman, On a conjecture of Gowers and Wolf, arXiv:2106.15437v2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.15437)

### Relative density reaches sparse prime subsets

**Remember:** Compare a set of primes with the primes themselves.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The upper relative density of a set A of primes is the limit superior, as N → ∞, of \|A ∩ \[1,N\]\|/π(N), where π(N) counts the primes at most N.

**Problem.** Every set of primes with positive upper relative density contains infinitely many nonconstant arithmetic progressions of each fixed length k ≥ 2.

**How the definition helps.** Relative density measures A against the primes, so A can have positive relative density while its density among integers is zero (our own explanation). Green and Tao extend Szemerédi’s theorem to sets dense relative to a suitable weight, and a sieve supplies such a weight for the primes.

**Wikipedia:** [Green–Tao theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green%E2%80%93Tao_theorem). It says: “the set A contains infinitely many arithmetic progressions of length k.”

**Sources:**

- [Green and Tao, The primes contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions, Annals of Mathematics 167 (2008), 481–547](https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2008.167.481)

### Rough weights make prime uniformity measurable

**Remember:** Compare primes with integers that avoid the same small prime divisors.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let P be the product of the primes below w, and φ(P) the number of residues modulo P coprime to P. The Cramér model M is P/φ(P) on integers coprime to P and zero elsewhere, so it has mean one and the same small-prime biases as the primes.

**Problem.** Let Λ be the von Mangoldt function, w = exp((log N)¹ᐟ¹⁰), and k ≥ 2 fixed. On \[1,N\], the order-k Gowers norm of Λ − M is O((log log N)⁻ᶜ) for some c = c(k) &gt; 0.

**How the definition helps.** The constant function fails, since the mean of (Λ(n) − 1)exp(2πin/3) tends to −1/2 by the prime number theorem in residue classes, and M removes such biases (our own explanation). Tao and Teräväinen’s quantitative uniformity theorem bounds what remains.

**Paper or page:** [Improved quadratic Gowers uniformity for the Möbius function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.09635). It says: “\\\|\\Lambda - \\Lambda <sub>Q</sub>\\\| <sub>U<sup>s</sup>(\[N\])</sub> \\ll (\\log \\log (N))<sup>-c</sup>”

**Sources:**

- [Tao and Teräväinen, Quantitative bounds for Gowers uniformity of the Möbius and von Mangoldt functions, JEMS 27 (2025), 1321–1384](https://doi.org/10.4171/jems/1404)

### Squared sieve weights dominate primes

**Remember:** Beyond the divisor cutoff, a prime contributes only its divisor one.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity), 11N13. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix a smooth χ supported on \[−1,1\] with 0 ≤ χ ≤ 1 and χ(0) = 1, and let S(m) be the sum of μ(d)χ(log d/log R) over divisors d of m, with μ the Möbius function. Let W be the product of the primes up to w and c the integral of \|χ′\|² over \[0,1\]. Set ν(n) = φ(W)log(R)S(Wn+1)²/(Wc) for N/2 ≤ n &lt; N, and ν(n) = 1 elsewhere.

**Problem.** Fix k ≥ 3, let N run through large primes, let w grow slowly enough, and set a = 1/(8k·2ᵏ) and R = Nᵃ. Then ν satisfies the k-linear forms condition, and ν(n) ≥ (a/2c)(φ(W)/W)log(Wn+1) whenever Wn + 1 is prime and N/2 ≤ n &lt; N.

**How the definition helps.** At a prime Wn + 1 &gt; R, only the divisor one has log d &lt; log R, so S = 1 and ν(n) = φ(W)log(R)/(Wc) (our own explanation). Since log(Wn+1) ≤ 2 log N for large N, this gives the lower bound. Proposition 8.3 of the cited exposition proves the linear forms condition by estimating products of these divisor sums.

**Wikipedia:** [Green–Tao theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green%E2%80%93Tao_theorem). It says: “To construct this set, Green and Tao used ideas from Goldston, Pintz, and Yıldırım's work on prime gaps.”

**Sources:**

- [Conlon, Fox and Zhao, The Green–Tao theorem: an exposition, EMS Surveys in Mathematical Sciences 1 (2014), 249–282](https://doi.org/10.4171/emss/6)
- [Green and Tao, The primes contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions, Annals of Mathematics 167 (2008), 481–547](https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2008.167.481)

### Unique square completion turns a 1-step nilspace into an abelian group

**Remember:** Fix an origin, then the fourth corner of a square is the sum.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.CO, math.DS. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A nilspace is a nonempty set X with cubes, maps from {0,1}ⁿ to X, that include all maps from {0,1} and are stable under affine maps between discrete cubes. Every corner, a map on a cube minus one vertex whose faces are cubes, extends to a cube. X is 1-step if every corner of a square extends in exactly one way.

**Problem.** Every 1-step nilspace X admits a free transitive action of an abelian group A. Its cubes are exactly the maps ω ↦ x+∑ᵢωᵢhᵢ for x ∈ X and increments hᵢ ∈ A.

**How the definition helps.** Fix an origin o and define x + y as the vertex that completes the square with corners o, x and y (our own explanation). The structure theorem for 1-step nilspaces proves the group laws and identifies the cubes with affine cubes of this group.

**Paper or page:** [Notes on nilspaces: algebraic aspects](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.03693v3). It says: “Then there is an abelian group A such that 𝒩 is a principal homogeneous space of A and the cubes on 𝒩 are the projections of the degree-1 cubes on A.”

**Sources:**

- [Pablo Candela, Notes on nilspaces: algebraic aspects, arXiv:1601.03693 (2017). Discrete Analysis, 2017:15, 59pp](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.03693v3)

### Weighted deletion extends arithmetic removal

**Remember:** Delete little weight, even when the support has tiny density.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Deleting a set B from a nonnegative function f on ℤ/Nℤ costs the sum of f(x) over x in B, divided by N, so cost is weight, not size. The weighted progression count averages ∏ⱼ fⱼ(x + (j−1)d) over independent uniform x and d.

**Problem.** Fix k ≥ 3 and ε &gt; 0, let N be a large prime, and let 0 ≤ fᵢ ≤ ν, where ν satisfies the k-linear forms condition. If the weighted progression count is below some c(k,ε) &gt; 0, a deletion of cost at most ε from each fᵢ leaves no progression whose jth term lies in the remaining support of fⱼ for every j.

**How the definition helps.** Cost counts the mass that enters the progression count, so a support of tiny density can still carry most of it (our own explanation). Conlon, Fox and Zhao’s relative arithmetic removal lemma gives the deletions, by applying a weighted removal theorem to coordinate sets that represent progressions.

**Paper or page:** [The Green-Tao theorem for affine curves over 𝔽(q)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.00839). It says: “Then there is a family of subsets”

**Sources:**

- [Conlon, Fox and Zhao, A relative Szemerédi theorem, Geometric and Functional Analysis 25 (2015), 733–762](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00039-015-0324-9)

### Sidon sets give error-correcting codes

**Remember:** Four elements summing to zero make a weight-four codeword.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B75 (Other combinatorial number theory), 94B05. arXiv math.CO, math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In a binary vector space, a set is Sidon if distinct pairs of distinct elements have distinct sums, that is, no four distinct elements sum to zero (our own).

**Problem.** Let n &gt; t ≥ 2. A Sidon set of size n + 1 exists in the t-dimensional binary vector space exactly when a certain binary linear code exists. The code has length n, dimension n − t, and no nonzero word with fewer than five nonzero coordinates.

**How the definition helps.** Translated to contain 0, the set gives n nonzero columns of a t-row matrix whose kernel has dimension at least n − t (our own proof). Distinct nonzero columns exclude kernel words of weight one and two, and the Sidon property, using 0 when needed, excludes weights three and four. So the kernel contains such a code, and conversely the columns of any such code’s parity-check matrix, with 0, form a Sidon set.

**Paper or page:** [Sidon sets, sum-free sets and linear codes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.07906v3). It says: “There is no Sidon set M ⊆ 𝔽₂ᵗ of size n + 1.”

**Sources:**

- [Sidon sets, sum-free sets and linear codes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.07906v3)

### Oriented quadratic algebras let twisted binary forms describe Picard groups

**Remember:** Orient the algebra first, then the form classes give its ideal classes.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11E16 (General binary quadratic forms), 11R65, 14F06. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let A be a quadratic algebra, locally free of rank two over a scheme S, and let N be a line bundle. An N-orientation of A is an isomorphism from A modulo the scalar submodule to the dual line bundle of N.

**Problem.** Fix a scheme on which 2 is not a zero divisor and a line bundle N. Fix discriminant and parity arising from an N-oriented quadratic algebra. The classes of primitive N-twisted binary quadratic forms with these invariants correspond to the Picard group of that oriented algebra.

**How the definition helps.** The orientation keeps track of the algebra when the quotient by scalars has no global basis. The paper shows that the discriminant and the parity classify the oriented algebras. The paper says that Wood's earlier bijection needs this refinement to give Picard groups.

**Paper or page:** [Recovering the Picard group of quadratic algebras from Wood's binary quadratic forms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.13422v5). It says: “Extending the notion of orientation of quadratic algebras to the non-free case is another key step, eventually leading us to the desired parametrization.”

**Sources:**

- [William Dallaporta, Recovering the Picard group of quadratic algebras from Wood's binary quadratic forms, arXiv:2111.13422v5 (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.13422v5)

### Primitive values distinguish binary forms

**Remember:** Use coprime inputs to tell primitive forms apart.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11E16 (General binary quadratic forms). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An integral binary quadratic form ax² + bxy + cy² is primitive if gcd(a, b, c) = 1. Its primitive values are its values at integer pairs with coprime coordinates.

**Problem.** Primitive integral binary quadratic forms with nonsquare discriminants are equivalent if they have the same primitive values. Equivalence means an invertible integer change of variables.

**How the definition helps.** Values at all pairs do not determine a form, since x² + xy + y² and x² + 3y² have the same values but different discriminants (our own). Primitive values separate them, because only the second takes the value 4 at a coprime pair, namely (1,1) (our own). Fouvry and Koymans prove that equal primitive value sets always force equivalence.

**Paper or page:** [Binary quadratic forms with the same value set](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.09575v2), [Binary quadratic forms with the same value set](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.09575v2). It says: “Let F and G be two primitive quadratic forms, with non square discriminants and with F(ℤ²ₚᵣᵢₘ) = G(ℤ²ₚᵣᵢₘ).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Forms with integer matrix need only 1 to 15 to be universal

**Remember:** Integer matrix means even cross terms.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11E25 (Sums of squares and representations by other particular quadratic forms), 11E12. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An integral quadratic form has integer matrix if, in integral coordinates, its symmetric coefficient matrix has integer entries. Equivalently, every mixed term has even coefficient.

**Problem.** If a positive definite quadratic form with integer matrix represents every integer from 1 through 15, it represents every positive integer.

**How the definition helps.** The matrix condition specifies exactly the class addressed by the Conway–Schneeberger 15 theorem (our own explanation). That theorem supplies the finite test for universality.

**Wikipedia:** [15 and 290 theorems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/15_and_290_theorems). It says: “The 15 theorem says that a quadratic form with integer matrix is universal if it takes the numbers from 1 to 15 as values.”

**Sources:**

### Weighting forms with extra symmetry gives Hurwitz class numbers modular behaviour

**Remember:** Count the square and hexagonal forms fractionally, and generating functions become modular.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11E41 (Class numbers of quadratic and Hermitian forms), 11F37. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For N &gt; 0, H(N) sums over SL₂(ℤ)-classes of positive definite integral binary quadratic forms of discriminant −N, imprimitive ones included, with each class weighted by 2 divided by the order of its stabilizer. Set H(0) = −1/12.

**Problem.** With these weights, the generating function Σ H(N) qᴺ is a mock modular form of weight 3/2. That is, Zagier showed that adding a simple correction term makes it transform like a modular form of weight 3/2.

**How the definition helps.** With these weights, Zagier’s theorem supplies the nonholomorphic correction and the weight-3/2 transformation law. Most classes have stabilizer ±1 and weight one, while the classes of x² + y² and x² + xy + y² have weights 1/2 and 1/3 (our own explanation).

**Wikipedia:** [Hurwitz class number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurwitz_class_number). It says: “forms are weighted by 2/g for g the order of their automorphism group, and where H(0) = –1/12.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Weighting lattices by one over their symmetries gives the mass formula

**Remember:** Count each lattice as one over its symmetries, and the total is computable.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11E41 (Class numbers of quadratic and Hermitian forms), 11E08. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Two positive definite integral quadratic forms are in the same genus when they are equivalent over the p-adic integers for every prime p (our own). The mass of a genus is the sum of 1/\|Aut(Λ)\| over its classes Λ, where Aut(Λ) is the finite symmetry group of the lattice.

**Problem.** For dimension n ≥ 2, the mass of a genus equals an explicit product of local factors, one for each prime.

**How the definition helps.** Weighting each class by one over its symmetries makes the mass a volume (our own explanation). The Smith–Minkowski–Siegel mass formula factors this volume into local factors, with a real factor that depends on the dimension and determinant.

**Wikipedia:** [Smith–Minkowski–Siegel mass formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smith%E2%80%93Minkowski%E2%80%93Siegel_mass_formula). It says: “a formula for the sum of the weights of the lattices (quadratic forms) in a genus, weighted by the reciprocals of the orders of their automorphism groups.”

**Sources:**

- [H. J. S. Smith, On the orders and genera of quadratic forms containing more than three indeterminates. Second notice, Proc. Roy. Soc. London 16 (1867) 197–208](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspl.1867.0036)

### Relative completion retains modular monodromy

**Remember:** Keep the reductive quotient before completing.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F06 (Structure of modular groups and generalizations; arithmetic groups), 20G30. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix a Zariski-dense homomorphism from a group Γ to a reductive algebraic group R over ℚ. The relative completion is the inverse limit of all extensions of R by unipotent groups that receive a Zariski-dense lift of Γ. With R trivial it is the ordinary rational unipotent completion (our own formulation).

**Problem.** The ordinary rational unipotent completion of the modular group SL₂(ℤ) is trivial. Its completion relative to the standard inclusion surjects onto the algebraic group SL₂ over ℚ.

**How the definition helps.** The relative completion surjects onto SL₂ by construction, since SL₂(ℤ) is Zariski dense in SL₂ (our own argument). A nontrivial unipotent image would give a nonzero homomorphism from SL₂(ℤ) to the additive group ℚ. None exists, because the abelianization of SL₂(ℤ) is finite.

**nLab:** [Malcev completion](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Malcev+completion). It says: “Mal'cev completion is a left adjoint functor to the embedding of the category of uniquely divisible nilpotent groups into the category of nilpotent groups.”

### Big theta quotients detect pairs

**Remember:** Take the largest quotient with the desired first action.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F27 (Theta series; Weil representation; theta correspondences), 11F70. arXiv math.NT, math.RT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For an orthogonal–symplectic dual pair over a p-adic field of odd residue characteristic, with the coverings the Weil representation needs, let π be an irreducible smooth representation of the first group. The largest quotient of the Weil representation that is a sum of copies of π has the form π ⊗ Θ(π), and Θ(π), a representation of the second group, is the big theta lift.

**Problem.** Take an irreducible smooth complex representation σ of the second group. The Weil representation surjects onto π tensored with σ exactly when Θ(π) surjects onto σ. Such a σ is unique up to isomorphism and is called the small theta lift.

**How the definition helps.** Every map from the Weil representation onto π ⊗ σ factors through this largest quotient π ⊗ Θ(π), so it is the same as a map from Θ(π) onto σ (our own). Howe duality proves that a nonzero Θ(π) has a unique irreducible quotient, which gives the uniqueness of σ.

**Paper or page:** [Equal rank local theta correspondence as a strong Morita equivalence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.13484v3). It says: “Θ(π) is either zero or has a unique irreducible quotient, so that θ(π) is irreducible.”

**Sources:**

- [Wee Teck Gan and Shuichiro Takeda, A proof of the Howe duality conjecture](https://doi.org/10.1090/jams/839)

### A three-block product excludes exceptional zeros

**Remember:** Four copies of a real zero overwhelm three poles.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands L-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a unitary cuspidal π that is not self-dual, with central character trivial on positive real scalars, let D(s) be the product of the nine Rankin–Selberg functions L(s,a×b̃) with a and b in the list (1,π,π̃). D contains L(s,π) and L(s,π̃) twice each, so a real zero of L(s,π) is a fourfold zero of D, while only the three dual pairs give poles at s = 1 (our own explanation).

**Problem.** For fixed rank and number field, some effective c &gt; 0 makes L(s,π) free of real zeros in \[1−c/log(3+C),1). Here C is the analytic conductor of π.

**How the definition helps.** Positivity of the coefficients of −D′/D and conductor bounds for the nine factors allow at most three real zeros of D near 1, counted with multiplicity. A real zero of L(s,π) would give four (our own explanation).

**Paper or page:** [Exceptional zeros of Rankin-Selberg L-functions and joint Sato-Tate distributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06482v2). It says: “is not self-dual, then L(s,π) has no exceptional zero.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Abelian quotient isolates zero-free factors

**Remember:** Divide out ζ, the one factor that carries the pole.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands L-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a full-level holomorphic cuspidal Hecke eigenform with normalized representation π and analytic conductor C, set R(s) = L(s,Symᵐπ × Symᵐπ)/ζ(s) for each m ≥ 1. Dividing by ζ(s) removes the trivial factor of the self-pairing, the factor that carries the pole at s = 1 (our own specialization).

**Problem.** There is an absolute, effectively computable c &gt; 0 such that R(s) has no real zeros for s ≥ 1−c/(m² log(3mC²)).

**How the definition helps.** The quotient R keeps only factors with no pole, to which the cited zero-free theorem applies (our own specialization). The theorem needs trivial central character and no complex multiplication, which full-level forms have.

**Paper or page:** [Exceptional zeros of Rankin-Selberg L-functions and joint Sato-Tate distributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06482v2). It says: “There exists an absolute, effectively computable constant”

**Sources:**

### Additive twists encode modular transformations

**Remember:** A rational additive twist records the cusp used in a transformation.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands L-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The completed additive twist at a rational x of a Dirichlet series ∑a(n)n⁻ˢ, absolutely convergent on Re s &gt; 1, is T(s,x) = γ(s)∑a(n)exp(2πinx)n⁻ˢ. The phase exp(2πinx) shifts the nth Fourier term by x, so the twist records a cusp (our own explanation). Here γ(s) = Qˢ∏Γ(λs+μ), with Q, λ &gt; 0, ∑λ = 1 and Re μ &gt; −λ/2 for each factor.

**Problem.** Fix positive integral N, a character χ modulo N and ω ≠ 0, and suppose T(s,a/q) = ωχ(b)q¹⁻²ˢT(1−s,−b/q), both sides entire of finite order, whenever N divides q &gt; 0 and ab ≡ 1 modulo q. Then for some positive integer k, the numbers a(n)n⁽ᵏ⁻¹⁾ᐟ² are the Fourier coefficients of a modular form of weight k, level N and character χ.

**How the definition helps.** Each functional equation relates the twists at a/q and −b/q, as a level-N matrix relates the two cusps (our own explanation). A converse theorem recovers modularity from these paired equations, after identifying the gamma factor and inverting the Mellin transform.

**Paper or page:** [An extension of Venkatesh's converse theorem to the Selberg class](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.00451v1). It says: “Given any α ∈ ℚ, define the complete twisted L-function”

**Sources:**

- [Andrew R. Booker, Michael Farmer, Min Lee, An extension of Venkatesh's converse theorem to the Selberg class](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.00451v1)

### Analytic conductor measures sum length

**Remember:** The square root of the conductor sets the central sum length.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands L-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For level-one Hecke–Maass cusp forms f and g, the central analytic conductor C of L(s,f×g) is its finite conductor times ∏(3+\|κ\|) over its gamma factors Γℝ(s+κ). It sets the length of the sum that captures the central value: about √C terms (our own explanation).

**Problem.** For Q &gt; 1 and ε &gt; 0, some smooth W depending only on Q and ε vanishes beyond Q¹ᐟ²⁺ᵋ. For every such pair with C ≤ Q, \|L(½,f×g)\|² ≪ Qᵋ∫\|S(t)\|²dt + Q⁻¹⁰⁰ over \|t\| ≤ log Q, where S(t) = ∑ₙ λf(n)λg(n)W(n)n⁻¹ᐟ²⁻ⁱᵗ.

**How the definition helps.** One bound C ≤ Q covers every pair, so the cited lemma can choose one weight W from Q and ε alone. Gamma-factor estimates in the functional equation give the square-root length (our own explanation).

**Paper or page:** [Uniform subconvexity bounds for GL(2) × GL(2) L-functions in the spectral aspect](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.05968v1). It says: “Then there exists a function W(x) depending on Q and ε only”

### Dual tensor products give squares

**Remember:** The trace of a tensor with its conjugate is an absolute square.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands L-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** At an unramified prime p, let A be the diagonal matrix of Satake parameters of a unitary cuspidal representation; its dual has the conjugate matrix Ā. The local Rankin–Selberg factor of the pair is 1/det(I−(A⊗Ā)p⁻ˢ), and every power of A⊗Ā has trace tr(Aʳ)tr(Āʳ) = \|tr(Aʳ)\|² (our own derivation).

**Problem.** In −L′(s)/L(s) for this product, the term at pʳ has coefficient (log p)\|tr(Aʳ)\|² for every integer r ≥ 1. Every such coefficient is nonnegative.

**How the definition helps.** Taking −L′/L of the local factor gives the coefficient (log p)tr((A⊗Ā)ʳ) at pʳ (our own derivation). This equals (log p)\|tr(Aʳ)\|², which is nonnegative.

**Paper or page:** [Exceptional zeros of Rankin-Selberg L-functions and joint Sato-Tate distributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06482v2). It says: “If Π ∈ 𝔄ₙ, then −L′/L(s, Π × Π̃) has non-negative Dirichlet coefficients.”

### Gamma poles delimit the critical integers

**Remember:** A critical integer avoids gamma poles on both sides.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands L-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For full-level holomorphic Hecke cusp forms of even weights k &gt; ℓ, normalize their Rankin–Selberg function so that the functional equation sends s to k+ℓ−1−s. An integer s is critical when the gamma factors, with arguments s and s−ℓ+1 and poles at the nonpositive integers, are finite at s and at k+ℓ−1−s (our own calculation).

**Problem.** The critical integers for the Rankin–Selberg function of these two forms are exactly ℓ, ℓ+1, …, k−1.

**How the definition helps.** Finiteness at s needs s−ℓ+1 ≥ 1, so s ≥ ℓ (our own calculation). Finiteness at the reflection needs k+ℓ−1−s ≥ ℓ, so s ≤ k−1.

### Isobaric sums count repeated poles

**Remember:** Each copy pairs with every dual copy of its block.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands L-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An isobaric sum Π is a list of unitary cuspidal blocks, repeats allowed, with central characters trivial on positive real scalars. L(s,Π×Π̃) multiplies the Rankin–Selberg factors over all ordered pairs of a block of Π and a dual block of Π̃, so a block that occurs m times meets its own dual m² times (our own count).

**Problem.** If each distinct block occurs m times, with m allowed to depend on the block, the pole order at 1 equals ∑ m².

**How the definition helps.** Only a block paired with its own dual gives a pole at 1, and that pole is simple, so the order is ∑m². The other factors do not vanish at 1, so nothing cancels.

### Pole correction makes convexity uniform

**Remember:** Cancel the pole without changing growth far from it.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands L-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For unitary cuspidal π and π′ over a number field, with central characters trivial on positive real scalars, let L(s) be their Rankin–Selberg function. Set R(s) = L(s)(s−1)/(s+1) when π′ is dual to π, the only case with a pole at 1, and R(s) = L(s) otherwise. The factor (s−1)/(s+1) kills the pole and stays bounded for Re s ≥ 0.

**Problem.** R is holomorphic for Re s &gt; −1. For σ ≥ 0, integers j ≥ 0 and ε &gt; 0, its jth derivative at σ+it is O(C(t) raised to max(1−σ,0)/2+ε), where C(t) is the analytic conductor at height t and the constant depends only on the ranks, field degree, j and ε.

**How the definition helps.** The correction cancels the only possible pole without changing size on Re s ≥ 0, so one convexity bound covers every pair. Strip estimates bound R, and Cauchy’s formula bounds its derivatives (our own explanation).

**Paper or page:** [Oscillations and first-ever negative Fourier coefficients of symmetric square L-functions over sparse set](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.18994v1), [A new zero-free region for Rankin-Selberg L-functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.16889v6). It says: “consider the holomorphic function”

**Remember:** A smooth twist at length X returns at length q²/X.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands L-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a level-one holomorphic Hecke cusp form of weight k with normalized coefficients λ(n), and a smooth weight v supported in \[1,2\], the Bessel transform of v is H(u) = ∫v(y)Jₖ₋₁(4π√(uy))dy over y &gt; 0. **Paper or page:** [Subconvexity for GL(1) twists of Rankin-Selberg L-functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.09646v5). It says: “v be a compactly supported smooth function on (0,∞).”

**Remember:** The Weil action can agree while monodromy differs.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F70 (Representation-theoretic methods; automorphic representations over local and global fields), 11F85. arXiv math.NT, math.RT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A two-dimensional Weil–Deligne parameter of a p-adic field is a complex Weil representation r, trivial on an open subgroup of inertia, together with a nilpotent operator N with r(w)Nr(w)⁻¹ = \|w\|N for every Weil element w. The operator N, the monodromy, carries information that r alone loses (our own).

**Problem.** The trivial representation of GL₂ and the Steinberg representation, the locally constant functions on the projective line modulo constants, have the same Weil action after semisimplification. Their full parameters differ.

**How the definition helps.** N is zero for the trivial representation and has rank one for Steinberg, so the parameters differ although r agrees (our own). This comes from the local Langlands calculation of the two parameters (our own).

### Noninvariant characters induce cusp forms

**Remember:** A character must move under conjugation to give a cusp form.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F70 (Representation-theoretic methods; automorphic representations over local and global fields), 11F41. arXiv math.NT, math.RT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a quadratic extension L of a number field F, a Hecke character of L is a continuous character of the idele class group of L, the ideles modulo the global scalars. It is regular if the nontrivial automorphism of L over F changes it; otherwise its induction splits into two characters of F (our own).

**Problem.** Automorphic induction transfers the character to a representation of GL₂ over F. This representation is cuspidal, meaning its constant terms vanish, exactly when the character is regular.

**How the definition helps.** Regularity removes exactly the characters whose induction splits as a sum of two characters (our own). For example, the trivial character induces the trivial character plus the quadratic character of L over F (our own). The quadratic automorphic induction theorem proves the cuspidality criterion.

**Paper or page:** [Vignéras orbifolds: isospectrality, regulators, and torsion homology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.07240v1). It says: “is cuspidal if and only if Ψ<sup>σ</sup> ≠ Ψ.”

### Crystalline periods detect good reduction

**Remember:** At p, crystalline replaces unramified as the test for good reduction.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 11G07. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a finite extension K of ℚₚ, a p-adic Galois representation V is crystalline if V ⊗ B<sub>crys</sub> has as many Galois-fixed dimensions as V, where B<sub>crys</sub> is Fontaine’s crystalline period ring. It is the p-adic substitute for being unramified, which fails at p even for good reduction (our own).

**Problem.** An elliptic curve over K has good reduction, a smooth model over the integers of K, exactly when its rational p-adic Tate module is crystalline.

**How the definition helps.** The crystalline test allows the ramification that p-power torsion has even under good reduction (our own). For example, y² = x³ − x has good reduction at 5, yet its Tate module over ℚ₅ has the ramified cyclotomic character as determinant (our own). The crystalline comparison theorem gives necessity, and Coleman and Iovita give sufficiency (our own).

**nLab:** [p-adic Hodge theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/p-adic+Hodge+theory). It says: “We can also apply this construction with Bcrys instead of BdR; if the dimension stays the same we say that V is crystalline.”

### Determinants retain small-characteristic information

**Remember:** A trace keeps one coefficient, while a determinant law keeps them all.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A d-dimensional determinant law on a group G over a commutative ring A gives, for each commutative A-algebra B, a unital multiplicative map D<sub>B</sub> from B\[G\] to B, compatible with scalar change and homogeneous of degree d. It records a whole characteristic polynomial, while its trace keeps only the coefficient of t in D(1+tx).

**Problem.** When d! is invertible in the coefficient ring, taking traces is a bijection from d-dimensional determinant laws to trace pseudocharacters. In small characteristic the trace can lose information.

**How the definition helps.** When d! is invertible, traces of powers recover the other coefficients, and the cited reconstruction theorem gives the bijection (our own explanation). In characteristic two, take a nontrivial 𝔽₄-valued character χ of a cyclic group of order three (our own example). Then χ⊕χ and 1⊕1 both have trace zero but determinants χ² ≠ 1.

**Paper or page:** [On the relation between pseudocharacters and Chenevier's determinants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.18034v1). It says: “a bijection between A-valued d-dimensional determinants on R and A-valued d-dimensional pseudocharacters on R.”

### Fontaine's (φ,Γ)-modules are Laurent F-crystals evaluated on one prism

**Remember:** Γ is the symmetry group of one prism, not extra data.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 14F30, 11S20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A Laurent F-crystal over the integers 𝒪 of a finite extension K of ℚₚ assigns each prism (A,I) over 𝒪 a finite projective module over p-completed A\[1/I\], compatibly with base change, with a compatible isomorphism from its Frobenius pullback. Its value at Wu’s cyclotomic prism is a φ-module over 𝐀(K), and Γ = Gal(K(μₚ∞)/K) acts on that prism by automorphisms (our own explanation).

**Problem.** (φ,Γ)-modules over 𝐀(K) are equivalent to Laurent F-crystals over 𝒪. Wu also shows that Laurent F-crystals are equivalent to ℤₚ-representations of Gal(K̄/K), which gives a new proof of Fontaine's theorem.

**How the definition helps.** Evaluation at the cyclotomic prism gives a module over 𝐀(K) with invertible linearized Frobenius, and prism automorphisms give the commuting semilinear Γ-action (our own explanation). Wu’s descent theorem rebuilds the crystal from this (φ,Γ)-module.

**Paper or page:** [Galois representations, (φ, Γ)-modules and prismatic F-crystals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.12105), [Galois representations, (φ, Γ)-modules and prismatic F-crystals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.12105), [Galois representations, (φ, Γ)-modules and prismatic F-crystals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.12105). It says: “Then (φ,Γ)-modules over 𝐀<sub>K</sub> are equivalent to prismatic F-crystals in 𝒪\_Δ\[1/I\]<sup>∧<sub>p</sub>-modules</sup> over (𝒪<sub>K</sub>)\_Δ.”

**Sources:**

- [Z. Wu, Galois representations, (φ,Γ)-modules and prismatic F-crystals, Documenta Mathematica 26 (2021) 1771–1798](https://doi.org/10.4171/dm/855)

### Frames make Galois lifts glue

**Remember:** Fixed matrices glue entry by entry.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix a continuous representation ρ̄ of a profinite group G on kⁿ, with k finite of characteristic p. A framed lift to a complete Noetherian local W(k)-algebra A with residue field k is a continuous homomorphism G → GLₙ(A) reducing to ρ̄, kept as actual matrices in the fixed basis, not up to conjugation.

**Problem.** Suppose every open subgroup of G has only finitely many continuous homomorphisms to the group of order p. Then one universal ring parametrizes the framed lifts to all complete Noetherian local algebras over the Witt vectors of k with residue field k.

**How the definition helps.** Because lifts are matrices, two compatible lifts glue entry by entry to a lift over the fibre product of rings (our own). Without a frame, gluing would also need a compatible choice of basis changes (our own). Schlessinger’s criterion turns this gluing and the finiteness hypothesis into a universal ring (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Deformation Theory of Galois Representations and the Taylor--Wiles Method](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.12202v1). It says: “We call the representing ring of it the universal lifting ring or universal framed deformation ring”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Isogeny degrees determine pairing type

**Remember:** Symplectic type means the pairing scales by a square.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 11G05. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For elliptic curves E, F over a number field and an odd prime p, a linear isomorphism u from E\[p\] to F\[p\] has symplectic type if it multiplies the Weil pairing by a nonzero square. That is, e<sub>F</sub>(uP,uQ) = e<sub>E</sub>(P,Q)ʳ for all P, Q ∈ E\[p\], with r a square in 𝔽ₚˣ (our own reformulation).

**Problem.** An isogeny of degree n prime to p induces an isomorphism of p-torsion of symplectic type exactly when n is a square modulo p.

**How the definition helps.** An isogeny of degree n multiplies the Weil pairing by n, by compatibility of the pairing with the dual isogeny (our own). So its torsion map has symplectic type exactly when n is a square modulo p (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Local points on twists of X(p) with applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.04294v3). It says: “is symplectic if (n/p) = 1 and anti-symplectic otherwise.”

**Sources:**

- [Local points on twists of X(p) with applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.04294v3)

### Kummer-tower (φ,τ)-modules are descent data on the Breuil–Kisin prism

**Remember:** The awkward τ-action is just gluing data over the self-product prism.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 14F30, 11S20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let (𝔖,E) be the Breuil–Kisin prism of a p-adic integer ring and A⁽²⁾ its prismatic self-product. A descent datum on an étale φ-module over p-completed 𝔖\[1/E\] is a Frobenius-compatible isomorphism between its two pullbacks to p-completed A⁽²⁾\[1/E\], satisfying the cocycle condition on the triple product. This is exactly the gluing data a crystal carries (our own).

**Problem.** Étale φ-modules over the completed 𝔖\[1/E\] with descent data over the completed A⁽²⁾\[1/E\] are equivalent to étale (φ,τ)-modules. A descent datum is determined by its value at τ.

**How the definition helps.** A descent datum is the gluing data every crystal has, so the ad hoc τ-action becomes standard descent. The work is computing A⁽²⁾ and its perfection, and showing that the value at τ fixes the datum.

**Paper or page:** [A prismatic approach to (φ, Ĝ)-modules and F-crystals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.12240). It says: “The category of étale φ-modules over A\[1/E\]<sup>∧<sub>p</sub></sup> with descent data over A<sup>(2)</sup>\[1/E\]<sup>∧<sub>p</sub></sup> is equivalent to the category of étale (φ,τ)-modules over A\[1/E\]<sup>∧<sub>p</sub></sup>”

**Sources:**

- [H. Du and T. Liu, A prismatic approach to (φ, Ĝ)-modules and F-crystals, preprint (2023), arXiv:2107.12240](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.12240)

### Lifts modulo strict conjugation make the deformation tangent space first Galois cohomology

**Remember:** The group law gives cocycles, and changes of basis give coboundaries.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 14D15. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A first-order deformation of a continuous representation ρ̄ of a profinite group G over a finite field k is a continuous lift to k\[ε\]/(ε²), up to conjugation by matrices that reduce to the identity. Writing a lift as g ↦ (1+εc(g))ρ̄(g), the group law makes c a cocycle, and these conjugations change c by coboundaries (our own).

**Problem.** The tangent space of the deformation functor of ρ̄ is H¹(G, ad ρ̄). Here ad ρ̄ is the matrix algebra over k, with G acting by conjugation through ρ̄.

**How the definition helps.** The tangent space is therefore cocycles modulo coboundaries, which is H¹(G, ad ρ̄) by definition (our own). Reading it as the tangent space of a ring needs Mazur’s representability theorem, under its hypotheses (our own).

**nLab:** [Galois deformation ring](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Galois+deformation+ring). It says: “where two lifts are considered equivalent if they are conjugate by an element of the kernel of the reduction map.”

**Sources:**

- [Barry Mazur, Deforming Galois representations, in Galois Groups over ℚ (1989)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4613-9649-9_7)

### Log prisms extend the crystalline correspondence to semistable lattices

**Remember:** Add a log structure, and crystalline becomes semistable.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 14F30. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Give the integers 𝒪 of a p-adic field the log structure of its closed point. A log prismatic F-crystal of height h assigns each log prism (A,I) a finite projective A-module M, compatibly with base change, with a linearized Frobenius φ\*M → M that is injective with cokernel killed by Iʰ.

**Problem.** On the log prismatic site of 𝒪, F-crystals of height h are equivalent to lattices in semistable representations with Hodge–Tate weights in \[0,h\]. Semistable representations include the Tate modules of curves with semistable reduction (our own gloss).

**How the definition helps.** The log structure is the only change from the crystalline case, and it moves the theorem from good to semistable reduction (our own). Du and Liu prove it by extending their (φ,Ĝ)-module construction to log prisms.

**Paper or page:** [A prismatic approach to (φ, Ĝ)-modules and F-crystals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.12240), [A prismatic approach to (φ, Ĝ)-modules and F-crystals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.12240). It says: “The category of prismatic F-crystals over (X,M<sub>X</sub>)\_Δ<sub>log</sub> of height h is equivalent to the category of lattices in semi-stable representations of G<sub>K</sub> with Hodge-Tate weights between 0 and h.”

**Sources:**

- [H. Du and T. Liu, A prismatic approach to (φ, Ĝ)-modules and F-crystals, preprint (2023), arXiv:2107.12240](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.12240)
- [T. Liu, A note on lattices in semi-stable representations, Mathematische Annalen 346 (2010) 117–138](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00208-009-0392-y)

### Oddness excludes nonmodular real representations

**Remember:** Complex conjugation must have opposite signs in the two directions.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 11F11. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A continuous two-dimensional representation of the absolute Galois group of ℚ is odd if complex conjugation has determinant −1. In odd characteristic this means its eigenvalues are 1 and −1, as for every representation from a modular form (our own).

**Problem.** Every continuous, odd, absolutely irreducible two-dimensional representation over a finite field of odd characteristic arises from a cuspidal Hecke eigenform. This is Serre’s modularity theorem.

**How the definition helps.** Oddness removes even examples, such as those with trivial complex conjugation (our own argument). For example, x³−4x+1 has discriminant 229, so its S₃ splitting field is totally real, and the two-dimensional representation of S₃ over 𝔽₅ is absolutely irreducible but even. Serre’s theorem supplies modularity under the stated hypotheses.

**Wikipedia:** [Serre's modularity conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serre%27s_modularity_conjecture). It says: “Additionally, assume ρ is odd, meaning the image of complex conjugation has determinant -1.”

**Sources:**

- [Khare and Wintenberger, Serre’s modularity conjecture (I)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-009-0205-7)
- [Khare and Wintenberger, Serre’s modularity conjecture (II)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-009-0206-6)

### Prismatic F-crystals over a p-adic integer ring are crystalline Galois lattices

**Remember:** Crystalline lattices are F-crystals on all prisms at once, with no choices.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 14F30, 11S20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A prismatic F-crystal over the integers 𝒪 of a p-adic field assigns each prism (A,I) over 𝒪 a finite projective A-module M, compatibly with base change, with a compatible isomorphism φ\*M ≅ M after inverting I. It uses every prism at once, so it needs no chosen uniformizer.

**Problem.** Prismatic F-crystals over 𝒪 are equivalent to Galois-stable ℤₚ-lattices in crystalline representations of Gal(K̄/K).

**How the definition helps.** Because the crystal involves no choices, it describes crystalline lattices integrally and canonically. Kisin’s Breuil–Kisin module, which depends on a uniformizer, is its value at one prism (Du and Liu, Theorem 4.1.10). Bhatt and Scholze proved the equivalence, and Du and Liu give a second proof.

**Paper or page:** [A prismatic approach to (φ, Ĝ)-modules and F-crystals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.12240), [A prismatic approach to (φ, Ĝ)-modules and F-crystals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.12240). It says: “There is an equivalence of the category of prismatic F-crystals in finite locally free 𝒪\_Δ-modules over (𝒪<sub>K</sub>)\_Δ and the category of Galois stable lattices in crystalline representations of G<sub>K</sub>.”

**Sources:**

- [B. Bhatt and P. Scholze, Prismatic F-crystals and crystalline Galois representations, Cambridge Journal of Mathematics 11 (2023)](https://doi.org/10.4310/cjm.2023.v11.n2.a3)
- [M. Kisin, Crystalline representations and F-crystals, in Algebraic Geometry and Number Theory, Progress in Mathematics](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-8176-4532-8_7)

### Rational Hodge–Tate crystals compute Galois cohomology of nearly Hodge–Tate representations

**Remember:** Reduce modulo the prism ideal, invert p, and require base change.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 14F30, 11S25. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A rational Hodge–Tate crystal over the integers 𝒪 of a p-adic field K assigns each prism (A,I) over 𝒪 a finite projective (A/I)\[1/p\]-module, compatibly with base change. A representation of Gal(K̄/K) on a C-vector space, with C the completed algebraic closure, is nearly Hodge–Tate if every Sen weight lies in ℤ+E′(π)⁻¹𝔪<sub>C</sub>, for a uniformizer π with Eisenstein polynomial E.

**Problem.** Evaluation at Fontaine’s perfect prism for C is an equivalence from rational Hodge–Tate crystals over 𝒪 to nearly Hodge–Tate C-representations. It matches prismatic cohomology with continuous Galois cohomology.

**How the definition helps.** The crystal carries one operator that plays the role of the Sen operator (our own reading), so Sen theory gets a canonical home on the prismatic site. The work is Sen theory over the Kummer tower, through locally analytic vectors (Theorem 7.12).

**Paper or page:** [Hodge--Tate prismatic crystals and Sen theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.07024), [Hodge--Tate prismatic crystals and Sen theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.07024), [Hodge--Tate prismatic crystals and Sen theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.07024), [Hodge--Tate prismatic crystals and Sen theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.07024). It says: “There exists a natural quasi-isomorphism RΓ((𝒪<sub>K</sub>)\_Δ,\*, 𝕄) ≃ RΓ(G<sub>K</sub>, W) where the right hand side is Galois cohomology.”

**Sources:**

- [H. Gao, Y. Min and Y. Wang, Hodge–Tate prismatic crystals and Sen theory, preprint (2023), arXiv:2311.07024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.07024)

### Reducibility ideals locate split traces

**Remember:** One ideal detects every quotient with a split trace.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take a two-dimensional Galois pseudocharacter T over a complete local ring with 2 invertible, whose residual trace is χ₁+χ₂ for distinct characters. Its reducibility ideal is the smallest ideal J with T modulo J a sum of characters lifting χ₁ and χ₂, so a quotient has a split trace exactly when its ideal contains J (our own).

**Problem.** In the cited family of Galois traces attached to modular forms, the reducibility ideal equals the maximal ideal. Among nonzero quotient rings, only the residue field gives a split trace.

**How the definition helps.** The smallest ideal turns a search for two characters into an inclusion test on ideals (our own). The hard step is the cited calculation that this ideal is the maximal ideal.

**Paper or page:** [Eisenstein degeneration of Euler systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.02078v2). It says: “The reducibility ideal of the pseudo-character t𝐟 is exactly 𝔪.”

**Sources:**

- [Eisenstein degeneration of Euler systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.02078v2)

### Requiring an étale Frobenius makes φ-modules match Galois representations

**Remember:** Invertible linearized Frobenius excludes multiplication by p.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 11S20, 14F30. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An étale φ-module over Fontaine’s ring 𝐀(K) is a finite free module M with a Frobenius-semilinear map whose linearization φ\*M → M is an isomorphism. This excludes, for example, M = 𝐀(K) with x ↦ p·φ(x), which has no nonzero Frobenius-fixed vectors.

**Problem.** For a finite extension K of ℚₚ, let K∞ adjoin all p-power roots of unity and let 𝐀 be Fontaine’s larger completed ring. Then M ↦ (M ⊗ 𝐀) fixed by Frobenius is an equivalence from étale φ-modules over 𝐀(K) to ℤₚ-representations of Gal(K̄/K∞).

**How the definition helps.** Fontaine’s equivalence identifies M ⊗ 𝐀 with the scalar extension of its fixed lattice, which needs the linearized Frobenius to be invertible (our own explanation). For x ↦ pφ(x), a fixed vector lies in pⁿ𝐀 for every n and so vanishes, losing rank one. The quoted Lubin–Tate theorem specializes to the cyclotomic case with coefficient field ℚₚ.

**Paper or page:** [Prismatic F-crystals and Lubin-Tate (φq,Γ)-modules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.07620). It says: “The functors Mod\_𝐀<sub>K</sub><sup>φ<sub>q</sub>,et</sup> → Rep\_𝒪<sub>L</sub>(G<sub>K∞</sub>), M ↦ (M⊗\_𝐀<sub>K</sub> 𝐀)<sup>φ = 1</sup>, (T⊗\_𝒪<sub>L</sub> 𝐀)<sup>G<sub>K∞</sub></sup> ↤ T form an equivalence of exact tensor categories.”

**Sources:**

- [J.-M. Fontaine, Représentations p-adiques des corps locaux (1ère partie), Modern Birkhäuser Classics (2007 reprint)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-8176-4575-5_6)
- [M. Kisin and W. Ren, Galois representations and Lubin–Tate groups, Documenta Mathematica 14 (2009) 441–461](https://doi.org/10.4171/dm/278)

### The self-product prism gives a one-line criterion for crystalline lattices

**Remember:** Crystalline means τ stays inside the self-product prism.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 14F30. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a p-adic integer ring 𝒪 with residue field k, let A = W(k)\[\[u\]\] with φ(u) = uᵖ, the Breuil–Kisin prism with ideal (E) for the Eisenstein polynomial E of a uniformizer π. Its prismatic self-product A⁽²⁾ is the universal prism over 𝒪 receiving two maps from A, so it is where a crystal’s two values on A are compared (our own description).

**Problem.** Liu’s (φ,Ĝ)-modules classify lattices in semistable representations with bounded Hodge–Tate weights; let τ be the Kummer generator moving compatible roots of π and fixing p-power roots of unity. The lattice is crystalline exactly when its Kisin module 𝔐 satisfies τ(𝔐) ⊆ A⁽²⁾ ⊗<sub>A</sub> 𝔐.

**How the definition helps.** Crystalline lattices come from F-crystals on all prisms, which glue over A⁽²⁾, so crystallinity becomes the condition that τ stays inside A⁽²⁾. Semistable lattices need a larger ring built from A⁽²⁾ (our own reading). The proof uses Du and Liu’s prismatic construction of (φ,Ĝ)-modules.

**Paper or page:** [A prismatic approach to (φ, Ĝ)-modules and F-crystals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.12240). It says: “Select τ ∈ Ĝ as the above. Then T̂(𝔐̂) is crystalline if and only if τ(𝔐) ⊂ A<sup>(2)</sup>⊗<sub>A</sub> 𝔐.”

**Sources:**

- [H. Du and T. Liu, A prismatic approach to (φ, Ĝ)-modules and F-crystals, preprint (2023), arXiv:2107.12240](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.12240)
- [T. Liu, A note on lattices in semi-stable representations, Mathematische Annalen 346 (2010) 117–138](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00208-009-0392-y)

### Alternation forces a square order

**Remember:** A perfect alternating pairing puts the finite group into pairs.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11G05 (Elliptic curves over global fields), 11G40. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A ℚ/ℤ-valued bilinear pairing b on an abelian group A is alternating if every element pairs to zero with itself, b(x,x) = 0. This is stronger than skew symmetry, which allows b(x,x) = ½ on a cyclic group of order two (our own).

**Problem.** If the Tate–Shafarevich group of an elliptic curve over a number field is finite, its order is a square.

**How the definition helps.** A finite group with a perfect alternating pairing splits into pairs of cyclic factors of equal order, so its order is a square (our own). For the Tate–Shafarevich group, Cassels proves alternation, and duality makes the pairing perfect when the group is finite (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Tate–Shafarevich group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate%E2%80%93Shafarevich_group). It says: “if the order of Ш is finite then it is a square.”

**Sources:**

- [Cassels, Arithmetic on Curves of Genus 1. IV. Proof of the Hauptvermutung](https://doi.org/10.1515/crll.1962.211.95)
- [Poonen and Stoll, The Cassels–Tate Pairing on Polarized Abelian Varieties](https://doi.org/10.2307/121064)

### Relaxed Selmer conditions pair with strict ones

**Remember:** Everything minus nothing at one prime equals half the local cohomology.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11G05 (Elliptic curves over global fields), 11R34. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For an elliptic curve over a number field, a prime p and one finite prime v, the relaxed p-Selmer group allows every local class at v and the strict group allows only zero there. Both keep the usual Selmer conditions, classes that come from curve points divided by p, at every other prime.

**Problem.** The 𝔽ₚ-dimension of the relaxed group minus that of the strict group equals half the dimension of the local first cohomology of the p-torsion at v.

**How the definition helps.** Under local Tate duality, allowing everything and allowing zero are opposite conditions, and the usual condition is its own orthogonal complement of half the local dimension (our own). The cited orthogonality theorem makes the images of the two dimension jumps exact annihilators inside the usual condition (our own). So the two jumps add to half the local dimension (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Increasing the p-Selmer rank by twisting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09207v3). It says: “The images of the two right-hand maps in the following exact sequences are orthogonal complements of each other under the sum of the local Tate pairings.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Exterior powers give determinant characters

**Remember:** Take the top exterior power before passing to the Galois action.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G09 (Drinfel'd modules; higher-dimensional motives, etc.). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The determinant of a rank-r Drinfeld module E is the rank-one Drinfeld module whose A-motive is the top exterior power ∧ʳM of the motive M of E, on which every linear map acts by its determinant. The cited theorem says it exists and is unique up to isomorphism.

**Problem.** At a prime different from the characteristic, the Galois action on the Tate module of the determinant module is the determinant of the Galois action on the Tate module of E.

**How the definition helps.** A linear map acts on the top exterior power by its determinant (our own explanation). The comparison between motives and Tate modules preserves exterior powers, which carries this to torsion.

**Paper or page:** [Pour une définition commune des courbes elliptiques et modules de Drinfeld](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.13160). It says: “Le $A$-motif $\\underline{D}$ provient d'un $A$-module de Drinfeld de rang $1$ et de caractéristique $\\delta<sub>E</sub>$. Ce module de Drinfeld est unique à isomorphisme près, et on le note $\\det E$.”
