### Frobenius determinants measure Drinfeld points

**Remember:** Take the determinant of one minus Frobenius to measure rational torsion.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11G09 (Drinfel'd modules; higher-dimensional motives, etc.). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For A = 𝔽q\[T\], measure a finite A-module by the product of the monic polynomials h in its splitting into cyclic modules A/(h). This is the polynomial version of a group’s order, and it is the monic determinant of any square presentation matrix (our own explanation).

**Problem.** For a Drinfeld module over a finite field, this measure of its rational points equals its Frobenius polynomial at 1, scaled to be monic. The Frobenius polynomial is the characteristic polynomial of the field-size power map on a Tate module away from the characteristic.

**How the definition helps.** Rational points are the points fixed by Frobenius, so away from the characteristic their torsion part is the cokernel of one minus Frobenius on the Tate module (our own explanation). Its measure is therefore det(1 − Frobenius), the Frobenius polynomial at 1. The cited theorem gives the full polynomial, including its characteristic factor.

**Paper or page:** [Convolutions of Goss and Pellarin L-series](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.14931). It says: “Then\\\[  \\bigl\[ E(\\mathbb {F}<sub>f</sub>) \\bigr\]\_{\\mathsf{A}} = \\gamma \\cdot \\Char (\\tau ^d,T<sub>\\lambda </sub>(E),1),  \\\]where $\\gamma \\in \\mathbb {F}<sub>q</sub><sup>\\times </sup>$ forces the right-hand expression to be monic in\~ $t$.”

**Sources:**

- [Wei-Cheng Huang and Matthew A. Papanikolas, Convolutions of Goss and Pellarin L-series](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.14931)

### Frobenius polynomials classify Drinfeld isogeny classes

**Remember:** The Frobenius polynomial determines the isogeny class over a finite field.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11G09 (Drinfel'd modules; higher-dimensional motives, etc.). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For A = 𝔽q\[T\], the Frobenius polynomial of a Drinfeld module over a finite field is the characteristic polynomial of the field-size power map on its rational Tate module at a prime other than the characteristic. Because Frobenius acts semisimply, this polynomial determines the Tate module with its Frobenius action (our own explanation).

**Problem.** Take two Drinfeld modules of the same rank and characteristic over the same finite field. Their Frobenius polynomials agree exactly when an isogeny, a nonzero map respecting both A-actions, exists over that field.

**How the definition helps.** An isogeny identifies the rational Tate modules compatibly with Frobenius, so the polynomials agree. Conversely, equal polynomials give isomorphic Tate modules by semisimplicity, and the Tate isogeny theorem turns this into an isogeny.

**Paper or page:** [Traces of Hecke operators on Drinfeld modular forms for 𝔽q\[T\]](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.04555). It says: “Then cφ(X) = cψ(X) if and only if φ is isogenous to ψ.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Ideal classes classify rank one Drinfeld modules

**Remember:** At rank one, period lattices become fractional ideals up to scaling.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G09 (Drinfel'd modules; higher-dimensional motives, etc.), 11R58. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let A be the functions on a smooth projective curve over a finite field that are regular away from a fixed place ∞. The period lattice of a Drinfeld module is the kernel of its exponential over the completed algebraic closure at ∞; in rank one it is a fractional ideal of A up to scaling (our own argument).

**Problem.** The ideal class group acts freely and transitively on the rank one Drinfeld modules up to isomorphism.

**How the definition helps.** Drinfeld uniformization identifies rank-one modules up to isomorphism with rank-one lattices up to scaling, that is, with ideal classes. Ideal multiplication acts freely and transitively on these classes (our own argument).

**Paper or page:** [Drinfeld Module and Weil pairing over Dedekind domain of class number two](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.16919). It says: “The set of isomorphism classes of A-Drinfeld modules is the principle homogeneous space of the class group of A”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Lattice enlargement composes ideal isogenies

**Remember:** Ideal isogenies enlarge the period lattice by inverse ideals.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G09 (Drinfel'd modules; higher-dimensional motives, etc.). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a Drinfeld module with period lattice Λ, the kernel of its exponential over the completed algebraic closure at ∞, and a nonzero ideal I of A, the quotient by I is the Drinfeld module with the larger lattice I⁻¹Λ. Here A is the ring of functions on a curve that are regular away from ∞.

**Problem.** Taking the quotient for I and then for J gives the quotient for IJ up to isomorphism.

**How the definition helps.** Enlarging the lattice twice gives J⁻¹I⁻¹Λ = (IJ)⁻¹Λ, the lattice for IJ (our own explanation). The result holds only up to isomorphism because normalizing the isogeny can rescale the target lattice, as the cited formula shows.

**Paper or page:** [Drinfeld Module and Weil pairing over Dedekind domain of class number two](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.16919). It says: “Then we have Λψ = Λφ · ∂(λ) I⁻¹.”

**Sources:**

- [Chuangqiang Hu and Xiao-Min Huang, Drinfeld Module and Weil pairing over Dedekind domain of class number two](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.16919)

### Forgetting signs lets twists share j

**Remember:** A modular curve sees torsion bases only up to curve automorphisms.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G18 (Arithmetic aspects of modular and Shimura varieties), 11F80. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For an open subgroup H of GL₂ over the profinite integers, a point of the modular curve X(H) above j is a full torsion basis of an elliptic curve with invariant j, up to H and up to automorphisms of the curve. For j outside {0,1728} these automorphisms are ±1, so bases are identified up to ±H (our own formulation).

**Problem.** Take an algebraic number j different from 0 and 1728 and an elliptic curve over ℚ(j) with that invariant. Some point of X(H) above j is rational over ℚ(j) exactly when a conjugate of ±H contains the curve’s Galois image on torsion.

**How the definition helps.** A ℚ(j)-rational point is a basis class fixed by Galois, which exists exactly when some conjugate of ±H contains the Galois image (our own). Because signs are forgotten, a quadratic twist, which changes the image only by signs, gives the same answer (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Degrees of points with rational j-invariant on X₀(n) and X₁(n)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.13199v1). It says: “there exists a point x ∈ Xᴴ(ℚ(j)) such that j(x) = j if and only if 𝒢ⱼ ≤ ±ℋ.”

**Sources:**

- [Degrees of points with rational j-invariant on X₀(n) and X₁(n)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.13199v1)

### Component graphs count torus rank

**Remember:** Each independent loop supplies one multiplicative direction in the Jacobian.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11G20 (Curves over finite and local fields), 14G20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The dual graph of a split semistable curve model has one vertex per irreducible component of the special fibre and one edge per node, joining the components through its two branches. Its independent loops number edges minus vertices plus one, when the graph is connected.

**Problem.** For a smooth projective geometrically connected curve of positive genus over ℚ with split semistable reduction at a prime, the torus rank of its Jacobian equals the number of independent loops of this graph. The torus rank counts multiplicative group factors in the connected part of the reduced Néron model.

**How the definition helps.** A line bundle on the special fibre is fixed by its restrictions to components and one gluing scalar per node, and rescaling the components removes vertices minus one of these scalars (our own explanation). The description of the Jacobian’s Néron model identifies the remaining parameters with its torus.

**Paper or page:** [Normal distribution of bad reduction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.15874v1). It says: “the toric rank of Jac(C) is equal to m − c + 1”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Ramification scales node thickness

**Remember:** An edge length is a valuation, so ramification multiplies it.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G20 (Curves over finite and local fields), 14G20. arXiv math.AG, math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In the dual graph of a split semistable model, a node with local equation xy = a gets length v(a), where v is the normalized valuation of the base ring. Such a model has a reduced special fibre whose only singularities are ordinary double points defined over the residue field.

**Problem.** Start with such a model over a complete discrete valuation ring. After a finite totally ramified extension of index e, the pulled-back model has the same graph with every length multiplied by e.

**How the definition helps.** After a totally ramified extension of index e, the node still has equation xy = a, and the new normalized valuation of a is e times the old (our own calculation). Total ramification keeps the residue field, so the special fibre and its graph do not change.

**Paper or page:** [Models of Bihyperelliptic Curves](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.09730v1). It says: “with the same dual graph as 𝒞, but with the lengths of all edges multiplied by e.”

**Sources:**

- [Models of Bihyperelliptic Curves](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.09730v1)

### Under semistability, invariant valuations determine the reduction graph of hyperelliptic curves

**Remember:** Require semistability before reading a reduction graph from invariants.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11G20 (Curves over finite and local fields), 14H45. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A curve over a local field is semistable if it has a proper flat model over the ring of integers whose special fibre is reduced, with only ordinary double points. Its dual graph has a vertex for each component and an edge for each double point.

**Problem.** For a hyperelliptic curve C of genus g ≥ 2 over a local field K of odd residue characteristic, the paper gives a finite list of invariants depending only on g. If C is semistable, their valuations determine the dual graph of the special fibre of its minimal regular model over the maximal unramified extension of K.

**How the definition helps.** Semistability removes the curves whose graph the invariants cannot see; the paper shows by a counterexample that, for genus at least two, no list of invariants works without it. This is the analog of Tate’s algorithm, where ord(j) gives the graph of a semistable elliptic curve.

**Paper or page:** [Invariants recovering the reduction type of a hyperelliptic curve](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.08487v3). It says: “They also determine the dual graph of the special fibre of the minimal regular model of C/Kᵘⁿʳ if C/K is semistable.”

**Sources:**

- [Lilybelle Cowland Kellock, Elisa Lorenzo, Invariants recovering the reduction type of a hyperelliptic curve, arXiv:2502.08487v3 (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.08487v3)

### Serre–Frobenius groups separate ordinary and supersingular curves

**Remember:** Close the powers of the normalized Frobenius tuple inside a torus.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G25 (Varieties over finite and local fields), 11G10, 11G20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For an abelian variety over 𝔽q, let u be the tuple of its Frobenius eigenvalues divided by √q, a point in a product of unit circles. Its Serre–Frobenius group is the closure of the powers uⁿ, and the normalized Frobenius trace over the degree-n extension is the coordinate sum of uⁿ.

**Problem.** Normalized Frobenius traces are equidistributed for the image of Haar probability measure under the coordinate sum. For elliptic curves the group is a circle exactly in the ordinary case, and the supersingular groups are exactly the cyclic groups of orders 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 and 12.

**How the definition helps.** Powers of a generator of a compact group equidistribute for Haar measure, so the traces follow its image under the coordinate sum (our own explanation). For elliptic curves one eigenvalue determines the group. The classification of eigenvalues gives roots of unity of the listed orders when supersingular, and otherwise an infinite and hence dense circle subgroup.

**Paper or page:** [Frobenius distributions of low dimensional abelian varieties over finite fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.02237), [Frobenius distributions of low dimensional abelian varieties over finite fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.02237). It says: “This group, which we call the Serre--Frobenius group, encodes the possible multiplicative relations between the Frobenius eigenvalues.”

**Sources:**

- [Santiago Arango-Piñeros, Deewang Bhamidipati, Soumya Sankar, Frobenius distributions of low dimensional abelian varieties over finite fields, International Mathematics Research Notices 2024, no. 16, 11989-12020, arXiv:2306.02237](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.02237)

### Regular dessins descend to moduli fields

**Remember:** A regular cover can move any chosen sheet to any other.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11G32 (Arithmetic aspects of dessins d'enfants, Bely? theory), 14H57. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A dessin is a connected cover of the sphere branched only over 0, 1 and ∞. It is regular if its symmetries act transitively on each unbranched fibre, so one unique symmetry moves any chosen sheet to any other. Its field of moduli is the fixed field of the Galois automorphisms that preserve its isomorphism class.

**Problem.** Every regular dessin admits defining equations over its field of moduli.

**How the definition helps.** Regularity lets one mark a point above the unbranched value 2 and choose, for each Galois conjugate, the unique isomorphism preserving the mark (our own argument). Uniqueness gives the cocycle condition, so Weil descent gives equations over the field of moduli.

**Wikipedia:** [Dessin d'enfant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dessin_d%27enfant). It says: “Due to the Galois correspondence between subgroups of Γ and algebraic number fields, the stabilizer corresponds to a field, the field of moduli of the dessin.”

**Sources:**

- [Marston Conder, Gareth Jones, Manfred Streit and Jürgen Wolfart, Galois actions on regular dessins of small genera, Proposition 1 (2013)](https://www.math.uni-frankfurt.de/~wolfart/Artikel/CoJoStWo.pdf)

### Zero-cycles with modulus give class field theory

**Remember:** The modulus D bounds ramification along the boundary, as a conductor does.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G45 (Geometric class field theory), 19F05, 14C25. arXiv math.AG, math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a proper variety X and an effective Cartier divisor D, the Chow group of zero-cycles with modulus CH₀(X\|D) is the free group on closed points outside D, modulo divisors of functions congruent to 1 along D. The functions live on normalizations of integral curves meeting X∖D, and the congruence uses the pulled-back divisor with its multiplicities.

**Problem.** Let U be smooth, connected and quasi-projective over a finite field, with normal proper compactification X whose boundary supports an effective Cartier divisor. Reciprocity identifies π₁ᵃᵇ(U) with the inverse limit of CH₀(X\|D) ⊗ ℤ/m over positive integers m and effective Cartier divisors D with that support.

**How the definition helps.** Raising the multiplicities of D allows more ramification along the same boundary, as a larger conductor does (our own explanation). The reciprocity theorem, using Bloch’s formula with modulus, identifies the finite quotients in the inverse limit.

**Paper or page:** [Bloch's formula for 0-cycles with modulus and higher dimensional Class Field Theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.01856), [Bloch's formula for 0-cycles with modulus and higher dimensional Class Field Theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.01856). It says: “The reciprocity maps {ρ₍X,D₎}\|D\|⊂C induce an isomorphism of pro-finite topological groups ρU : lim D,m CH₀(X\|D) ⊗ ℤ/m ≅ π₁ᵃᵇ(U).”

**Sources:**

- [Federico Binda, Amalendu Krishna and Shuji Saito, Bloch's formula for 0-cycles with modulus and higher dimensional class field theory, arXiv:2002.01856](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.01856)

### Invariant metrics scale heights exactly

**Remember:** An invariant metric turns pullback into exact multiplication of heights.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G50 (Heights), 14G40. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let f be an endomorphism of a projective variety over a number field, with an ample line bundle L and an isomorphism f\*L ≅ L⊗q for some integer q &gt; 1. A continuous adelic metric on L is invariant if this isomorphism is an isometry at every place, so pulling back along f multiplies its height exactly by q (our own explanation).

**Problem.** For such a map, invariant norms exist, and the height h that they define satisfies h(f(P)) = qh(P).

**How the definition helps.** Heights pull back with maps and add over tensor products, so an isometry f\*L ≅ L⊗q gives h(f(P)) = qh(P) with no error term (our own explanation). Arbitrary metrics give this only up to bounded error. The existence theorem builds invariant metrics by repeated pullback and taking qth roots, starting from an integral model.

**Paper or page:** [Specialization of canonical heights on abelian varieties](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.07664v1). It says: “In particular, there exists a canonical height”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Alternating Kummer products give symmetric powers

**Remember:** Alternating the relative product makes the Kummer tensors symmetric.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with K-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Over the affine line minus 0 and 1, with coordinate z, the Kummer motive K is the degree-one cohomology of the multiplicative line relative to the points 1 and 1/z. In its n-fold product, take degree-n cohomology relative to the faces where some coordinate equals 1 or 1/z, and keep the part where each swap of two coordinates acts by −1.

**Problem.** This part of the relative cohomology motive is the symmetric tensor power Symⁿ(K).

**How the definition helps.** The relative product theorem identifies the whole group with K⊗ⁿ twisted by the sign character, because swapping two degree-one classes already gives a sign (our own explanation). So the sign part is the symmetric part of K⊗ⁿ, namely Symⁿ(K).

**Paper or page:** [A construction of the polylogarithm motive](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.00789), [A construction of the polylogarithm motive](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.00789). It says: “𝒦⊗ⁿ ≃ 𝒞ₙ ⊗ sgnₙ”

**Sources:**

- [A construction of the polylogarithm motive](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.00789)

### Clean polylogarithms erase product terms

**Remember:** Project away products before taking a single-valued period.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with K-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A clean polylogarithm applies the Dynkin projection, which kills exactly the sums of products of positive-weight elements, to the de Rham image of the formal iterated integral of a multiple polylogarithm. Only then does it take the single-valued period, keeping the real part in odd weight and the imaginary part in even weight, where weight counts the integrations.

**Problem.** Suppose a rational linear combination of formal integrals of the same positive weight equals a sum of products of positive-weight elements. The corresponding clean functions then sum to zero with the same coefficients.

**How the definition helps.** A combination equal to a sum of products is killed by the projection before any number is computed, so its clean value is zero. Ordinary single-valued evaluation preserves products and can leave them nonzero (our own comparison).

**Paper or page:** [Clean Single-Valued Polylogarithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04344), [Clean Single-Valued Polylogarithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04344). It says: “The kernel of Π is generated by all non-trivial products”

**Sources:**

- [Clean Single-Valued Polylogarithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04344)

### Clean polylogarithms reverse interior letters

**Remember:** After products vanish, reversal preserves odd lengths and negates even lengths.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with K-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The clean value of a formal iterated integral with fixed endpoints applies the Dynkin projection, which kills all products, to its de Rham image and then takes the single-valued period. It keeps the real part in odd length and the imaginary part in even length.

**Problem.** In a clean iterated integral of length n &gt; 0, reversing the interior letters multiplies it by (−1)ⁿ⁺¹ without exchanging endpoints.

**How the definition helps.** The shuffle antipode identity expresses the word plus (−1)ⁿ times its reversal as a sum of products from nonempty proper cuts (our own explanation). The Dynkin projection kills those products. Evaluating the remaining two terms gives the claimed sign with unchanged endpoints.

**Paper or page:** [Clean Single-Valued Polylogarithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04344). It says: “Iᶜˢᵛ(x₀; xₙ, …, x₁; xₙ₊₁) = (−1)ⁿ⁺¹ Iᶜˢᵛ(x₀; x₁, …, xₙ; xₙ₊₁).”

**Sources:**

- [Clean Single-Valued Polylogarithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04344)

### Clean projection gives tetralogarithm reduction

**Remember:** Remove all products, then fix the constant on real inputs.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with K-theory), 33B30. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** I₃,₁(x,y) is the clean value of the nested integral from 0 to 1 with successive poles x, 0, 0, y: project the weight-four formal integral away from products of lower-weight integrals, then take the imaginary part of its single-valued value. L₄ is the clean value of the fourth polylogarithm in the same way.

**Problem.** For x,y∉{0,1}, with y∉{x,1−x} and all displayed arguments of L₄ outside {0,1}, I₃,₁(1−x,y)+I₃,₁(x,y)=L₄((1−x)/(1−y))−L₄((1−y)/x)−3L₄(y/(1−x))−3L₄(y/x)+L₄(y/(y−1))−L₄((1−x)y/(x(1−y)))/2−L₄(xy/((1−x)(1−y)))/2+L₄((1−y)y/((1−x)x))/2.

**How the definition helps.** Because products are projected away, the two sides can be compared through their symbols modulo products, and Gangl matched these symbols. Any constant left over is zero, since both sides are imaginary parts that vanish on real inputs.

**Paper or page:** [Clean Single-Valued Polylogarithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04344v2). It says: “This constant must be 0 since each side vanishes on the real line, as we take the imaginary part in the definition of the functions.”

**Sources:**

- [Steven Charlton, Claude Duhr and Herbert Gangl, Clean Single-Valued Polylogarithms (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04344v2)

### Cobrackets rule out classical tetralogarithms

**Remember:** A nonzero two-by-two split rules out a classical expression.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with K-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On polylogarithm symbols modulo products, the (2,2) cobracket of a weight-four symbol splits it after its second letter, takes both halves modulo products, and subtracts the result with the halves exchanged. Weight means tensor length.

**Problem.** The weight-(2,2) cobracket vanishes on every rational sum of classical tetralogarithm symbols modulo products. Thus a nonzero value rules out any such expression.

**How the definition helps.** The symbol of the classical tetralogarithm has a repeated logarithm as its second half, and that tensor is half the shuffle square of a logarithm, so it vanishes modulo products (our own explanation). Linearity extends this to rational sums.

**Paper or page:** [Cluster Polylogarithms I: Quadrangular Polylogarithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.01564). It says: “For $k\\geq 2$ iterated truncated coproduct $\\overline{\\Delta }<sup>\[k-1\]</sup>$ vanishes on $\\mathcal{D}<sub>k-1</sub>\\mathcal{L}\_\\bullet (\\mathrm{F})$”

**Sources:**

- [Cluster Polylogarithms I: Quadrangular Polylogarithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.01564)

### Divisor differences compare elliptic regulators

**Remember:** Equal divisor differences give equal regulator periods without integrating twice.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with K-theory), 19F27. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On an elliptic curve, the diamond product of the divisors of two functions is the formal sum of the differences P−Q, with P a zero or pole of the first and Q of the second, weighted by the product of their multiplicities. It is taken modulo \[−P\] = −\[P\].

**Problem.** Take two pairs of rational functions on an elliptic curve E over ℚ, with rational zeros and poles. Assume their symbols extend across every point. Equal diamond products give equal regulator values on a generator of H₁(E,ℤ)⁻, the subgroup where complex conjugation acts by negation.

**How the definition helps.** Bloch’s formula evaluates the regulator on the generator of H₁(E,ℤ)⁻ by applying the elliptic dilogarithm to this diamond product, so equal diamond products give equal values (our own). The elliptic dilogarithm changes sign under negation, so it respects \[−P\] = −\[P\].

**Paper or page:** [A shifted Mahler measure identity for Boyd's family](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.09974). It says: “r<sub>E</sub>(\\{ f,g\\} )\[\\gamma \]=D<sup>E</sup>((f)\\diamond (g)), \\end{align\*}where $\[\\gamma \]$ is a generator of $H<sub>1</sub>(E,\\mathbb {Z})<sup>-$</sup>.”

**Sources:**

- [A shifted Mahler measure identity for Boyd's family, Lemma 2.1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.09974)

### Five-term relations give a regulator

**Remember:** The five-term identity lets the dilogarithm act on classes of symbols.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with K-theory), 19F27. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The pre-Bloch group of a subfield F of ℂ is the free abelian group on symbols \[x\], for x in F other than 0 and 1, modulo the five-term relation \[x\]−\[y\]+\[y/x\]−\[(1−x⁻¹)/(1−y⁻¹)\]+\[(1−x)/(1−y)\] = 0 for distinct x, y.

**Problem.** The Bloch–Wigner dilogarithm D gives a homomorphism \[x\] ↦ D(x) from the pre-Bloch group to ℝ.

**How the definition helps.** A map out of a quotient is well defined once it kills the defining relations (our own explanation). The analytic five-term identity says exactly that D kills each one.

**nLab:** [dilogarithm](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/dilogarithm). It says: “The Bloch–Wigner dilogarithm is defined by D(z) ≔ Im(Li₂(z)) + arg(1−z) log\|z\|.”

**Sources:**

- [Don Zagier, Polylogarithms, Dedekind zeta functions, and the algebraic K-theory of fields (1990)](https://people.mpim-bonn.mpg.de/zagier/files/scanned/PolylogsDedekindZetaAndKTheory/fulltext.pdf)

### Integrable symbols exclude path dependence

**Remember:** Adjacent wedge tests remove the local obstruction to path independence.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with K-theory). arXiv math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On a smooth complex variety with the zeros and poles of the chosen rational functions removed, represent each function f by the form df/f and ordered lists of forms by tensors. A sum of tensors is integrable if, for each adjacent pair of positions, replacing the two forms by their wedge product and summing gives zero.

**Problem.** An integrable tensor gives a homotopy-invariant linear combination of logarithmic iterated integrals. Homotopies fix both endpoints and stay in the open variety.

**How the definition helps.** Chen’s variation formula for these closed forms has only adjacent wedge terms, so integrability makes it vanish (our own explanation). Without it, dx/x followed by dy/y from (1,1) to (2,2) gives (log 2)² moving first in x, but zero moving first in y (our own example).

**nLab:** [iterated integral](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/iterated+integral), [polylogarithm](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/polylogarithm). It says: “Iterated integrals include nested integration of differential forms”

**Sources:**

- [A. B. Goncharov, A simple construction of Grassmannian polylogarithms](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aim.2013.03.018)

### Matrix inversion gives the antipode

**Remember:** The antipode inverts the whole variation matrix.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with K-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Arrange the formal coefficients of multiple polylogarithms in their variation matrix V, triangular with ones on the diagonal. The coproduct then acts as matrix multiplication: for the transpose W, it sends Wᵢⱼ to the sum of Wᵢₖ ⊗ Wₖⱼ over k.

**Problem.** The antipode, the operation undoing a coproduct under multiplication, sends V entry by entry to V⁻¹.

**How the definition helps.** The antipode axiom then reads S(W)W = I, so S(W) = W⁻¹ (our own calculation). Transposing gives S(V) = V⁻¹, since the coefficient algebra is commutative.

**Paper or page:** [Hopf algebras of multiple polylogarithms, and holomorphic 1-forms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.08337), [Hopf algebras of multiple polylogarithms, and holomorphic 1-forms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.08337). It says: “The antipode satisfies S(V) = V⁻¹.”

**Sources:**

- [Hopf algebras of multiple polylogarithms, and holomorphic 1-forms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.08337)

### Multiplication identifies torsion logarithm fibers

**Remember:** Multiplication sends torsion to zero and rescales each graded piece invertibly.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with K-theory), 14F40. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For the fundamental group π of a complex elliptic curve at zero, take its rational group ring modulo the (n+1)st power of the ideal of sums whose coefficients add to zero. The pointed logarithm system transports this vector space along loops by multiplication and marks the element 1 at zero.

**Problem.** For N ≥ 1, multiplication by N identifies this system with its pullback, whose fiber at P is the original fiber at NP. Thus every point killed by N has a canonical identification of its fiber with the fiber at zero.

**How the definition helps.** Multiplication by N sends each loop γ to γᴺ, so it maps the truncated group ring to itself, keeps 1 and respects transport (our own argument). On degree k of the graded ring it acts by Nᵏ, which is invertible over ℚ. At a point killed by N, the pullback fibre is the fibre at zero.

**nLab:** [Poincaré line bundle](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Poincar%C3%A9+line+bundle). It says: “The canonical line bundle on the product of an abelian group (abelian variety) and its dual Picard scheme.”

**Sources:**

- [Sprang, The algebraic de Rham realization of the elliptic polylogarithm via the Poincaré bundle, Sections 2 and 4](https://doi.org/10.2140/ant.2020.14.545)

### Nested cuts make coproducts coassociative

**Remember:** Cut twice, and nested subsequences ignore which cut came first.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with K-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Goncharov’s coproduct cuts an iterated integral I(a₀; a₁,…,aₙ; aₙ₊₁) at every subsequence of its interior letters. Each term pairs the integral over the kept letters with the product of the integrals over the gaps between consecutive kept points, endpoints included.

**Problem.** Goncharov’s coproduct is coassociative. Applying it again to the first factor or to the second factor gives the same three-factor sum.

**How the definition helps.** Both double expansions sum over the same pairs of nested subsequences, so they agree term by term (our own). One side chooses the larger subsequence first, and the other chooses the smaller one and then extra letters in each gap. For the coproduct defined by periods, one first needs the theorem that it equals this cut formula.

**Paper or page:** [Hopf algebras of multiple polylogarithms, and holomorphic 1-forms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.08337). It says: “Goncharov’s coproduct is coassociative.”

**Sources:**

- [Hopf algebras of multiple polylogarithms, and holomorphic 1-forms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.08337)

### Nonzero boundaries exclude Bloch classes

**Remember:** A dilogarithm sum counts in K₃ only when its boundary vanishes.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with K-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The rational Bloch group of an infinite field F consists of rational sums ∑aᵢ\[xᵢ\] with xᵢ ≠ 0, 1, taken modulo the five-term dilogarithm relation. A sum belongs to it when its boundary ∑aᵢ xᵢ ∧ (1 − xᵢ) in the rational exterior square of F× is zero.

**Problem.** Suslin’s theorem: the rational Bloch group of F is isomorphic to rational indecomposable K₃ of F, that is, K₃(F) ⊗ ℚ modulo the image of Milnor K₃.

**How the definition helps.** Suslin’s exact sequence maps indecomposable K₃ onto the Bloch group with torsion kernel, so tensoring with ℚ gives the isomorphism. The zero-boundary condition removes symbols such as \[t\] over ℚ(t), whose boundary t ∧ (1 − t) is nonzero (our own example).

**Wikipedia:** [Bloch group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloch_group). It says: “0 \\rightarrow \\operatorname{Tor}(K<sup>\*</sup>, K<sup>\*</sup>)<sup>\\sim</sup> \\rightarrow \\operatorname{K}<sub>3</sub>(K)<sub>ind</sub> \\rightarrow \\operatorname{B}<sub>2</sub>(K) \\rightarrow 0”

**Sources:**

- [A. A. Suslin, K₃ of a field, and the Bloch group](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/tm1914)

### Orbit sums descend to elliptic curves

**Remember:** Sum over the whole orbit, so the representative does not matter.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with K-theory), 33B30. arXiv math.NT, math.CA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The elliptic curve E = ℂ×/qℤ, with 0 &lt; \|q\| &lt; 1, identifies x with qx. Its elliptic dilogarithm sums the Bloch–Wigner dilogarithm over the whole orbit: Dᴱ(x) = ∑ₖ D(qᵏx), k ∈ ℤ.

**Problem.** The orbit sum is absolutely convergent and gives a well-defined function on E. It also changes sign under x ↦ 1/x.

**How the definition helps.** Replacing x by qx only shifts the summation index, so the sum depends only on the point of E (our own). Replacing k by −k and using D(1/z) = −D(z) gives the sign change. Absolute convergence follows from D(z) = O(\|z\|(1 + \|log\|z\|\|)) near zero, and from inversion for the other tail.

**Paper or page:** [A shifted Mahler measure identity for Boyd's family](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.09974v1). It says: “The elliptic dilogarithm Dᴱ extends by linearity to a map from ℤ\[E(ℚ)\]⁻ to ℂ.”

**Sources:**

- [Don Zagier, The Bloch–Wigner–Ramakrishnan polylogarithm function (1990)](https://people.mpim-bonn.mpg.de/zagier/files/doi/10.1007/BF01453591/fulltext.pdf)
- [Quanli Yang, Hang Liu and Guoping Tang, A shifted Mahler measure identity for Boyd's family (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.09974v1)

### Orbit sums give elliptic doubling

**Remember:** Each orbit term doubles classically, so the orbit sum doubles too.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with K-theory), 14H52. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On E = ℂ×/qℤ with 0 &lt; \|q\| &lt; 1, the elliptic dilogarithm sums the Bloch–Wigner dilogarithm over the orbit: Dᴱ(z) = ∑ₙ D(qⁿz), n ∈ ℤ. Here D(z) = Im Li₂(z) + arg(1 − z) log\|z\|.

**Problem.** For every P ∈ E, twice the sum of Dᴱ(Q) over the four points with 2Q = P equals Dᴱ(P).

**How the definition helps.** The classical doubling formula D(w²) = 2(D(w) + D(−w)) applies to every orbit term (our own argument). With w² = z, the four halves are w, −w, √q w and −√q w: the first pair gives the even orbit indices and the second the odd ones. Absolute convergence lets the sums be regrouped.

**nLab:** [Feynman diagram](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Feynman+diagram). It says: “Spencer Bloch, Pierre Vanhove, The elliptic dilogarithm for the sunset graph, IHES preprint P-13-24, pdf”

**Sources:**

- [Bloch and Vanhove, The elliptic dilogarithm for the sunset graph, Appendix A](https://www.math.uchicago.edu/~bloch/mysunset/sunset.pdf)

### Path truncation makes monodromy unipotent

**Remember:** Truncate at degree n, and every loop minus one becomes nilpotent.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with K-theory). arXiv math.AG, math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Work on the projective line minus 0, 1 and ∞, with a tangential base point at 0. The degree-n truncation divides the rational group algebra of loops by Jⁿ⁺¹, where J is spanned by all γ − 1, so any n + 1 loop differences multiply to zero.

**Problem.** Continuing the finite polylogarithm system around any loop gives a unipotent operator M: some power of M − I is zero.

**How the definition helps.** Hain realizes the finite polylogarithm monodromy on a quotient of a degree-n truncation, where (γ − 1)ⁿ⁺¹ acts as zero (our own argument). Without truncation this fails: in the full completion a loop around zero maps to a generator of a cyclic quotient, and no power of its difference from one vanishes.

**Paper or page:** [Chern-Simons invariants of hyperbolic three-manifolds, mixed Tate motives, and motivic path torsor of augmented character varieties](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.11950), [Chern-Simons invariants of hyperbolic three-manifolds, mixed Tate motives, and motivic path torsor of augmented character varieties](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.11950). It says: “It has unipotent monodromy at each point of {0,1,∞}.”

**Sources:**

- [Chern-Simons invariants of hyperbolic three-manifolds, mixed Tate motives, and motivic path torsor of augmented character varieties](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.11950)
- [R. Hain, Classical polylogarithms](https://doi.org/10.1090/pspum/055.2/1265550)

### Projecting products makes relations exact

**Remember:** Project products to zero before you evaluate.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with K-theory), 33B30. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Apply to a formal polylogarithm (a formal iterated integral, graded by its number of integrations) the projection Π, whose kernel is exactly the span of products of positive-weight elements. Then evaluate as a single-valued function, keeping its real part in odd weight and its imaginary part in even weight.

**Problem.** If a rational sum of formal polylogarithms of one weight equals a sum of products of positive-weight elements, its clean single-valued evaluation is zero.

**How the definition helps.** Π kills every product, so the sum is zero before evaluation. Proposition 2.4 identifies the kernel of Π, and linearity passes from single products to sums (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Clean Single-Valued Polylogarithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04344v2). It says: “The kernel of Π is generated by all non-trivial products”

**Sources:**

- [Steven Charlton, Claude Duhr and Herbert Gangl, Clean Single-Valued Polylogarithms (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04344v2)

### Rational Bloch regulators are injective

**Remember:** Tensor with ℚ, and the dilogarithm map forgets nothing.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with K-theory), 19F27. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a number field F, the rational Bloch group consists of rational sums ∑a\[x\], x ∈ F outside {0, 1}, modulo the five-term relations. A sum belongs to it when its boundary ∑a x ∧ (1 − x) in Λ²(F× ⊗ ℚ) is zero, and rational coefficients erase all torsion.

**Problem.** Choose one embedding σ from each conjugate pair of nonreal embeddings of F. The map with coordinates ∑aD(σ(x)), where D is the Bloch–Wigner dilogarithm, is injective on the rational Bloch group.

**How the definition helps.** Every map to a real vector space kills torsion, so injectivity can only hold once rational coefficients remove it. On what remains, Borel’s regulator theorem gives injectivity, and the comparison with the dilogarithm regulator identifies the coordinates (our own).

**nLab:** [Bloch group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Bloch+group). It says: “Now the point is that restricted to the Bloch group proper the Borel regulator is injective.”

**Sources:**

- [Don Zagier, Polylogarithms, Dedekind zeta functions, and the algebraic K-theory of fields (1990)](https://people.mpim-bonn.mpg.de/zagier/files/scanned/PolylogsDedekindZetaAndKTheory/fulltext.pdf)
- [A. A. Suslin, K₃ of a field, and the Bloch group (1990)](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/tm1914)

### Regulator forms kill Steinberg relations

**Remember:** η(f, 1 − f) is exact, with the dilogarithm as primitive.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with K-theory), 19D45. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On an open set U of a smooth complex curve where f and g have no zeros or poles, the regulator form is η(f,g) = log\|f\| d arg g − log\|g\| d arg f. Its class is taken modulo differentials of single-valued functions, and η(f, 1 − f) = dD(f) for the Bloch–Wigner dilogarithm D.

**Problem.** A Steinberg symbol {f,g} is bimultiplicative and satisfies {f, 1 − f} = 0. Sending it to the class of η(f,g) gives a well-defined map to closed real 1-forms on U modulo exact ones.

**How the definition helps.** The Steinberg relation goes to the class of dD(f), which is zero. Roy proves that η is closed and bimultiplicative, so the other relations hold as well.

**Paper or page:** [Generalized Mahler measures of Laurent polynomials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.04601). It says: “\\eta \\left(x, 1-x\\right) = d D\\left(x\\right).”

**Sources:**

- [Generalized Mahler measures of Laurent polynomials, Lemma 2.1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.04601)

### Residues identify elliptic polylogarithms

**Remember:** Fix the residues at the torsion points, and the class is fixed.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with K-theory), 14F40. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On a complex elliptic curve, remove the D² points of order dividing D, for D ≥ 2. The elliptic polylogarithm is the compatible sequence of degree-one classes, with coefficients in the logarithm sheaf, whose residue is D² − 1 at zero and −1 at each other removed point. The logarithm sheaf transports truncated power series in two loop variables along paths.

**Problem.** Exactly one compatible sequence has these residues, so the elliptic polylogarithm is well defined. The residues are read through the splitting at each removed point given by multiplication by D, and have zero components in all positive degrees.

**How the definition helps.** Sprang’s exact sequence shows that, over all truncations together, a class is fixed by its residues, and that residues occur when their scalar parts sum to zero (our own reading). Here (D² − 1) − (D² − 1) = 0. Sprang then computes residues of explicit forms from the Poincaré line bundle to represent the class.

**nLab:** [Poincaré line bundle](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Poincar%C3%A9+line+bundle). It says: “The canonical line bundle on the product of an abelian group (abelian variety) and its dual Picard scheme.”

**Sources:**

- [Sprang, The algebraic de Rham realization of the elliptic polylogarithm via the Poincaré bundle, Definition 3.2 and Theorem 5.8](https://doi.org/10.2140/ant.2020.14.545)

### Steinberg symbols yield elliptic identities

**Remember:** Diamond the divisors of f and 1 − f, and get zero.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with K-theory), 19D45. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For rational functions f and g on an elliptic curve, the diamond product (f) ⋄ (g) sums P − Q over each zero or pole P of f and Q of g, weighted by the product of signed multiplicities. A point and its negative carry opposite signs. Bloch’s formula says the regulator of the Steinberg symbol {f,g} is Dᴱ((f) ⋄ (g)).

**Problem.** Take a nonconstant rational function f on an elliptic curve over ℚ. Assume its zeros, its poles and all points where f equals one are rational. Applying the elliptic dilogarithm linearly to div(f) ⋄ div(1−f) gives zero.

**How the definition helps.** Every Steinberg symbol satisfies {f, 1 − f} = 0, so its regulator is zero. Bloch’s formula equates that regulator with Dᴱ((f) ⋄ (1 − f)) (our own proof).

**Paper or page:** [A shifted Mahler measure identity for Boyd's family](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.09974). It says: “r<sub>E</sub>(\\{ f,g\\} )\[\\gamma \]=D<sup>E</sup>((f)\\diamond (g)), \\end{align\*}where $\[\\gamma \]$ is a generator of $H<sub>1</sub>(E,\\mathbb {Z})<sup>-$</sup>.”

**Sources:**

- [A shifted Mahler measure identity for Boyd's family, Lemma 2.1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.09974)
- [Yang, Liu and Tang, A Mahler Measure Identity Involving a Genus 2 Family, Section 1](https://ccj.pku.edu.cn/Article/DownLoad?id=364490499&type=ArticleFile)

### Three terms compute next-to-Milnor cohomology

**Remember:** Next to the top degree, cohomology is a kernel modulo trilogarithm images.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with K-theory), 19E15. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a field F of characteristic zero, m ≥ 3 and V = F× ⊗ ℚ, Goncharov’s complex has B₂(F) ⊗ Λᵐ⁻²V in degree m − 1, with B₂(F) the rational dilogarithm symbols modulo their relations. Its outgoing differential sends \[x\]₂ ⊗ β to (1 − x) ∧ x ∧ β. Its incoming boundaries are the trilogarithm images \[x\]₂ ⊗ (x ∧ α).

**Problem.** Take the kernel of this differential modulo the span of \[x\]₂ ⊗ (x ∧ α), for x ∈ F outside {0, 1} and α ∈ Λᵐ⁻³V. It is the rational motivic cohomology of F in degree m − 1 and weight m, defined using algebraic cycles.

**How the definition helps.** The complex makes this cohomology one explicit kernel modulo one explicit family of boundaries (our own). Bolbachan’s comparison theorem identifies the result with motivic cohomology defined using algebraic cycles.

**Wikipedia:** [Goncharov conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goncharov_conjecture). It says: “Goncharov defined the following complex called Γ(F,n) placed in degrees \[1,n\]”

**Paper or page:** [On Goncharov's conjecture in next to Milnor degree](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06271). It says: “is true when i = m − 1 and m ∈ ℤ, m ≥ 2.”

**Sources:**

- [On Goncharov's conjecture in next to Milnor degree](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06271)

### Top polylogarithm cohomology gives Milnor K-theory

**Remember:** The last differential’s image is exactly the Steinberg relations.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with K-theory), 19D45. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For an infinite field F, V = F× ⊗ ℚ and m ≥ 2, Goncharov’s last differential maps B₂(F) ⊗ Λᵐ⁻²V to ΛᵐV by \[x\] ⊗ α ↦ (1 − x) ∧ x ∧ α. Here B₂(F) is the rational dilogarithm symbol space modulo five-term relations. Its image is the span of the wedges containing a pair 1 − x, x (our own).

**Problem.** For m ≥ 2, the top cohomology of this complex is the rational Milnor K-group of F in degree m.

**How the definition helps.** Rational Milnor K-theory in degree m is ΛᵐV modulo the wedges containing a pair 1 − x, x (our own). Top cohomology is ΛᵐV modulo the image of the last differential, which is the same span.

**Wikipedia:** [Goncharov conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goncharov_conjecture). It says: “Goncharov defined the following complex called Γ(F,n) placed in degrees \[1,n\]”

**Sources:**

- [A. B. Goncharov, Geometry of configurations, polylogarithms, and motivic cohomology](https://doi.org/10.1006/aima.1995.1045)

### Truncated cuts vanish in lower depth

**Remember:** Each surviving factor must spend a nonzero letter.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with K-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A formal iterated integral class has depth at most d if, modulo products, words with at most d nonzero interior letters represent it. The truncated cobracket drops every term of the cobracket with a weight-one factor, so each surviving factor needs a nonzero letter.

**Problem.** For k ≥ 2, this k-factor operation vanishes on classes of depth at most k − 1. On depth k its value therefore depends only on the class modulo lower depth.

**How the definition helps.** Depth-zero factors are powers of logarithms: truncation removes the weight-one ones, and the others are products, which vanish (our own). So k surviving factors use k nonzero letters, while the cut formula keeps total depth at most the input depth. Inputs of depth k − 1 therefore give zero.

**Paper or page:** [Cluster Polylogarithms I: Quadrangular Polylogarithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.01564). It says: “For $k\\geq 2$ iterated truncated coproduct $\\overline{\\Delta }<sup>\[k-1\]</sup>$ vanishes on $\\mathcal{D}<sub>k-1</sub>\\mathcal{L}\_\\bullet (\\mathrm{F})$”

**Sources:**

- [Cluster Polylogarithms I: Quadrangular Polylogarithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.01564)

### Weight frames split the dilogarithm

**Remember:** One middle weight, one cut: log(1 − z) ⊗ log z.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with K-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Represent the dilogarithm by its framed period matrix, a triangular matrix whose entries next to the diagonal are, in units of the diagonal periods, log(1 − z) and log z. The reduced coproduct cuts the frame at each intermediate weight and pairs the two pieces, and the dilogarithm has only weight one in between.

**Problem.** For z ∈ ℂ outside {0,1}, the reduced coproduct is log(1 − z) ⊗ log z. Each logarithm represents a class modulo 2πiℤ in the integral normalization.

**How the definition helps.** With one intermediate weight there is one cut, and it pairs the two entries next to the diagonal (our own). The scalar Li₂(z) alone does not record both. Building the period matrix and proving independence of the basis are the real work.

**Paper or page:** [Chern-Simons invariants of hyperbolic three-manifolds, mixed Tate motives, and motivic path torsor of augmented character varieties](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.11950), [Chern-Simons invariants of hyperbolic three-manifolds, mixed Tate motives, and motivic path torsor of augmented character varieties](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.11950). It says: “log(1 − z) ⊗ log(z)”

**Sources:**

- [Chern-Simons invariants of hyperbolic three-manifolds, mixed Tate motives, and motivic path torsor of augmented character varieties](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.11950)

### Weight-one symbols multiply by shuffling

**Remember:** A symbol lists weight-one pieces, and products shuffle the lists.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with K-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The symbol of a weight-n formal polylogarithm is its iterated coproduct into n factors, each projected to weight one. The shuffle product of two tensors sums all interleavings that keep the order within each.

**Problem.** The symbol of a product equals the shuffle product of the two symbols.

**How the definition helps.** The coproduct is multiplicative, so each weight-one slot of a product’s symbol takes weight one from one factor and a scalar from the other (our own). Choosing which slots come from the first factor gives every shuffle once.

**Paper or page:** [Hopf algebras of multiple polylogarithms, and holomorphic 1-forms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.08337). It says: “Δ₁,…,₁ is a morphism of graded Hopf algebras.”

**Sources:**

- [Hopf algebras of multiple polylogarithms, and holomorphic 1-forms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.08337)

### Fourier signs bound lattice packing

**Remember:** One sign controls the lattice and the other controls its dual.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11H31 (Lattice packing and covering (number-theoretic aspects)), 11H60. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An admissible function for radius r is a real radial Schwartz function f on ℝⁿ with f(x) ≤ 0 for ‖x‖ ≥ r and f(0) = f̂(0) &gt; 0. Its Fourier transform f̂(ξ) = ∫ f(x) exp(−2πix·ξ) dx must be ≥ 0 everywhere.

**Problem.** If such a function exists, any lattice packing by balls of radius r/2 has density at most the volume of one such ball. For a unit-covolume lattice with shortest length r, the bound is sharp.

**How the definition helps.** On a lattice with minimal distance r the signs give ∑ f(v) ≤ f(0), and on its dual ∑ f̂(u) ≥ f̂(0) (our own). Poisson summation makes the first sum the second divided by the covolume, so the covolume is at least one. Density is ball volume over covolume, which gives the bound.

**Paper or page:** [Algebraic proof of modular form inequalities for optimal sphere packings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.14659v3). It says: “f(0) = f̂(0) &gt; 0”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Short vectors encode Littlewood’s conjecture

**Remember:** Diagonal scaling turns small products into short lattice vectors.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11H46 (Products of linear forms), 11J13. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For real α and β, the lattice Λ of all (qα − p, qβ − r, q) with p, r, q ∈ ℤ records both approximation errors and their common denominator. Its forward orbit is the set of diag(a, b, 1/(ab))Λ for a, b ≥ 1, and each such map keeps the product of the three coordinates.

**Problem.** Let d(t) denote the distance to the nearest integer. The lower limit of q·d(qα)·d(qβ) over positive integers q is zero exactly when this orbit has noncompact closure.

**How the definition helps.** Diagonal maps keep the coordinate product, so a small q·d(qα)·d(qβ) becomes a short nonzero vector in the orbit (our own). The dynamical correspondence for Littlewood’s conjecture makes this exact. Mahler’s compactness criterion turns arbitrarily short vectors into noncompact closure.

**Wikipedia:** [Littlewood conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Littlewood_conjecture). It says: “failure of Littlewood's conjecture corresponds to relative compactness of the orbit”

**Sources:**

- [Manfred Einsiedler, Anatole Katok and Elon Lindenstrauss, Invariant measures and the set of exceptions to Littlewood’s conjecture](https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2006.164.513)

### Shortest vectors test extreme packings

**Remember:** Minimal vectors pin down the form and balance its inverse.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11H55 (Quadratic forms (reduction theory, extreme forms, etc.)), 11H31. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take the minimal vectors of a positive definite form Q, the nonzero integer vectors v with the smallest value vᵀQv. Q is perfect if the matrices vvᵀ span all symmetric matrices, so these lengths pin down Q (our own). Q is eutactic if Q⁻¹ = ∑ λᵥvvᵀ with every λᵥ &gt; 0.

**Problem.** A lattice packing has locally maximal density among lattice packings exactly when its form is perfect and eutactic.

**How the definition helps.** The two conditions replace comparison with all nearby packings by two linear tests on the minimal vectors (our own). Voronoi’s theorem proves that together they characterize a local maximum of density.

**Paper or page:** [The lattice packing problem in dimension 9 by Voronoi's algorithm](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.20719v1). It says: “is extreme if and only if it is perfect and eutactic.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Critical lattices detect Dirichlet improvement

**Remember:** Better approximation keeps the moving lattice away from the critical locus.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11J13 (Simultaneous homogeneous approximation, linear forms), 11H06. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix a plane norm ν and put η(u,t) = max(ν(u), \|t\|) on ℝ³. Follow the lattice of all (exp(s)(p − qx), exp(−2s)q) with p ∈ ℤ², q ∈ ℤ, s ≥ 0, which turns good approximations of x into short vectors (our own). The critical locus is the set of unit-covolume lattices whose shortest nonzero η-length is as large as possible.

**Problem.** Call x uniformly improvable if, for some c below the sharp universal bound and all large T, there are integers 1 ≤ q ≤ T and p ∈ ℤ² with Tν(qx − p)² ≤ c. This holds exactly when the moving lattice eventually avoids a neighborhood of the critical locus.

**How the definition helps.** The scaling turns the two bounds on q and on ν(qx − p) into one test of shortest η-length (our own). By Mahler’s compactness criterion, lattices with shortest length bounded below form a compact set (our own). So avoiding a neighborhood of the maximizers means a uniform gap below the maximum (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Abundance of Dirichlet-improvable pairs with respect to arbitrary norms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.10298v2), [Abundance of Dirichlet-improvable pairs with respect to arbitrary norms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.10298v2). It says: “x ∈ DIν if and only if the forward aₛ-orbit of Λₓ eventually avoids an open neighborhood of ℒη”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Geodesic heights order quadratic roots

**Remember:** Each root is a geodesic top; small moduli give high tops.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11J71 (Distribution modulo one). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For squarefree D &gt; 1 with D ≢ 1 modulo 4, each solution r of r² ≡ D modulo m gives the hyperbolic semicircle with endpoints (r ± √D)/m. Its top lies at horizontal position r/m and height √D/m, so the cutoff m ≤ X becomes height at least √D/X (our own).

**Problem.** Take the fractions r/m with 1 ≤ m ≤ X, one representative 0 ≤ r &lt; m per solution, counted with repetition. As X grows, the fraction of them in each fixed arc approaches the length of the arc.

**How the definition helps.** Theorem 5.1 identifies these semicircles with lifts of finitely many closed geodesics on the modular surface. Corollary 2.7 counts geodesic tops above a given height in an arc, with leading term proportional to the arc length. Dividing by the total count cancels the constant (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Fine-scale distribution of roots of quadratic congruences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.02854v3), [Fine-scale distribution of roots of quadratic congruences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.02854v3). It says: “For a finite interval I ⊂ ℝ, 1 ≤ α &lt; β ≤ ∞ and probability measure λ with bounded density”

**Sources:**

- [J. Marklof and M. Welsh, Fine-scale distribution of roots of quadratic congruences](https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2022-0081)

### Independent coordinate functions prevent diagonal concentration

**Remember:** No nonzero character sees a constant polynomial phase.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11J71 (Distribution modulo one). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Real polynomials p₁, …, pₖ are independent modulo constants if no nonzero real linear combination of them is constant, so every nonzero integer combination P is a nonconstant polynomial.

**Problem.** Let p₁, …, pₖ be independent modulo constants and let aₙ be distinct integers. For almost every real x, the fraction of the vectors (aₙp₁(x), …, aₙpₖ(x)) modulo one in each box approaches the volume of the box.

**How the definition helps.** Weyl’s criterion reduces the claim to equidistribution of aₙP(x) for each nonzero integer combination P. Each P is nonconstant, so it has local differentiable inverses away from finitely many critical points, and the one-dimensional metric theorem applies for almost every x. Countably many P leave a null set, while a dependence such as p₁ = p₂ would confine the vectors to the diagonal (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Metric uniform distribution on analytic curves](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.06909v1). It says: “The set {1, p₁, …, pₖ} is linearly independent over ℝ.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Macroscopic pair counts detect uniformity

**Remember:** Pair differences square each Fourier coefficient of the points.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11J71 (Distribution modulo one). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The pair measure of N circle points gives each of the N² ordered differences xᵢ − xⱼ modulo one mass 1/N², tested on fixed arcs. Its Fourier coefficient at frequency k is \|(1/N) ∑ⱼ exp(2πikxⱼ)\|².

**Problem.** The fraction of ordered differences in every arc approaches its length exactly when the original sequence has the same property. Omitting pairs with equal indices gives the same equivalence.

**How the definition helps.** So the pair measure’s Fourier coefficients tend to zero exactly when those of the points do (our own). Weyl’s criterion turns both limits into uniform distribution. The N equal-index pairs have total mass 1/N, so omitting them does not change the limits.

**Paper or page:** [Weak Poissonian Correlations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.11813v1). It says: “The sequence (xₙ) is uniformly distributed mod 1.”

**Sources:**

- [Weak Poissonian Correlations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.11813v1)

### Period torsors bound transcendence degree

**Remember:** The group dimension caps the number of independent periods.

*True by definition.* MSC 11J81 (Transcendence (general theory)), 14C15, 14F40. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a Nori motive over ℚ, the period torsor is the space of comparisons between its de Rham and Betti cohomology that respect every map and tensor operation in the category it generates. After extending scalars, the motivic Galois group acts on it freely and transitively, so both have the same dimension.

**Problem.** The number of algebraically independent entries of the actual comparison matrix is at most the dimension of the motivic Galois group of the motive.

**How the definition helps.** The actual comparison is one complex point of this torsor, and its matrix entries are coordinate values there. A point’s coordinates have transcendence degree at most the dimension of the space containing it (our own argument). Tensor reconstruction supplies the torsor structure, so that dimension is the dimension of the motivic Galois group.

**Paper or page:** [Functional Transcendence of Periods and the Geometric André–Grothendieck Period Conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.05182v2). It says: “The scheme Spec ℙ̃(k) is naturally a torsor for the motivic Galois group Gₘₒₜ(k, γ) base-changed to k.”

**Sources:**

- [Huber and Müller-Stach, Periods and Nori Motives](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-319-50926-6)

### Quotients bound p-adic period fields

**Remember:** Subtract the symmetry that fixes the embedded classes.

*True by definition.* MSC 11J81 (Transcendence (general theory)), 14F40. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix a pure motive M over ℚ̄ in Ancona and Fratila’s category, with good reduction at a chosen prime above p. Its period space parametrizes the embeddings of specialized algebraic cycle classes into de Rham cohomology before reduction that respect all maps and tensor products in the category generated by M. GdR acts on this space, with stabilizer Gcrys.

**Problem.** The transcendence degree of André’s p-adic periods over ℚ̄ is at most dim GdR − dim Gcrys. These are the tensor symmetry groups of de Rham cohomology before reduction and of crystalline cohomology after reduction.

**How the definition helps.** André’s periods are coordinates of one point of the period space, so their transcendence degree is at most its dimension (our own argument). The homogeneous-space theorem computes that dimension as dim GdR − dim Gcrys.

**Paper or page:** [Algebraic classes in mixed characteristic and André's p-adic periods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.09213v2). It says: “trdegℚ̄ 𝒫ₚ(M) ≤ trdegℚ̄ 𝒫ₚ(⟨M⟩) ≤ dim GdR(M) − dim Gcrys(M).”

**Sources:**

- [Giuseppe Ancona, Dragos Fratila, Algebraic classes in mixed characteristic and André's p-adic periods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.09213v2)

### Relative periods isolate moving relations

**Remember:** Fix the constant motives before testing relations among moving periods.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11J81 (Transcendence (general theory)), 14F40. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix a finitely generated extension k of ℂ and a Zariski-dense real analytic arc on a model of k extending past both endpoints. Relative comparisons are tensor isomorphisms between de Rham and Betti realizations that agree with the usual comparison on every constant object, and the relative formal period ring is their coordinate ring.

**Problem.** Evaluation identifies the relative formal period ring with the ring of analytic period germs. A germ records a function only near the chosen arc point.

**How the definition helps.** Fixing the constant comparisons leaves only relations among the varying periods to test (our own interpretation). Injectivity of evaluation says that a formal relation holds whenever it vanishes on the germs. Bakker and Tsimerman prove injectivity with their functional transcendence theorem.

**Paper or page:** [Functional Transcendence of Periods and the Geometric André–Grothendieck Period Conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.05182v2). It says: “The relative period ring ℙ̃(k/ℂ) is an integral domain, and the evaluation map evₖ is an isomorphism.”

**Sources:**

- [Ben Bakker, Jacob Tsimerman, Functional Transcendence of Periods and the Geometric André–Grothendieck Period Conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.05182v2)

### Counting only reduced fractions frees multiplicative Khintchine from monotonicity

**Remember:** Count each rational point once, and monotonicity is no longer needed.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11J83 (Metric theory), 11J13. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Approximate α ∈ ℝᵏ by reduced fractions p₁/q, …, pₖ/q, each numerator coprime to the common denominator q, and measure the error as the product of the k errors \|αᵢ − pᵢ/q\|. Coprimality counts each rational point once and leaves φ(q) numerators per coordinate.

**Problem.** Let ψ map positive integers to \[0, 1/2\]. Almost every α has infinitely many reduced approximations with product error at most ψ(q)/qᵏ exactly when ∑<sub>q≥1</sub> ψ(q)(φ(q)/q)ᵏ(log(q/(φ(q)ψ(q))))ᵏ⁻¹ diverges, with φ Euler’s totient and terms with ψ(q) = 0 read as zero.

**How the definition helps.** Counting only reduced fractions produces the totient weight (φ(q)/q)ᵏ in the series (our own). The multiplicative Duffin–Schaeffer theorem supplies overlap estimates that prove the divergence case without monotonicity.

**Paper or page:** [The Duffin-Schaeffer Conjecture for multiplicative Diophantine approximation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.11257v1). It says: “The recent result of Koukoulopoulos and Maynard provides an elegant way of removing monotonicity when only counting reduced fractions.”

**Sources:**

- [Lorenz Frühwirth, Manuel Hauke, The Duffin-Schaeffer Conjecture for multiplicative Diophantine approximation, arXiv:2403.11257v1 (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.11257v1)
- [R. J. Duffin, A. C. Schaeffer, Khintchine’s problem in metric Diophantine approximation, Duke Mathematical Journal 8(2), 243–255 (1941)](https://doi.org/10.1215/S0012-7094-41-00818-9)

### Reduced fractions remove monotonicity from Khintchine's theorem

**Remember:** Count each fraction once, in lowest terms, and monotonicity is not needed.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11J83 (Metric theory), 11J04. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix a positive function f on the positive integers. A reduced approximation to α is p/q with q &gt; 0, gcd(p,q) = 1 and \|α − p/q\| &lt; f(q)/q. There are φ(q) such centers per unit interval, which gives the test series ∑ φ(q)f(q)/q.

**Problem.** For every f, almost every real α has infinitely many reduced approximations exactly when ∑ φ(q)f(q)/q diverges. Khintchine’s test without coprimality needs f monotone, since Duffin and Schaeffer found a non-monotone f whose series diverges while almost no α is approximable.

**How the definition helps.** The totient series is the total length of the reduced target intervals, up to a factor 2 (our own). Convergence then gives the null case by Borel–Cantelli (our own). The Duffin–Schaeffer theorem of Koukoulopoulos and Maynard proves the divergence case for arbitrary f.

**Wikipedia:** [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duffin–Schaeffer<sub>theorem</sub>](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/https%3A//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duffin%E2%80%93Schaeffer_theorem). It says: “has infinitely many solutions in coprime integers p,q with q &gt; 0 if and only if”

**Paper or page:** [General Duffin--Schaeffer-type counterexamples in diophantine approximation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16565), [Independence inheritance and Diophantine approximation for systems of linear forms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.03929). It says: “Duffin and Schaeffer provided a famous counterexample to show that Khintchine's theorem fails without monotonicity assumption.”

**Sources:**

- [Sam Chow, Manuel Hauke, Andrew Pollington, Felipe A. Ramírez, General Duffin--Schaeffer-type counterexamples in diophantine approximation, arXiv:2504.16565 (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16565)
- [R. J. Duffin, A. C. Schaeffer, Khintchine's problem in metric Diophantine approximation, Duke Mathematical Journal (1941)](https://doi.org/10.1215/s0012-7094-41-00818-9)
