### Unshifted pair correlations force uniformity

**Remember:** At zero shift the density pairs with itself.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11K06 (General theory of distribution modulo 1), 11K38. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Count ordered pairs of distinct indices i, j ≤ N with xᵢ − xⱼ within circular distance s/N of a shift γ. A circle sequence has Poissonian pair correlation at γ if this count divided by N tends to 2s for every s &gt; 0.

**Problem.** Poissonian pair correlation at shift zero forces uniform distribution, so each interval gets a limiting fraction of points equal to its length. For every nonzero shift, some sequence has Poissonian pair correlation at that shift but is not uniformly distributed.

**How the definition helps.** At shift zero the statistic compares the point density with itself, which forces the density to be constant (our own). The unshifted pair correlation theorem makes this exact. The cited shifted construction gives a nonuniform sequence for each nonzero shift.

**Paper or page:** [On Inhomogeneous Poissonian Pair Correlations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16542v1), [On Inhomogeneous Poissonian Pair Correlations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16542v1). It says: “that has γ-PPC but is not uniformly distributed.”

**Sources:**

- [On Inhomogeneous Poissonian Pair Correlations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16542v1)

### Anchored variation gives exact quadrature error

**Remember:** A function mixes boxes, so its error mixes box errors.

*True by definition.* MSC 11K38 (Irregularities of distribution, discrepancy). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The variation of f on \[0,1)ᵈ is the least total mass of a finite signed measure ν on (0,1\]ᵈ with f(x) = c + ∫ 1\[x ∈ \[0,t)\] dν(t). So f is a constant plus a signed mixture of anchored boxes \[0,t), the points below t in every coordinate.

**Problem.** The largest absolute integration error, sample average minus integral, over functions of variation at most one equals the star discrepancy. Star discrepancy is the largest absolute difference between sample fraction and volume over the boxes \[0,t).

**How the definition helps.** Integration error is the ν-integral of box errors, so it is at most the mass of ν times the star discrepancy, and the infimum gives the upper bound (our own). A unit point mass at one box gives that box’s error exactly, so the supremum reaches the star discrepancy.

**Wikipedia:** [Low-discrepancy sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low-discrepancy_sequence). It says: “The Koksma–Hlawka inequality is sharp in the following sense”

**Sources:**

- [C. Aistleitner and J. Dick, Functions of bounded variation, signed measures, and a general Koksma–Hlawka inequality (2015)](https://doi.org/10.4064/aa167-2-4)

### Dual digital nets retain exactly surviving frequencies

**Remember:** A Walsh frequency survives precisely when its induced input frequency is zero.

*True by definition.* MSC 11K38 (Irregularities of distribution, discrepancy). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A binary digital net sends every u ∈ {0,1}ᵐ to the point whose coordinate j has binary digits Cⱼu modulo two, followed by zeros. On the net, the Walsh function of a mask k reads (−1) raised to w·u, with w = ∑ⱼ Cⱼᵀkⱼ modulo two over the digit positions present. The dual net is the set of masks with w = 0.

**Problem.** The sample average of a Walsh function equals one for dual masks and zero otherwise. For an absolutely convergent series of Walsh functions, sample average minus uniform integral equals the sum of coefficients at nonzero dual masks.

**How the definition helps.** Averaging (−1) raised to w·u over all u gives one if w = 0 and zero otherwise (our own). Absolute convergence permits termwise averaging. Only the constant Walsh function has nonzero integral, so the error is the sum of coefficients at nonzero dual masks.

**Paper or page:** [Optimal periodic L²-discrepancy and diaphony bounds for higher order digital sequences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.05747v1). It says: “and where 𝒟 is the so-called dual net”

**Sources:**

- [Optimal periodic L²-discrepancy and diaphony bounds for higher order digital sequences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.05747v1)

### Extreme discrepancy removes lower-dimensional Haar terms

**Remember:** Taking differences of both box ends discards terms that ignore a coordinate.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11K38 (Irregularities of distribution, discrepancy). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let F(t) be the sample fraction in \[0,t) minus its volume. Center F in each coordinate in turn, subtracting its average over that coordinate, and call the result G. Centering removes only parts that ignore some coordinate, and these cancel in every box error.

**Problem.** For a box \[a,b), take its error as the sample fraction minus the volume. The integral of the squared error over all endpoint pairs with a ≤ b in every coordinate equals ∫\|G(t)\|² dt over the unit cube.

**How the definition helps.** A box error is the alternating sum of F over the box’s corners, where parts ignoring a coordinate cancel, so G gives the same box errors (our own). For mean-zero g on \[0,1\], integrating \|g(b) − g(a)\|² over a ≤ b gives ∫\|g\|². Apply this in each coordinate to G.

**Paper or page:** [Point sets with optimal order of extreme and periodic discrepancy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.05781v1). It says: “and D its anchored discrepancy function with Haar coefficients”

**Sources:**

- [Point sets with optimal order of extreme and periodic discrepancy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.05781v1)

### Greedy squared error gives uniform distribution

**Remember:** Each new point goes where the squared box error grows least.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11K38 (Irregularities of distribution, discrepancy). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Choose each new point to minimize ∫ (count in \[0,t) − N·vol\[0,t))² dt over the unit cube, where \[0,t) holds the points below t in every coordinate.

**Problem.** From any fixed nonempty finite starting list, the root mean square count error divided by N is O(N⁻¹⁄²). The fraction of points in each box approaches its volume.

**How the definition helps.** Averaged over a uniformly random next point, the cross term vanishes and each box’s squared error grows by at most one (our own). So the greedy choice adds at most one per step, and after N steps the integral is O(N) (our own). The root mean square error over N is then O(N⁻¹ᐟ²), and the cited theorem gives uniform distribution.

**Paper or page:** [Uniformly distributed sequences generated by a greedy minimization of the L² discrepancy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.06298v4). It says: “is uniformly distributed modulo 1.”

**Sources:**

- [Uniformly distributed sequences generated by a greedy minimization of the L² discrepancy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.06298v4)

### Index coordinates transfer discrepancy bounds

**Remember:** A box in the new coordinate selects a block of the old sequence.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11K38 (Irregularities of distribution, discrepancy). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Lift N points of \[0,1)ᵈ into \[0,1)ᵈ⁺¹ by attaching j/N to the jth point, counting from zero, so a box in the new coordinate selects a block of consecutive points (our own). Extreme L² discrepancy is the square root of the integral, over all boxes \[a,b) with a ≤ b, of the squared difference between actual and expected count.

**Problem.** For every infinite sequence in the d-dimensional unit cube, infinitely many prefixes have extreme L² discrepancy at least c(d)(log N)ᵈ⁄². Here N is the prefix length and c(d) is positive.

**How the definition helps.** A block is the difference of two prefixes, so the lifted discrepancy is at most twice the largest prefix discrepancy plus two from rounding (our own). The lower bound for finite point sets in dimension d + 1 makes the lifted discrepancy at least a constant times (log N)ᵈᐟ² (our own). Hence some prefix is that large for infinitely many N (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Exact order of extreme Lᵖ discrepancy of infinite sequences in arbitrary dimension](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.06461v1), [Point sets with optimal order of extreme and periodic discrepancy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.05781v1). It says: “for infinitely many N ∈ ℕ.”

**Sources:**

- [Exact order of extreme Lᵖ discrepancy of infinite sequences in arbitrary dimension](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.06461v1)

### Interlaced digits raise digital net order

**Remember:** Interlacing pushes the largest input digits up by nearly a factor α.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11K38 (Irregularities of distribution, discrepancy). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Interlacing of factor α merges each group of α coordinates of a binary digital net into one coordinate. It places digit j of coordinate r at position α(j − 1) + r, for 1 ≤ r ≤ α. The order-α weight of a dual mask, a digit selection with even sum on every input, adds its α largest selected positions in each coordinate.

**Problem.** Suppose every nonzero dual mask of the original αd-dimensional net has order one weight greater than m−t′. Every nonzero dual mask of the interlaced d-dimensional net then has order α weight greater than αm−αt′−dα(α−1)/2.

**How the definition helps.** Splitting an output dual mask back gives an input dual mask (our own). Each input coordinate’s leading position j moves to αj − (α − r), so each group’s α largest positions lose at most α(α − 1)/2 against α times the old leaders. Summing over the d groups gives the bound.

**Paper or page:** [Optimal periodic L²-discrepancy and diaphony bounds for higher order digital sequences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.05747v1). It says: “is an order 1 digital (t′, αd)-sequence over ℤ₂”

**Sources:**

- [Optimal periodic L²-discrepancy and diaphony bounds for higher order digital sequences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.05747v1)

### Low discrepancy forces mesoscopic counts

**Remember:** At a wider scale, each point sees the expected number of neighbors.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11K38 (Irregularities of distribution, discrepancy). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For 0 &lt; β &lt; 1 and s &gt; 0, count ordered pairs of distinct indices i, j ≤ N whose points lie within circular distance s/Nᵝ, and divide by N²⁻ᵝ. The radius is wider than the typical gap 1/N, so each arc should hold about 2sN¹⁻ᵝ points (our own).

**Problem.** Suppose the largest absolute difference between sample fraction and length over all arcs is o(N⁻ᵝ). Then the normalized count tends to 2s for every fixed s &gt; 0.

**How the definition helps.** Discrepancy o(N⁻ᵝ) is smaller than the arc length 2s/Nᵝ, so every arc, whatever its center, holds 2sN¹⁻ᵝ + o(N¹⁻ᵝ) points (our own). Summing over the N centers counts ordered pairs, and the N self-pairs do not affect the limit (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Weak Poissonian box correlations of higher order](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.11105v2). It says: “Then the sequence has (k, β)-Poissonian box correlations”

**Sources:**

- [Weak Poissonian box correlations of higher order](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.11105v2)

### Normalized height lets roots reflect

**Remember:** Reflect through the unit circle without changing angles or normalized height.

*True by definition.* MSC 11K38 (Irregularities of distribution, discrepancy). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a monic polynomial P with P(0) ≠ 0, the normalized height is h(P) = ∫₀¹ log⁺(\|P(exp(2πit))\|/√\|P(0)\|) dt, with log⁺ the positive part of the logarithm. Dividing by √\|P(0)\| makes each root factor \|z − r\|/√\|r\|, which on \|z\| = 1 does not change when r is replaced by 1/r̄.

**Problem.** Replacing each root r outside the unit disk by 1/r̄ preserves the height and every angular sector count. So the angular count bound 4√(Nh(P)/π) for degree N reduces to polynomials with all roots in the closed unit disk.

**How the definition helps.** Reflection keeps each root factor and each root argument, so it keeps the boundary modulus, the height and the sector counts (our own). The estimate for roots in the disk then applies.

**Paper or page:** [Hilbert transforms and the equidistribution of zeros of polynomials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.00105v4). It says: “If P is a monic polynomial of degree N with P(0) ≠ 0, then 𝒟(P) ≤ (4/√π)√(N h(P)).”

**Sources:**

- [E. Carneiro et al., Hilbert transforms and the equidistribution of zeros of polynomials (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfa.2021.109199)

### Pure eigenvalues bound hyper-Kloosterman sums

**Remember:** The sum is a signed trace of r eigenvalues of the same size.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11L05 (Gauss and Kloosterman sums; generalizations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a prime p, r ≥ 3 and a ∈ 𝔽ₚˣ, the hyper-Kloosterman sum Kᵣ(a) sums exp(2πi(x₁ + ⋯ + xᵣ)/p) over tuples in (𝔽ₚˣ)ʳ with product a. By the trace formula it is a signed trace of Frobenius on compactly supported cohomology, which is pure of weight w when every eigenvalue has absolute value p raised to w/2.

**Problem.** The absolute value of Kᵣ(a) is at most r times p to the power (r−1)/2.

**How the definition helps.** Deligne shows that only degree r − 1 contributes, that it has dimension r, and that it is pure of weight r − 1. So Kᵣ(a) is up to sign a sum of r numbers of absolute value p raised to (r − 1)/2, and the triangle inequality gives the bound (our own final step).

**Paper or page:** [The sixth moment of Dirichlet L-functions at the central point](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.01457v1). It says: “where the hyper-Kloosterman sum”

**Sources:**

- [Pierre Deligne, Applications de la formule des traces aux sommes trigonométriques, SGA 4½, section 7 (1977)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BFb0091523)

### Rank and purity bound Kloosterman sums

**Remember:** Rank counts the eigenvalues and purity bounds their sizes.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11L05 (Gauss and Kloosterman sums; generalizations), 11T23, 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a finite field 𝔽𝓆 and nontrivial additive character ψ, the rank-r Kloosterman sum at a ∈ 𝔽𝓆ˣ sums ψ(x₁ + ⋯ + xᵣ) over tuples with product a. Up to sign it is the Frobenius trace at a on the Kloosterman sheaf, which is pure of weight w when every eigenvalue has modulus q raised to w/2.

**Problem.** For r ≥ 2 the sum has modulus at most r times q raised to (r − 1)/2.

**How the definition helps.** Deligne proves that the sheaf has rank r and is pure of weight r − 1, so the sum is a sum of r eigenvalues of modulus q raised to (r − 1)/2. The triangle inequality gives the bound (our own deduction).

**Wikipedia:** [Kloosterman sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kloosterman_sum). It says: “Geometrically the sum is taken along a 'hyperbola' XY = ab”

**Sources:**

### Symmetric powers bound Kloosterman angles

**Remember:** Uₘ is a symmetric power trace, and SL(2) fixes nothing there.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11L05 (Gauss and Kloosterman sums; generalizations), 11T23, 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For an odd prime p, nontrivial ψ and a ∈ 𝔽ₚˣ, write the Kloosterman sum K(a) = ∑ₓ ψ(x + a/x) as −2√p cos θ(a) with θ(a) ∈ \[0, π\]. The Chebyshev polynomial Uₘ(cos θ) = sin((m + 1)θ)/sin θ is the trace of the angle θ on degree-m symmetric tensors of SL(2), which have no invariant vector.

**Problem.** For each fixed integer m ≥ 1, the sum of Uₘ(cos θ(a)) over a ≠ 0 has modulus O(√p). The constant depends only on m.

**How the definition helps.** Katz identifies the geometric symmetry group of the normalized Kloosterman sheaf as SL(2), so Uₘ(cos θ(a)) is a Frobenius trace on a sheaf with no geometric invariants. The trace formula and Deligne’s bound then give a sum of size O(√p).

**Wikipedia:** [Chebyshev polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chebyshev_polynomials). It says: “Similarly, the Chebyshev polynomials of the second kind Uₙ are defined by”
