### Distinct tuples give Poisson moments

**Remember:** Count distinct tuples to read the Poisson moments directly.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N13 (Primes in congruence classes). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Pick a class uniformly among the φ(q) classes coprime to q, and let Z count its primes up to N. Its kth falling factorial Z(Z−1)⋯(Z−k+1) counts ordered lists of k distinct primes in the class, which is what a prime-tuple hypothesis estimates.

**Problem.** Assume Leung's Conjecture 1.1, a uniform estimate for how often prescribed shifts of an integer are all prime, and let N/(φ(q)log N) tend to λ &gt; 0. Then each fixed falling factorial moment of order k tends to λᵏ, and Z approaches the Poisson distribution of mean λ.

**How the definition helps.** Falling factorial moments count only distinct primes, exactly the tuples the hypothesis covers (our own explanation). Leung groups these tuples and estimates their prime counts under the hypothesis. The limiting factorial moments determine the Poisson distribution (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Moments of primes in progressions to a large modulus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.07941v2). It says: “Let k ≥ 1 be an integer. Suppose φ(q) ≍ N/log N.”

**Sources:**

- [Sun-Kai Leung, Moments of primes in progressions to a large modulus](https://doi.org/10.1515/forum-2024-0292)

### Empty classes determine least primes

**Remember:** The first prime has not arrived exactly when the class is empty.

*True by definition.* MSC 11N13 (Primes in congruence classes). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Pick a class uniformly among the φ(q) classes coprime to q, let P be its least prime, and set T = P/(φ(q)log q). Then T &gt; t exactly when the class has no prime up to tφ(q)log q.

**Problem.** Assume Leung’s Conjecture 1.1, a uniform estimate for how often prescribed shifts of an integer are all prime. As q tends to infinity, the probability that T exceeds any fixed t &gt; 0 tends to exp(−t).

**How the definition helps.** So the tail of T is the chance that a prime count is zero (our own explanation). At that cutoff Leung's conditional Poisson limit applies with mean t, since log φ(q) is asymptotic to log q. A Poisson variable of mean t is zero with probability exp(−t).

**Paper or page:** [Moments of primes in progressions to a large modulus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.07941v2). It says: “Let t &gt; 0 be a fixed real number.”

**Sources:**

- [Sun-Kai Leung, Moments of primes in progressions to a large modulus](https://doi.org/10.1515/forum-2024-0292)

### Good moduli give prime lower bounds

**Remember:** No zero near one, so nothing cancels the main term.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N13 (Primes in congruence classes), 11M06. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A modulus q ≥ 2 is good when no Dirichlet L-function modulo q has a zero close to the line Re(s) = 1: every zero σ+it satisfies 1−σ ≥ c/log(q(1+\|t\|)), for a fixed small absolute c &gt; 0.

**Problem.** For a good modulus q and every a coprime to q, the class of a contains at least Cx/(φ(q) log x) primes up to x once x ≥ qᴰ. Here φ(q) counts the invertible classes, and C, D &gt; 0 depend only on c.

**How the definition helps.** With no zero near 1, the explicit formula has no term that can cancel the main term x/φ(q) (our own explanation). Otherwise a real zero close to 1 could remove almost all primes from some classes. The proof bounds how many zeros come near the line Re(s) = 1 (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Recent results on large gaps between primes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.07176v2). It says: “Let q be a good modulus. Then π(x;q,a) ≫ x/(φ(q) log x),”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Residue ratios determine joint errors

**Remember:** Subtract the class average, and only the ratio of classes remains.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N13 (Primes in congruence classes), 11M06. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The centered error E(x;a) compares the prime-power count in class a with the average over all invertible classes modulo q ≥ 3: E(x;a) = φ(q)(ψ(x;a)−M(x))/√x. Here ψ(x;a) sums log p over prime powers pᵏ ≤ x congruent to a, and M(x) is the average of ψ(x;a) over the φ(q) classes.

**Problem.** Assume every nontrivial zero of a Dirichlet L-function modulo q has real part ½, none equals ½, and their positive imaginary parts (with multiplicity, over the primitive characters inducing characters modulo q) are linearly independent over ℚ. Then, with x sampled on \[1,X\] by density 1/(x log X), the pair (E(x;α),E(x;β)) for reduced α, β has a limiting distribution that depends only on αβ⁻¹ modulo q.

**How the definition helps.** Subtracting the class average removes the principal character, so each error becomes a sum of character values at the class times sums over zeros (our own explanation). Under linear independence the limiting law sees the two classes only through χ(αβ⁻¹). The proof controls the zeros with large imaginary part (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Joint distributions of error terms for primes in arithmetic progressions modulo 11](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.05427v1). It says: “where a ≡ αβ⁻¹ mod q.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Smoothing sharpens least prime bounds

**Remember:** Fade the weight to zero at x, and high zeros fade too.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N13 (Primes in congruence classes), 11M06. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For q ≥ 2 and a coprime to q, weight each prime power n = pᵏ ≤ x with n ≡ a modulo q by (log p)·log(x/n). The factor log(x/n) fades the weight to zero at x, so in the explicit formula each zero ρ enters with 1/ρ² instead of 1/ρ (our own).

**Problem.** Assume the generalized Riemann hypothesis, which puts every nontrivial zero of every Dirichlet L-function on the line Re(s) = ½. The least prime congruent to a modulo q is then O((φ(q)log q)²), with an absolute implied constant.

**How the definition helps.** With 1/ρ² the sum over zeros converges absolutely, so under the hypothesis the weighted sum is about x/φ(q) with error O(√x log q) (our own). Prime powers with k ≥ 2 add only O(√x). So the main term wins once x is a large constant times (φ(q) log q)².

**Wikipedia:** [Linnik's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linnik%27s_theorem). It says: “where φ is the totient function”

**Sources:**

- [Youness Lamzouri, Xiannan Li and Kannan Soundararajan, Conditional bounds for the least quadratic non-residue and related problems](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0025-5718-2015-02925-1)

### Square-root weights expose prime bias

**Remember:** At weight one over root p, prime squares tilt toward three.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N13 (Primes in congruence classes). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Weight each odd prime p by 1/√p, the weight at the central point s = ½, and subtract the weighted count of primes p ≤ x with p ≡ 1 modulo 4 from that with p ≡ 3. At this weight the prime squares are no longer negligible, since they contribute about ½∑1/p, which grows like ½ log log x (our own).

**Problem.** Assume all nontrivial zeros of the L-function of the nonprincipal character modulo 4 have real part ½. Then for x outside a set with ∫dx/x finite, the weighted difference is ½ log log x plus a constant plus an error tending to zero.

**How the definition helps.** In log L(s,χ) at s = ½ the primes enter with sign χ(p), while the prime squares enter with χ(p)² = 1 and weight 1/(2p) (our own). These square terms give ½ log log x, and higher powers converge. The cited prime-product theorem controls the rest outside the exceptional set.

**Paper or page:** [Euler Products at the Centre and Applications to Chebyshev's Bias](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.01512v1). It says: “for all x outside a set of finite logarithmic measure.”

**Sources:**

- [Arshay Sheth. Euler Products at the Centre and Applications to Chebyshev's Bias](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.01512v1)

### Squared weights halve the exponent

**Remember:** Squaring doubles the modulus, so the weights reach half the level.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N13 (Primes in congruence classes), 11N36, 11N05. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Primes have level of distribution ϑ when their errors in progressions are small on average over all moduli up to almost x<sup>ϑ</sup>: ∑<sub>q≤xᵇ</sub> E(x;q) = O(x/(log x)ᴬ) for every A &gt; 0 and b &lt; ϑ. Here E(x;q) is the largest \|θ(t;q,a)−t/φ(q)\| over invertible a and 2 ≤ t ≤ x, where θ(t;q,a) sums log p over primes p ≤ t in the class a.

**Problem.** Fix a nonzero integer a and η &gt; 0, let R ≤ x<sup>(ϑ/2−η)</sup>, and let \|λ(d)\| ≤ 1 with λ(d) = 0 when gcd(d,a) &gt; 1. Then ∑(∑<sub>d≤R, d\|p−a</sub> λ(d))² log p over primes x &lt; p ≤ 2x equals x∑<sub>d,e≤R</sub> λ(d)λ(e)/φ(lcm(d,e)) up to O(x/(log x)ᴬ) for every A &gt; 0.

**How the definition helps.** Expanding the square gives one progression condition modulo lcm(d,e) ≤ R² &lt; x<sup>ϑ</sup>, which lies inside the level of distribution (our own). Each modulus q occurs at most τ(q)² times, where τ counts divisors. Cauchy–Schwarz with E(2x;q) = O(x log x/q) and the polylogarithmic bound for ∑<sub>q≤R²</sub> τ(q)⁴/q absorbs these multiplicities.

**Wikipedia:** [Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombieri%E2%80%93Vinogradov_theorem). It says: “averaged over the moduli q up to Q.”

**Sources:**

- [Enrico Bombieri, On the large sieve (1965)](https://doi.org/10.1112/S0025579300005313)

### The Siegel correction isolates progression bias

**Remember:** Put the exceptional zero into the main term, not the error.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N13 (Primes in congruence classes). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The Siegel-corrected model M(n) is the sieve model D/φ(D) on n coprime to D, and 0 otherwise, multiplied by 1−χ(n)n<sup>(β−1)</sup> when an exceptional zero exists. Here D is the product of primes below Q = exp((log N)<sup>(1/10)</sup>), and the exceptional zero is a real zero β ∈ (1−c₀/log Q, 1) of L(s,χ) for a primitive real character χ of conductor below Q.

**Problem.** For a sufficiently small absolute c₀ &gt; 0 and every arithmetic progression P in \[1,N\], \|∑<sub>n∈P</sub>(Λ(n)−M(n))\| ≤ CN exp(−c(log N)<sup>(1/10)</sup>). The positive constants c and C are effective.

**How the definition helps.** The factor 1−χ(n)n<sup>(β−1)</sup> is the term that an exceptional zero adds to the prime count, so M absorbs it and one error bound covers both cases (our own explanation). The Landau–Page theorem shows there is at most one such zero. Tao and Teräväinen prove the estimate in Proposition 2.2.

**Paper or page:** [Improved quadratic Gowers uniformity for the Möbius function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.09635). It says: “qSiegel is the conductor for the character χSiegel for the Siegel zero β”

**Sources:**

- [Tao and Teräväinen, Quantitative bounds for Gowers uniformity of the Möbius and von Mangoldt functions, JEMS 27 (2025), 1321–1384](https://doi.org/10.4171/jems/1404)

### The W-trick removes parity bias

**Remember:** One class coprime to W, rescaled to mean one, looks random.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N13 (Primes in congruence classes). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The W-tricked prime weight F(n) = φ(W)Λ(Wn+b)/W looks at primes in one class b modulo W and is rescaled to have mean one. Here W is the product of primes at most √(log log N), and 1 ≤ b ≤ W is coprime to W. Λ(m) = log p when m is a positive power of a prime p, and 0 otherwise.

**Problem.** For each fixed k ≥ 2, the order-k Gowers norm of F−1 on the integers from 1 to ⌊(N−b)/W⌋ is O((log log N)<sup>(−c)</sup>), uniformly in b, with c &gt; 0 depending on k.

**How the definition helps.** A class coprime to W removes the bias of primes against small prime divisors, and φ(W)/W makes the mean one, so F looks like the constant 1 (our own). Tao and Teräväinen’s Corollary 1.5 gives the quantitative Gowers bound.

**Wikipedia:** [Green–Tao theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green%E2%80%93Tao_theorem). It says: “The proof is an extension of Szemerédi's theorem.”

**Sources:**

- [Tao and Teräväinen, Quantitative bounds for Gowers uniformity of the Möbius and von Mangoldt functions, JEMS 27 (2025), 1321–1384](https://doi.org/10.4171/jems/1404)

### Three factors extend modulus ranges

**Remember:** Split the level any way you like into three bounded factors.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N13 (Primes in congruence classes), 11N35. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A sequence λ is triply well factorable at level Q if, for every way to write Q = Q₁Q₂Q₃ with each Qᵢ ≥ 1, λ splits as a product convolution: λ(q) = ∑ u₁(q₁)u₂(q₂)u₃(q₃) over q₁q₂q₃ = q. Here each uᵢ has \|uᵢ\| ≤ 1 and vanishes above Qᵢ, so the proof may choose the three factor sizes it needs.

**Problem.** Fix a nonzero integer a and A, ε &gt; 0, and let Q ≤ x<sup>(3/5−ε)</sup>. For λ triply well factorable at level Q, ∑ λ(q)(π(x;q,a) − π(x)/φ(q)) over q ≤ Q coprime to a is O(x/(log x)ᴬ), where π(x;q,a) counts primes up to x congruent to a modulo q.

**How the definition helps.** Because a factorization exists for every split, Maynard can choose the three factor ranges that each sum in the proof needs (our own explanation). A single fixed split could leave a factor outside the range an estimate requires (our own). Maynard’s estimates for these sums then reach moduli up to x<sup>(3/5−ε)</sup>.

**Paper or page:** [On Chen's theorem, Goldbach's conjecture and almost prime twins II](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.05727v4). It says: “The proof combines various techniques in sieve methods, such as weighted sieve, Chen's switching principle”

**Sources:**

- [J. Maynard, Primes in arithmetic progressions to large moduli II: Well-factorable estimates, Theorem 1.1.](https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid%3Ad75350eb-1358-474a-b070-0b4b5ad720b2)

### Three factors reach larger moduli

**Remember:** Any three-way split of the level gives a factorization.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N13 (Primes in congruence classes), 11N36. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Weights λ are triply well factorable at level Q if, for every split Q = Q₁Q₂Q₃ with Qᵢ ≥ 1, λ(q) = ∑ u₁(d₁)u₂(d₂)u₃(d₃) over d₁d₂d₃ = q for some uᵢ with \|uᵢ\| ≤ 1 that vanish above Qᵢ. So the proof can fix the three factor sizes after it sees the sum.

**Problem.** Fix a nonzero integer a and A, ε &gt; 0, and take triply well factorable weights at level Q ≤ x<sup>(3/5−ε)</sup>. Let E(q) be the number of primes up to x congruent to a modulo q minus π(x)/φ(q); then ∑ λ(q)E(q) over q ≤ Q coprime to a is O(x/(log x)ᴬ).

**How the definition helps.** The definition lets the proof choose three factor sizes after splitting the prime sum (our own explanation). An arbitrary weight supported on q ≤ Q has no such guarantee (our own). Maynard’s estimates for sums over products of variables control the signed errors (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Elliott–Halberstam conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliott%E2%80%93Halberstam_conjecture). It says: “This conjecture was proven for all θ &lt; 1/2 by Enrico Bombieri”

**Sources:**

- [James Maynard, Primes in arithmetic progressions to large moduli II, Theorem 1.1](https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:d75350eb-1358-474a-b070-0b4b5ad720b2)

### A saddle point cancels linear terms

**Remember:** Choose the contour where the first derivative vanishes.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N25 (Distribution of integers with specified multiplicative constraints). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The saddle point α &gt; 0 is where xˢZ(s,y) is smallest on the positive real axis, that is, where the derivative of log Z(s,y) equals −log x; here Z(s,y) = ∏<sub>p≤y</sub>(1−p<sup>(−s)</sup>)<sup>(−1)</sup>. Let D be the second derivative of log Z(s,y) at α.

**Problem.** Let Ψ(x,y) count positive integers at most x with no prime factor above y, and put u=log x/log y. Uniformly for x≥y≥max(2,log x), Ψ(x,y)=xᵅZ(α,y)/(α√(2πD)) times 1+O(1/u).

**How the definition helps.** At α the linear term of log(xˢZ(s,y)) vanishes, so on the line α+it the integrand is approximately Gaussian with exponent −Dt²/2 (our own calculation). Gaussian integration gives the factor 1/√(2πD). Hildebrand and Tenenbaum bound the remaining terms and the integral away from α.

**Paper or page:** [Smooth integers and the Dickman ρ function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.08973v6). It says: “where α &gt; 0 is defined as the minimum of s ↦ ζ(s,y)xˢ”

**Sources:**

- [Smooth integers and the Dickman ρ function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.08973v6)

### A saddle point explains Dickman decay

**Remember:** The saddle solves exp(ξ) = 1+uξ, so ξ ≈ log u.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N25 (Distribution of integers with specified multiplicative constraints). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The saddle point ξ(u) of the Dickman function is the positive solution of exp(ξ)−1 = uξ, the point where I(z)−uz is stationary, with I(z) = ∫₀ᶻ (exp(t)−1) dt/t. Here ρ is the Dickman function: ρ = 1 on \[0,1\] and uρ′(u) = −ρ(u−1) for u &gt; 1.

**Problem.** As u tends to infinity, log ρ(u)=−u(log u+log log u−1+O(log log u/log u)), where ρ is the Dickman function.

**How the definition helps.** Tenenbaum’s theorem gives log ρ(u) = −uξ + I(ξ) − ½ log I″(ξ) + O(1), so everything reduces to the size of ξ. The equation exp(ξ) = 1+uξ gives ξ = log u + log log u + O(log log u/log u) (our own). Since I(ξ) = u(1+O(1/ξ)) and log I″(ξ) = O(log u), the expansion follows (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Smooth integers and the Dickman ρ function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.08973v6). It says: “For $u \\ge 1$ we have $\\rho (u) = (\\sqrt{2\\pi I''(\\xi (u))})<sup>-1</sup>e<sup>\\gamma -u\\xi +I(\\xi )</sup>(1+O(u<sup>-1</sup>)).$”

**Sources:**

- [Smooth integers and the Dickman ρ function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.08973v6)

### Broken sticks model largest primes

**Remember:** After the first break, the leftover stick restarts at a smaller scale.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N25 (Distribution of integers with specified multiplicative constraints). arXiv math.NT, math.PR. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Break a unit stick by removing a uniform random fraction of what remains, again and again, independently. Let M be the longest piece; the ranked pieces follow the Poisson–Dirichlet law with parameter one.

**Problem.** Let N be uniform on {1,…,x} and P(N) its largest prime factor, with P(1) = 1; as x → ∞, log P(N)/log x converges in distribution to M. Moreover P(M ≤ t) = ρ(1/t) for 0 &lt; t ≤ 1, where ρ = 1 on \[0,1\] and uρ′(u) = −ρ(u−1) for u &gt; 1.

**How the definition helps.** After the first break the remaining stick is a smaller copy of the whole, so F(t) = P(M ≤ t) satisfies F(t) = ∫₀ᵗ F(t/(1−v)) dv for 0 &lt; t &lt; 1 (our own derivation). With g(u) = F(1/u) this becomes ug(u) = ∫<sub>u−1</sub><sup>u</sup> g(v) dv, whose derivative is the Dickman equation. Billingsley’s theorem gives the arithmetic limit.

**Paper or page:** [Multiplicative arithmetic functions and the generalized Ewens measure](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.00601v3). It says: “where PD(θ) is the Poisson-Dirichlet distribution with parameter θ”

### Hypergraphs let one density formula cover every pattern of coprimality conditions

**Remember:** Draw an edge wherever a common prime power is forbidden.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N25 (Distribution of integers with specified multiplicative constraints), 05C65. arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix positive integers r and j ≤ m and a family H of j-element subsets (edges) of the positions {1,…,m}. An m-tuple is H-wise relatively r-prime if, for every nonzero prime ideal 𝔭, the positions whose entries lie in 𝔭ʳ contain no edge, so they form an independent set of H.

**Problem.** Take j ≤ m and rm ≥ 2, over the ring of integers of a number field or over 𝔽q\[x\]. The density of H-wise relatively r-prime m-tuples is a product over primes 𝔭. The factor for 𝔭 is Σₖ iₖ(H)(1 − 1/N(𝔭ʳ))ᵐ⁻ᵏ(1/N(𝔭ʳ))ᵏ, where iₖ(H) counts independent sets of size k.

**How the definition helps.** At each prime 𝔭, the positions with entries in 𝔭ʳ form an independent set, and the local factor sums over these sets by size k (our own explanation). Lemmas 2.2 and 2.4 do this count. A separate limit argument passes from finitely many primes to the full density (our own).

It says: “we define the notion of j-wise relative r-primality with respect to a fixed j-uniform hypergraph H. This allows us to provide further generalisations to several results on natural densities”

### Prime-prefix densities sum to one

**Remember:** Each integer stops at its first rejected prime; the stops fill everything.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N25 (Distribution of integers with specified multiplicative constraints). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Read the prime factorization of n from the smallest prime up, keeping the part m read so far; the next prime power pᵃ passes if p ≤ θ(m). The set B holds 1 and the integers whose every step passes, where θ(1) ≥ 2 and θ(m) is at least every prime factor of m.

**Problem.** Suppose the fraction of integers up to x belonging to B tends to zero. For m in B put w(m)=(1/m)∏ (1−1/p), taking the product over primes p≤θ(m). Then ∑ w(m) over B equals one.

**How the definition helps.** Every integer outside B stops at a first failed step, so these integers split into classes indexed by the passed part m ∈ B (our own explanation). The class of m is m times the integers with no prime factor ≤ θ(m), which has density w(m) by the Chinese remainder theorem. The hypothesis that B has density zero lets the cited theorem pass to the infinite sum.

### Reciprocal smooth weights yield Dickman

**Remember:** Weight by one over n, and prime exponents become independent.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N25 (Distribution of integers with specified multiplicative constraints). arXiv math.NT, math.PR. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Pick a y-smooth integer n, one with no prime factor above y, with probability c(y)/n, where c(y) = ∏<sub>p≤y</sub>(1−1/p); then the exponents of the primes p ≤ y are independent geometric variables. Measure the size of n by Z = log n/log y.

**Problem.** As y tends to infinity, Z converges in distribution to a Dickman variable D. Its Laplace transform, the mean E\[exp(−tD)\], equals exp(∫₀¹ (exp(−tu)−1) du/u) for t≥0.

**How the definition helps.** Independence makes E\[exp(−tZ)\] a product over primes p ≤ y (our own derivation). Its logarithm is a sum over prime powers, and the terms with exponent at least two vanish in the limit since ∑1/p² converges. Partial summation with Mertens’ estimate turns the rest into the displayed integral.

### Square-root intervals center squarefull counts

**Remember:** Width H on the square-root scale gives each b a fixed share.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N25 (Distribution of integers with specified multiplicative constraints). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A squarefull integer, one where every prime exponent is at least two, is uniquely a²b³ with b squarefree. Count them in (x, (√x+H)²\], an interval of width H on the square-root scale, so for each b the allowed a fill an interval of length H/b<sup>(3/2)</sup>.

### Fixed square divisors prevent Gaussian limits

**Remember:** No fixed prime square, so f(P(n)) is not always zero.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11N32 (Primes represented by polynomials; other multiplicative structures of polynomial values). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Require that no prime square divides every value P(n). Otherwise a Rademacher random multiplicative function f, which gives primes independent fair signs and vanishes on integers with a repeated prime factor, is zero at every P(n) (our own).

**Problem.** Let P be an irreducible integer quadratic, or a product of at least two pairwise nonproportional integer linear factors, with positive leading coefficient and no fixed prime square divisor. Then for some κ &gt; 0, the sum of f(P(n)) over 1 ≤ n ≤ N with P(n) &gt; 0, divided by √(κN), converges in distribution to a standard normal variable.

**How the definition helps.** The condition removes the case where the sum is identically zero, such as n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3), which 4 always divides (our own). The real work shows that enough values P(n) are squarefree and that the surviving terms have a normal limit (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Random Chowla's Conjecture for Rademacher Multiplicative Functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.05952v2). It says: “Suppose that there is no prime p for which p² ∣ P(n) for all n ∈ ℕ.”

**Sources:**

- [Jake Chinis, Besfort Shala. Random Chowla's Conjecture for Rademacher Multiplicative Functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.05952v2)

### Beta prefixes control sieve moduli

**Remember:** Test odd prefixes for the upper bound, even ones for the lower.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11N35 (Sieves). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix D ≥ z ≥ 2 and β ≥ 1. The beta-sieve keeps a squarefree d with all prime factors below z, written p₁ &gt; p₂ &gt; … &gt; p<sub>r</sub>, only if p₁⋯p<sub>m−1</sub>·p<sub>m</sub><sup>(β+1)</sup> ≤ D for every tested length m. The upper weight tests odd m, the lower weight tests even m, and a kept d gets sign (−1)ʳ.

**Problem.** Give rejected integers weight zero. Then both weights vanish above D, and the lower and upper sums over divisors of n bound the indicator that n has no prime factor below z.

**How the definition helps.** Group the dropped terms by their first failed prefix; each group sums to zero or to the prefix’s sign, which has the right sign for that bound (our own proof). Tested prefixes keep d ≤ D directly. An untested last prime fits under its predecessor’s allowance since β ≥ 1, or lies below z if it stands alone.

**Paper or page:** [Polynomials represented by norm forms via the beta sieve](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.08949v2). It says: “there is a choice of upper and lower bound sieve weights Λ± (taking values in {−1,0,1}), and explicit constants”

**Sources:**

- [H. Iwaniec, Rosser’s sieve, Acta Arithmetica 36 (1980), 171–202.](https://doi.org/10.4064/aa-36-2-171-202)
- [Alec Shute, Polynomials represented by norm forms via the beta sieve, §4.](https://doi.org/10.1017/S1474748025000076)

### Linear sieve sums recover Buchstab

**Remember:** Adding the two delay equations gives one delay equation.

*True by definition.* MSC 11N35 (Sieves). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The linear sieve functions f and F are the continuous solutions of the coupled delay equations (sf(s))′ = F(s−1) and (sF(s))′ = f(s−1) for s &gt; 2. They start from f = 0 on \[1,2\] and sF(s) = 2exp(γ) on \[1,3\], with γ Euler’s constant.

**Problem.** Let ω(s) equal 1/s on \[1,2\] and extend continuously by (sω(s))′ = ω(s − 1) for s &gt; 2. Then f(s) + F(s) = 2 exp(γ)ω(s) for all s ≥ 1.

**How the definition helps.** Adding the equations gives (s(f+F)(s))′ = (f+F)(s−1), the Buchstab equation, and f+F = 2exp(γ)/s on \[1,2\] (our own derivation). Each next unit interval is fixed by the previous one, so f+F = 2exp(γ)ω.

**Wikipedia:** [Buchstab function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buchstab_function). It says: “the unique continuous function”

**Paper or page:** [Weighted sieves with switching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.19063v3). It says: “(f(s)+o(1))”

**Sources:**

- [W. B. Jurkat and H.-E. Richert, An improvement of Selberg’s sieve method I, Acta Arithmetica 11 (1965), 217–240.](https://doi.org/10.4064/aa-11-2-217-240)

### Waring counts control power moduli

**Remember:** Crowded fractions a/qᵏ mean many sums of kth powers.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N35 (Sieves). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Δ is the large sieve constant for the fractions a/qᵏ, reduced, with q ≤ Q: the least Δ with ∑\|T(a/qᵏ)\|² ≤ Δ·∑\|coefficients\|² for every trigonometric polynomial T on N consecutive integer frequencies. R(t) counts ordered ways to write t as a sum of s positive kth powers, and it measures how tightly these fractions can cluster (our own).

**Problem.** Take integers k ≥ 2, s ≥ 1 and Q ≥ 1 with Qᵏ &lt; N &lt; Q²ᵏ. Suppose R(t) ≤ C for every integer 1 ≤ t ≤ sQᵏ. For each ε &gt; 0, Δ ≤ cNQᵋ(CQ²ᵏ/N)¹⁄ˢ, where c depends only on ε, k and s.

**How the definition helps.** Fractions a/qᵏ that crowd into a short interval give near-coincidences that turn into representations as sums of s kth powers. Baier and Lynch use R(t) ≤ C to bound the number of denominators in such a cluster, which bounds Δ.

**Paper or page:** [Large sieve inequalities with power moduli and Waring's problem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.07613v2). It says: “uniformly in positive integers n ≤ sQᵏ”

**Sources:**

- [S. Baier and S. B. Lynch, Large sieve inequalities with power moduli and Waring's problem, Lemma 2.1.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.07613v2)

### A sieve quotient counts primes

**Remember:** Mₖ over four is the prime count the weights reach.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N36 (Applications of sieve methods). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Maynard’s quotient Mₖ is the supremum of ∑Jᵢ/I over real piecewise smooth F on \[0,1\]ᵏ, zero unless ∑tᵢ ≤ 1, with I = ∫F² and each Jᵢ positive. Jᵢ integrates F along coordinate i, squares, and integrates over the other coordinates; ∑Jᵢ/I measures how many shifts the sieve weight makes prime (our own).

**Problem.** Take k distinct integer shifts h₁,…,hₖ whose residues omit at least one class modulo every prime. Infinitely many integers n give at least ⌈Mₖ/4⌉ primes among n+h₁,…,n+hₖ.

**How the definition helps.** With level ½ from the Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem, Maynard’s estimates make the weighted average number of primes among the n+hᵢ arbitrarily close to Mₖ/4 on arbitrarily large intervals (our own explanation). An average above ⌈Mₖ/4⌉−1 forces some n with at least ⌈Mₖ/4⌉ primes.

**Paper or page:** [Primes in Tuples of Linear Forms in Number Fields and Function Fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.04705v1). It says: “Then there are infinitely many integers α ∈ A such that at least rₖ of the aᵢα + hᵢ, 1 ≤ i ≤ k are prime.”

**Sources:**

- [James Maynard, Small gaps between primes, Annals of Mathematics 181 (2015), 383–413](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2015/181-1/p07)

### An extra power raises GPY averages

**Remember:** Raise the log power to k+ℓ, and the square sees more primes.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N36 (Applications of sieve methods). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The GPY weight is w(n) = (∑ μ(d)(log(R/d))<sup>(k+ℓ)</sup>/(k+ℓ)!)², summed over divisors d ≤ R of ∏(n+hᵢ), for k distinct shifts hᵢ, 0 ≤ ℓ ≤ k and R &gt; 1. The extra power ℓ lets the weight favour n for which ∏(n+hᵢ) has at most k+ℓ prime factors (our own).

**Problem.** For shifts that omit a residue class modulo each prime, fixed 0 &lt; r &lt; ¼ and R = xʳ, take the w-weighted mean over x &lt; n ≤ 2x of the number of primes among the n+hᵢ. It tends to r · 2(2ℓ+1)/(ℓ+1) · k/(k+2ℓ+1).

**How the definition helps.** The prime-weighted sum and the total weight have main terms of the same shape, a product of local densities times factorials in k and ℓ (our own explanation). Goldston, Pintz and Yıldırım evaluate both. The local densities cancel in the ratio, and the factorials give the limit (our own calculation).

**Wikipedia:** [Goldston–Pintz–Yıldırım sieve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldston%E2%80%93Pintz%E2%80%93Y%C4%B1ld%C4%B1r%C4%B1m_sieve). It says: “introduce another parameter 0 ≤ ℓ ≤ k”

**Sources:**

- [D. A. Goldston, J. Pintz and C. Y. Yıldırım, Primes in Tuples I, Annals of Mathematics 170 (2009), 819–862](https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2009.170.819)

### Fiber integrals bound Maynard weights

**Remember:** Cauchy–Schwarz on each line, with weights that sum to k.

*True by definition.* MSC 11N36 (Applications of sieve methods). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take k ≥ 2 and a square-integrable F on the simplex tᵢ ≥ 0, ∑tᵢ ≤ 1, with I = ∫F² &gt; 0. Jᵢ is the integral, over the other coordinates, of the square of the integral of F along the line in coordinate i, a line of length L = 1 − ∑<sub>j≠i</sub> tⱼ.

**Problem.** For this version of the Maynard quotient, ∑ Jᵢ/I ≤ k log k/(k−1).

**How the definition helps.** Since ∫₀ᴸ dt/(L+(k−1)t) = log k/(k−1), Cauchy–Schwarz on each line gives (∫F dtᵢ)² ≤ (log k/(k−1))∫F²·(L+(k−1)tᵢ) dtᵢ (our own derivation). Summed over i, the weights L+(k−1)tᵢ add to k at every point, so ∑Jᵢ ≤ (k log k/(k−1))·I.

**Paper or page:** [Primes in Tuples of Linear Forms in Number Fields and Function Fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.04705v1). It says: “M<sub>k</sub>=\\sup \_{F\\in \\mathcal{S}<sub>k</sub>}\\frac{\\sum <sub>m=1</sub><sup>k</sup>J<sup>(m)</sup><sub>k</sub>(F)}{I<sub>k</sub>(F)}”

**Sources:**

- [D. H. J. Polymath, Variants of the Selberg sieve, and bounded intervals containing many primes, Research in the Mathematical Sciences 1 (2014), 12](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40687-014-0012-7)
- [James Maynard, Small gaps between primes, Annals of Mathematics 181 (2015), 383–413](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2015/181-1/p07)

### Balanced correlations cancel imaginary twists

**Remember:** Zero total exponent cancels the common phase.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N37 (Asymptotic results on arithmetic functions), 11N64. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Integer exponents k₁,…,k\_ℓ, one per shift hⱼ, are balanced when they sum to zero. Then a common twist n<sup>(it)</sup> cancels from ∏ f(n+hⱼ)<sup>(kⱼ)</sup>, because each (n+hⱼ)<sup>(it)</sup> is close to n<sup>(it)</sup> and the powers add to zero.

**Problem.** Let f be multiplicative with \|f\| ≤ 1 and ∑ₚ(1−Re(f(p)χ̅(p)p<sup>(−it)</sup>))/p finite for some real t and Dirichlet character χ. For fixed nonnegative shifts and balanced exponents, the average of ∏ f(n+hⱼ)<sup>(kⱼ)</sup>, with conjugates for negative kⱼ, converges.

**How the definition helps.** If f is close to χ(n)n<sup>(it)</sup>, each factor carries a phase near n<sup>(itkⱼ)</sup>, and balance makes these phases multiply to one, since (n+h)<sup>(it)</sup>/n<sup>(it)</sup> → 1 (our own explanation). Theorem 2.14 proves convergence for the remaining factors.

**Paper or page:** [Furstenberg systems of pretentious and MRT multiplicative functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.03121). It says: “are integers such that ∑(j=1,…,ℓ) kⱼ = 0, then the limit”

**Sources:**

- [Furstenberg systems of pretentious and MRT multiplicative functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.03121)

### Character distance controls residue means

**Remember:** Far from every character modulo Q, so every coprime class averages out.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N37 (Asymptotic results on arithmetic functions). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A function f with \|f\| ≤ 1 pretends to no character modulo Q when D(f,χ)² = ∑ₚ(1−Re(f(p)χ̅(p)))/p is infinite for every Dirichlet character χ modulo Q. These characters are exactly what is needed to pick out each invertible class modulo Q.

**Problem.** Let f be multiplicative and pretend to no character modulo Q. For each positive a coprime to Q, the logarithmic average (weights 1/n) of f(Qn+a) over n ≤ X tends to zero.

**How the definition helps.** By character orthogonality, the indicator of the class a is a combination of the characters modulo Q, so the average splits into averages of f·χ̅ (our own explanation). Infinite distance gives each of these logarithmic cancellation. Replacing Q/(Qn+a) by 1/n adds only a summable error.

**Paper or page:** [On multiplicative recurrence along linear patterns](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.03504). It says: “such that 𝔻(f,χ) = +∞ for all Dirichlet characters of modulus Q.”

**Sources:**

- [On multiplicative recurrence along linear patterns](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.03504)

### Local parity factors shifted correlations

**Remember:** Each prime flips the sign with its own local odds.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N37 (Asymptotic results on arithmetic functions). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a prime set P with ∑<sub>p∈P</sub> 1/p finite, λ(m) is −1 raised to the number of prime factors of m from P, counted with multiplicity. For a finite nonempty set H of distinct positive shifts, η(p,H) is the density of n for which p divides ∏<sub>h∈H</sub>(n+h) to an odd power, the n where the local sign at p is −1.

**Problem.** For each n, multiply λ(n+h) over h in H. As X grows, the average of these products for n ≤ X tends to the product of 1−2η(p,H) over p in P. When the shifts are distinct modulo p, η(p,H)=\|H\|/(p+1).

**How the definition helps.** The product of λ(n+h) over H is a product of local signs over p ∈ P, and the sign at p is −1 with density η(p,H), so it averages to 1−2η(p,H) (our own calculation). The Chinese remainder theorem makes finitely many primes independent, and the convergent reciprocal sum controls the rest. For distinct residues at most one shift is divisible by p, and an odd exponent has density 1/(p+1) for each.

**Paper or page:** [On variants of Chowla's conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.10962). It says: “Moreover, for every non-exceptional prime, ηₚᴴ = d/(p+1).”

**Sources:**

- [On variants of Chowla's conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.10962)

### Logarithmic means need no frequency search

**Remember:** Harmonic weights allow a test against the constant function alone.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N37 (Asymptotic results on arithmetic functions). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For f with \|f(n)\| ≤ 1, the logarithmic mean up to X is ∑<sub>n≤X</sub> f(n)/n divided by ∑<sub>n≤X</sub> 1/n. Its distance is measured to the constant 1 alone, D(f,1;X)² = ∑<sub>p≤X</sub>(1−Re f(p))/p, because weights 1/n already average every twist n<sup>(it)</sup>, t ≠ 0, to zero (our own).

**Problem.** For multiplicative f the absolute logarithmic mean is at most C exp(−D(f,1;X)²/2) for X ≥ 2, with absolute C.

**How the definition helps.** Halász’s bound for ordinary means must search over twists n<sup>(it)</sup>, since these have ordinary means of modulus about 1/\|1+it\| (our own comparison). Under weights 1/n such twists do not matter, so only the distance to 1 enters. Lemma 2.2 gives the bound.

**Paper or page:** [On multiplicative recurrence along linear patterns](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.03504). It says: “\|𝔼ˡᵒᵍ(n ≤ X) f(n)\| ≪ exp(−(1/2)∑(p ≤ X) (1−Re f(p))/p).”

**Sources:**

- [On multiplicative recurrence along linear patterns](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.03504)

### Multiplicativity at two prevents anticorrelation of size one

**Remember:** Powers of two follow f(2), so evenness cannot carry a sign.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11N37 (Asymptotic results on arithmetic functions), 11N64. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take f real, multiplicative, with \|f\| ≤ 1, and completely multiplicative at 2: f(2ʲ) = f(2)ʲ for every j ≥ 1. This excludes the function that is 1 on odd n and −1 on even n, for which f(n)f(n+1) = −1 always.

**Problem.** Suppose f takes a negative value. Average f(n)f(n+1) over n=1,…,X. For all sufficiently large X, the modulus of this average is at most 1−δ for some δ &gt; 0 depending on f.

**How the definition helps.** That function has f(4) = −1 ≠ f(2)², so the condition removes the obvious way to make the average −1 (our own check). Matomäki and Radziwiłł prove the bound in the extension after Corollary 2.

**Wikipedia:** [Kaisa Matomäki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaisa_Matom%C3%A4ki). It says: “Her research includes results on the distribution of multiplicative functions over short intervals of numbers”

**Sources:**

- [Kaisa Matomäki and Maksym Radziwiłł, Multiplicative functions in short intervals (2016)](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2016/183-3/p06)

### Nonproportional forms exclude self correlation

**Remember:** A determinant rules out comparing a sign to itself.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11N37 (Asymptotic results on arithmetic functions). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Two linear forms a₁n+b₁ and a₂n+b₂ with positive integer coefficients are nonproportional when a₁b₂ ≠ a₂b₁, so neither is a constant multiple of the other.

**Problem.** For nonproportional forms, the logarithmic average (weights 1/n) of λ(a₁n+b₁)λ(a₂n+b₂) tends to zero. Here λ is the Liouville function, −1 raised to the number of prime factors counted with multiplicity.

**How the definition helps.** Proportional forms satisfy v(a₁n+b₁) = u(a₂n+b₂) for fixed positive integers u, v, so the product λ(a₁n+b₁)λ(a₂n+b₂) is the constant λ(u)λ(v) (our own calculation). Tao’s logarithmic two-point theorem gives cancellation for all other pairs.

**Paper or page:** [On multiplicative recurrence along linear patterns](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.03504). It says: “Let a₁, a₂, b₁, b₂ be natural numbers such that a₁b₂ − a₂b₁ ≠ 0.”

**Sources:**

- [On multiplicative recurrence along linear patterns](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.03504)
- [Terence Tao, The logarithmically averaged Chowla and Elliott conjectures for two-point correlations (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1017/fmp.2016.6)

### Prime parity factors the mean

**Remember:** Each prime in P scales the mean by (p−1)/(p+1).

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N37 (Asymptotic results on arithmetic functions). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a set P of primes, λ<sub>P</sub>(n) is −1 raised to the number of prime factors of n from P, counted with multiplicity. So λ<sub>P</sub> is completely multiplicative, with value −1 at primes in P and 1 at other primes.

**Problem.** The ordinary mean of λ for P tends to the product of 1−2/(p+1) over primes p in P. The product is zero exactly when ∑1/p over P diverges.

**How the definition helps.** At each p in P the exponent is j with density (1−1/p)/pʲ, so the local sign averages to 1−2/(p+1) (our own calculation). The Wintner–Wirsing mean-value theorem multiplies these local averages. The factors lie in (0,1), so the product is zero exactly when ∑<sub>p∈P</sub> 1/p diverges.

**Paper or page:** [On variants of Chowla's conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.10962). It says: “lim(x → ∞) (1/x)∑(n ≤ x) λ<sub>P</sub>(n) = ∏(p ∈ P)(1−2/(p+1)).”

**Sources:**

- [On variants of Chowla's conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.10962)

### Shifted powers can spoil Gaussian limits

**Remember:** A pure power P = nᵈ just copies the original sum.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11N37 (Asymptotic results on arithmetic functions). arXiv math.NT, math.PR. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A Steinhaus random multiplicative function f gives each prime an independent uniform point on the unit circle and is completely multiplicative. For degree d, exclude the polynomials w(x+c)ᵈ, with w an integer and c rational, which are a constant times a dth power of a linear form.

**Problem.** Take an integer polynomial P of degree d ≥ 2 outside the excluded family, with P(n)&gt;0 for all sufficiently large n. Sum f(P(n)) over positive n ≤ N with P(n)&gt;0 and divide by √N. The result converges in distribution to a complex normal variable with independent real and imaginary parts, each normal with mean zero and variance ½.

**How the definition helps.** For P(n) = nᵈ, f(n)ᵈ is again a Steinhaus function, so the sum has the law of ∑f(n) (our own example). Harper’s first-moment bound makes that sum divided by √N tend to zero in probability, so no normal limit holds (our own deduction). The polynomial limit theorem gives the normal law outside the excluded family.

**Paper or page:** [Random Chowla's Conjecture for Rademacher Multiplicative Functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.05952). It says: “converge in distribution to a standard complex Gaussian.”

**Sources:**

- [Random Chowla's Conjecture for Rademacher Multiplicative Functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.05952)
- [Adam J. Harper, Moments of random multiplicative functions, I (2020)](https://doi.org/10.1017/fmp.2019.7)

### Square products predict Gaussian limits

**Remember:** Square products drive the fourth moment; Gaussian means three.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N37 (Asymptotic results on arithmetic functions). arXiv math.NT, math.PR. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let f give primes independent fair signs, multiply them on squarefree integers, and vanish elsewhere. For a set S of squarefree integers, the square energy counts ordered quadruples from S whose product is a perfect square; these are exactly the terms that survive in the fourth moment of ∑<sub>n∈S</sub> f(n).

**Problem.** For each large N choose a set A of squarefree integers in \[1,N\] with \|A\| ≥ N exp(−√(log N log log N)/3). Assume subsets S ⊆ A satisfy \|S\|/\|A\| → 1 and their square energies divided by \|S\|² tend to three. The sum of f(n) over A divided by √\|A\| converges in distribution to the normal law with mean zero and variance one.

**How the definition helps.** E\[f(a)f(b)f(c)f(d)\] is 1 when abcd is a square and 0 otherwise, since a prime with odd exponent gives a mean-zero sign (our own expansion). So square energy (3+o(1))\|S\|² says the fourth moment matches the normal value 3. The cited theorem turns this, with the size conditions, into the normal limit.

**Paper or page:** [Central limit theorems for random multiplicative functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.06098). It says: “and satisfying E□(𝒮) = (3+o(1))\|𝒮\|². Then as f ranges over Rademacher random multiplicative functions”

**Sources:**

- [Central limit theorems for random multiplicative functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.06098)

### Tao’s averages test twisted characters

**Remember:** Compare prime values with a character times a rotating phase.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N37 (Asymptotic results on arithmetic functions). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A twisted character is g(n) = χ(n)n<sup>(it)</sup>, a Dirichlet character χ modulo q times a rotating phase n<sup>(it)</sup> with real t. The distance from f to g up to X is the square root of ∑<sub>p≤X</sub>(1−Re(f(p)g̅(p)))/p.

**Problem.** Fix distinct nonnegative integers a, b and ε &gt; 0, and let f, h be multiplicative with modulus at most one and with logarithmic average (weights 1/n) of f(n+a)h(n+b) of modulus at least ε for large X. Then each of f, h is within distance C of some χ(n)n<sup>(it)</sup> with modulus q ≤ C and \|t\| ≤ CX, where C depends only on a, b, ε.

**How the definition helps.** A correlation can come from a phase alone: f(n) = n<sup>i</sup> and its conjugate h give f(n+a)h(n+b) → 1, yet f is far from every untwisted character (our own example). So the model must allow n<sup>(it)</sup> as well as χ. Tao’s theorem proves that such a model always exists.

**Paper or page:** [Gap problems for integer-valued multiplicative functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.11636). It says: “Then there are primitive Dirichlet characters”

**Sources:**

- [Gap problems for integer-valued multiplicative functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.11636)
- [Terence Tao, The logarithmically averaged Chowla and Elliott conjectures for two-point correlations (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1017/fmp.2016.6)

### Generating functions give Landau’s asymptotic

**Remember:** Mark each distinct prime by z and read the count from its coefficient.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N60 (Distribution functions associated with additive and positive multiplicative functions). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Mark each distinct prime factor by z: S(x,z) = ∑<sub>n≤x</sub> z<sup>(ω(n))</sup>, where ω(n) counts distinct prime divisors. Then the coefficient of zᵏ is the number of n ≤ x with exactly k distinct prime divisors.

**Problem.** Fix an integer k≥1 and put L=log log x. As x grows, the count with ω(n)=k is asymptotic to xLᵏ⁻¹/((k−1)! log x).

**How the definition helps.** Selberg–Delange gives S(x,z) ≈ x exp(zL)G(z)/(Γ(z) log x), with G analytic near zero and G(0) = 1 (our own calculation). Since 1/Γ(z) = z+O(z²), the coefficient of zᵏ comes mainly from L<sup>(k−1)</sup>/(k−1)! in exp(zL). Cauchy’s formula on \|z\| = 1/L controls the error.

**Paper or page:** [Probabilistic interpretation of the Selberg--Delange Method in analytic number theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.17535v1). It says: “Let f: ℕ → ℂ be an admissible function with average value ρ.”

**Sources:**

- [Probabilistic interpretation of the Selberg--Delange Method in analytic number theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.17535v1)

### Poisson normalization yields a product

**Remember:** Remove the Poisson term and each prime leaves a summable error.

*True by definition.* MSC 11N60 (Distribution functions associated with additive and positive multiplicative functions). arXiv math.NT, math.PR. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let N have the zeta distribution, P(N = n) = 1/(ζ(s)nˢ) for s &gt; 1, so the events p \| N are independent with probabilities p<sup>(−s)</sup> and ω(N), the number of distinct prime factors, is a sum of independent indicators. Divide E\[exp(zω(N))\] by exp(μ(s)(exp(z)−1)), the same quantity for a Poisson variable with the same mean μ(s) = ∑ₚ p<sup>(−s)</sup>.

**Problem.** As s decreases to 1, the quotient converges locally uniformly for complex z. Its limit is the product over primes of (1+w/p)exp(−w/p), where w=exp(z)−1.

**How the definition helps.** Each prime gives the factor (1+w/pˢ)exp(−w/pˢ) with w = exp(z)−1, where the Poisson division cancels the linear term (our own calculation). So each factor differs from 1 by O(1/p²) on bounded sets of z, and the product converges uniformly as s decreases to 1.

**Paper or page:** [Large deviations for number of irreducible divisors of the Dirichlet series distribution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.14234v1). It says: “The random variables ω(Xₛ), s &gt; 1, converges mod-Poisson as s ↘ 1”

### Sparse exceptions permit bounded values

**Remember:** Every exceptional prime at least doubles the value.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N60 (Distribution functions associated with additive and positive multiplicative functions), 11N64. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For positive integer valued multiplicative f, a prime p is exceptional when f(p) ≠ 1, and the exceptional primes are measured only by ∑1/p over them, not by the size of f(p). Each exceptional prime that divides n exactly once at least doubles f(n), so many of them force f(n) to be large (our own).

**Problem.** For a finite C, consider the fraction of integers n ≤ X satisfying f(n) ≤ C. For some C this fraction has positive limit superior exactly when the exceptional primes have finite reciprocal sum.

**How the definition helps.** If ∑1/p diverges, a typical n has many exceptional primes to the first power, each multiplying f(n) by at least 2, so f(n) ≤ C almost never holds (our own reading). The cited theorem proves the density criterion with all prime powers pᵛ. Higher powers drop out since their reciprocals have a convergent sum (our own simplification).

**Paper or page:** [Gap problems for integer-valued multiplicative functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.11636). It says: “if and only if ∑(pᵛ ∶ f(pᵛ) ≠ 1) 1/pᵛ &lt; ∞.”

**Remember:** Delete the zeros, then count opposite signs that become neighbors.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N64 (Other results on the distribution of values or the characterization of arithmetic functions). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Count sign changes of a real sequence after deleting its zeros: a sign change is a pair of consecutive remaining terms with opposite signs.

**Problem.** A real multiplicative f has more than cX sign changes up to X, for some c &gt; 0 and all large X, exactly when f takes a negative value and has at least δX nonzero values up to X for some δ &gt; 0 and all large X.

**How the definition helps.** Deleting zeros lets the count see changes even when every pair of neighbours contains a zero, as for the repeating values 1, 0, −1, 0 (our own example). Corollary 3 proves the criterion.

### Uniform distance gives one model

**Remember:** A uniformly close model can be chosen once.

### Counting remainders continue Beurling zeta

**Remember:** Subtract the linear count; the leftover sets where zeta stays holomorphic.

*True by definition.* MSC 11N80 (Generalized primes and integers). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The remainder R(x) = N(x) − κ(x−1) is what is left of the count N(x) of Beurling generalized integers of size at most x after removing a linear main term. Generalized integers are the products of generalized primes, reals greater than one tending to infinity, counted by factorization and including the empty product 1.

**Problem.** Suppose κ &gt; 0 and \|R(x)\| ≤ Cx<sup>θ</sup> with θ &lt; 1. Then the Beurling zeta function ζ(s) = ∑v<sup>(−s)</sup> over generalized integers v extends to Re s &gt; θ, holomorphic except for a simple pole at 1 with residue κ.

**How the definition helps.** The linear term κ(x−1) gives exactly the pole κ/(s−1), and the remainder gives an integral that converges further left (our own calculation). For Re s &gt; 1, partial summation gives ζ(s) = κ/(s−1) + s∫₁<sup>∞</sup> R(x)x<sup>(−s−1)</sup> dx. The bound on R makes this integral holomorphic on Re s &gt; θ.

**Paper or page:** [Distribution of Beurling primes and zeroes of the Beurling zeta function I. Distribution of the zeroes of the zeta function of Beurling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.09045v3). It says: “\|ζ(s) − κ/(s−1)\| ≤ A\|s\|/(σ−θ)”

### Prime labels preserve Möbius inversion

**Remember:** Count by labels, not sizes, and Möbius inverts each prime factor.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11N80 (Generalized primes and integers). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Beurling generalized integers are the formal products of prime labels, each with a real size greater than one and sizes tending to infinity, counted separately even when sizes agree; the empty product has size 1. The Möbius weight of a product is (−1)ᵏ if it uses k distinct labels and 0 if a label repeats.

**Problem.** Form the Beurling zeta series by summing exp(−s log v) over all products of size v, including multiplicities. Wherever this series converges absolutely, its reciprocal equals the same series with each term multiplied by its Möbius weight.

**How the definition helps.** Products counted by labels have one factorization each, so expanding ∏(1−v<sup>(−s)</sup>) over prime sizes v gives every product with its Möbius weight (our own). Grouping by size only adds these weights; for primes of sizes 2 and 4, the size-4 term gets −1 from the prime and 0 from 2·2 (our own). Absolute convergence justifies multiplying and regrouping (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Beurling zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beurling_zeta_function). It says: “A Beurling generalized integer is a number that can be written as a product of Beurling generalized primes.”

**Paper or page:** [The average order of the Möbius function for Beurling primes](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.06866v2). It says: “Here Mℙ(x) is the partial sum of the Möbius function over 𝒩 not exceeding x.”

### Relative density excludes Goldbach obstructions

**Remember:** Measure density inside the prime class that can reach the target.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11P32 (Goldbach-type theorems; other additive questions involving primes), 11P55. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let P be the primes congruent to 1 modulo 3, so any three of them sum to a multiple of 3. A set A ⊆ P has relative lower density liminf \|A ∩ \[1,X\]\|/\|P ∩ \[1,X\]\|, its lower share of P.

**Problem.** Suppose A has relative lower density greater than one half in P. Then every sufficiently large odd multiple of 3 is a sum of three elements of A. This can fail at density one half.

**How the definition helps.** Strict inequality excludes a residue obstruction at density one half (our own example). Keeping the primes in P that are ±1 modulo 5 gives relative density one half, by the prime number theorem in progressions, yet no three of them sum to 0 modulo 5. Alsetri’s theorem proves that density above one half suffices.

**Paper or page:** [Density ternary Goldbach for primes in a fixed residue class](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.09648v3). It says: “Then A+A+A contains every sufficiently large odd integer n which satisfies n ≡ 0 mod 3.”

### Dickman weights isolate smooth density

**Remember:** Weight by power density times smooth density, then substitute m = xᵈ.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method), 11P05. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** w(β) sums exp(2πiβm) over integers Zᵈ &lt; m ≤ Xᵈ, weighting m by m<sup>(1/d−1)</sup>/d, the density of dth powers near m, times ϱ(log m/(d log Z)), the density of Z-smooth numbers near m<sup>(1/d)</sup>. Here ϱ is the Dickman function: ϱ = 1 on \[0,1\] and uϱ′(u) = −ϱ(u−1) for u &gt; 1.

**Problem.** Fix an integer d ≥ 3, B &gt; 0 and sufficiently small η &gt; 0, and set Z = X raised to η. For \|β\| &lt; (log X)ᴮ/Xᵈ, one has w(β) = ϱ(1/η)XI(Xᵈβ) + O(X/log Z + Z). Here I(t) = ∫₀¹ exp(2πitvᵈ) dv.

**How the definition helps.** The substitution m = xᵈ turns the weight m<sup>(1/d−1)</sup>/d into dx, so without the Dickman factor the sum is the integral X·I(Xᵈβ) for unrestricted dth powers (our own calculation). The Dickman factor is replaced by its value ϱ(1/η) at the top end x = X. Rome and Yamagishi bound the error of this replacement.

**Paper or page:** [Integral solutions to systems of diagonal equations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.09256v2). It says: “Then w(β) = ϱ((d log X)/(d log Z)) X I(Xᵈβ) + O(X/log Z + Z).”

### Disjoint supports multiply local sums

**Remember:** Functions on disjoint pieces vary independently, so their averages multiply.

*True by definition.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method), 11P05. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a finite subscheme Z of a curve over a finite field K, with function algebra R and a K-linear map λ: R → K, let S(Z,λ) be the average of ψ(λ(xᵏ)) over x in R, for fixed k ≥ 1 and a nontrivial additive character ψ of K into the unit circle. When Z is a disjoint union Z₁ ⊔ Z₂, R = R₁ × R₂, so x splits into two independent components (our own).

**Problem.** If Z is the disjoint union of Z₁ and Z₂, then S(Z,λ) = S(Z₁,λ₁)S(Z₂,λ₂), where λᵢ applies λ to functions on Zᵢ extended by zero. Moreover, λ is nondegenerate, meaning that it factors through no proper quotient of R, exactly when λ₁ and λ₂ are nondegenerate.

**How the definition helps.** A uniform x in R₁ × R₂ is a pair of independent uniform components, and λ(xᵏ) = λ₁(x₁ᵏ) + λ₂(x₂ᵏ), so ψ turns the sum into a product and the averages multiply (our own explanation). Ideals of R₁ × R₂ are products of ideals, so ker λ contains a nonzero ideal exactly when some ker λᵢ does (our own).

**Paper or page:** [The asymptotic in Waring's problem over function fields via singular sets in the circle method](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.14053v1). It says: “Then we have \\\[ S<sub>Z</sub>(\\overline{\\alpha})=S<sub>Z<sub>1</sub></sub>(\\overline{\\alpha}<sub>Z<sub>1</sub></sub>)S<sub>Z<sub>2</sub></sub>(\\overline{\\alpha}<sub>Z<sub>2</sub></sub>) \\\]”

### Real solution density makes positivity local

**Remember:** A smooth zero with positive weight sends positive mass near zero.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For smooth F: ℝˢ → ℝʳ and a smooth compactly supported weight w ≥ 0, the real solution density is the limit, as ε decreases to 0, of the w-mass of points with F(x) in \[−ε,ε\]ʳ divided by (2ε)ʳ, when the limit exists. It measures the w-weighted size of the zero set of F (our own).

**Problem.** Assume F has derivative of rank r at every zero in the support of w. Then the normalized mass has a finite limit, which is positive if w is positive at any zero.

**How the definition helps.** Where the derivative has rank r, local coordinates turn F into the first r coordinates, so the mass near zero becomes an integral over the other coordinates that is continuous in the value of F (our own proof). It is positive wherever the weight is positive at a zero. A partition of unity near the compact zero set combines the charts, and the rest of the support maps away from zero.

**Paper or page:** [Solving quadratic forms in restricted variables with the circle method](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17949v1). It says: “can be interpreted as a local density over the reals inside the compact set 𝔅.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Residues modulo sixteen select sums of twelve fourth powers

**Remember:** Modulo sixteen, a fourth power records whether its base is odd.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method), 11P05. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Modulo 16, a fourth power is 0 if its base is even and 1 if its base is odd, so a sum of twelve fourth powers is congruent to its number of odd bases (our own). An integer is admissible when its residue modulo 16 lies in 1,…,12, the counts possible with at least one odd base.

**Problem.** Every sufficiently large admissible integer is a sum of twelve fourth powers of positive integers. No integer outside the admissible classes is such a sum with an odd base.

**How the definition helps.** Residues 13 to 15 would need more than twelve odd bases, and residue 0 forces every base to be even (our own explanation). Brüdern and Wooley prove existence for large admissible integers in Corollary 1.3.

**Wikipedia:** [Waring's problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waring%27s_problem). It says: “any sufficiently large number congruent to 1 through 14 mod 16 could be written as a sum of 14 fourth powers”

**Sources:**

- [J. Brüdern and T. D. Wooley, On smooth Weyl sums over biquadrates and Waring’s problem (2022)](https://www.math.purdue.edu/~twooley/publ/20220507smbiq.pdf)

### Smooth cutoffs suppress Poisson tails

**Remember:** Smooth weights remove boundary terms in repeated integration by parts.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method), 11L07. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** I is the oscillatory integral of exp(2πi\[β₁F₁(x)+β₂F₂(x)−c·x/q\]) over ℝˢ against the smooth compactly supported cutoff W(x/P), for fixed quadratic forms F₁, F₂, real β = (β₁,β₂), a real vector c and a positive integer q. Because the cutoff is smooth with compact support, integration by parts never leaves boundary terms (our own).

**Problem.** Fix δ &gt; 0 and take P sufficiently large. If \|c\| ≥ (q/P)(1+P²\|β\|)Pᵟ, then \|I\| ≤ C(A)Pˢ/(P\|c\|/q)ᴬ for each integer A ≥ 1. The constants may depend on the forms, W and δ.

**How the definition helps.** When \|c\| is this large, the phase has derivative of size about P\|c\|/q in the direction of c on the whole scaled support (our own explanation). Each integration by parts gains that factor with no boundary term, which gives decay to any power A. A sharp cutoff would leave boundary terms; on \[0,1\] its Fourier transform has size 1/(πt) at positive half-integers t.

**Paper or page:** [A two-dimensional delta symbol method and its application to pairs of quadratic forms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.11355v1). It says: “I<sub>q</sub>(\\vec{\\mathrm{w}},\\mathbf{u})\\ll<sub>N</sub> P<sup>s</sup>(P\|\\mathbf{u}\|/q)<sup>-N</sup>\\ll P<sup>s-N\\delta</sup>”

**Sources:**

- [J. Li, S. L. Rydin Myerson and P. Vishe, A two-dimensional delta symbol method and its application to pairs of quadratic forms](https://www.maths.dur.ac.uk/users/pankaj.vishe/2dDelta.pdf)

**Remember:** A good moment below twelve leaves a factor for the arc saving.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method), 11P05, 11L15. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For the smooth Weyl sum g(α) = ∑ exp(2πiαx⁴) over x ≤ P with no prime factor above R, an exponent Δ is admissible for the moment of order t if ∫₀¹\|g\|ᵗ dα = O(P<sup>(t−4+Δ)</sup>), uniformly for 1 ≤ R ≤ P<sup>η</sup> with some fixed η &gt; 0. With Δ = 0 at t below 12, a twelfth moment over E only has to pay for the extra 12−t factors of \|g\| (our own).

**How the definition helps.** On E, write \|g\|¹² = \|g\|ᵗ·\|g\|<sup>(12−t)</sup> and bound the second factor by (εP)<sup>(12−t)</sup> (our own calculation). The moment bound with Δ = 0 then gives P<sup>(t−4)</sup>·(εP)<sup>(12−t)</sup> = P⁸ε<sup>(12−t)</sup>.

**Wikipedia:** [Hardy–Ramanujan–Littlewood circle method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy%E2%80%93Ramanujan%E2%80%93Littlewood_circle_method). It says: “one takes a sufficiently high power of the generating function”

### Bailey pairs generate identity chains

**Remember:** Keep the relation, and each new pair can start the next step.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11P84 (Partition identities; identities of Rogers-Ramanujan type), 11B65. arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A Bailey pair relative to a is two sequences α, β linked by βₙ = ∑<sub>r=0</sub><sup>n</sup> αᵣ/((q;q)<sub>n−r</sub>(aq;q)<sub>n+r</sub>) for all n ≥ 0, where (x;q)ₘ = ∏<sub>0≤j&lt;m</sub>(1−xqʲ) and no denominator vanishes. Bailey’s lemma maps pairs to pairs with the same a, so each output can be fed back in.

**How the definition helps.** The lemma’s output satisfies the same defining relation, so it can serve as the next input, which gives a chain (our own reading). The work lies in the finite summation identity that proves this.

**Remember:** The image of uniform boundary measure stays uniform if the center stays fixed.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R06 (PV-numbers and generalizations; other special algebraic numbers; Mahler measure). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A finite Blaschke product B is a constant of modulus one times factors (z−a)/(1−āz) with \|a\| &lt; 1, so it maps the unit circle to itself. B is centered when B(0) = 0, and then it carries uniform measure on the circle to uniform measure.

**How the definition helps.** For centered B, a harmonic function composed with B keeps its value at 0, which is its circle average, so B preserves uniform measure and the average of log\|P\| (our own proof). Without centering this fails: B(z) = (z+½)/(1+z/2) moves 0 to ½, and the average of log\|z−2\| changes from log 2 to log(3/2) (our own example).

### Constant terms count lattice walks

**Remember:** The constant coefficient keeps exactly the walks that return to the origin.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R06 (PV-numbers and generalizations; other special algebraic numbers; Mahler measure). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

The constant coefficient of Sⁿ counts walks of n unit steps on ℤ² that return to the origin (our own).

In coordinates u+v and u−v each step is two independent signs, so a return needs balanced signs in each coordinate. Katagiri’s comparison with root-of-unity averages identifies this constant coefficient with the measure.

**Remember:** A cyclotomic polynomial in one monomial still has measure zero.

On the torus such a monomial is itself uniform on the unit circle, so the factor has the same measure as Φₙ, which is zero.

**Problem.** A nonzero Laurent polynomial over ℤ has logarithmic Mahler measure zero exactly when it is a signed monomial times a product of extended cyclotomic factors.

**How the definition helps.** Each factor has measure zero because its monomial is uniform on the circle and Jensen’s formula gives Φₙ measure zero (our own explanation). Boyd proves the converse for integer polynomials. A monomial clears negative exponents without changing the measure.

### Dilogarithms evaluate triangular Mahler measure

**Remember:** D is a primitive of the regulator form; integrals become endpoint values.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R06 (PV-numbers and generalizations; other special algebraic numbers; Mahler measure), 11G55. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For 0 &lt; \|z\| &lt; 1, the Bloch–Wigner dilogarithm is D(z) = Im Li₂(z) + arg(1−z) log\|z\|, where Li₂(z) = ∑ₙ≥₁ zⁿ/n² and arg is the principal argument; extend D continuously to zero and the unit circle. Its differential is the regulator form: dD(z) = log\|z\| d arg(1−z) − log\|1−z\| d arg z.

**Problem.** The uniform circle average of log\|1 + x + y\| over x and y equals D(exp(πi/3))/π. This average is the logarithmic Mahler measure.

**How the definition helps.** On the unit circle dD(−x) = −log\|1+x\| d arg x, so the integral left by Jensen’s formula is an endpoint difference of D (our own calculation). Jensen’s formula keeps the arc where \|1+x\| ≥ 1, from exp(−2πi/3) to exp(2πi/3). The endpoint values of D(−x) are D(exp(πi/3)) and its negative, giving the stated average.

**Wikipedia:** [Mahler measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahler_measure). It says: “m(1+x+y)=3√3/(4π) L(χ₋₃,2)”

**Paper or page:** [Generalized Mahler measures of Laurent polynomials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.04601). It says: “\\eta \\left(x, 1-x\\right) = d D\\left(x\\right).”

**Sources:**

- [Generalized Mahler measures of Laurent polynomials, Lemma 2.1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.04601)
- [Smyth, On measures of polynomials in several variables](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0004972700006894)

### Dominant coefficients exclude p-adic zeros

**Remember:** One strictly largest term cannot cancel on the p-adic unit torus.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R06 (PV-numbers and generalizations; other special algebraic numbers; Mahler measure). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A Laurent polynomial over ℂₚ has a dominant coefficient if one coefficient has strictly larger p-adic absolute value than every other. On the unit torus, where every coordinate has absolute value one, each term has the size of its coefficient, so the dominant term outweighs all the others.

**Problem.** A nonzero Laurent polynomial over ℂₚ has no zero on the unit torus exactly when it has a dominant coefficient.

**How the definition helps.** If one term dominates, the strict p-adic triangle inequality forbids cancellation, so there is no zero (our own explanation). The converse uses the lemma’s factorization into a monomial times one plus a polynomial with coefficients of absolute value below one. Our own example 1 − t has tied coefficients and vanishes at t = 1.

**Paper or page:** [A note on p-adic higher Mahler measures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.05724). It says: “Then $f$ does not vanish in any point of $T<sub>p</sub><sup>n$</sup> if and only if we have\\begin{align}  f(t<sub>1</sub>, \\cdots , t<sub>n</sub>)=at<sub>1</sub><sup>l<sub>1</sub></sup>\\cdots t<sub>n</sub><sup>l<sub>n</sub></sup>(1+g(t<sub>1</sub>, \\cdots , t<sub>n</sub>)) \\end{align}for some $a \\in \\mathbb {C}<sub>p</sub><sup>\\times </sup>, (l<sub>1</sub>, \\cdots , l<sub>n</sub>) \\in \\mathbb {Z}<sup>n$</sup> and $g \\in \\mathfrak {m}<sub>p</sub>\[t<sub>1</sub><sup>\\pm 1</sup>, \\dots ,t<sub>n</sub><sup>\\pm 1</sup>\]$.”

**Sources:**

- [A note on p-adic higher Mahler measures, Lemma 2.5](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.05724)

### Exact symbols give boundary integrals

**Remember:** Each term supplies a primitive, so only the boundary remains to integrate.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R06 (PV-numbers and generalizations; other special algebraic numbers; Mahler measure), 11G55. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On the smooth locus of an irreducible surface P(x,y,z) = 0, away from zeros and poles, require x∧y∧z to be a finite rational combination of terms f∧(1−f)∧g. Here ∧ is taken in the third exterior power, with rational coefficients, of the group of nonzero rational functions. Each such term has a known primitive for its regulator form, so the form log\|z\| dθ∧dφ gets a primitive β (our own explanation).

**Problem.** Let Γ be the chain of roots with \|z\| ≥ 1 above \|x\| = \|y\| = 1, counted with multiplicity and oriented by the angles θ, φ of x, y. If Γ is piecewise smooth in this open set, with its boundary, then m(P) minus the measure of the leading coefficient in z is an integral over the boundary of Γ.

**How the definition helps.** Jensen’s formula writes the difference of measures as the integral of log\|z\| dθ∧dφ over Γ divided by (2π)², and the decomposition makes this form exact. Trieu’s regulator identities give the primitive β as a weighted sum over the terms (our own explanation). Stokes’ theorem then replaces the integral over Γ by the integral of β over the oriented boundary.

**Paper or page:** [The Mahler measure of exact polynomials and special L-values of K3 surfaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.00893). It says: “\\mathrm{m}(P) - \\mathrm{m}(\\tilde P) = \\dfrac {(-1)<sup>n-1</sup>}{(2\\pi i)<sup>n-1</sup>} \\int <sub>\\partial \\Gamma </sub> \\rho (\\xi ).”

**Sources:**

- [The Mahler measure of exact polynomials and special L-values of K3 surfaces, Theorem 1.11](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.00893)

### Exterior roots give regulator integrals

**Remember:** Follow the big roots y as x circles; they carry the measure.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R06 (PV-numbers and generalizations; other special algebraic numbers; Mahler measure), 19F27. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let P(x,y) = 0 define an elliptic curve. As x runs counterclockwise once around the unit circle, γ is the oriented path traced on the curve by the roots y with \|y\| &gt; 1, counted with multiplicity. These are exactly the roots that Jensen’s formula keeps in the average of log\|P\| over y.

**Problem.** Assume γ is a finite union of smooth paths, and let P\* be the leading coefficient of P in y. Then m(P) − m(P\*), where m is the average of log\|·\| over the unit torus, equals −1/(2π) times the integral along γ of η = log\|x\| d arg y − log\|y\| d arg x.

**How the definition helps.** Jensen’s formula gives m(P) − m(P\*) as 1/(2π) times the integral of log\|y\| d arg x over the roots on γ (our own explanation). On γ, log\|x\| = 0, so η reduces to −log\|y\| d arg x. This gives the factor −1/(2π).

**Paper or page:** [Determinants of Mahler measures and special values of L-functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.14714). It says: “m(P) − m(P\*) = −1/(2π) ∫γₚ η(x,y).”

**Sources:**

- [Determinants of Mahler measures and special values of L-functions, Theorem 2.1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.14714)

### Short relation bounds imply equidistribution

**Remember:** Large height means no short target monomial collapses to a constant.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R06 (PV-numbers and generalizations; other special algebraic numbers; Mahler measure). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A monomial map between tori replaces each target variable by a product of integer powers of the source variables. Its Boyd height is the least largest-absolute-coordinate of a nonzero exponent vector whose target monomial becomes constant after composing with the map, or infinity if there is none. So with large height every target monomial with small exponents stays nonconstant, and its source average is zero.

**Problem.** Fix the target torus and let the Boyd heights tend to infinity. Then for every continuous g on the target, the source average of g composed with the map tends to the target average of g, and the same holds for g = log\|P\| with P a fixed nonzero Laurent polynomial.

**How the definition helps.** Each fixed nonconstant monomial eventually stays nonconstant on the source, so its source average equals its target average zero (our own argument). Trigonometric polynomials approximate every continuous function uniformly, which gives the first claim. For log\|P\| the Boyd–Lawton theorem controls the region near zeros, where uniform approximation fails.

**Paper or page:** [General Boyd-Lawton Theorems with Multivariable Limits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05910). It says: “If $g\\colon {\\mathbb {T}}<sup>n\\to</sup> {\\mathbb {C}}$ is continuous, then\\\[  \\int \_{{\\mathbb {T}}<sup>n</sup>} g \\,  d \\tau <sub>n</sub> \\;  = \\;  \\lim <sub>\\mu \\left( q<sub>A</sub> \\right)\\to \\infty </sub>\\;  \\int \_{{\\mathbb {T}}<sup>m}</sup> g \\circ q<sub>A</sub> \\;  d \\tau \_m,  \\\]”

**Sources:**

- [General Boyd-Lawton Theorems with Multivariable Limits, Corollary 6.1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05910)

### Tempered faces prevent tame obstructions

**Remember:** Cyclotomic edge roots make every boundary tame symbol torsion.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R06 (PV-numbers and generalizations; other special algebraic numbers; Mahler measure), 19D45. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A two-variable Laurent polynomial is tempered if, on every edge of its Newton polygon, the edge polynomial has only roots of unity as nonzero roots. The edge polynomial takes the coefficients at successive lattice points of the edge, zeros included, as the coefficients of a one-variable polynomial. Every boundary tame symbol of x and y is ± a power of an edge root, so temperedness makes them all torsion (our own).

**Problem.** Take an irreducible tempered polynomial over ℚ whose Newton polygon has positive area. On its smooth complete curve every tame symbol of x and y is a root of unity, so their symbol has no boundary obstruction with rational coefficients.

**How the definition helps.** At a point with uniformizer t, write x = tᵐa and y = tⁿb with units a, b, so the tame symbol is (−1)ᵐⁿaⁿ/bᵐ (our own calculation). For (m,n) ≠ (0,0) the lowest-order terms cancel along one edge, so the leading unit in its primitive direction is an edge root. Our own example x + y + 2 is not tempered, and its symbol at x = 0 is −1/2.

**Paper or page:** [A shifted Mahler measure identity for Boyd's family](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.09974). It says: “Qₖ(x,y) and Qₖ(x−1,y) are tempered polynomials.”

**Sources:**

- [A shifted Mahler measure identity for Boyd's family, Lemma 3.1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.09974)
- [Yang, Liu and Tang, A Mahler Measure Identity Involving a Genus 2 Family, Section 1](https://ccj.pku.edu.cn/Article/DownLoad?id=364490499&type=ArticleFile)

### Monic polynomials are Hermite equivalent exactly when their rings ℤ\[X\]∕(f) are isomorphic

**Remember:** For monic polynomials, compare the rings, not the norm forms.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R09 (Polynomials (irreducibility, etc.)), 11R54. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The norm form of a monic integer polynomial f of degree n sends integer coordinates (a₀,…,aₙ₋₁) to the norm of a₀ + a₁X + … + aₙ₋₁Xⁿ⁻¹ in ℤ\[X\]/(f), the determinant of multiplication by that element (our own description). Two monic polynomials are Hermite equivalent when an invertible integer change of coordinates turns one norm form into the other.
