### Almost uniform convergence gives Egorov’s theorem one exceptional set

**Remember:** Discard one set of arbitrarily small measure to get uniform convergence.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A20 (Measurable and nonmeasurable functions, sequences of measurable functions, modes of convergence). arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Convergence is almost uniform if, for every ε &gt; 0, convergence is uniform outside some measurable set of measure less than ε.

**Problem.** On a finite measure space, suppose real measurable functions converge to a real measurable limit outside a set of measure zero. Then they converge almost uniformly.

**How the definition helps.** Finite measure makes the error sets of pointwise convergence small, so they can be gathered into one small exceptional set (our own). For each k, the points where some error after index N exceeds 1/k form sets that decrease in N to measure zero, so their measures tend to zero (our own). Choose N for each k with measures summing below ε; outside their union, convergence is uniform (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Egorov's Theorem](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Egorov's_Theorem). It says: “Then fₙ converges a.u. to f.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Borel sets on the target make measurable functions compose

**Remember:** Test only Borel sets, so a Borel map after it is safe.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A20 (Measurable and nonmeasurable functions, sequences of measurable functions, modes of convergence), 28A05. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A Lebesgue measurable function f : ℝ → ℂ pulls back each Borel set of ℂ to a Lebesgue measurable set. Only Borel sets are tested on the target, though the source allows all Lebesgue sets.

**Problem.** If f is Lebesgue measurable and g is Borel measurable, then g ∘ f is Lebesgue measurable. In particular, continuous functions of measurable functions, and sums and products of measurable functions, are measurable.

**How the definition helps.** For each Borel B, g⁻¹(B) is Borel, so f⁻¹(g⁻¹(B)) is Lebesgue measurable (our own). A pair of measurable functions is measurable because open rectangles from a countable basis have measurable preimages (our own). Addition and multiplication are continuous functions of this pair (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Measurable function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measurable_function). It says: “Indeed, two Lebesgue-measurable functions may be constructed in such a way as to make their composition non-Lebesgue-measurable.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Completeness preserves measurability after changes on a null set

**Remember:** A complete measure lets you change a function anywhere on a null set.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A20 (Measurable and nonmeasurable functions, sequences of measurable functions, modes of convergence), 28A12. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A measure is complete when every subset of a measurable set of measure zero is measurable.

**Problem.** On a complete measure space, a real function that agrees with a measurable function outside a null set is measurable.

**How the definition helps.** For each Borel set, its new inverse image combines the old inverse image outside the null set with a subset inside it (our own). Completeness makes that subset measurable (our own). Without completeness, the indicator of a nonmeasurable subset of a measurable null set agrees almost everywhere with zero (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Lebesgue measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebesgue_measure). It says: “However, as a measure on only the Borel sets, it is not complete: a subset of a Borel set of measure zero need not itself be Borel.”

**Paper or page:** [Function A.E. Equal to Measurable Function in Complete Measure Space is Measurable](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Function_A.E._Equal_to_Measurable_Function_in_Complete_Measure_Space_is_Measurable). It says: “Then g is Σ-measurable.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Finite test sets give local convergence in measure

**Remember:** Measure the bad sets one finite piece at a time.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A20 (Measurable and nonmeasurable functions, sequences of measurable functions, modes of convergence). arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Functions fₙ converge locally in measure to f when, for each measurable set of finite measure and each ε &gt; 0, the measure of the part of that set where \|fₙ − f\| &gt; ε tends to zero.

**Problem.** Almost everywhere convergence of real measurable functions implies local convergence in measure on any measure space.

**How the definition helps.** On a set of finite measure, continuity from above applies to decreasing sets (our own). There, the points with some error above ε from index n onward form sets that decrease to a null set, so their measures tend to zero (our own). Global convergence can fail: on ℝ the indicators of \[n, n+1\] tend to zero pointwise, yet each has measure one (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Convergence in measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_in_measure). It says: “if (fₙ) converges to f almost everywhere, then (fₙ) converges to f locally in measure.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Measurable level sets stay measurable under pointwise limits

**Remember:** Check measurability one rational threshold at a time.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A20 (Measurable and nonmeasurable functions, sequences of measurable functions, modes of convergence). arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A real function is measurable when, for every rational q, the set where it exceeds q is measurable; this test is equivalent to testing all Borel preimages.

**Problem.** If real-valued measurable functions converge pointwise to a real-valued function, then their limit is measurable.

**How the definition helps.** The limit exceeds t exactly when, for some rational q &gt; t, all late enough terms exceed q (our own). So that set is a countable union of countable intersections of measurable sets (our own). The generator theorem equates the threshold test with the test on all Borel sets (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Pointwise Limit of Measurable Functions is Measurable](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Pointwise_Limit_of_Measurable_Functions_is_Measurable). It says: “Then the pointwise limit limₙ→∞ fₙ: X → ℝ̄ is also Σ-measurable.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The subsequence test makes continuous functions preserve convergence in measure

**Remember:** Follow each almost everywhere convergent subsequence through the continuous function.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A20 (Measurable and nonmeasurable functions, sequences of measurable functions, modes of convergence). arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** On a finite measure space, fₙ converge in measure to f exactly when every subsequence has a further subsequence converging to f almost everywhere. The usual definition asks that, for each ε &gt; 0, the measure where \|fₙ − f\| &gt; ε tends to zero.

**Problem.** On a finite measure space, suppose real measurable functions fₙ converge in measure to a real measurable function f. For every continuous real function h, the functions h(fₙ) converge to h(f) in measure.

**How the definition helps.** Continuity of h carries the almost everywhere convergence of each further subsequence over to h(fₙ), so h(fₙ) passes the test (our own). The subsequence criterion does the work, by choosing indices whose error-set measures are summable (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Convergence in measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_in_measure). It says: “converges to f locally in measure if and only if every subsequence has in turn a subsequence that converges to f almost everywhere.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Counting measure turns nonnegative series into integrals

**Remember:** Counting measure gives each term of the series weight one.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A25 (Integration with respect to measures and other set functions), 28A12. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Counting measure on ℕ gives a finite set its number of elements and an infinite set measure ∞. Each singleton thus has mass one.

**Problem.** For any nonnegative function on ℕ, its integral for counting measure equals the sum of its values, even when the sum is infinite.

**How the definition helps.** On a finite set, each value contributes exactly once because its singleton has mass one (our own). Monotone convergence does the work of passing from finite initial segments to the whole sum (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Integral of Positive Function with respect to Counting Measure on Natural Numbers](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Integral_of_Positive_Function_with_respect_to_Counting_Measure_on_Natural_Numbers). It says: “Then: ∫ f dμ = ∑ₙ₌₁<sup>∞</sup> f(n)”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Differences of positive integrals make the signed integral linear

**Remember:** Add the nonnegative pieces before subtracting their integrals.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A25 (Integration with respect to measures and other set functions). arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a real measurable f with finite integral of \|f\|, define ∫f as ∫f⁺ − ∫f⁻. Here f⁺ = max(f, 0) and f⁻ = max(−f, 0).

**Problem.** The Lebesgue integral is linear on real integrable functions. If f = a − b with nonnegative integrable a and b, then ∫f = ∫a − ∫b.

**How the definition helps.** If f = a − b, then a + f⁻ = b + f⁺, so additivity of nonnegative integrals gives ∫a − ∫b = ∫f⁺ − ∫f⁻ (our own). So any splitting into nonnegative integrable parts computes the integral, without finding the positive and negative parts of a sum (our own). Add or scale the two parts separately, exchanging them when the scalar is negative (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Integral of Integrable Function is Homogeneous](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Integral_of_Integrable_Function_is_Homogeneous), [Integral of Integrable Function is Additive](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Integral_of_Integrable_Function_is_Additive). It says: “Then λf is μ-integrable, and: ∫ λf dμ = λ ∫ f dμ”

### Large-power norms find essential suprema

**Remember:** Large powers detect every height that occurs on positive measure.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28A25 (Integration with respect to measures and other set functions), 28A20. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The essential supremum of \|f\| is the least M in \[0, ∞\] with \|f\| ≤ M almost everywhere, so it ignores peaks on sets of measure zero (our own). For finite p ≥ 1, the p-norm of f is (∫\|f\|ᵖ)<sup>(1/p)</sup>.

**Problem.** On a probability space, the p-norms of a measurable function tend to the essential supremum of its absolute value as p tends to infinity. Both norms and limit may equal infinity.

**How the definition helps.** Each height below the essential supremum is exceeded on a set of positive measure, and the pth root of that measure tends to one (our own). The essential supremum bounds every p-norm because the space has measure one (our own). Without ignoring null sets, the indicator of one point in \[0, 1\] would have supremum one but every p-norm zero (our own).

**nLab:** [essential supremum](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/essential+supremum). It says: “But we ignore things that happen only on a null set.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Tail infima prove Fatou

**Remember:** Take the infimum before integrating, then let the tail move.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A25 (Integration with respect to measures and other set functions). arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The limit inferior of a sequence is the supremum over n of the infimum of its tail from n onward, so it is the limit of increasing tail infima.

**Problem.** For nonnegative measurable functions, the integral of their pointwise limit inferior is at most the limit inferior of their integrals.

**How the definition helps.** The tail formula gives increasing measurable functions without choosing a subsequence at each point (our own). Each tail infimum has integral at most the infimum of the integrals over that tail (our own). Monotone convergence identifies the limit of these integrals with the integral of the pointwise limit inferior (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Fatou's Lemma for Integrals/Positive Measurable Functions](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Fatou's_Lemma_for_Integrals/Positive_Measurable_Functions). It says: “∫ lim inf fₙ dμ ≤ lim inf ∫ fₙ dμ”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Testing a density on every measurable set makes it unique

**Remember:** Test where one density is larger than the other.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A25 (Integration with respect to measures and other set functions), 28A12. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A density of a finite measure ν relative to μ is a nonnegative measurable function g with ∫<sub>E</sub> g dμ = ν(E) for every measurable set E.

**Problem.** Two densities of the same finite measure relative to the same measure μ are equal outside a μ-null set.

**How the definition helps.** Test on the set where one density exceeds the other: the integrals there agree and are finite, so the positive difference vanishes μ-almost everywhere (our own). Exchanging the densities handles the opposite difference (our own). Matching only total mass would not suffice, since the indicators of either half of \[0, 1\] both have mass one half (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Radon-Nikodym Theorem](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Radon-Nikodym_Theorem). It says: “then: g₁ = g₂ μ-almost everywhere.”

### The Lebesgue integral lets limits pass inside the integral

**Remember:** Measure each level of a simple function, then approximate from below.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A25 (Integration with respect to measures and other set functions), 28A20. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The Lebesgue integral of a nonnegative measurable f is the supremum of the integrals of nonnegative simple functions s ≤ f, where each value of s counts times the measure of its level set. For an integrable real function, subtract the integral of its negative part from that of its positive part (our own).

**Problem.** If nonnegative measurable functions increase pointwise to f, their integrals tend to ∫f. If measurable real functions converge pointwise to f under a common integrable absolute bound, their integrals tend to ∫f.

**How the definition helps.** Measurability passes to pointwise limits, and the hypotheses ensure that each limit has a defined integral (our own). The monotone convergence theorem handles increasing nonnegative functions, and the dominated convergence theorem handles the common integrable bound (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Lebesgue integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebesgue_integral), [Dominated convergence theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominated_convergence_theorem). It says: “The main purpose of the Lebesgue integral is to provide an integral notion where limits of integrals hold under mild assumptions.”

**Sources:**

- [H. Lebesgue, Intégrale, longueur, aire, Ann. Mat. Pura Appl. 7 (1902), 231–359, doi:10.1007/BF02420592](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02420592)

### The lower-sum definition makes the Lebesgue integral monotone

**Remember:** A higher function admits every lower test of a smaller one.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A25 (Integration with respect to measures and other set functions). arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a nonnegative measurable function, define its integral as the supremum of integrals of nonnegative simple functions below it. A simple function takes finitely many values, with a measurable set of points for each value.

**Problem.** If nonnegative measurable functions f and g satisfy f ≤ g, then ∫f dμ ≤ ∫g dμ.

**How the definition helps.** Every simple function below f also lies below g, so the supremum for g includes every test for f (our own). Defining the integral by limits instead requires proving that all increasing simple approximations give the same limit (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Integral of Positive Measurable Function is Monotone](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Integral_of_Positive_Measurable_Function_is_Monotone). It says: “This can be summarized by saying that ∫ · dμ is monotone.”

### The lower-test integral makes Markov’s bound a single comparison

**Remember:** Use the threshold as a lower bound wherever the function reaches it.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A25 (Integration with respect to measures and other set functions), 28A20. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a nonnegative measurable function, the Lebesgue integral is the supremum of integrals of nonnegative simple functions below it. A simple function takes only finitely many values on measurable sets.

**Problem.** For a nonnegative measurable function f and any t &gt; 0, the measure of {f ≥ t} is at most (∫f dμ)/t. In particular, convergence in Lᵖ implies convergence in measure for every finite p ≥ 1.

**How the definition helps.** The function equal to t on {f ≥ t} and zero elsewhere is a simple function below f, with integral t·μ({f ≥ t}) (our own). So ∫f, the supremum over such functions, is at least that, which is the bound (our own). Applying the bound to \|fₙ − f\|ᵖ at threshold εᵖ shows that Lᵖ convergence gives convergence in measure (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Markov's Inequality](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Markov's_Inequality). It says: “μ({x ∈ A : \|f(x)\| ≥ t}) ≤ (1/t) ∫ₐ \|f\| dμ”

### Absolute integrability rules out conflicting orders in Fubini’s theorem

**Remember:** Integrate the absolute value before trusting a change of order.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A35 (Measures and integrals in product spaces), 28A25. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A real measurable function is integrable when its absolute value has finite integral, so its positive and negative parts both have finite integrals. A measure space is σ-finite if countably many sets of finite measure cover it.

**Problem.** For an integrable function on a product of two σ-finite measure spaces, almost every slice in either direction is integrable. Both orders of integration give the integral over the product.

**How the definition helps.** Absolute integrability makes both parts finite, so Tonelli’s theorem lets us integrate the positive and negative parts separately. On pairs of positive integers with counting measure, put 1 at (i,i), −1 at (i,i+1), and zero elsewhere (our own). Every row sums to zero, but the first column sums to one and all later columns sum to zero (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Fubini's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fubini%27s_theorem). It says: “Use the condition that the functions are integrable to write them as the difference of two positive integrable functions and apply Tonelli's theorem to each of these.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Measurable rectangles make every section of a product set measurable

**Remember:** Taking a section commutes with complements and countable unions.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A35 (Measures and integrals in product spaces), 28A20. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The product σ-algebra is the smallest σ-algebra containing all rectangles A × B with measurable sides. The vertical section of a set E at x is the set of y with (x, y) ∈ E.

**Problem.** Every vertical or horizontal section of a set in the product σ-algebra is measurable in the corresponding factor.

**How the definition helps.** Rectangles have measurable sections, and taking a section commutes with complements and countable unions (our own). So the sets with measurable sections form a σ-algebra containing every rectangle, hence the whole product σ-algebra (our own). Completion can break this: in the plane every subset of a vertical line is Lebesgue measurable, including one with a nonmeasurable section (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Vertical Section of Measurable Set is Measurable](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Vertical_Section_of_Measurable_Set_is_Measurable). It says: “where Eₓ is the x-vertical section of E.”

### Requiring σ-finite measures makes Tonelli's theorem true

**Remember:** σ-finite spaces can be cut into countably many finite pieces.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A35 (Measures and integrals in product spaces), 28A12. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A measure space is σ-finite when it is a countable union of sets of finite measure.

**Problem.** For two σ-finite measure spaces, consider a nonnegative function measurable for the product σ-algebra. Its two iterated integrals both equal its integral against the product measure.

**How the definition helps.** σ-finiteness lets Tonelli’s theorem pass from finite pieces to the whole product by monotone convergence (our own). Give \[0, 1\] Lebesgue measure in one factor and counting measure, which is not σ-finite, in the other. The diagonal indicator then has iterated integrals zero and one, so they cannot both equal its product integral.

**Wikipedia:** [Fubini's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fubini%27s_theorem). It says: “This shows that Tonelli's theorem can fail for spaces that are not σ-finite no matter which product measure is chosen.”

### Testing box volumes identifies the product as Lebesgue measure

**Remember:** A product of boxes is a box, and their volumes multiply.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A35 (Measures and integrals in product spaces), 28A12. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Borel Lebesgue measure on ℝⁿ is the unique Borel measure that gives each half-open box its volume, the product of its side lengths. A product measure gives each measurable rectangle A × B the measure of A times the measure of B.

**Problem.** The product of Borel Lebesgue measures on ℝᵐ and ℝⁿ is Borel Lebesgue measure on ℝᵐ⁺ⁿ.

**How the definition helps.** A half-open box in ℝᵐ⁺ⁿ is a box in ℝᵐ times a box in ℝⁿ, so the product measure gives it its volume, and uniqueness forces equality (our own). This uses the fact that the product of the Borel σ-algebras of ℝᵐ and ℝⁿ is the Borel σ-algebra of ℝᵐ⁺ⁿ (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Product measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Product_measure). It says: “the completion procedure is needed to extend the Borel measure into the Lebesgue measure, or to extend the product of two Lebesgue measures to give the Lebesgue measure on the product space.”

**Paper or page:** [Existence and Uniqueness of Lebesgue Measure](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Existence_and_Uniqueness_of_Lebesgue_Measure). It says: “Then Lebesgue measure, the extension of λⁿ to the Borel σ-algebra ℬ(ℝⁿ), exists and is unique.”

### Standard Borel spaces always have conditional distributions

**Remember:** Standard Borel means countable or a copy of the real line.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A05 (Classes of sets (Borel fields, σ-rings, etc.), measurable sets, Suslin sets, analytic sets), 60A10, 60B05. arXiv math.PR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A measurable space is standard Borel if its σ-algebra is the Borel σ-algebra of a Polish topology, one given by a complete separable metric. Up to isomorphism these are the countable discrete spaces and ℝ, where a law is fixed by countably many numbers (our own).

**Problem.** On a standard Borel probability space, every sub-σ-algebra admits a regular conditional distribution of the identity. Given an input probability, every Markov kernel between standard Borel spaces has a Bayesian inverse, unique almost surely under the output law.

**How the definition helps.** Because the space is countable or a copy of ℝ, conditional probabilities of countably many generating sets fit together into a regular conditional distribution (our own). Disintegrating the joint law of input and output over the output gives the Bayesian inverse (our own). A countable generating class makes it unique outside one null set of the output law (our own).

It says: “They provide a setting for many constructions in probability theory, including conditional probability, disintegration, and countable products.”

### The partition definition of total variation makes it the least dominating measure

**Remember:** Total variation is the largest absolute sum over finite partitions.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28A10 (Real- or complex-valued set functions), 28A25. arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The total variation \|μ\|(A) is the largest total absolute mass that a finite measurable partition of A can show. It is the supremum, over such partitions, of the sum of \|μ(piece)\| for signed or complex μ (our own).

**Problem.** Always \|μ(A)\| ≤ \|μ\|(A). Every positive measure ν with \|μ(A)\| ≤ ν(A) for all measurable A satisfies \|μ\|(A) ≤ ν(A).

**How the definition helps.** The one-piece partition gives \|μ(A)\| ≤ \|μ\|(A) (our own). If ν dominates, each partition sum ∑\|μ(Aᵢ)\| is at most ∑ν(Aᵢ) = ν(A), so the supremum is at most ν(A) (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Total Variation is Smallest Measure exceeding Modulus of Measure](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Total_Variation_is_Smallest_Measure_exceeding_Modulus_of_Measure). It says: “\|μ(A)\| ≤ ν(A) for each A ∈ Σ.”

### Total variation adds both signs

**Remember:** Count both signs as positive mass.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A10 (Real- or complex-valued set functions). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite signed measure μ, split the space into measurable sets P and N. Every measurable subset of P has mass ≥ 0, and every measurable subset of N has mass ≤ 0. Then \|μ\|(A) = μ(A ∩ P) − μ(A ∩ N), a sum of two nonnegative measures (our own).

**Problem.** The total variation of a finite signed measure is a nonnegative measure.

**How the definition helps.** A sum of two nonnegative measures is a nonnegative measure, so the theorem holds at once (our own). The Hahn decomposition theorem supplies P and N (our own). The value equals the supremum of absolute partition sums, so it does not depend on the choice of P and N (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Variation of Signed Measure is Measure](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Variation_of_Signed_Measure_is_Measure). It says: “Then \|μ\| is a measure.”

### Finite mass controls small sets

**Remember:** Finite mass turns null-to-null into small-to-small.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A12 (Contents, measures, outer measures, capacities). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A finite measure ν is absolutely continuous with respect to μ if it vanishes on every measurable set of μ-mass zero. Finiteness makes ν of a decreasing sequence of sets tend to ν of their intersection (our own).

**Problem.** Suppose ν is finite and absolutely continuous with respect to μ. For every ε &gt; 0, some δ &gt; 0 ensures ν(A) &lt; ε for every measurable A with μ(A) &lt; δ.

**How the definition helps.** If the bound fails for some ε, choose sets Aₙ with μ(Aₙ) ≤ 2⁻ⁿ and ν(Aₙ) ≥ ε (our own). The unions of their tails decrease to a μ-null set that keeps ν-mass at least ε, a contradiction (our own). Without finiteness it fails: take ν counting measure on the positive integers and μ({n}) = 2⁻ⁿ (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Characterization of Absolutely Continuous Measures](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Characterization_of_Absolutely_Continuous_Measures). It says: “for each ε &gt; 0 there exists δ &gt; 0 such that for each A ∈ Σ with μ(A) &lt; δ, we have ν(A) &lt; ε.”

### Truly continuous measures give Radon–Nikodym without σ-finiteness

**Remember:** One set of finite measure carries almost all of ν.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A12 (Contents, measures, outer measures, capacities), 28A25. arXiv math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A real finitely additive set function ν is truly continuous with respect to μ if, for each ε &gt; 0, it is small away from one set of finite measure. Precisely, some measurable E with μ(E) &lt; ∞ and some δ &gt; 0 give \|ν(F)\| &lt; ε whenever μ(E ∩ F) &lt; δ.

**Problem.** A real finitely additive ν has an integrable density with respect to μ exactly when ν is truly continuous with respect to μ. A density f satisfies ν(E) = ∫<sub>E</sub> f dμ for every measurable E.

**How the definition helps.** True continuity is the finite-measure control that the Radon–Nikodym theorem needs when μ is not σ-finite (our own). On an uncountable set with the countable–cocountable σ-algebra, let μ be counting measure and let ν give cocountable sets mass one. Then ν is absolutely continuous, but for each finite E its complement F has μ(E ∩ F) = 0 and ν(F) = 1 (our own).

**nLab:** [Radon–Nikodym derivative](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Radon%E2%80%93Nikodym+derivative). It says: “The following example shows that the condition of being truly continuous is necessary in the non-σ-finite case.”

- [David H. Fremlin, Measure Theory, Volume 2, Chapter 23](https://www1.essex.ac.uk/maths/people/fremlin/mt.htm)

### Measure densities multiply

**Remember:** Changing the reference measure twice multiplies the two weights.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28A15 (Abstract differentiation theory, differentiation of set functions), 28A25. arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A density dν/dμ is a nonnegative measurable function whose μ-integral over each measurable set is its ν-measure. Equivalently, integrating a nonnegative g against ν is integrating g·(dν/dμ) against μ (our own).

**Problem.** Let ν, μ and λ be σ-finite positive measures on one space, with ν vanishing on μ-null sets and μ vanishing on λ-null sets. Then dν/dλ = (dν/dμ)(dμ/dλ) outside a λ-null set, for finite versions of the densities.

**How the definition helps.** Apply the integration rule twice: ν(A) = ∫<sub>A</sub> (dν/dμ) dμ = ∫<sub>A</sub> (dν/dμ)(dμ/dλ) dλ for each measurable A (our own). The rule follows from indicators by monotone convergence, and the Radon–Nikodym theorem makes the density unique λ-almost everywhere (our own).

**nLab:** [absolutely continuous measure](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/absolutely+continuous+measure). It says: “This measure f ν is absolutely continuous with respect to ν.”

### Continuous sections keep substitution measurable

**Remember:** Measurable in the point, continuous in the value.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A20 (Measurable and nonmeasurable functions, sequences of measurable functions, modes of convergence), 26B40. arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Carathéodory function W(x, y), with x in an open set Ω of Euclidean space and y in a Euclidean space, is Lebesgue measurable in x for each fixed y. Outside one null set of x, it is continuous in y, so limits in y pass through W (our own).

**Problem.** For each Lebesgue measurable map u from Ω into the space of y values, x ↦ W(x, u(x)) is Lebesgue measurable.

**How the definition helps.** Approximate u by measurable maps uₖ with countably many values; each x ↦ W(x, uₖ(x)) is measurable by measurability in x (our own). Continuity in y makes W(x, uₖ(x)) tend to W(x, u(x)) outside the fixed null set (our own). Without continuity, the indicator of {(a, a) ∣ a ∈ A} for nonmeasurable A ⊂ ℝ has measurable sections, but u(x) = x gives the indicator of A (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Carathéodory function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carath%C3%A9odory_function). It says: “the mapping ξ ↦ W(x, ξ) is continuous for almost every x ∈ Ω.”

### Defining convergence in measure by truncated distances makes it metrizable

**Remember:** Cap each pointwise error at one, then integrate.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A20 (Measurable and nonmeasurable functions, sequences of measurable functions, modes of convergence), 46E30. arXiv math.CA, math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For real measurable f and g and each measurable set E of finite measure, put ρ<sub>E</sub>(f, g) = ∫<sub>E</sub> min{\|f − g\|, 1} dμ, the error capped at one. Local convergence in measure is convergence in all these pseudometrics, and ρ<sub>E</sub> grows with E (our own).

**Problem.** On a finite measure space, convergence in measure comes from one metric on measurable functions, once functions equal almost everywhere are identified.

**How the definition helps.** On a finite measure space, ρ<sub>X</sub> dominates every ρ<sub>E</sub>, so the single pseudometric ρ<sub>X</sub> gives the topology. It is zero exactly when the functions agree almost everywhere, so it is a metric on the classes (our own). Splitting the integral at a positive error threshold gives the usual test for convergence in measure (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Convergence in measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_in_measure). It says: “When μ(X) &lt; ∞, we may consider only one metric ρ<sub>X</sub>, so the topology of convergence in finite measure is metrizable.”

### Defining the Lebesgue integral by horizontal slices gives the layer cake formula

**Remember:** Add up the areas of the horizontal slabs.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A25 (Integration with respect to measures and other set functions), 26A42. arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For nonnegative measurable f, slice the region under its graph horizontally; the slice at height t has measure F(t) = μ{x ∣ f(x) &gt; t}. Define ∫f dμ as the improper Riemann integral of F over (0, ∞). To allow infinite values, take the supremum of ∫ₐᵇ min{F(t), M} dt over 0 &lt; a &lt; b &lt; ∞ and M &gt; 0 (our own).

**Problem.** Let f be nonnegative and measurable. Its integral equals the integral over t from 0 to ∞ of μ{f &gt; t}, also when both are infinite.

**How the definition helps.** With this definition the formula is the definition itself, as Wikipedia notes. The real content is that the slice integral agrees with the simple-function integral (our own). Check it for simple functions, then pass to increasing limits by monotone convergence (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Lebesgue integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebesgue_integral). It says: “The Lebesgue integral may then be defined as the improper Riemann integral of f∗:”

### Bounded mass controls vague tests

**Remember:** Bounded total mass keeps far-out tails small in every integral.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A33 (Spaces of measures, convergence of measures). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Measures μₙ converge vaguely to μ if ∫f dμₙ → ∫f dμ for every continuous f that is zero outside a compact set. A uniform bound on total masses keeps the far-out part of a test tending to zero at infinity small in every integral (our own).

**Problem.** Suppose finite positive Borel measures on the line converge vaguely to a finite measure and have uniformly bounded masses. Their integrals converge against every continuous function vanishing at infinity.

**How the definition helps.** Replace a test g vanishing at infinity by a compactly supported one within ε of it everywhere; the mass bound M makes every integral error at most Mε (our own). Without the bound, mass n at the point n tends vaguely to zero, but its integral against 1/(1 + \|x\|) tends to one (our own).

### Lipschitz tests bound closed-set masses

**Remember:** Fade a closed set’s indicator to zero just beyond its boundary.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A33 (Spaces of measures, convergence of measures). arXiv math.PR, math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A bounded Lipschitz test is a bounded real function f on a metric space with \|f(x) − f(y)\| ≤ L·d(x, y) for some finite L. Such tests can fade the indicator of a closed set C to zero within distance 1/n, as fₙ(x) = max(0, 1 − n·dist(x, C)) (our own).

**Problem.** Suppose Borel probabilities on a metric space converge against every bounded Lipschitz test to a Borel probability P. For every closed C, their masses on C have limit superior at most P(C).

**How the definition helps.** Each probability Pₖ satisfies Pₖ(C) ≤ ∫fₙ dPₖ, which tends to ∫fₙ dP, so lim sup Pₖ(C) ≤ ∫fₙ dP (our own). As n grows, fₙ decreases to the indicator of the closed set C, so ∫fₙ dP tends to P(C) by bounded convergence (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Convergence of measures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_of_measures). It says: “lim sup Pₙ(C) ≤ P(C) for all closed sets C of space S”

Without σ-finiteness, take length and counting measure on \[0, 1\]. Summing lengths of horizontal sections gives the diagonal mass zero, while adding length along the diagonal gives it mass one, and every rectangle keeps its mass (our own).

### New densities reweight fiber laws

**Remember:** Weight each fiber, then move its total weight to the image law.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28A50 (Integration and disintegration of measures). arXiv math.PR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Disintegrate m along φ into a probability kernel of fiber laws mᵧ, where mᵧ lives on φ⁻¹({y}) for almost every y under the image law ν. These fiber laws average back to m: ∫mᵧ(A) dν(y) = m(A) for every Borel A.

**How the definition helps.** Reweighting by ρ acts fiber by fiber, so the weight on each fiber, h(y), is the new image density (our own). Integrating h over an image event gives its reweighted probability, and ρmᵧ/h(y) stays on the same fiber (our own). Integrating these laws against hν cancels h and recovers ρm, and fibers with h(y) equal to 0 or ∞ have zero hν-mass (our own).
