### Standard probability spaces make every measure-algebra map come from a point map

**Remember:** Standard spaces have enough points, so set maps come from point maps.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A60 (Measures on Boolean rings, measure algebras), 60A10. arXiv math.PR, math.DS. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A probability space is standard if, after removing null sets, it is isomorphic to an interval with Lebesgue measure, a countable set of atoms, or a disjoint union of both. Its measure algebra is the Boolean algebra of measurable sets, with sets that differ by a null set treated as equal.

**Problem.** Between standard probability spaces, every probability-preserving Boolean homomorphism of measure algebras comes from inverse images under a measure-preserving point map. The point map is determined up to null sets.

**How the definition helps.** On a standard space, countably many events separate points, so an event map pins down each image point; this is the spatial realization theorem (our own). The perforated interval, a set of inner measure zero and outer measure one, has the same measure algebra as the interval. A point map realizing this identity would equal the identity almost everywhere, so the perforated set would contain a set of full length, which it does not (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Standard probability space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_probability_space). It says: “It may seem that every homomorphism of measure algebras has to correspond to some measure preserving map, but it is not so. However, for standard probability spaces each F corresponds to some f.”

**Sources:**

- [V. A. Rokhlin, On the fundamental ideas of measure theory, Mat. Sbornik 25 (67) (1949), 107–150; English translation, AMS Translations 71 (1952), 1–54](http://ma.huji.ac.il/~matang02/rohlin.pdf)

### Flat norms contract boundaries

**Remember:** Flat norm is the cheapest split into small piece plus boundary.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A75 (Length, area, volume, other geometric measure theory). arXiv math.MG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The flat norm of a Euclidean k-current T is the cheapest way to write T as a piece plus a boundary. It is the infimum of mass(R) + mass(S) over all T = R + ∂S with finite-mass currents R of dimension k and S of dimension k + 1, or ∞ if none exists (our own).

**Problem.** The boundary operator is a contraction for the flat norm on Euclidean currents of finite flat norm.

**How the definition helps.** Each decomposition T = R + ∂S gives ∂T = ∂R, because ∂∂S = 0 (our own). So ∂T = 0 + ∂R is a decomposition of cost mass(R) ≤ mass(R) + mass(S) (our own). Taking the infimum gives flat(∂T) ≤ flat(T) (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Current (mathematics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Current_%28mathematics%29). It says: “they are close in the flat norm if they coincide up to a small deformation.”

**Sources:**

- [Herbert Federer and Wendell H. Fleming, Normal and Integral Currents (1960)](https://doi.org/10.2307/1970227)

### Lipschitz charts preserve rectifiability

**Remember:** Lipschitz pieces of ℝᵐ cover all but a null set.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A75 (Length, area, volume, other geometric measure theory). arXiv math.MG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A set is countably m-rectifiable if countably many Lipschitz images of subsets of ℝᵐ cover it, apart from a set of m-dimensional Hausdorff measure zero.

**Problem.** A Lipschitz map between metric spaces sends a countably m-rectifiable set to a countably m-rectifiable set, for m ≥ 1.

**How the definition helps.** Composing each chart with the given map gives another Lipschitz chart (our own). An L-Lipschitz map multiplies each covering diameter by at most L, so the exceptional set still has zero m-dimensional Hausdorff measure (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Rectifiable set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rectifiable_set). It says: “Equivalently, the fᵢ may be taken to be Lipschitz continuous without altering the definition.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Normal components count boundary crossings

**Remember:** The projected area factor turns a boundary integral into a crossing count.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A75 (Length, area, volume, other geometric measure theory). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A set E has finite perimeter when the distributional gradient of its indicator is a finite vector measure. Its reduced boundary is the set of points where this gradient, divided by its total variation on shrinking centered balls, tends to a unit vector, the normal.

**Problem.** Let E be a bounded set of finite perimeter in ℝⁿ, and integrate the absolute last component of its normal over the reduced boundary against (n−1)-dimensional Hausdorff measure. The result equals the integral over horizontal coordinates x′ of the number of reduced boundary points on the vertical line through x′.

**How the definition helps.** The reduced boundary carries a normal and, by De Giorgi's theorem, a tangent plane at almost every point, so the projection formula can be stated (our own). Projecting that plane onto the horizontal coordinates scales area by the absolute last component of the normal (our own). The area formula integrates this factor and counts the points in each fiber (our own).

**Paper or page:** [The Petty projection inequality for sets of finite perimeter](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.07103v1). It says: “\\int\_{\\partial<sup>\\ast</sup>E}g(x)\|\\nu<sup>E<sub>y</sub></sup>(x)\|d\\mathcal{H}<sup>n-1</sup>(x)=\\int\_{\\mathbb{R}<sup>n-1</sup>}dx<sup>\\prime</sup>\\int\_{(\\partial<sup>\\ast</sup>E)\_{x<sup>\\prime</sup>}}g(x<sup>\\prime</sup>,y)d\\mathcal{H}<sup>0</sup>(y).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Reduced boundaries ignore null holes

**Remember:** Removing a null set does not change the measured boundary.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A75 (Length, area, volume, other geometric measure theory). arXiv math.CA, math.MG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A set has finite perimeter if the distributional gradient of its indicator is a finite vector measure; this gradient sees the set only through integrals, so it ignores null sets. The reduced boundary is where the gradient, divided by its total variation on shrinking centered balls, tends to a unit vector.

**Problem.** Changing a set of finite perimeter on a Lebesgue null set preserves its reduced boundary. Its perimeter measure equals normalized (n−1)-dimensional Hausdorff measure restricted to that boundary in ℝⁿ.

**How the definition helps.** The reduced boundary is built from the gradient measure alone, and that measure does not change when the set changes on a null set. Removing a countable dense set from an open ball makes every point of the ball a topological boundary point, but the reduced boundary stays the sphere (our own). De Giorgi's structure theorem identifies the perimeter measure with normalized (n−1)-dimensional Hausdorff measure on the reduced boundary.

**Paper or page:** [Rectifiability; a survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.00540v3). It says: “Let E ⊂ ℝⁿ be a set of finite perimeter. Then ∂∗E is (n−1)-rectifiable”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Covering fixes packing premeasure

**Remember:** Pack each piece, then take the cheapest countable cover.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A78 (Hausdorff and packing measures). arXiv math.MG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For s &gt; 0, the packing premeasure of E packs disjoint balls centered in E with diameters at most δ and takes the supremum of the sums of diameterˢ, in the limit δ → 0. Packing measure then takes the cheapest countable cover: the infimum over countable covers of E of the sums of the pieces' premeasures.

**Problem.** Packing measure is countably subadditive and gives countable sets zero measure in every positive dimension. Packing premeasure need not do either.

**How the definition helps.** Covering by countably many pieces builds in countable subadditivity, by joining nearly optimal covers with summable errors (our own). A singleton holds at most one packing ball, so its premeasure is 0 for s &gt; 0, and every countable set has packing measure zero (our own). The rationals in \[0, 1\] have positive one-dimensional premeasure, since equally spaced rational centers carry arbitrarily fine disjoint balls of total diameter at least one-half (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Packing dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Packing_dimension). It says: “the packing measure of S is the infimum of the packing pre-measures of countable covers of S.”

**Sources:**

- [Claude Tricot, Two definitions of fractional dimension (1982)](https://doi.org/10.1017/s0305004100059119)

### Diameter powers reveal dimension

**Remember:** On small sets, raising the exponent makes every cover cheaper.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A78 (Hausdorff and packing measures), 28A80. arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For s ≥ 0, cover the set by countably many nonempty sets of diameter at most δ, each set of diameter d costing dˢ, which falls as s grows once d &lt; 1 (cost one per set when s = 0). The unnormalized Hausdorff measure at s is the limit, as δ → 0, of the cheapest total cost. The Hausdorff dimension is the infimum of exponents where this measure is zero.

**Problem.** For a subset of Euclidean space, Hausdorff measure is infinite below its dimension and zero above it. At the dimension itself, it can be zero, finite positive, or infinite.

**How the definition helps.** Raising the exponent cheapens every fine cover: for t &lt; s, the cost at s is at most δˢ⁻ᵗ times the cost at t (our own). So finite measure at t forces zero measure at s, and positive measure at s forces infinite measure at t (our own). This gives one cutoff without computing any of the measures (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Strictly Positive Hausdorff Measure implies Infinite Lower Dimensional Measure](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Strictly_Positive_Hausdorff_Measure_implies_Infinite_Lower_Dimensional_Measure). It says: “ℋˢ(F) &gt; 0 ⇒ ∀ t ∈ \[0, s) : ℋᵗ(F) = +∞”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Frostman bounds force positive measure

**Remember:** Little mass per small ball forces every cover to cost enough.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A78 (Hausdorff and packing measures). arXiv math.MG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An s-Frostman probability on E is a Borel probability μ with μ(E) = 1 that puts little mass in small balls. Some finite C gives μ(B(x, r)) ≤ Crˢ for every center x and radius r &gt; 0 (our own).

**Problem.** A Borel subset of Euclidean space carrying a Frostman probability of exponent s &gt; 0 has positive s-dimensional Hausdorff measure.

**How the definition helps.** Each set of a cover can carry only a little mass, but together they carry mass one, so the cover cannot be cheap (our own). A nonempty set of diameter d &gt; 0 lies in a ball of radius 2d, so it carries mass at most C(2d)ˢ, and singletons carry none (our own). Summing over any countable cover of E gives a sum of diameter powers at least 1/(2ˢC) at every scale (our own).

**Paper or page:** [A Study Guide to "Kaufman and Falconer estimates for radial projections"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.11847v1). It says: “If a Borel set X supports an s-Frostman probability measure μ, then ℋˢ(X) &gt; 0.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Hausdorff dimension respects countable unions

**Remember:** A countable union of sets of measure zero still has measure zero.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A78 (Hausdorff and packing measures). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Hausdorff measure is built from countable covers: at each scale δ, take the infimum of the sums of s-th powers of diameters over countable covers by sets of diameter at most δ, then let δ → 0. Because the covers are countable, this measure is countably subadditive (our own). Hausdorff dimension is the infimum of exponents giving zero measure.

**Problem.** The Hausdorff dimension of a countable union is the supremum of the dimensions of its members.

**How the definition helps.** Above the supremum, every member has measure zero, so countable subadditivity makes the union null too; monotonicity gives the reverse inequality (our own). Box dimension, which counts boxes of one size at a time, fails this: each point has box dimension zero, but the rationals in \[0, 1\] have box dimension one (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Hausdorff dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff_dimension). It says: “If X=\\bigcup<sub>i\\in I</sub>X<sub>i</sub> is a finite or countable union, then \\dim\_{\\operatorname{Haus}}(X) =\\sup<sub>i\\in I</sub> \\dim\_{\\operatorname{Haus}}(X<sub>i</sub>).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Mass bounds give dimension bounds

**Remember:** A cover must pay enough to carry all the mass.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A78 (Hausdorff and packing measures). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Hausdorff measure at exponent s is the limit, as δ → 0, of the cheapest sum of s-th powers of diameters over countable covers by sets of diameter at most δ. Hausdorff dimension is the infimum of exponents giving zero measure, so positive s-dimensional measure gives dimension at least s.

**Problem.** Let a finite measure μ give a Borel set F ⊂ ℝ positive mass, with μ(I) ≤ C·diam(I)ˢ for some C, some s &gt; 0 and every sufficiently small closed interval I. Then F has Hausdorff dimension at least s.

**How the definition helps.** Each set of a fine cover lies in a closed interval of the same diameter, so it carries mass at most C times its diameter to the power s (our own). The cover carries all of μ(F), so its cost is at least μ(F)/C (our own). So the s-dimensional measure of F is positive and its dimension is at least s (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Constructing self-similar subsets within the fractal support of Lacunary Wavelet Series for their multifractal analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.17712). It says: “μ(U) ≤ c \|U\|ᵗ”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Packing dimension respects countable unions

**Remember:** Cover each piece first, then put all the covers together.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A78 (Hausdorff and packing measures), 28A80. arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The upper box dimension of a bounded set is the limit superior of log N(r)/log(1/r) as r → 0, where N(r) is the fewest radius-r balls that cover it. Modified upper box dimension first cuts the set into countably many bounded pieces: it is the infimum, over countable covers, of the supremum of the pieces' upper box dimensions. In Euclidean space this equals packing dimension.

**Problem.** The packing dimension of a countable union of subsets of Euclidean space equals the supremum of their packing dimensions.

**How the definition helps.** Above the supremum, each piece has a countable cover whose upper box dimensions stay below the bound (our own). All these covers together form one countable cover of the union, and monotonicity gives the reverse inequality (our own). The theorem identifying modified upper box dimension with packing dimension justifies the cover formula.

**Wikipedia:** [Packing dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Packing_dimension). It says: “the packing dimension of S is equal to the upper modified box dimension of S”

**Sources:**

- [Claude Tricot Jr., Two definitions of fractional dimension (1982)](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0305004100059119)

### Disjoint pieces give unique addresses

**Remember:** The first place where two addresses differ puts them in disjoint pieces.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A80 (Fractals), 37B10. arXiv math.DS. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Finitely many injective contractions on a compact metric space have a unique nonempty compact attractor A, equal to the union of its images. Strong separation means these images are pairwise disjoint. A point's address is the infinite list of maps whose nested images of A, first map outermost, all contain the point.

**Problem.** If the space and the family are nonempty and strong separation holds, each point of A has exactly one address.

**How the definition helps.** Disjoint images make the first map of an address unique, and injectivity gives a unique point of A to locate at the next step (our own). Repeating this choice builds the whole address, and the contraction mapping theorem supplies the attractor (our own). Without separation, the two half-size copies of \[0, 1\] meet at 1/2, which then has two addresses (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Applications of the Tarski-Kantorovitch Fixed-Point Principle to the study of Infinite Iterated Function Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.04650v1). It says: “the canonical projection π : Λ(I) → A is bijective.”

**Sources:**

- [Applications of the Tarski-Kantorovitch Fixed-Point Principle to the study of Infinite Iterated Function Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.04650v1)

### Graph norms let closed operators commute with integrals

**Remember:** Integrate the point and its image together.

*True by definition.* MSC 28B05 (Vector-valued set functions, measures and integrals). arXiv math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A closed operator T has a graph {(x, Tx)} that is closed in the product of the two Banach spaces. With the graph norm ‖x‖ + ‖Tx‖, its domain becomes a Banach space on which T is bounded (our own).

**Problem.** If f takes values in the domain of T and both f and Tf are Bochner integrable, T commutes with integration. In particular, the integral of f belongs to the domain.

**How the definition helps.** Integrate the pair (f, Tf) in the product space; its Bochner integral is (∫f, ∫Tf) (our own). Simple approximations can take values in the closed graph, so this integral lies in the graph (our own). Hence ∫f is in the domain and T(∫f) = ∫Tf (our own).

**Paper or page:** [A Representation of Matrix-Valued Harmonic Functions by the Poisson Integral of Non-commutative BMO Functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.11752v2). It says: “T\\left(\\int \_E f(x)\\, d\\mu (x) \\right)=\\int \_E T(f(x))\\, d\\mu (x),”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Separable range rules out invisible vectors

**Remember:** A separable range lets scalar tests detect strong measurability.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28B05 (Vector-valued set functions, measures and integrals). arXiv math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Banach-valued function is weakly measurable if every continuous linear functional turns it into a measurable scalar function, and strongly measurable if it is an almost everywhere norm limit of simple functions. It is essentially separably valued if, outside a null set, its values lie in a separable subspace, where countably many functionals compute norms (our own).

**Problem.** Pettis's theorem says that weak measurability gives strong measurability when the range is essentially separable.

**How the definition helps.** In a separable subspace, countably many functionals compute the norm, so weak measurability makes distances to a countable dense set measurable, and this yields simple approximations (our own). Without separability, t ↦ eₜ from \[0, 1\] into ℓ²(\[0, 1\]) is weakly measurable, since each functional is nonzero at only countably many t (our own). It is not strongly measurable, because distinct eₜ lie √2 apart and a separable subspace holds only countably many of them (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Kernel-Summability Methods and the Silverman-Toeplitz Theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.06770v3). It says: “A function v : E → X is strongly measurable if, and only if, the two following conditions are satisfied: v is weakly measurable; v is essentially separably valued.”

**Sources:**

- [B. J. Pettis, On integration in vector spaces (1938)](https://doi.org/10.1090/s0002-9947-1938-1501970-8)

### Stone's condition lets an abstract Daniell integral come from a measure

**Remember:** Truncate at height one, and the integral finds its measure.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28C05 (Integration theory via linear functionals (Radon measures, Daniell integrals, etc.), representing set functions and measures), 28A12. arXiv math.FA, math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Daniell's setting is a vector lattice T₀ of real functions on X with a positive linear functional I that respects monotone limits: if φₙ decreases to 0, then I(φₙ) → 0. Stone's condition asks that min(φ, 1) is in T₀ whenever φ is. Then, for nonnegative φ, min(nφ, 1) increases to the indicator of {φ &gt; 0} (our own).

**Problem.** Under Stone’s condition, some measure μ on a σ-algebra of subsets of X represents I. Every φ in T₀ is μ-measurable and satisfies I(φ) = ∫φ dμ.

**How the definition helps.** The truncations supply the indicators that a measure needs, so the sets {φ &gt; 0} become measurable (our own). The Daniell–Stone theorem extends I to these indicators and supplies the representing measure.

**Paper or page:** [The Daniell Integral: Integration without measure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.14964v1), [The Daniell Integral: Integration without measure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.14964v1). It says: “with the property that χX ∧ φ ∈ T₀ whenever φ ∈ T₀. Let I be an I-integral on T₀. Then there is a σ-algebra 𝒜 on X and a measure μ on 𝒜”

**Sources:**

- [Adriaan de Clercq, The Daniell Integral: Integration without measure, arXiv:2211.14964 (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.14964v1)

### Compatible finite quotient averages give Haar measure on profinite groups

**Remember:** On each finite quotient, average with equal weight for every point.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28C10 (Set functions and measures on topological groups or semigroups, Haar measures, invariant measures), 20E18. arXiv math.FA, math.GR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A profinite group G is an inverse limit of finite groups, so each continuous function is uniformly close to one that factors through a finite quotient G/N by an open normal subgroup (our own). Integrate such a function by averaging its values over G/N with equal weight (our own).

**Problem.** These finite averages determine Haar probability measure on any profinite group, without using Haar’s general existence theorem.

**How the definition helps.** Translations permute each finite quotient, so the averages are translation invariant (our own). Passing to a finer quotient keeps the average, because every fibre has the same number of points (our own). Density extends the averages to a positive linear functional, and the Riesz representation theorem makes it a regular Borel probability measure (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Compact group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_group). It says: “In the profinite case there are many subgroups of finite index, and Haar measure of a coset will be the reciprocal of the index.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Defining Haar measure on Baire sets makes the regularity conditions unnecessary

**Remember:** On Baire sets, invariant measures are regular for free.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28C10 (Set functions and measures on topological groups or semigroups, Haar measures, invariant measures), 43A05. arXiv math.FA, math.GR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On a locally compact Hausdorff group, the Baire σ-algebra is generated by the compact sets that are countable intersections of open sets. A left Haar measure on it is a nonzero left-invariant Baire measure, finite on compact Baire sets; such measures are automatically regular.

**Problem.** Every locally compact Hausdorff group has a left Haar measure, unique up to a positive constant. On the Baire sets this can be stated without any regularity condition.

**How the definition helps.** Baire measures finite on compact Baire sets are automatically regular, so no separate regularity hypothesis is needed. Haar's theorem supplies existence and uniqueness up to a positive factor (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Haar measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure). It says: “Some authors define a Haar measure on Baire sets rather than Borel sets. This makes the regularity conditions unnecessary as Baire measures are automatically regular.”

**Sources:**

- [A. Haar, Der Massbegriff in der Theorie der kontinuierlichen Gruppen, Annals of Mathematics 34 (1933)](https://doi.org/10.2307/1968346)

### Left invariant volume forms give Haar measure on Lie groups

**Remember:** Translate a volume form at the identity to get invariant volume everywhere.

*True by definition.* MSC 28C10 (Set functions and measures on topological groups or semigroups, Haar measures, invariant measures), 22E15. arXiv math.DG, math.GR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On an n-dimensional Lie group, take a nonzero alternating n-form at the identity and spread it by left translation to a smooth volume form ω. Since ω is left-invariant by construction, integrating \|ω\| gives a left-invariant measure.

**Problem.** Every Lie group has a left Haar measure, a nonzero regular Borel measure unchanged by left translations, given by its left invariant volume form.

**How the definition helps.** Left translation preserves ω by construction, so the measure given by \|ω\| is left-invariant (our own). It is a smooth positive density, so it is positive on nonempty open sets, finite on compact sets and regular (our own). This replaces Haar's general existence proof.

**Wikipedia:** [Haar measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure). It says: “On an n-dimensional Lie group, Haar measure can be constructed easily as the measure induced by a left-invariant n-form. This was known before Haar's theorem.”

**Sources:**

- [A. Haar, Der Massbegriff in der Theorie der kontinuierlichen Gruppen, Annals of Mathematics 34 (1933)](https://doi.org/10.2307/1968346)

### The Haar scaling definition makes compact groups unimodular

**Remember:** Left translation cannot rescale the finite mass of the whole group.

*True by definition.* MSC 28C10 (Set functions and measures on topological groups or semigroups, Haar measures, invariant measures), 22C05. arXiv math.FA, math.GR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix a right Haar measure ν on a locally compact Hausdorff group. Left translation by g rescales ν by one positive number, the modular factor Δ(g): ν(g⁻¹S) = Δ(g)ν(S) for every Borel S. The group is unimodular if every factor equals one.

**Problem.** The modular function is multiplicative. Every compact Hausdorff group is unimodular.

**How the definition helps.** Two translations rescale by the product of their factors, so Δ is multiplicative (our own). On a compact group, the whole group has finite positive measure and translation does not change it, so Δ(g) = 1.

**Wikipedia:** [Haar measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure). It says: “Thus, by uniqueness up to a constant scaling factor of the Haar measure, there exists a function Δ from the group to the positive reals, called the Haar modulus, modular function or modular character”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Inner regularity is what Kolmogorov's extension theorem needs beyond Euclidean spaces

**Remember:** Compact sets inside every event let finite laws glue into one process.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28C15 (Set functions and measures on topological spaces (regularity of measures, etc.)), 60G05, 28A35. arXiv math.PR, math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A measure on a topological space is inner regular if every measurable set is approximated from inside by compact sets: its measure is the supremum of the measures of its compact subsets. A consistent family gives a probability on each finite product, and these agree under the projections between products.

**Problem.** Consistent inner regular probability laws on the finite products of Hausdorff spaces extend uniquely to a probability on the product σ-algebra of the infinite product. Borel probabilities on Polish spaces are inner regular, so Euclidean spaces need no extra assumption.

**How the definition helps.** Inner regularity lets countable additivity be checked on compact sets. Nested compact sets with the finite intersection property have a common point, so a decreasing sequence of cylinder events cannot lose all its mass (our own). Without such a condition the extension can fail, as an example of Andersen and Jessen shows (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Kolmogorov extension theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolmogorov_extension_theorem). It says: “In fact, any collection of measurable spaces together with a collection of inner regular measures defined on the finite products of these spaces would suffice, provided that these measures satisfy a certain compatibility relation.”

**Sources:**

- [A. Kolmogoroff, Grundbegriffe der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung, Springer, 1933](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-49888-6)

### Measures that respect directed unions of open sets have a support

**Remember:** Null open sets join into one null open set.

*True by definition.* MSC 28C15 (Set functions and measures on topological spaces (regularity of measures, etc.)), 28A12. arXiv math.FA, math.GN. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Borel measure is τ-additive if, for every directed family of open sets (any two members lie in a third), the union has measure equal to the supremum of the members' measures. The null open sets form such a family, since the union of two is again one, so their union is null (our own).

**Problem.** Every τ-additive Borel measure has a support, a smallest closed set of full measure.

**How the definition helps.** The complement of the union of all null open sets is closed and has full measure, and it is the smallest such set. For a general Borel measure that union can fail to be null. Every Radon measure on a Hausdorff space is τ-additive, so the definition covers the usual examples.

**nLab:** [tau-additive measure](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/tau-additive+measure), [valuation (measure theory)](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/valuation+%28measure+theory%29), [correspondence between measure and valuation theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/correspondence+between+measure+and+valuation+theory). It says: “the union of all null open sets is null”

**Sources:**

- [Tobias Fritz, Paolo Perrone, Sharwin Rezagholi, Probability, valuations, hyperspace: Three monads on Top and the support as a morphism (2019); arXiv:1910.03752](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.03752)

### Proper maps keep Radon measures locally finite

**Remember:** Compact inverse images keep mass finite near every target point.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28C15 (Set functions and measures on topological spaces (regularity of measures, etc.)). arXiv math.GN. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Radon measure is locally finite and approximates each Borel set from inside by compact sets. A continuous map is proper if inverse images of compact sets are compact, so its pushforward, which gives each Borel set the measure of its inverse image, stays finite on compact sets.

**Problem.** A proper continuous map between locally compact Hausdorff spaces sends a Radon measure to a Radon measure in the inner-regular convention.

**How the definition helps.** Properness makes the inverse image of a compact neighbourhood compact, so the pushforward is locally finite. Compact sets inside the inverse image of a Borel set map to compact sets inside that set with at least as much mass, which gives inner regularity (our own). Without properness, the map from ℝ to one point gives that point infinite Lebesgue mass (our own).

**nLab:** [Radon measure](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Radon+measure). It says: “is a Borel measure m on X such that m is locally finite and inner regular on all Borel subsets.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Proper maps preserve Radon measures

**Remember:** Compact sets cannot collect infinite mass from far away.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28C15 (Set functions and measures on topological spaces (regularity of measures, etc.)). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A continuous map is proper if inverse images of compact sets are compact, so its pushforward measure stays finite on compact sets (our own). On locally compact metric spaces, a Radon measure is finite on compact sets and approximates each Borel set from inside by compact sets.

**Problem.** A continuous proper map between locally compact metric spaces sends a Radon measure to a Radon measure.

**How the definition helps.** A compact target set has compact inverse image and therefore finite pushforward mass (our own). Compact sets inside the inverse image of a Borel set map to compact subsets of that set with at least the same mass (our own). Without properness, a constant map sends the entire length of the real line to one point (our own).

**nLab:** [Radon measure](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Radon+measure). It says: “The pushforward measure H∗μ is a Radon measure on Y defined as follows.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Regularity makes the measure in the Riesz representation theorem unique

**Remember:** Regularity picks one measure for each positive functional on continuous functions.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28C15 (Set functions and measures on topological spaces (regularity of measures, etc.)), 28C05. arXiv math.CA, math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A regular Borel measure is finite on compact sets and is fixed by its values on open and compact sets. It is outer regular: each Borel set has the infimum over open sets containing it as its measure. It is inner regular: each open set, and each Borel set of finite measure, has the supremum over its compact subsets as its measure.

**Problem.** For a locally compact Hausdorff space X, each positive linear functional on compactly supported continuous functions is integration against a unique regular Borel measure. The dual of C₀(X) consists of the finite regular complex Borel measures.

**How the definition helps.** Test integrals fix the masses of compact sets, and regularity then fixes the masses of open and Borel sets (our own). The Riesz–Markov–Kakutani theorem supplies existence. On \[0, Ω\], with Ω the first uncountable ordinal, evaluation at Ω is also represented by the nonregular Dieudonné measure, which gives {Ω} mass zero instead of one.

**Wikipedia:** [Riesz–Markov–Kakutani representation theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riesz%E2%80%93Markov%E2%80%93Kakutani_representation_theorem). It says: “Without the condition of regularity the Borel measure need not be unique.”

**Sources:**

- [S. Kakutani, Concrete representation of abstract (M)-spaces, Annals of Mathematics 42 (1941), 994–1024](https://doi.org/10.2307/1968778)

### Finite energy protects Brownian null sets

**Remember:** Finite-energy shifts keep Brownian null sets; other shifts change them all.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28C20 (Set functions and measures and integrals in infinite-dimensional spaces (Wiener measure, Gaussian measure, etc.)). arXiv math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Cameron–Martin space of Brownian motion on \[0, 1\], started at zero, consists of the paths h(t) = ∫₀ᵗ h′(s) ds with square-integrable velocity h′. These are the paths of finite energy ∫₀¹ h′(s)² ds.

**Problem.** Brownian path measure and its translate have the same null sets for shifts in the Cameron–Martin space. All other continuous shifts starting at zero give mutually singular measures.

**How the definition helps.** The Cameron–Martin theorem says that shifting Brownian motion by h keeps its null sets exactly when h has finite energy, and gives singularity for all other shifts. For example, t ↦ √t has h′(t)² = 1/(4t), whose integral diverges at zero, so this shift gives a singular law (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Notions of null sets in infinite-dimensional Carnot groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.14524v1). It says: “A Gaussian measure γ is quasi-invariant under translation by elements of its Cameron–Martin space H.”

**Sources:**

- [R. H. Cameron and W. T. Martin, Transformations of Wiener Integrals Under Translations (1944)](https://doi.org/10.2307/1969276)

### Linear functional tests show continuous linear maps preserve Gaussian laws

**Remember:** Compose a linear functional with the operator to test the image law.

*True by definition.* MSC 28C20 (Set functions and measures and integrals in infinite-dimensional spaces (Wiener measure, Gaussian measure, etc.)), 60G15. arXiv math.PR, stat.ML. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A probability law on a separable Banach space is Gaussian if every continuous linear functional sends it to a normal law on ℝ, counting constants as normal with variance zero.

**Problem.** A continuous linear map B between separable Banach spaces sends each Gaussian law to a Gaussian law. The output means and covariances of linear tests come from composing those tests with B.

**How the definition helps.** Gaussianity is a test by functionals, so it passes through B: for a functional L on the output, L∘B is a functional on the input and sends the law to a normal law (our own). The same composition gives the output means and covariances (our own). This avoids densities, which fail in infinite dimensions because there is no Lebesgue measure there.

**Wikipedia:** [Gaussian measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_measure). It says: “Even so, it is possible to define Gaussian measures on infinite-dimensional spaces, the main example being the abstract Wiener space construction.”

**Paper or page:** [Gaussian Process Priors for Systems of Linear Partial Differential Equations with Constant Coefficients](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.14319v4). It says: “be a linear continuous map. Then B∗γ is a Gaussian measure”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Weighted spaces carry Gaussian sequences

**Remember:** Independent standard Gaussians fit in weighted ℓ², not in ordinary ℓ².

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28C20 (Set functions and measures and integrals in infinite-dimensional spaces (Wiener measure, Gaussian measure, etc.)). arXiv math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Choose positive weights wₖ with finite sum. The weighted ℓ² space holds the sequences x with ∑wₖxₖ² &lt; ∞, normed by the square root of this sum. For independent standard Gaussians ξₖ, the sum ∑wₖξₖ² then has finite expectation ∑wₖ (our own).

**Problem.** Independent standard Gaussian coordinates define a Borel probability on the weighted space, but not on ordinary ℓ².

**How the definition helps.** Finite expectation makes the weighted norm finite almost surely, and truncations converge in that norm to a measurable random element (our own). In ordinary ℓ², the strong law makes the average of the first n squares tend to one, so the sum of squares diverges almost surely (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Abstract Wiener space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_Wiener_space). It says: “the cylinder set measure on B, unlike the cylinder set measure on H, will extend to a countably additive measure”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Sober measurable spaces make measurable Gelfand duality hold by definition

**Remember:** Each zero-one probability picks exactly one point.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28A05 (Classes of sets (Borel fields, σ-rings, etc.), measurable sets, Suslin sets, analytic sets), 46L05. arXiv math.FA, math.OA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A measurable space is sober if its zero-one probabilities recover its points: every countably additive probability taking only the values 0 and 1 is the Dirac measure at exactly one point. Equivalently, evaluation identifies the space with the measurable spectrum of its algebra of bounded measurable functions (our own).

**Problem.** The functors L∞ and Sp give a duality between sober measurable spaces and spatial σ-C\*-algebras, the commutative σ-C\*-algebras of the form L∞(X). A σ-C\*-algebra is a C\*-algebra closed under countable bounded monotone suprema.

**How the definition helps.** Sobriety says exactly that evaluation from the space to its measurable spectrum, the characters preserving bounded increasing sequential suprema, is an isomorphism (our own). The idempotent adjunction between bounded measurable functions and measurable spectra then restricts to a duality on sober spaces and spatial algebras.

**nLab:** [sober measurable space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/sober+measurable+space), [measurable Gelfand duality](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/measurable+Gelfand+duality). It says: “As usual with idempotent adjunctions, we have that the center is equivalently given by”

**Sources:**

- [Tobias Fritz, Antonio Lorenzin, Categories of abstract and noncommutative measurable spaces, Advances in Mathematics 488 (2026) 110793; arXiv:2504.13708](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13708)

### Take inclusion-exclusion as an axiom of constructive measures

**Remember:** Union plus intersection balances the two original sets.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28A10 (Real- or complex-valued set functions), 03F60. arXiv math.CA, math.LO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A valuation on a lattice of sets is a nonnegative function μ with μ(∅) = 0 that satisfies inclusion–exclusion for two sets: μ(A ∪ B) + μ(A ∩ B) = μ(A) + μ(B).

**Problem.** In constructive mathematics, a measure with the two-set law as an axiom satisfies the inclusion-exclusion formula for every finite family of sets.

**How the definition helps.** Induct on the number of sets, applying the two-set law to the union of the first n sets and the next one (our own). Distributing intersection over that union produces the smaller intersections that the induction handles (our own). With infinite values, put the union and the even intersections on one side and the odd intersections on the other, so nothing is subtracted (our own).

**nLab:** [inclusion-exclusion](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/inclusion-exclusion), [Cheng space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Cheng+space). It says: “On the other hand, we may adopt (\*) as the proper clause in the definition of measure.”

**Sources:**

- [Errett Bishop, Henry Cheng, Constructive measure theory, Memoirs of the AMS 116 (1972)](https://doi.org/10.1090/memo/0116)
- [Errett Bishop, Douglas Bridges, Constructive Analysis, Grundlehren 279, Springer (1985)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-61667-9)

### The Carathéodory extension theorem becomes a Kan extension of transformations

**Remember:** Add disjoint sets whenever their countable union stays in the algebra.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28A12 (Contents, measures, outer measures, capacities), 18A40. arXiv math.CT, math.CA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A premeasure on a Boolean algebra of sets takes values in \[0, ∞\] and gives ∅ zero. It adds the values of every countable disjoint family whose union lies in the algebra (our own).

**Problem.** A premeasure on a Boolean algebra of sets extends to a measure on the σ-algebra it generates. In the paper's language, this extension is a Kan extension of strict transformations.

**How the definition helps.** Countable additivity for unions already in the algebra gives the compatibility condition needed to extend the assignment (our own). The paper represents premeasures as strict transformations and identifies Carathéodory extension with their Kan extension. Its extension theorem supplies the proof.

**Paper or page:** [A categorical proof of the Carathéodory extension theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.01720). It says: “To prove this result categorically, we represent (pre)measures and outer measures by certain (co)lax and strict transformations. The Carathéodory extension then corresponds to a Kan extension of strict transformations.”

**Sources:**

- [Ruben Van Belle, A categorical proof of the Carathéodory extension theorem, arXiv:2210.01720 (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.01720)

### Area lifts preserve nonlinear integrals

**Remember:** Adjoin volume before measuring the size of a vector measure.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28A33 (Spaces of measures, convergence of measures), 28B05. arXiv math.FA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Lift a finite vector measure v on the closed domain to V = (ℒ, v), adjoining Lebesgue measure ℒ on the domain as an extra coordinate. Area-strict convergence means the lifts converge against every continuous vector test and their total variation masses converge to the limit lift's mass (our own).

**Problem.** Let finite vector measures on the closure of a bounded Euclidean domain converge area-strictly. Then integrals of continuous functions of position and unit direction against the lifted total variation converge, where the unit direction is the density of the lifted measure relative to its variation.

**How the definition helps.** Area-strict convergence is exactly the strict convergence of the lifts that Reshetnyak's continuity theorem needs (our own). On \[0, 1\], put density n on the first 1/n fraction of each of n equal cells and zero elsewhere; these converge weakly to length with mass one (our own). Their lifted masses tend to two, but the lift of length has mass √2, so area-strict convergence fails (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Relaxation of functionals with linear growth: interactions of emerging measures and free discontinuities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.12687v1). It says: “vε → σ weakly∗ and strictly in ℳ(Ω̄; ℝᵈ).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Comparing distribution functions up to constants characterizes vague convergence of signed measures

**Remember:** Compare masses of intervals, not mass accumulated from minus infinity.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28A33 (Spaces of measures, convergence of measures), 28A20. arXiv math.PR, math.CA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** With Fₙ(x) = μₙ((−∞, x\]) and F(x) = μ((−∞, x\]), compare distribution functions only after shifting each Fₙ by a real constant cₙ. Fₙ + cₙ converges to F locally in measure if, for each bounded interval I and ε &gt; 0, the length of {x ∈ I ∣ \|Fₙ(x) + cₙ − F(x)\| &gt; ε} tends to zero.

**Problem.** Finite signed measures μₙ on ℝ converge vaguely to μ exactly when two things hold. Their total variations are uniformly bounded on each bounded interval, and some real constants cₙ make Fₙ + cₙ converge to F in Lebesgue measure on every bounded interval.

**How the definition helps.** The constants absorb distribution-function offsets from mass escaping to the left (our own). A unit mass at −n tends vaguely to zero, and subtracting one makes its distribution function eventually zero on each bounded interval (our own). The paper’s characterization theorem gives the equivalence under locally uniform bounds on total variation.

**Paper or page:** [Vague and basic convergence of signed measures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11377v1). It says: “it is locally uniformly bounded in variation and the corresponding sequence of distribution functions either converges in Lebesgue measure up to constants, converges basically, or converges almost basically.”

**Sources:**

- [Michael Staněk, Vague and basic convergence of signed measures, arXiv:2406.11377 (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11377v1)

### Metric tangent measures let one test rectifiability in any complete metric space

**Remember:** Countably many Lipschitz charts cover the set up to Hausdorff measure zero.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A75 (Length, area, volume, other geometric measure theory), 28A78, 53C23. arXiv math.MG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A set E is countably n-rectifiable if countably many Lipschitz images of subsets of ℝⁿ cover E outside an n-dimensional Hausdorff null set. At x, positive lower n-density means ℋⁿ(E ∩ B(x,r)) ≥ crⁿ for some c &gt; 0 and all sufficiently small r &gt; 0 (our own).

**Problem.** For a measurable set E of finite n-dimensional Hausdorff measure in a complete metric space, rectifiability is equivalent to positive lower density and a unique measured tangent at almost every point. That tangent is a normed ℝⁿ with normalized Hausdorff measure.

**How the definition helps.** Rectifiability uses distances and Hausdorff measure, so both charts and measured tangents make sense without an ambient Euclidean space (our own). The paper’s Theorem 1.1 proves the equivalence by relating the tangent condition to small-scale bi-Lipschitz approximations.

**Paper or page:** [Characterising rectifiable metric spaces using tangent spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.12371v3). It says: “We also introduce a generalisation of Preiss's tangent measures that is suitable for the setting of arbitrary metric spaces and formulate our characterisation in terms of tangent measures.”

**Sources:**

- [David Bate, Characterising rectifiable metric spaces using tangent spaces, arXiv:2109.12371v3 (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.12371v3)

### Countable tests fix weak density versions

**Remember:** Each vector tests separately; countably many tests share one null set.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28B05 (Vector-valued set functions, measures and integrals). arXiv math.FA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A weak-star density of a measure m with values in the dual X\* is a function ζ to X\* that is tested one vector at a time. For each v in X, t ↦ ζ(t)(v) is integrable and ∫<sub>A</sub> ζ(t)(v) dμ(t) = m(A)(v) for every measurable A (our own).

**Problem.** On a finite Lebesgue interval, two weak-star densities of the same vector measure agree almost everywhere if the original Banach space is separable.

**How the definition helps.** For each v, two densities give scalar functions that agree outside a null set that depends on v (our own). For separable X, the union of these null sets over a countable dense set of v is null, and continuity gives ζ₁ = ζ₂ off it (our own). Without separability, on ℓ¹(\[0,1\]) the density ζ(t) = evaluation at coordinate t represents zero yet has norm one everywhere (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Global entropy solutions to a degenerate parabolic-parabolic chemotaxis system for flux-limited dispersal](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.03887v3). It says: “If X is separable, then any ζ₁ and ζ₂ that satisfy the conditions on ζ coincide a.e. in {g &gt; 0}.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Prevalence gives infinite-dimensional spaces a measure meaning of almost every

**Remember:** A shy set is invisible to one probe, from every position.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28C20 (Set functions and measures and integrals in infinite-dimensional spaces (Wiener measure, Gaussian measure, etc.)), 37C20. arXiv math.CA, math.DS. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In a complete metric vector space, a Borel set B is shy if one compactly supported Borel probability μ gives zero mass to every translate v + B. Subsets of such sets are also shy, and the complement of a shy set is prevalent (our own).

**Problem.** Subsets, translates and countable unions of shy sets are shy, and prevalent sets are dense. In this sense, almost every Cᵏ map of ℝⁿ into itself has only hyperbolic periodic points, for integers k ≥ 1.

**How the definition helps.** One probe measure works for every translate at once, so shyness plays the role of Lebesgue measure zero without a Lebesgue measure on the space (our own). The prevalence theorem of Hunt, Sauer and Yorke gives the closure and density properties (our own). Their hyperbolicity theorem uses a probe supported on a finite-dimensional family of perturbations (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Prevalent and shy sets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prevalent_and_shy_sets), [Generic property](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generic_property). It says: “the notions of prevalence and shyness are notions of almost everywhere and measure zero that are well-suited to the study of infinite-dimensional spaces”

**Sources:**

- [B. R. Hunt, T. Sauer, J. A. Yorke, Prevalence: a translation-invariant almost every on infinite-dimensional spaces, Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 27 (1992) 217–238](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0273-0979-1992-00328-2)

## 30 Functions of a complex variable

### Conjugation makes the complex modulus multiplicative

**Remember:** Conjugation respects products, so the squared modulus does too.

*True by definition.* MSC 30A99 (General properties of functions of one complex variable). arXiv math.CV. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** The conjugate of z = x + iy is z̄ = x − iy, and conjugation respects products. The modulus is \|z\| = √(z z̄), the nonnegative square root, which equals √(x² + y²).

**Problem.** For all complex numbers z and w, \|zw\| = \|z\|\|w\|.

**How the definition helps.** Since the conjugate of zw is z̄ w̄, \|zw\|² = (z z̄)(w w̄) = \|z\|²\|w\|² (our own). Taking nonnegative square roots gives \|zw\| = \|z\|\|w\| (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Absolute value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_value). It says: “\|z\| = √(z · z̄).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### A complex derivative as an i-linear map gives Cauchy–Riemann at once

**Remember:** The derivative's value on i is i times its value on 1.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 30A05 (Monogenic and polygenic functions of one complex variable), 26B05. arXiv math.CV. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Identify ℂ with ℝ². Call f complex differentiable at z if it is real differentiable there and its derivative L commutes with multiplication by i, so L(iv) = iL(v) for every v.

**Problem.** Let f = u + iv be complex differentiable at a point. Then ∂u/∂x = ∂v/∂y and ∂u/∂y = −∂v/∂x at that point.

**How the definition helps.** The two equations are the real and imaginary parts of L(i) = iL(1) (our own). Here L(1) = uₓ + ivₓ and L(i) = uᵧ + ivᵧ, while iL(1) = −vₓ + iuₓ (our own). This matches the difference-quotient definition because such an L is multiplication by L(1) (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Cauchy–Riemann equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%E2%80%93Riemann_equations). It says: “the partial derivatives of u and v exist and satisfy the Cauchy–Riemann equations at that point.”

**Paper or page:** [Cauchy-Riemann Equations/Necessary Condition](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Cauchy-Riemann_Equations/Necessary_Condition). It says: “The following two equations, known as the Cauchy-Riemann equations, hold for the partial derivatives of u and v:”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Real differentiability makes the Cauchy–Riemann test sufficient

**Remember:** First a real linear approximation; then Cauchy–Riemann makes it complex.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 30A05 (Monogenic and polygenic functions of one complex variable). arXiv math.CV. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A function f is real differentiable at z if a real linear map L approximates f(z + h) − f(z) with an error that is small compared with \|h\| as h → 0.

**Problem.** Write f = u + iv and suppose f is real differentiable at a point. There f has a complex derivative exactly when its partial derivatives satisfy uₓ = vᵧ and uᵧ = −vₓ.

**How the definition helps.** Real differentiability supplies the linear map L, and the equations say L is multiplication by uₓ + ivₓ, which is complex differentiability (our own proof). Partial derivatives alone are not enough: f(x + iy) = xy/√(x² + y²), with f(0) = 0, has zero partial derivatives at 0. Yet its difference quotient along the diagonal has opposite one-sided limits (our own example).

**Paper or page:** [Cauchy-Riemann Equations/Sufficient Condition](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Cauchy-Riemann_Equations/Sufficient_Condition). It says: “u and v be differentiable in their entire domain”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The Wirtinger derivative test makes holomorphic functions harmonic

**Remember:** The Laplacian factors through ∂/∂z̄, which kills holomorphic functions.

*True by definition.* MSC 30A05 (Monogenic and polygenic functions of one complex variable), 31A05. arXiv math.CV. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Call a continuously differentiable f holomorphic if ∂f/∂z̄ = ½(∂f/∂x + i∂f/∂y) is zero, the Cauchy–Riemann equations in one line. On twice continuously differentiable functions, 4 ∂/∂z ∂/∂z̄ is the Laplacian, where ∂/∂z = ½(∂/∂x − i∂/∂y).

**Problem.** The real and imaginary parts of a holomorphic function are harmonic: their second partial derivatives in x and y sum to zero.

**How the definition helps.** The Laplacian of f is 4 ∂/∂z(∂f/∂z̄), which is zero (our own). Holomorphic functions have power series, so f has continuous second derivatives and the mixed partials agree (our own). The Laplacian is a real operator, so it also kills the real and imaginary parts (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Wirtinger derivatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wirtinger_derivatives). It says: “The second Wirtinger derivative is also related with complex differentiation; ∂f/∂z̄ = 0 is equivalent to the Cauchy-Riemann equations in a complex form.”

**Paper or page:** [Real and Imaginary Parts of Holomorphic Function are Harmonic](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Real_and_Imaginary_Parts_of_Holomorphic_Function_are_Harmonic). It says: “Then u and v are harmonic functions.”

**Sources:**

- [W. Wirtinger, Zur formalen Theorie der Funktionen von mehr komplexen Veränderlichen, Mathematische Annalen 97 (1927), 357–375](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01447872)

### Circle averages give Cauchy’s bounds on Taylor coefficients

**Remember:** A coefficient is a circle average, and averages never exceed the maximum.

*True by definition.* MSC 30A10 (Inequalities in the complex plane), 30E20, 30B10. arXiv math.CV. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Suppose f is holomorphic near the closed disk with center a and radius r &gt; 0. Its nth Taylor coefficient at a is the average over θ of f(a + reⁱᶿ)exp(−inθ), divided by rⁿ, and the factor exp(−inθ) has magnitude one (our own).

**Problem.** Suppose f is holomorphic near a closed disk centered at a, with radius r and largest boundary magnitude M. Its nth Taylor coefficient at a has magnitude at most M divided by the nth power of r.

**How the definition helps.** An average of values of magnitude at most M has magnitude at most M, so the coefficient is at most M/rⁿ (our own proof). The real work is Cauchy’s integral formula, which identifies these circle averages with Taylor coefficients (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Cauchy's integral formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%27s_integral_formula). It says: “then the coefficients aₙ satisfy Cauchy's estimate”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Absolute convergence lets a power series change its center

**Remember:** Inside the radius, absolute sums are finite, so regrouping is safe.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 30B10 (Power series (including lacunary series) in one complex variable). arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The radius of convergence R of ∑ aₙzⁿ is the supremum of the r ≥ 0 with ∑ \|aₙ\|rⁿ finite, or ∞ if there is no bound. So inside the radius the series converges absolutely, and its terms may be regrouped freely.

**Problem.** A power series with radius R has a power series about each point a with \|a\| &lt; R. The new series agrees with the old sum throughout \|z − a\| &lt; R − \|a\|.

**How the definition helps.** Write z = a + (z − a) and expand each aₙzⁿ by the binomial theorem (our own proof). The absolute values of all the resulting terms sum to ∑ \|aₙ\|rⁿ with r = \|a\| + \|z − a\| &lt; R, which is finite. So the terms may be grouped by powers of z − a without changing the sum.

**Wikipedia:** [Power series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_series). It says: “The series converges absolutely inside its disc of convergence”

**Sources:**

- [Walter Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed. (1976), Theorem 8.4](https://www.lehman.edu/faculty/rbettiol/lehman_teaching/2020mat320/baby_Rudin.pdf)

### An everywhere convergent Taylor series exposes Liouville’s theorem

**Remember:** A bounded entire series can keep only its constant term.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 30B10 (Power series (including lacunary series) in one complex variable). arXiv math.CV. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** An entire function is one given by a single power series ∑ aₙzⁿ that converges at every point of the plane, so the same coefficients serve on every circle. Equivalently, it is complex differentiable at every point.

**Problem.** Every bounded entire function is constant.

**How the definition helps.** Cauchy’s estimate on the circle of radius r gives \|aₙ\| ≤ M/rⁿ for the global bound M, with the same aₙ for every r. Letting r grow forces aₙ = 0 for every n ≥ 1 (our own proof). The real work is proving that an entire function has one global series and proving Cauchy’s estimate (our own proof).

**Paper or page:** [Liouville's Theorem (Complex Analysis)](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Liouville's_Theorem_(Complex_Analysis)). It says: “Let f: ℂ → ℂ be a bounded entire function. Then f is constant.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Complex differentiability on a disk gives a Taylor series

**Remember:** Holomorphic at a point means differentiable on a whole disk around it.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 30B10 (Power series (including lacunary series) in one complex variable). arXiv math.CV. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A function is holomorphic at a point if it is complex differentiable at every point of some open disk about that point. A derivative at the single point is not enough (our own).

**Problem.** A function holomorphic at a point has a power series expansion on some disk about that point.

**How the definition helps.** The disk contains a circle and its interior, so Cauchy’s integral formula applies there and expands f as a power series (our own). A derivative at one point is not enough: f(z) = \|z\|² has a derivative at zero and nowhere else, so it has no power series there (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Complex analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_analysis). It says: “Complex functions that are differentiable at every point of an open subset Ω of the complex plane are said to be holomorphic on Ω.”

**Paper or page:** [Holomorphic Function is Analytic](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Holomorphic_Function_is_Analytic). It says: “Then f is complex analytic on D.”

### Differentiation preserves a power series radius

**Remember:** The nth root of n tends to one, so growth is unchanged.

*True by definition.* MSC 30B10 (Power series (including lacunary series) in one complex variable), 40A30. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The radius of convergence of ∑ aₙ(z − c)ⁿ is 1/limsup \|aₙ\|<sup>(1/n)</sup>, with 1/0 = ∞ and 1/∞ = 0. It depends only on how fast the coefficients grow, and the series converges inside it and diverges outside it.

**Problem.** A complex power series and its termwise derivative have the same radius of convergence.

**How the definition helps.** The derivative times (z − c) has coefficients n aₙ, and n<sup>(1/n)</sup> → 1, so the limsup is unchanged (our own). Multiplying by z − c does not change convergence away from c (our own). The Cauchy–Hadamard theorem links the coefficient formula to the disk of convergence (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Radius of Convergence of Derivative of Complex Power Series](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Radius_of_Convergence_of_Derivative_of_Complex_Power_Series). It says: “Then R = R′.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Holomorphic as one power series on a disk gives antiderivatives there

**Remember:** Integrate each power, and the radius of convergence stays the same.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 30B10 (Power series (including lacunary series) in one complex variable), 30A05. arXiv math.CV. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** On an open disk, describe a holomorphic function by one power series about the centre that converges on the whole disk. A theorem of Cauchy says this agrees with the usual definition by a complex derivative at each point.

**Problem.** Every holomorphic function on an open disk has an antiderivative defined throughout the disk.

**How the definition helps.** Integrate the series term by term: each coefficient aₙ becomes aₙ/(n + 1), which keeps the radius of convergence (our own). So the new series converges on the whole disk, and termwise differentiation gives back f (our own). Cauchy’s integral formula supplies one Taylor expansion valid on the entire disk.

**Wikipedia:** [Analyticity of holomorphic functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analyticity_of_holomorphic_functions). It says: “The argument, first given by Cauchy, hinges on Cauchy's integral formula and the power series expansion of the expression”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Log-convexity controls reciprocal signs

**Remember:** Ratios that never decrease make every later reciprocal coefficient nonpositive.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 30B10 (Power series (including lacunary series) in one complex variable). arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A positive sequence aₙ is log-convex if the ratios aₙ/aₙ₋₁ of successive terms never decrease, that is, aₙ² ≤ aₙ₋₁aₙ₊₁ for every n ≥ 1.

**Problem.** For a power series of positive radius with positive log-convex coefficients, its reciprocal has nonpositive coefficients beyond the constant.

**How the definition helps.** Induction shows each reciprocal coefficient bₙ with n ≥ 1 is at most zero, starting from b₁ = −a₁/a₀² (our own). Subtracting (aₙ/aₙ₋₁) times the degree n−1 product identity from the degree n one gives a₀bₙ = ∑ⱼ₌₁ⁿ⁻¹ ((aₙ/aₙ₋₁)aₙ₋₁₋ⱼ − aₙ₋ⱼ)bⱼ, and log-convexity makes each bracket nonnegative (our own). Without log-convexity, coefficients 1, 1, ½ give a reciprocal with quadratic coefficient ½ (our own).

**Paper or page:** [On Kaluza's sign criterion for reciprocal power series](https://arxiv.org/abs/1010.5337v3). It says: “b₀ = 1/a₀ &gt; 0 and bₙ ≤ 0 for all n ∈ {1, 2, …}.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### One absolutely convergent boundary point controls the closed disk

**Remember:** The boundary magnitudes bound the terms everywhere inside.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 30B10 (Power series (including lacunary series) in one complex variable), 40A30. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A power series ∑ aₙzⁿ converges absolutely at a point of modulus R if ∑ \|aₙ\|Rⁿ is finite. That sum then bounds the series on the whole closed disk \|z\| ≤ R, since there \|aₙzⁿ\| ≤ \|aₙ\|Rⁿ.

**Problem.** Suppose a power series converges absolutely at a point of modulus R. It converges uniformly to a continuous function on the closed disk of radius R.

**How the definition helps.** The bound \|aₙzⁿ\| ≤ \|aₙ\|Rⁿ holds on the whole closed disk, so the Weierstrass M-test gives uniform convergence, and the uniform limit of polynomials is continuous (our own argument). Plain convergence at one boundary point is not enough: ∑ zⁿ/n, from n = 1, converges at −1 but diverges at 1.

**Wikipedia:** [Power series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_series). It says: “Absolute convergence at every point of the boundary”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Power series make holomorphic circle averages equal the center value

**Remember:** Only the constant term survives a full turn.

*True by definition.* MSC 30B10 (Power series (including lacunary series) in one complex variable). arXiv math.CV. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A function is holomorphic if it is complex differentiable at each point of its open domain. Equivalently, near each point a it is a convergent power series ∑ cₙ(z − a)ⁿ, and each power with n ≥ 1 averages to zero on a circle about a (our own proof).

**Problem.** A function holomorphic on an open set containing a closed disk equals its circle average at the disk center.

**How the definition helps.** On a circle centred at a, each term cₙ(z − a)ⁿ with n ≥ 1 averages to zero, leaving the constant term f(a) (our own proof). Cauchy’s formula gives a centred Taylor series on a slightly larger disk, and uniform convergence on the circle lets us average term by term (our own proof).

**Paper or page:** [Mean Value Theorem for Holomorphic Functions](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Mean_Value_Theorem_for_Holomorphic_Functions). It says: “f(z) = (1/2π) ∫₀²π f(z + r eⁱᶿ) dθ”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Power series make holomorphic functions differentiable to every order

**Remember:** Differentiate the power series term by term to get another power series.

*True by definition.* MSC 30B10 (Power series (including lacunary series) in one complex variable), 30E20. arXiv math.CV. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Call a function analytic if it equals a convergent power series near each point of its open domain. Cauchy’s integral formula shows that every holomorphic function, one with a complex derivative at every point, is analytic.

**Problem.** Every holomorphic function has complex derivatives of all orders, and those derivatives are holomorphic.

**How the definition helps.** A power series differentiates term by term into another power series with the same radius of convergence, so the derivative of an analytic function is analytic (our own). The step repeats for every order (our own). Cauchy’s integral formula supplies the local series for a holomorphic function.

**nLab:** [holomorphic function](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/holomorphic+function). It says: “The theorem that every continuously complex-differentiable function is analytic is soft and due to Augustin Cauchy; the theorem that every complex-differentiable function is continuously differentiable is hard and due essentially to Édouard Goursat”

**Paper or page:** [Holomorphic Function is Analytic](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Holomorphic_Function_is_Analytic). It says: “Let f be a function holomorphic on some open ball D = B(a, r). Then f is complex analytic on D.”

**Sources:**

- [É. Goursat, Sur la définition générale des fonctions analytiques, d'après Cauchy, Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 1 (1900), 14–16](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9947-1900-1500519-7)

### Two power series give Laurent series two convergence radii

**Remember:** Positive powers converge inside a circle, negative powers outside one.

*True by definition.* MSC 30B10 (Power series (including lacunary series) in one complex variable). arXiv math.CV. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A Laurent series about a is a power series in z − a plus a power series in 1/(z − a) without constant term. It converges at z when both series converge there separately.

**Problem.** If a Laurent series about a converges on a nonempty open set, the interior of its convergence set away from a is an annulus. The inner radius may be zero and the outer radius infinite.

**How the definition helps.** The first series converges for \|z − a\| &lt; R and the second for 1/\|z − a\| &lt; 1/r, so together they give the annulus r &lt; \|z − a\| &lt; R (our own). Each radius comes from the convergence theorem for power series (our own). Separate convergence stops symmetric partial sums from hiding cancellation between the two series (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Laurent series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurent_series). It says: “both the positive- and negative degree power series converge.”

### A bounded approach angle keeps Abel’s boundary limit valid

**Remember:** Stay in a wedge at 1, and the series follows its sum.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 30B30 (Boundary behavior of power series in one complex variable; over-convergence), 30B10. arXiv math.CV. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Fix M &gt; 1. The Stolz sector at 1 is the set of z in the open unit disk with \|1 − z\| ≤ M(1 − \|z\|), a region shaped like a wedge near 1 whose closure meets the boundary circle only at 1.

**Problem.** Suppose a power series about zero converges at 1. Its values inside any fixed Stolz sector tend to that same sum as z approaches 1.

**How the definition helps.** After summation by parts, the error is a tail sum multiplied by a factor of size about \|1 − z\|/(1 − \|z\|), which the sector bounds by M (our own explanation). Outside a sector the limit can fail: a known series converges at 1 but is unbounded near boundary points arbitrarily close to 1.

**Wikipedia:** [Abel's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abel%27s_theorem). It says: “provided that z → 1 entirely within a single Stolz sector”
