### Gaussian thermal correlations use pairs

**Remember:** A fermionic Gaussian state is fixed by pairs, with crossing signs.

*True by definition.* MSC 82B10 (Quantum equilibrium statistical mechanics (general)). arXiv math-ph, cond-mat.stat-mech. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An even quasi-free fermion state is a fermionic Gaussian (our own): all odd moments of fields linear in creation and annihilation operators vanish. Each even moment is the sum, over pairings of its ordered fields, of the product of the paired two-field moments. Each pairing gets a factor −1 for each crossing of its arcs.

**Problem.** For a free fermion thermal state of the cited model with finite normalizing trace, the four-field moment has three terms. Pairings (12)(34), (13)(24), and (14)(23) have signs +, −, and +, respectively.

**How the definition helps.** The definition gives the four-field moment as the three pairings directly, with no new thermal trace (our own). Only (13)(24) has crossing arcs, so it alone gets the minus sign (our own). The cited result does the hard step: it proves that the thermal state is quasi-free.

**Paper or page:** [On the semiclassical regularity of thermal equilibria](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.07911v1). It says: “is quasi-free and its one-particle reduced density matrix operator is given”

**Sources:**

- [Jacky J. Chong, Laurent Lafleche, Chiara Saffirio, On the semiclassical regularity of thermal equilibria](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.07911v1)

### A shared field separates spins

**Remember:** One shared field carries all the mean-field dependence.

*True by definition.* MSC 82B20 (Lattice systems (Ising, dimer, Potts, etc.) and systems on graphs arising in equilibrium statistical mechanics), 82B26. arXiv cond-mat.stat-mech, math.PR. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take n spins sᵢ ∈ {−1,1} with coupling a &gt; 0 and fixed site fields hᵢ. Add one real field y with joint density proportional to exp(−ny²/(2a) + ∑ᵢ(hᵢ + y)sᵢ) (our own). Each spin then feels only its own field hᵢ plus the shared field y (our own).

**Problem.** Given the extra field and fixed site fields, all spins are independent. At fixed positive inverse temperature, concentration of the extra field at one value gives the corresponding product limit for any fixed set of spins.

**How the definition helps.** Fixing y makes the weight a product of one-spin factors, and integrating y out recovers the mean-field interaction exactly (our own). Each one-spin probability is continuous in y, so concentration of y gives the product limit (our own). The hard step in the cited model is proving that concentration for almost every choice of site fields (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Propagation of chaos in the Random field Curie-Weiss model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.01866v1). It says: “Assume that the function G(y) has a unique, non-degenerate global maximum in some point y₀.”

**Sources:**

- [Matthias Löwe, Zakhar Kabluchko, Propagation of chaos in the Random field Curie-Weiss model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.01866v1)

### Continuity excludes a decimated Ising law

**Remember:** Distant spins must lose their influence when nearby spins are fixed.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 82B20 (Lattice systems (Ising, dimer, Potts, etc.) and systems on graphs arising in equilibrium statistical mechanics). arXiv math.PR, cond-mat.stat-mech. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A law on a finite-spin lattice is quasilocal if each finite-region event has a version of its conditional probability that is continuous in the exterior configuration. That is, for every ε &gt; 0, two exteriors that agree on a large enough finite neighborhood give probabilities within ε.

**Problem.** Take the cited square-lattice Ising model, with nearest-neighbor coupling on one axis and power-law coupling of exponent 1 &lt; α ≤ 2 on the other. In its plus state at sufficiently low temperature, keeping only the sites with both coordinates even destroys quasilocality.

**How the definition helps.** A jump in a conditional probability that no version can remove rules out quasilocality, and hence any Gibbs description (our own). Fixing the kept spins in an alternating pattern lets distant boundary choices select different phases of the removed spins (our own). The hard estimate shows a lasting gap in the expected central spin over exterior events of positive probability (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Decimations for Two-dimensional Ising and Rotator Models I](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.07950v1), [Decimations for Two-dimensional Ising and Rotator Models I](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.07950v1). It says: “is non-quasilocal, hence non-Gibbs, and so are all decimated Gibbs measures.”

### Normalization excludes uniform heights

**Remember:** Messages count only if each site’s weights have a finite sum.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 82B20 (Lattice systems (Ising, dimer, Potts, etc.) and systems on graphs arising in equilibrium statistical mechanics). arXiv math-ph, math.PR. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For positive edge weights Q on a tree, a boundary law is a family of positive messages u<sub>xy</sub>, one per directed edge, with u<sub>xy</sub>(i) = c<sub>xy</sub> ∏<sub>z∼x,z≠y</sub> b<sub>zx</sub>(i). Here b<sub>zx</sub>(i) = ∑ⱼ Q<sub>xz</sub>(i,j)u<sub>zx</sub>(j), and c<sub>xy</sub> &gt; 0 does not depend on the height i. It is normalizable if ∑ᵢ ∏<sub>z∼x</sub> b<sub>zx</sub>(i) is finite at every vertex x, so the incoming messages give a probability distribution there (our own).

**Problem.** A normalizable boundary law defines a unique tree-indexed Markov chain among the Gibbs measures. For positive summable edge weights depending only on height differences, a constant boundary law solves the recursion yet gives no probability distribution at a vertex.

**How the definition helps.** The finite single-site sum is what turns the incoming messages into probabilities at a vertex. A constant message gives every integer height the same positive weight, so that sum diverges (our own). Once the sum is finite, the boundary-law theorem builds the Markov chain (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Gradient Gibbs measures with periodic boundary laws of a generalized SOS model on a Cayley tree](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.00867v1). It says: “defines a unique tree-indexed Markov chain μ ∈ 𝒢(γ)”

### Path recoloring switches current sources

**Remember:** Switch the colors along a path to move its odd endpoints.

*True by definition.* MSC 82B20 (Lattice systems (Ising, dimer, Potts, etc.) and systems on graphs arising in equilibrium statistical mechanics). arXiv cond-mat.stat-mech, math.PR. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A current puts a nonnegative integer on each edge of a finite graph, read as that many copies of the edge. Each copy is colored red or blue, and the sources of a color are the vertices that meet an odd number of copy ends of that color.

**Problem.** Fix the copies and distinct vertices x and y joined by a path of copies. Equally many colorings have source sets (A, {x,y}) as (A △ {x,y}, ∅), where △ denotes symmetric difference.

**How the definition helps.** Swapping the colors along one fixed simple path from x to y changes both colors’ parities exactly at x and y (our own). Swapping again restores the coloring, so the swap pairs the two sets of colorings (our own). Using this count for Ising spins needs the expansion of the interaction weights into currents (our own).

**Paper or page:** [A geometric perspective on the scaling limits of critical Ising and φ⁴ models in dimension d](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.04248v3). It says: “for which there exists a sub-current $\\mathbf{n} ' \\leq \\mathbf m $ supported on $\\mathcal{E} \_2$ with $\\partial \\mathbf{n} '=B$”

### The one-line projection of the Ising model has continuous one-sided predictions

**Remember:** A continuous prediction from the past need not extend to both sides.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 82B20 (Lattice systems (Ising, dimer, Potts, etc.) and systems on graphs arising in equilibrium statistical mechanics), 60K35, 37D35. arXiv math.PR, cond-mat.stat-mech. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A regular g-measure is a stationary process on finitely many symbols whose next symbol, given the whole past, has strictly positive probabilities that depend continuously on the past. Continuity means that long enough agreement on the recent past makes these probabilities close. The Schonmann projection restricts the plus phase of the zero-field square-lattice nearest-neighbor ferromagnetic Ising model to one lattice line.

**Problem.** At sufficiently low temperature, the Schonmann projection is a regular g-measure. At low temperature it is also non-Gibbsian, because its conditional probabilities given both sides are discontinuous.

**How the definition helps.** Regularity asks only for continuity given the past, while the Gibbs property asks for continuity given both sides (our own). Low-temperature estimates for the Schonmann projection prove the one-sided continuity and an essential discontinuity for two-sided conditioning (our own).

**Paper or page:** [The Schonmann projection as a g-measure-, how Gibbsian is it?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.10622v2). It says: “We prove that they are g-measures, which means that their conditional probabilities have a continuous dependence on one-sided boundary condition.”

**Sources:**

- [Aernout van Enter, Senya Shlosman, The Schonmann projection as a g-measure-, how Gibbsian is it?, arXiv:2102.10622v2 (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.10622v2)

### Tree messages give Gibbs transitions

**Remember:** Sum out a branch once, then use its weight at each edge.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 82B20 (Lattice systems (Ising, dimer, Potts, etc.) and systems on graphs arising in equilibrium statistical mechanics), 60K35. arXiv math-ph, math.PR. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On a regular tree with d children per nonroot vertex, let Q(i,j) be positive symmetric weights on a finite spin space. A homogeneous boundary law is a positive vector u with u(i) = c·b(i)ᵈ, where b(i) = ∑ⱼ Q(i,j)u(j) and c &gt; 0 is constant. Then u(j) is the summed weight of a whole branch whose top spin is j (our own).

**Problem.** The corresponding equilibrium law has independent child branches given the parent spin i. The probability of child spin j equals Q(i,j)u(j)/b(i).

**How the definition helps.** Since u(j) sums a whole branch, Q(i,j)u(j)/b(i) is the share of the branch weight with child spin j, which is a transition probability (our own). The recursion makes this tree law agree with the prescribed conditional probabilities in every finite region (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Infinite-volume states with irreducible localization sets for gradient models on trees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.05398v1). It says: “Pμ(i,j) = u(j) Q(i−j)/(Q ∗ u)(i)”

**Sources:**

- [Alberto Abbondandolo, Florian Henning, Christof Kuelske, Pietro Majer, Infinite-volume states with irreducible localization sets for gradient models on trees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.05398v1)

### Local swaps commute rows

**Remember:** The crossing slides past each column, swapping the two rows.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 82B23 (Exactly solvable models; Bethe ansatz). arXiv math-ph, cond-mat.stat-mech. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A periodic six-vertex transfer matrix is the trace, over the horizontal arrow space, of the ordered product of a row’s vertex weights L<sub>aj</sub> or M<sub>bj</sub> at columns j. An invertible crossing operator R on the two horizontal spaces a and b satisfies the local swapping rule if R L<sub>aj</sub> M<sub>bj</sub> = M<sub>bj</sub> L<sub>aj</sub> R at every column (our own). So R slides past one column while swapping the two rows’ weights (our own).

**Problem.** Periodic six-vertex row transfer matrices commute if an invertible crossing operator satisfies the local swapping relation with the row weights.

**How the definition helps.** Slide R across the row one column at a time, then take the trace around both closed rows, where cyclicity cancels R against its inverse (our own). This replaces multiplying large matrices with checking one local identity (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Switch Operators for the Six-Vertex Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.08089v3). It says: “Consider a six-vertex model and attach a cross vertex. Then the following relationship between partition functions holds.”

**Sources:**

- [Evelyn Choi, Jadon Geathers, Slava Naprienko, Switch Operators for the Six-Vertex Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.08089v3)

### Path reversal gives fluctuation symmetry

**Remember:** Reversing a path negates its log probability ratio.

*True by definition.* MSC 82C05 (Classical dynamic and nonequilibrium statistical mechanics (general)). arXiv cond-mat.stat-mech. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Path entropy production, in units of Boltzmann’s constant, is ln(p(x)/p(xᴿ)), where p(x) is the density of a finite chain trajectory x and xᴿ is its time reversal. It is defined where both densities are positive, and reversing the path negates it (our own).

**Problem.** For the paper’s centered, stable Gaussian Markov chains, the entropy produced per step has a rate function I. It describes exponential decay of probabilities as the path length grows and satisfies I(−w) = I(w) + w.

**How the definition helps.** Swapping each path with its reverse negates the log ratio and gives a finite-time symmetry for its distribution (our own). Once the rate function exists, this symmetry passes to it as I(−w) = I(w) + w (our own). Proving existence for these Gaussian chains is the harder step.

**Paper or page:** [Large deviations for quadratic functionals of stable Gauss-Markov chains and entropy production](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.08059v1). It says: “and I(−w) = I(w) + w for all w ∈ ℝ.”

**Sources:**

- [Marco Zamparo, Massimiliano Semeraro, Large deviations for quadratic functionals of stable Gauss-Markov chains and entropy production](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.08059v1)

### Path support restores fluctuation equality

**Remember:** Forward-impossible paths must stay impossible when reversed.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 82C05 (Classical dynamic and nonequilibrium statistical mechanics (general)). arXiv cond-mat.stat-mech. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let p and r be densities, against one common measure, of forward paths and of reversed paths from the reverse experiment. Absolute continuity requires every event impossible forward to be impossible under the reversed law. On forward paths set σ = ln(p/r), with σ = +∞ when r = 0 &lt; p.

**Problem.** Under this condition the forward mean of exp(−σ) equals one. In general it equals one minus the reverse probability of the set where p vanishes.

**How the definition helps.** Averaging exp(−σ) under p integrates r over the set where p &gt; 0 (our own). The missing mass is the reverse probability of the set where p = 0, which absolute continuity makes zero (our own). After free expansion from half a box, a reverse path can end in the initially empty half, so its reversal starts where the forward law vanishes (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Fluctuation theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluctuation_theorem). It says: “This condition is known as the condition of ergodic consistency.”

**Sources:**

- [Yûto Murashita, Ken Funo, and Masahito Ueda, Nonequilibrium equalities in absolutely irreversible processes](https://doi.org/10.1103/physreve.90.042110)

### Subtracting steady heat makes excess finite

**Remember:** Subtract the running cost before adding up the transient cost.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 82C05 (Classical dynamic and nonequilibrium statistical mechanics (general)). arXiv cond-mat.stat-mech. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take a finite continuous-time ring chain with stationary law π and heat flow h(x) at state x. The centered flow f = h − ∑ᵧπ(y)h(y) removes the steady heat rate, and the excess heat from x is V(x) = ∫₀∞ 𝔼ₓ\[f(Xₜ)\] dt when this converges.

**Problem.** Suppose the chain can reach every state from every other state. Then V is the unique solution of LV = −f with stationary mean zero, where the generator L gives the initial rate of change of an expected observable.

**How the definition helps.** Centering removes the steady heat rate, whose time integral diverges on a driven ring with nonzero mean heat flow (our own). Irreducibility makes the centered expectation decay exponentially, so the integral converges, and integrating its time derivative gives LV = −f (our own). Two solutions differ by a harmonic function, which is constant on a finite irreducible chain, so mean zero fixes V (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Drazin-Inverse and heat capacity for driven random walks on the ring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.04974v4). It says: “for a function f having ⟨f⟩ˢ = 0, then V₍f₎ = −Lᴰ⁻¹f.”

**Sources:**

- [Faezeh Khodabandehlou, Irene Maes, Drazin-Inverse and heat capacity for driven random walks on the ring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.04974v4)

### Transport distance bounds lost work

**Remember:** Transport distance is the least kinetic cost of moving the density.

*True by definition.* MSC 82C35 (Irreversible thermodynamics, including Onsager-Machlup theory). arXiv cond-mat.stat-mech. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The squared transport distance between two densities of finite second moment is the least kinetic cost ∫₀¹∫ρ\|v\|² dx dt of moving one into the other in unit time. The minimum is over paths of densities ρ and velocity fields v that satisfy ∂ₜρ + div(ρv) = 0 in the weak sense.

**Problem.** Consider particles in a changing potential at fixed temperature, with negligible inertia and constant positive friction. Mean work minus free energy change is at least friction times squared transport distance divided by the process duration.

**How the definition helps.** The observed motion is one admissible path, so after rescaling to unit time its cost bounds the minimum, which gives the inverse duration factor (our own). The paper’s work balance identifies friction times this cost with mean work minus free energy change. The dynamic transport theorem identifies the minimum with the least mean squared displacement over endpoint couplings (our own).

**Paper or page:** [On the relation between information and power in stochastic thermodynamic engines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.03986v1). It says: “𝒲 ≥ Δℱ + (γ/t𝒻) W₂²(p(0, ·), p(t𝒻, ·))”

**Sources:**

- [Amirhossein Taghvaei, Olga Movilla Miangolarra, Rui Fu, Yongxin Chen and Tryphon T. Georgiou, On the relation between information and power in stochastic thermodynamic engines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.03986v1)

### Matched moments conserve energy

**Remember:** Match the moments that collisions must leave unchanged.

*True by definition.* MSC 82C40 (Kinetic theory of gases in time-dependent statistical mechanics), 35Q20. arXiv math-ph. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A relaxation collision term νᵢ(Gᵢ − fᵢ) pushes the distribution fᵢ of species i toward a target Gᵢ at rate νᵢ. Choose the targets so that this term has zero particle-number moment for each species. Its energy and momentum moments, summed over species with each species’ own measure, must also vanish.

**Problem.** Assume each species has a nonzero, nonnegative integrable distribution with finite particle, energy, and momentum moments. The collision term preserves each species’ particle number and the mixture’s total energy and momentum.

**How the definition helps.** The conserved quantities are exactly these moments of the collision term, so they vanish by construction, without tracking individual collisions (our own). The real work is proving that targets with a common temperature and bulk velocity exist (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Relativistic BGK model for gas mixtures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05349v1). It says: “Thus, the partial particle four-flow and the energy-momentum tensor of gas mixtures are conserved”

**Sources:**

- [Byung-Hoon Hwang, Myeong-Su Lee, Seok-Bae Yun, Relativistic BGK model for gas mixtures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05349v1)

## 83 Relativity and gravitational theory

### Einstein synchronisation makes equal one-way light speeds a convention

**Remember:** The far clock reads midway, so out and back take equally long.

*True by definition.* MSC 83A05 (Special relativity). arXiv physics.class-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For two clocks at rest a fixed distance apart in an inertial frame, Einstein synchronisation gives a reflection the time midway between sending and return. If light leaves the first clock at τ₁ and comes back at τ₂, the second clock reads (τ₁ + τ₂)/2 when it reflects the light.

**Problem.** With Einstein synchronisation of distant clocks, the one-way speed of light is the same in both directions.

**How the definition helps.** The midpoint rule gives each leg duration (τ₂ − τ₁)/2 (our own). Both legs cover the same distance, so dividing by that duration gives equal one-way speeds (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Einstein synchronisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_synchronisation). It says: “Since it is meaningless to measure a one-way velocity prior to the synchronisation of distant clocks, experiments claiming a measure of the one-way speed of light can often be reinterpreted as verifying the Laue–Weyl's round-trip condition.”

**Sources:**

- [Einstein, A. (1905). Zur Elektrodynamik bewegter Körper. Annalen der Physik 322(10), 891–921.](https://doi.org/10.1002/andp.19053221004)

### Invariant mass, built from energy and momentum, is the same for everyone

**Remember:** Energy squared minus momentum squared is the same in every frame.

*True by definition.* MSC 83A05 (Special relativity). arXiv physics.class-ph, math-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The invariant mass is the nonnegative m with m²c⁴ = E² − \|p\|²c², where E and p are the total energy and momentum. Thus mc is the Minkowski length of the four-momentum (E/c, p) (our own).

**Problem.** The invariant mass of a system is the same in every inertial frame and stays constant for an isolated system. The combined invariant mass of all decay products of an isolated particle equals its rest mass.

**How the definition helps.** Lorentz transformations preserve the Minkowski square of the four-momentum (E/c, p), so they preserve m (our own). Four-momentum conservation gives the complete set of decay products the same four-momentum as the parent, hence the same invariant mass (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Mass in special relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_in_special_relativity). It says: “The term "relativistic mass" tends not to be used in particle and nuclear physics and is often avoided by writers on special relativity, in favor of referring to the body's relativistic energy.”

**Sources:**

- [L. B. Okun, The Concept of Mass, Physics Today 42 (1989), 31–36](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.881171)

### Proper time as spacetime length makes the inertial twin older

**Remember:** In flat spacetime, the straight timelike path takes the most proper time.

*True by definition.* MSC 83A05 (Special relativity), 53B30. arXiv gr-qc, physics.class-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Proper time along a future-directed timelike path is the time a clock carried along it shows (our own): its Minkowski length divided by c. In an inertial frame it equals ∫√(1 − \|v\|²/c²) dt.

**Problem.** In flat spacetime, compare one inertial leg with two future-directed timelike inertial legs between the same events. The single leg gives at least as much proper time, with equality only if all legs have the same velocity.

**How the definition helps.** The straight displacement is the sum of the two leg displacements, so the reversed triangle inequality makes its Minkowski length at least the sum of theirs. Equality requires proportional future-directed displacements, hence identical velocities (our own). Dividing by c gives the proper-time comparison (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Proper time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proper_time), [Minkowski spacetime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minkowski_spacetime), [Twin paradox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twin_paradox). It says: “For two similarly directed time-like vectors u and w, the inequality is ‖u + w‖ ≥ ‖u‖ + ‖w‖, where the equality holds when the vectors are linearly dependent.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Proper time makes four-acceleration perpendicular to four-velocity

**Remember:** Proper time gives four-velocity a fixed length, c.

*True by definition.* MSC 83A05 (Special relativity), 70H40. arXiv physics.class-ph, gr-qc. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Parametrize a future-directed timelike path by proper time τ, defined by c²dτ² = c²dt² − \|dx\|², so that the four-velocity U = dX/dτ has constant Minkowski square c² (our own). The four-acceleration is A = dU/dτ.

**Problem.** Along any twice differentiable timelike path in flat spacetime, four-velocity and four-acceleration are perpendicular. Perpendicularity uses the Minkowski scalar product, the spacetime version of a dot product.

**How the definition helps.** Since U·U = c² is constant, differentiating it gives 2U·A = 0, which is the claimed perpendicularity (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Four-acceleration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four-acceleration). It says: “The scalar product of a particle's four-velocity and its four-acceleration is always 0.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Rapidity makes relativistic velocities along one line simply add

**Remember:** Rapidity is a boost’s hyperbolic angle, and angles add.

*True by definition.* MSC 83A05 (Special relativity). arXiv physics.class-ph, math-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For signed velocity v along an oriented line with \|v\| &lt; c, rapidity is the unique real w satisfying tanh w = v/c.

**Problem.** Let frame B move relative to A with rapidity w₁, and C relative to B with rapidity w₂, along one line. Then C moves relative to A with rapidity w₁ + w₂, which is Einstein’s formula (u + v)/(1 + uv/c²) in terms of velocities.

**How the definition helps.** Einstein’s formula divided by c is exactly the addition formula tanh(w₁ + w₂) = (tanh w₁ + tanh w₂)/(1 + tanh w₁ tanh w₂) (our own). Since tanh is injective, the combined rapidity is w₁ + w₂ (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Rapidity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapidity). It says: “The simplicity of this formula contrasts with the complexity of the corresponding velocity-addition formula.”

**Sources:**

- [H. Minkowski, Die Grundgleichungen für die elektromagnetischen Vorgänge in bewegten Körpern, Nachrichten von der Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften zu Göttingen (1908), 53–111](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Translation:The_Fundamental_Equations_for_Electromagnetic_Processes_in_Moving_Bodies)

### Spacelike separation permits order reversal

**Remember:** Only spacelike pairs can swap their order.

*True by definition.* MSC 83A05 (Special relativity), 01A60. arXiv physics.hist-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Two events are spacelike separated when their squared interval c²Δt² − \|Δx\|² is negative. Then no signal at or below light speed can travel from one to the other (our own).

**Problem.** Two distinct events occur in opposite time orders for some two future-directed inertial observers, ones moving at constant velocity, exactly when their separation is spacelike.

**How the definition helps.** A boost with velocity v gives the transformed time difference the sign of Δt − v·Δx/c² (our own). For \|Δx\| &gt; c\|Δt\|, choose velocities along Δx on opposite sides of the simultaneity speed c²Δt/\|Δx\| (our own). Otherwise \|v\| &lt; c prevents reversal (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Spacetime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacetime). It says: “From a different reference frame, the orderings of these non-causally-related events can be reversed.”

**Sources:**

- [Hermann Minkowski, Raum und Zeit (1908 address, reprinted 1988)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-322-89451-9_11)

### Horizons exclude overcharged solutions

**Remember:** Too much charge leaves no real horizon radius.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 83C57 (Black holes). arXiv gr-qc, astro-ph.HE. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A Reissner–Nordström black hole is a spherical, nonrotating charged mass, in Einstein–Maxwell theory with zero cosmological constant, that has an event horizon. The horizon is the boundary beyond which light cannot escape. In geometric units, with mass M &gt; 0 and charge Q, its possible radii solve r² − 2Mr + Q² = 0.

**Problem.** For positive M, a Reissner–Nordström black hole has \|Q\| ≤ M. At equality the two horizon radii coincide.

**How the definition helps.** A horizon needs a real root, and r² − 2Mr + Q² = 0 has one exactly when M² ≥ Q² (our own). At equality the two roots coincide at r = M (our own). For \|Q\| &gt; M the singularity is naked, and showing that the larger root bounds the escape region needs the causal structure of the solution.

**Wikipedia:** [Reissner–Nordström metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reissner%E2%80%93Nordstr%C3%B6m_metric). It says: “have no event horizon (the term under the square root becomes negative) and would display a naked singularity.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Curvature density makes gravity coordinate invariant

**Remember:** Pull back the metric and the whole curvature density follows.

*True by definition.* MSC 83C05 (Einstein's equations (general structure, canonical formalism, Cauchy problems)). arXiv gr-qc, math-ph. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Einstein–Hilbert action integrates the scalar curvature, the double trace of the curvature tensor, against the metric volume measure. In coordinates this measure is √\|det g\| times coordinate volume, so both pieces come from the metric alone.

**Problem.** Let a smooth map of a compact spacetime region onto itself have a smooth inverse. Pulling the metric back by this map leaves the Einstein–Hilbert action unchanged.

**How the definition helps.** The scalar curvature and the metric volume both pull back with the metric, so the change of variables formula keeps the integral fixed. The factor √\|det g\| supplies exactly the Jacobian that formula needs, and bare coordinate volume would miss it (our own).

**nLab:** [Einstein-Hilbert action](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Einstein-Hilbert+action). It says: “This functional is invariant under the action of diffeomorphisms on X”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Largest Cauchy developments are unique

**Remember:** The largest solution contains every other solution from the same data.

*True by definition.* MSC 83C05 (Einstein's equations (general structure, canonical formalism, Cauchy problems)). arXiv gr-qc, math.DG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A vacuum development solves Einstein’s vacuum equations and realizes the given initial data on a Cauchy surface, one crossed exactly once by every inextendible timelike path. A development is largest if every other development embeds into it, preserving the metric, the initial data and the time direction.

**Problem.** Given connected vacuum initial data, any two largest developments agree up to a map that preserves the spacetime metric and fixes the initial data.

**How the definition helps.** Being largest gives embeddings in both directions, and each composite fixes the initial surface pointwise and preserves its future unit normal (our own). So the composite has identity derivative at a point, and an isometry of a connected spacetime is fixed by its value and derivative at one point (our own). The composites are identities, so the embeddings are inverse isometries (our own).

**Paper or page:** [On the genericity of singularities in spacetimes with weakly trapped submanifolds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.09651v2). It says: “any other spacetime satisfying these conditions can be isometrically embedded therein.”

**Sources:**

- [Yvonne Choquet-Bruhat and Robert Geroch (1969), Global aspects of the Cauchy problem in general relativity](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01645389)

### The Einstein tensor makes Einstein’s equations conserve stress–energy

**Remember:** A divergence-free left side forces a divergence-free right side.

*True by definition.* MSC 83C05 (Einstein's equations (general structure, canonical formalism, Cauchy problems)), 83C40. arXiv gr-qc, math.DG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Einstein tensor G = Ric − ½Rg subtracts half the trace R of the Ricci curvature Ric, times the metric g, so its divergence vanishes for every metric. Einstein’s equations set G proportional to the stress–energy tensor T, the density and flow of energy and momentum.

**Problem.** Einstein’s equations with a nonzero constant of proportionality force T to have zero covariant divergence. This is the local conservation law for energy and momentum in curved spacetime.

**How the definition helps.** Taking the divergence of both sides of Einstein’s equations gives zero divergence for T at once. The contracted Bianchi identity says the divergence of Ric is half the gradient of R. The trace term subtracts exactly that gradient (our own). With Ric alone on the left, a conserved T would force R to be constant (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Einstein tensor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_tensor). It says: “The (contracted) Bianchi identities automatically ensure the covariant conservation of the stress–energy tensor in curved spacetimes:”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Wave coordinates reveal Einstein’s wave operator

**Remember:** Let the coordinates solve waves to expose waves in the metric.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 83C05 (Einstein's equations (general structure, canonical formalism, Cauchy problems)), 35Q75. arXiv gr-qc, math-ph. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Wave coordinates are coordinate functions that each solve the source-free scalar wave equation of the metric. Equivalently, the metric trace of the connection coefficients vanishes, and that trace carries the extra second derivatives that hide the wave operator (our own).

**Problem.** In wave coordinates, the highest derivatives in the vacuum Einstein equations form a wave operator on each metric component. The coefficients of this operator depend on the metric itself.

**How the definition helps.** The extra second derivatives in the Ricci tensor are derivatives of that trace, which the coordinate condition sets to zero (our own). Each metric component then obeys a wave equation whose lower-order terms involve at most first derivatives (our own). Constructing such coordinates and showing that the condition persists is a separate step.

**Wikipedia:** [Harmonic coordinates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_coordinates). It says: “relative to a harmonic coordinate chart, the Ricci curvature is given by”

**Paper or page:** [On Axially Symmetric Perturbations of Kerr Black Hole Spacetimes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.08326v1). It says: “The linearized Einstein equations in harmonic gauge is purely a hyperbolic differential equation system”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Fermi–Walker transport keeps frames orthonormal

**Remember:** Correct for acceleration without changing inner products.

*True by definition.* MSC 83C10 (Equations of motion in general relativity and gravitational theory), 83A05. arXiv gr-qc, math.DG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fermi–Walker transport moves a vector X along an observer with proper-time velocity U, normalized by g(U,U) = −1, and acceleration A. It adds a correction to parallel transport: ∇<sub>U</sub> X = g(A,X)U − g(U,X)A. This correction is an infinitesimal Lorentz transformation in the plane of U and A, so it preserves inner products (our own).

**Problem.** Axes that start mutually perpendicular and normalized retain their inner products under Fermi–Walker transport. A time axis initially equal to U stays equal to U.

**How the definition helps.** The correction is antisymmetric with respect to g, so the inner-product derivatives cancel (our own). For X = U the right side is A, since g(A,U) = 0 and g(U,U) = −1, so U itself is transported (our own). Uniqueness of solutions keeps a time axis that starts at U equal to U (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Fermi–Walker transport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermi%E2%80%93Walker_transport). It says: “then the vector field X is Fermi–Walker transported along the curve.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Timelike geodesics give all test bodies the same free fall

**Remember:** The geodesic equation uses the initial position and velocity, not the mass.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 83C10 (Equations of motion in general relativity and gravitational theory), 53C22. arXiv gr-qc, math.DG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A test body, one with negligible self-gravity and internal structure, falls freely along a timelike geodesic: its proper-time velocity has zero covariant derivative along its path. This equation involves only the metric and the body’s position and velocity, not its mass (our own).

**Problem.** Two freely falling test bodies at the same event with the same initial velocity follow the same path as long as the geodesic exists.

**How the definition helps.** Both bodies solve the same geodesic equation with the same initial data, which has a unique solution for a smooth metric (our own). Newtonian gravity gets this only if all bodies have the same ratio of gravitational to inertial mass (our own). The physical work is in justifying the geodesic law for test bodies (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Geodesics in general relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geodesics_in_general_relativity). It says: “Importantly, the world line of a particle free from all external, non-gravitational forces is a particular type of geodesic. In other words, a freely moving or falling particle always moves along a geodesic.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Null updates give linear metric inverses

**Remember:** Add a null square to flat space; it squares to zero.

*True by definition.* MSC 83C20 (Classes of solutions; algebraically special solutions, metrics with symmetries for problems in general relativity and gravitational theory), 83C57. arXiv gr-qc, math-ph. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Kerr–Schild metric is the flat metric η plus H k ⊗ k, where H is a scalar function. Here k is a null covector, one of zero squared length under the inverse of η, so raising one index makes the perturbation square to zero (our own).

**Problem.** Write v for the vector corresponding to k under the flat metric. The inverse metric equals the inverse flat metric minus H v ⊗ v.

**How the definition helps.** With N = H v ⊗ k, the square of N contains k(v) = 0, so (I + N)(I − N) = I (our own). Raising the remaining index turns this into the stated inverse metric (our own).

**nLab:** [Kerr-Schild spacetime](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Kerr-Schild+spacetime). It says: “where k is a lightlike vector field with respect to both metrics, and H is any scalar function.”

**Sources:**

- [G. C. Debney, R. P. Kerr, and A. Schild (1969), Solutions of the Einstein and Einstein-Maxwell Equations](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1664769)

### Static symmetry excludes rotating Kerr

**Remember:** Static means steady and without twist.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 83C20 (Classes of solutions; algebraically special solutions, metrics with symmetries for problems in general relativity and gravitational theory). arXiv gr-qc. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A spacetime region is stationary if a timelike field, one inside the light cone, has a flow that preserves the metric. It is static if such a field is also perpendicular to a family of hypersurfaces filling the region.

**Problem.** A static metric admits local coordinates in which its coefficients are independent of time and all mixed time and space coefficients vanish. The rotating Kerr metric shows why stationarity alone does not suffice, even near spatial infinity.

**How the definition helps.** Take coordinates on one perpendicular slice and carry them along the Killing flow, which preserves the metric, so the coefficients do not depend on time (our own). Perpendicularity of the field to the slices sets the mixed coefficients to zero (our own). Rotating Kerr is stationary near infinity but has no hypersurface-orthogonal timelike Killing field there.

**Wikipedia:** [Static spacetime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Static_spacetime). It says: “Thus, the Kerr solution provides an example of a stationary spacetime that is not static”

**Sources:**

- [Kerr (1963), Gravitational Field of a Spinning Mass as an Example of Algebraically Special Metrics](https://doi.org/10.1103/physrevlett.11.237)

### Vacuum twist has a potential

**Remember:** In vacuum, twist is locally a gradient.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 83C20 (Classes of solutions; algebraically special solutions, metrics with symmetries for problems in general relativity and gravitational theory). arXiv gr-qc, math-ph. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The twist of the timelike Killing field K of a stationary metric measures how its flow lines wind around each other (our own). It is the one-form ⋆(α ∧ dα), where α is the one-form metric-dual to K and ⋆ is the Hodge dual in four oriented dimensions.

**Problem.** If the Ricci tensor vanishes, the twist of K is locally the differential of a real function. A single such function exists on each simply connected region.

**How the definition helps.** A local potential exists exactly when the twist has zero exterior derivative, by the Poincaré lemma (our own explanation). The curvature identity for a Killing field expresses that derivative through the Ricci tensor paired with K, so it vanishes in vacuum. Path integration then gives a single potential on a simply connected region.

**Wikipedia:** [Stationary spacetime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stationary_spacetime). It says: “the twist 4-vector ωμ is curl-free”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Conformal rescaling extends flat spacetime to a finite diamond

**Remember:** Shrink infinity to a boundary without tipping the light cones.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 83C30 (Asymptotic procedures (radiation, news functions, H -spaces, etc.) in general relativity and gravitational theory), 53C50. arXiv gr-qc, math.DG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A conformal diagram multiplies the metric by a positive function that brings infinity to a finite boundary, in coordinates where the new metric extends smoothly to that boundary. Light rays keep their directions, because the rescaling does not change which vectors are null.

**Problem.** In two-dimensional Minkowski spacetime, the arctangent of each light coordinate maps the whole plane onto a finite square in light coordinates. In time and space coordinates this is a diamond with null edges.

**How the definition helps.** In units c = 1, the coordinates U = arctan(t − x) and V = arctan(t + x) each range over (−π/2, π/2), giving the finite square (our own). Multiplying the metric by cos²(U)cos²(V) gives −dU dV, smooth up to the boundary (our own). Each edge has constant U or V and is therefore null (our own).

**nLab:** [Penrose diagram](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Penrose+diagram). It says: “which makes events at timelike/spacelike/lightlike infinity of the spacetime appear at respective boundary points of its Penrose diagram.”

**Wikipedia:** [Penrose diagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penrose_diagram). It says: “spacetime distances that are considered infinitely far away are compactified into finite locations in the diagram.”

**Sources:**

- [Roger Penrose (1963), Asymptotic Properties of Fields and Space-Times](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.10.66)

### Hawking energy ignores normal rescaling

**Remember:** One light expansion gains what the other loses.

*True by definition.* MSC 83C40 (Gravitational energy and conservation laws; groups of motions). arXiv gr-qc, math-ph. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a closed spacelike surface of area A, take future null normals ℓ, n with g(ℓ,n) = −2. In geometric units the Hawking energy is √(A/(16π)) \[1 + (1/(16π))∫θℓθₙ dA\] (our own). The expansion θₖ of a normal k, the tangential trace of its covariant derivative, measures how fast area grows along k.

**Problem.** Hawking energy stays fixed when the null normals are multiplied by a smooth positive function and its reciprocal, respectively.

**How the definition helps.** The energy uses the expansions only through their product θℓθₙ, which reciprocal scalings preserve, while the area stays fixed (our own). Scaling ℓ by f scales θℓ by f, and scaling n by 1/f scales θₙ by 1/f (our own). Derivatives of f point along the normals and drop out of the tangential trace (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Hawking energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawking_energy). It says: “measure the divergence of these families of null geodesics”

**Sources:**

- [Hawking (1968), Gravitational Radiation in an Expanding Universe](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1664615)

### Killing fields give conserved matter currents

**Remember:** A Killing field’s derivative is antisymmetric, so symmetric stress kills it.

*True by definition.* MSC 83C40 (Gravitational energy and conservation laws; groups of motions), 53C50. arXiv gr-qc, math-ph. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Killing field X is a vector field whose flow preserves the metric. Equivalently, its dual covector has antisymmetric covariant derivative, ∇ₐXᵦ + ∇ᵦXₐ = 0.

**Problem.** Contracting a symmetric, divergence-free stress tensor with a Killing field gives a divergence-free current.

**How the definition helps.** The product rule for Jᵃ = TᵃᵇXᵦ gives one term containing the divergence of T, which vanishes by hypothesis (our own). The remaining contraction Tᵃᵇ∇ₐXᵦ vanishes because its factors are symmetric and antisymmetric in the same indices (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Killing vector field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killing_vector_field). It says: “we can construct the conserved quantity Jᵃ := TᵃᵇXᵦ satisfying”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Komar flux ignores intervening vacuum

**Remember:** With no Ricci curvature between surfaces, the same Komar flux crosses both.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 83C40 (Gravitational energy and conservation laws; groups of motions). arXiv gr-qc, math-ph. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In an oriented four-dimensional stationary spacetime, let α be the one-form dual to the stationary Killing field. The Komar flux through an oriented closed surface S is the integral over S of ⋆dα, up to normalization. This integrand is closed wherever the Ricci tensor vanishes (our own).

**Problem.** Suppose two closed surfaces together bound a compact oriented three-dimensional region in four-dimensional spacetime. If the Ricci tensor vanishes throughout the region, the same stationary symmetry gives equal Komar fluxes with consistent orientations.

**How the definition helps.** The Killing-field identity gives the exterior derivative of ⋆dα in terms of the Ricci tensor, so the flux form is closed in the vacuum region (our own). Stokes’ theorem then equates the difference of the two surface fluxes to an integral of zero (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Komar mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Komar_mass). It says: “This demonstrates that enclosing any amount of vacuum will not change our volume integral.”

**Sources:**

- [Arthur Komar (1959), Covariant Conservation Laws in General Relativity](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.113.934)

### Advanced time crosses the Schwarzschild horizon

**Remember:** Label inward light rays to keep time finite at the future horizon.

*True by definition.* MSC 83C57 (Black holes). arXiv gr-qc, astro-ph.HE. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Outside a Schwarzschild black hole of mass M &gt; 0, with G = c = 1, define advanced time v = t + r + 2M ln(r/(2M) − 1). It is constant along each ingoing radial light ray (our own), and it replaces t while the areal radius r and the angles stay.

**Problem.** The Schwarzschild metric, which specifies spacetime intervals outside the black hole, extends smoothly across its future horizon in advanced time. It remains invertible there.

**How the definition helps.** Substituting dv = dt + dr/(1 − 2M/r) gives the radial metric −(1 − 2M/r)dv² + 2dv dr (our own). Its coefficients are smooth at r = 2M and its determinant is −1 (our own). The angular metric there is a positive multiple of the round sphere metric (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Eddington–Finkelstein coordinates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddington%E2%80%93Finkelstein_coordinates). It says: “the metric is explicitly non-singular at the Schwarzschild radius”

**Sources:**

- [David Finkelstein, Past-Future Asymmetry of the Gravitational Field of a Point Particle (1958).](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.110.965)

### Event horizons can cross flat regions

**Remember:** To find the horizon, follow light all the way out.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 83C57 (Black holes), 83C75. arXiv gr-qc, math.DG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The event horizon of an asymptotically flat spacetime is the boundary of the black hole region. That region holds the events from which no future causal signal reaches future null infinity, where escaping light rays end. So the horizon depends on the whole future, not on the local geometry (our own).

**Problem.** Suppose a spherical thin shell collapses through its Schwarzschild radius with empty, flat spacetime inside. Part of the event horizon then lies in that flat interior.

**How the definition helps.** Because the horizon depends on eventual escape, events in a flat region can lie on it (our own). Trace the outgoing horizon ray backward from where it meets the shell at the Schwarzschild radius (our own). Before that meeting the ray runs inside the shell, where spacetime is flat (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Apparent horizon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apparent_horizon). It says: “Event horizons can, in principle, arise and evolve in exactly flat regions of spacetime”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Irreducible mass bounds extraction

**Remember:** Horizon area written as a mass: a floor that never drops.

*True by definition.* MSC 83C57 (Black holes). arXiv gr-qc, astro-ph.HE. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The irreducible mass of a Kerr black hole is its horizon area A written as a mass, √(A/(16π)) in units G = c = 1. The Kerr mass formula M² = Mᵢᵣᵣ² + J²/(4Mᵢᵣᵣ²) shows that the total mass M is never below it.

**Problem.** Suppose a Kerr black hole settles into another Kerr black hole in a process covered by the classical area theorem. Then the final total mass is at least the initial irreducible mass.

**How the definition helps.** The area theorem says horizon area never decreases, so the irreducible mass never decreases (our own). The Kerr mass formula then gives final mass ≥ final irreducible mass ≥ initial irreducible mass (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Kerr metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerr_metric). It says: “M² = Mᵢᵣᵣ² + J²c²/(4Mᵢᵣᵣ²G²).”

**Sources:**

- [Demetrios Christodoulou (1970), Reversible and Irreversible Transformations in Black-Hole Physics](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.25.1596)
- [J. M. Bardeen, B. Carter and S. W. Hawking (1973), The four laws of black hole mechanics](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01645742)

### Killing tensors conserve the Carter quantity

**Remember:** Feed it three equal velocities and its derivative vanishes.

*True by definition.* MSC 83C57 (Black holes), 83C40. arXiv gr-qc, math.DG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A rank-two Killing tensor is a symmetric tensor field K whose covariant derivative vanishes after symmetrizing over all three inputs. Equivalently, (∇ᵤK)(u,u) = 0 for every vector u (our own).

**Problem.** Along an affinely parametrized geodesic with velocity u, the value K(u,u) stays constant. In the rotating Kerr black hole, a special Killing tensor gives the Carter constant this way, up to combinations of known constants.

**How the definition helps.** Along the geodesic ∇ᵤu = 0, so the derivative of K(u,u) is (∇ᵤK)(u,u), which the definition makes zero (our own). For Kerr, the work is constructing the special Killing tensor (our own).

**nLab:** [Killing tensor](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Killing+tensor). It says: “For every Killing tensor K on (X,g) the dynamics of the relativistic particle on X has a further conserved quantity.”

**Wikipedia:** [Killing tensor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killing_tensor). It says: “Every Killing tensor corresponds to a constant of motion on geodesics.”

**Sources:**

- [Martin Walker and Roger Penrose (1970), On quadratic first integrals of the geodesic equations for type {22} spacetimes](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01649445)
- [Brandon Carter (1968), Global Structure of the Kerr Family of Gravitational Fields](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.174.1559)

### Kruskal coordinates remove the horizon singularity

**Remember:** Exponentiate the light coordinates and the horizon becomes an ordinary place.

*True by definition.* MSC 83C57 (Black holes), 83C15. arXiv gr-qc, math-ph. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Kruskal coordinates replace the Schwarzschild light coordinates t ∓ r\* by exponentials, U = −exp(−(t − r\*)/(4M)) and V = exp((t + r\*)/(4M)), where r\* = r + 2M ln(r/(2M) − 1), G = c = 1 and angles are unchanged. In them UV = (1 − r/(2M))exp(r/(2M)), and the dU dV coefficient −32M³exp(−r/(2M))/r stays smooth and nonzero at r = 2M (our own).

**Problem.** In units G = c = 1, the Schwarzschild metric extends smoothly across its horizon at r = 2M. This radius is not a curvature singularity.

**How the definition helps.** The metric coefficient that blew up at r = 2M becomes smooth and nonzero, so the metric extends across the horizon (our own). Since UV has nonzero derivative in r at r = 2M, r is a smooth function of UV there, and the sphere part r² dΩ² stays regular (our own).

**nLab:** [Kruskal–Szekeres coordinates](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Kruskal%E2%80%93Szekeres+coordinates). It says: “for maximaly extended Schwarzschild spacetime.”

**Wikipedia:** [Kruskal–Szekeres coordinates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kruskal%E2%80%93Szekeres_coordinates). It says: “Note that the metric is perfectly well defined and non-singular at the event horizon.”

**Sources:**

- [Martin Kruskal (1960), Maximal Extension of Schwarzschild Metric](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.119.1743)

### Radial potential locates photon spheres

**Remember:** Light circles at the potential's peak, so it falls off.

*True by definition.* MSC 83C57 (Black holes). arXiv gr-qc, astro-ph.HE. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Outside a Schwarzschild black hole of mass M, with G = c = 1, the radial potential of a light ray is V(r) = L²(1 − 2M/r)/r². Here L is the ray's angular momentum and r is the areal radius, with sphere area 4πr². The ray moves radially like a particle with (dr/dλ)² = E² − V(r), so circular orbits sit at stationary points of V (our own).

**Problem.** Outside a Schwarzschild black hole of mass M, circular light orbits have areal radius 3M. They are unstable under radial perturbations.

**How the definition helps.** A circular orbit needs V′(r) = 0, and for L ≠ 0 this holds outside the horizon only at r = 3M (our own). There V has a maximum, so a small radial push grows (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Schwarzschild geodesics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwarzschild_geodesics). It says: “the unstable orbit &lt;math&gt;r<sub>crit</sub> ={3\\over 2}r<sub>s</sub>&lt;/math&gt;.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Surface gravity detects affine flow

**Remember:** Surface gravity is how much the horizon's Killing flow accelerates along itself.

*True by definition.* MSC 83C57 (Black holes). arXiv gr-qc. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On a Killing horizon, a null surface to which a Killing field K is normal, the surface gravity κ is the factor in ∇ₖK = κK wherever K ≠ 0. It measures how far the flow parameter of K is from an affine one, which has zero covariant acceleration.

**Problem.** Along a horizon orbit where K ≠ 0, the flow parameter is affine exactly when κ vanishes along the orbit. At each such point, κ vanishes exactly when the gradient of the squared length g(K,K) vanishes.

**How the definition helps.** The first claim reads the definition directly: zero acceleration means ∇ₖK = 0 (our own). The Killing equation makes the gradient of g(K,K) equal to −2∇ₖK = −2κK, which gives the second claim. This is the full spacetime gradient, so it can be nonzero although g(K,K) = 0 on the horizon.

**Wikipedia:** [Surface gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_gravity). It says: “kᵃ ∇ₐ kᵇ = κ kᵇ implies −kᵃ ∇ᵇ kₐ = κ kᵇ”

**Sources:**

- [Bardeen, Carter, Hawking (1973), The four laws of black hole mechanics](https://doi.org/10.1007/bf01645742)

### Null frame coefficients detect geodesics

**Remember:** No sideways acceleration means a light ray follows a geodesic.

*True by definition.* MSC 83C60 (Spinor and twistor methods in general relativity and gravitational theory; Newman-Penrose formalism). arXiv gr-qc, math-ph. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Pick real null fields ℓ, n with g(ℓ,n) = −1 and orthonormal spacelike fields e₁, e₂ perpendicular to both, and set m = (e₁ + i e₂)/√2. The spin coefficient κ = −g(m, ∇ₗℓ) records the two sideways components of the acceleration ∇ₗℓ, in one sign convention (our own).

**Problem.** The curves tangent to ℓ can be reparametrized as geodesics exactly when κ vanishes along them.

**How the definition helps.** Since g(ℓ,ℓ) = 0, the acceleration ∇ₗℓ is perpendicular to ℓ, so it has no n part (our own). Thus κ = 0 exactly when the acceleration is a multiple of ℓ, the test for a reparametrization to be a geodesic (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Newman–Penrose formalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newman%E2%80%93Penrose_formalism). It says: “shows that ℓᵃ is tangent to a geodesic if and only if κ = 0”

**Sources:**

- [Newman, Penrose (1962), An Approach to Gravitational Radiation by a Method of Spin Coefficients](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1724257)

### Incomplete geodesics need not encounter curvature

**Remember:** A geodesic can just stop, with no curvature blowing up.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 83C75 (Space-time singularities, cosmic censorship, etc.), 53C50. arXiv gr-qc, math.DG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A spacetime is geodesically incomplete if some geodesic, a path with parallel velocity in an affine parameter, stops at a finite parameter value and cannot be continued. The definition asks only that a path end, not that curvature blow up.

**Problem.** Assume a spacetime has a noncompact Cauchy surface, a closed future trapped surface, and Ric(k,k) ≥ 0 for every lightlike k. Then Penrose's theorem gives a future light ray that ends at finite affine parameter, and this alone does not require any curvature to diverge.

**How the definition helps.** Incompleteness only asks for a ray that stops, so curvature may stay bounded. For example, delete one event from flat spacetime: a straight light ray toward it stops at finite parameter, yet curvature is zero (our own). Penrose's theorem does the separate work of deriving incompleteness from trapping.

**nLab:** [Penrose singularity theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Penrose+singularity+theorem). It says: “the singularity theorem makes statements about non-extendible curves but not explicitly about "singularities" in the sense of points of diverging curvature”

**Sources:**

- [Roger Penrose (1965), Gravitational Collapse and Space-Time Singularities](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.14.57)

### Null convergence bounds the distance to focusing

**Remember:** Converging light only converges faster, so it soon focuses.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 83C75 (Space-time singularities, cosmic censorship, etc.). arXiv gr-qc. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The expansion θ of a family of light rays in four dimensions is the rate of change of log cross-sectional area density along each ray, in an affine parameter. Null convergence asks Ric(k,k) ≥ 0 for every null k, and then for rays leaving a surface orthogonally, which have no rotation, the Raychaudhuri equation gives θ′ ≤ −θ²/2 (our own).

**Problem.** Light rays leave a spacelike two-surface orthogonally, and one ray starts with expansion θ₀ &lt; 0. Under null convergence, that ray reaches a focal point, where the area density vanishes, within affine length 2/\|θ₀\| if it extends that far.

**How the definition helps.** From θ′ ≤ −θ²/2 we get (1/θ)′ ≥ 1/2, so 1/θ climbs from −1/\|θ₀\| to 0 within affine length 2/\|θ₀\| (our own). Then θ tends to −∞, so the area density collapses there or earlier (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Raychaudhuri equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raychaudhuri_equation). It says: “As the expansion gives the rate of change of the logarithm of the area density”

**Sources:**

- [Raychaudhuri (1955), Relativistic Cosmology. I](https://doi.org/10.1103/physrev.98.1123)

### Conformal time measures light travel

**Remember:** Conformal time: light crosses one comoving unit per tick.

*True by definition.* MSC 83F05 (Relativistic cosmology), 53C50. arXiv gr-qc, math.DG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In a homogeneous, isotropic universe with scale factor a(t), conformal time η is defined by dη = dt/a(t), with light speed one. In a flat universe it makes the metric a²(−dη² + dx²), so time and fixed spatial coordinates carry the same factor (our own).

**Problem.** In a spatially flat homogeneous universe, a radial light ray travels one unit of fixed-coordinate distance per unit of conformal time. The particle horizon radius in those coordinates is the conformal time elapsed since the start of the model, if finite.

**How the definition helps.** For a radial light ray ds = 0, so \|dx/dη\| = 1 (our own). Integrating from the start gives the particle horizon radius as the elapsed conformal time, when it is finite (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Cosmological horizon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmological_horizon). It says: “the particle horizon is equal to the conformal time that has passed since the Big Bang, times the speed of light.”

**Paper or page:** [Bonnet-Myers rigidity theorem for globally hyperbolic Lorentzian length spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.17017v3). It says: “γ(t) = (t, ± ∫ₜ₀ᵗ 1/f(λ) dλ)”

**Sources:**

- [Bonnet-Myers rigidity theorem for globally hyperbolic Lorentzian length spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.17017v3)

### Bondi news controls energy loss

**Remember:** Energy leaves at the rate of the news squared.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 83C30 (Asymptotic procedures (radiation, news functions, H -spaces, etc.) in general relativity and gravitational theory), 83C40. arXiv gr-qc, math-ph. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Near outgoing light infinity in Bondi coordinates, write the angular metric as r²q + rC + O(1), with q the unit sphere metric and C the trace-free shear. The Bondi news N = ∂ᵤC is the rate of change of that shear in retarded time u, and Bondi energy is the sphere average of the Bondi mass aspect (our own).

**Problem.** In four-dimensional vacuum general relativity with a smooth asymptotically flat Bondi expansion, Bondi energy never increases with retarded time. It has zero instantaneous loss exactly when the news vanishes in every direction.

**How the definition helps.** The vacuum Bondi mass-loss law makes the energy derivative a negative constant times the sphere integral of \|N\|², because the angular divergence term integrates to zero (our own). A continuous nonnegative integrand has zero integral exactly when it vanishes everywhere (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Masses at null infinity for Einstein's equations in harmonic coordinates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.01487v2). It says: “They satisfy the Bondi mass loss law”

**Sources:**

- [H. Bondi, M. G. J. van der Burg, and A. W. K. Metzner (1962), Gravitational waves in general relativity, VII. Waves from axi-symmetric isolated system](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1962.0161)
- [R. K. Sachs (1962), Gravitational waves in general relativity VIII. Waves in asymptotically flat space-time](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1962.0206)

### Bulk symmetries act conformally at infinity

**Remember:** A bulk symmetry preserves the boundary metric up to scale.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 83C30 (Asymptotic procedures (radiation, news functions, H -spaces, etc.) in general relativity and gravitational theory). arXiv gr-qc. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A smooth conformal compactification adds a boundary on which the rescaled metric h = Ω²g extends smoothly and nondegenerately, where Ω &gt; 0 inside, Ω = 0 on the boundary and dΩ ≠ 0 there. The boundary keeps only a conformal metric, the induced metric up to smooth positive rescaling.

**Problem.** Take a smooth conformal compactification with timelike boundary, whose induced metric has one negative direction. Any interior Killing field that extends smoothly to the boundary generates local maps that preserve the boundary metric up to positive rescaling.

**How the definition helps.** A Killing field preserves g, so it changes h = Ω²g only by a factor: ℒₖh = 2(KΩ/Ω)h (our own). Taking the h-trace shows KΩ/Ω is smooth up to the boundary, so KΩ = 0 there and K is tangent to it (our own). Restricted to the boundary, the identity says the flow changes the induced metric only by scale (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Geometric reflective boundary conditions for asymptotically Anti-de Sitter spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.20661). It says: “then it is tangent to ℐ”

**Sources:**

- [Geometric reflective boundary conditions for asymptotically Anti-de Sitter spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.20661)

### Cotton curvature supplies boundary stress

**Remember:** Cotton–York curvature is built to obey the boundary constraints.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 83C30 (Asymptotic procedures (radiation, news functions, H -spaces, etc.) in general relativity and gravitational theory). arXiv gr-qc. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On an oriented three-dimensional Lorentzian manifold, the Cotton–York tensor is the curl of Ric − (R/4)h: take its covariant derivative and contract the derivative index and first index with the volume form. It measures how curvature varies, and it is symmetric, trace-free and divergence-free for every metric h.

**Problem.** On a three-dimensional conformal boundary, whose metric h is fixed only up to a positive factor, take a constant multiple of the Cotton–York tensor as stress data. It is trace-free and divergence-free for each h, and changing h to Ω²h multiplies it by Ω⁻¹, as boundary stress data require.

**How the definition helps.** Because the identities hold for every metric, the curvature-built tensor meets the stress constraints for all representatives at once (our own). Its rescaling law is the one required of boundary stress, so the choice is consistent across the conformal class. The work lies in proving those curvature identities (our own assessment).

**Paper or page:** [Geometric reflective boundary conditions for asymptotically Anti-de Sitter spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.20661), [Geometric reflective boundary conditions for asymptotically Anti-de Sitter spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.20661). It says: “is symmetric, trace-free with respect to the metric h and divergence-free for the Levi-Civita connection D of h.”

**Sources:**

- [Geometric reflective boundary conditions for asymptotically Anti-de Sitter spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.20661)

### Dominant energy bounds total momentum

**Remember:** Keep local energy large enough to pay for local momentum.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 83C40 (Gravitational energy and conservation laws; groups of motions). arXiv gr-qc. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Initial data, a spatial metric with its bending in spacetime, give an energy density μ and a momentum density J through the constraint equations. The dominant energy condition requires μ ≥ \|J\| everywhere, so local energy always covers local momentum.

**Problem.** Take smooth complete three-dimensional initial data without boundary, with integrable μ and J satisfying the dominant energy condition. If the metric error decays as 1/r and the bending as 1/r², each derivative gaining one inverse power through orders two and one, then total energy E is at least total momentum \|P\|.

**How the definition helps.** The condition removes negative-mass examples such as zero bending with metric (1 − a/√(1+r²))⁴ times the Euclidean metric, 0 &lt; a &lt; 1 (our own). This metric is complete with energy −2a and zero momentum, but its scalar curvature is negative, so μ &lt; 0 breaks the bound (our own). The spacetime positive mass theorem supplies the global estimate.

**Paper or page:** [The case of equality for the spacetime positive mass theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.01984v3). It says: “Suppose (M,g,k) is a complete asymptotically flat initial data set satisfying the dominant energy condition (DEC) μ ≥ \|J\|. Then E ≥ \|P\|.”

**Sources:**

- [Sven Hirsch and Yiyue Zhang, The case of equality for the spacetime positive mass theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.01984v3)

### Nearly round spheres recover total mass

**Remember:** Escaping spheres must even out their bending faster than 1/r.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 83C40 (Gravitational energy and conservation laws; groups of motions), 53C21. arXiv gr-qc, math.DG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Nearly round spheres are surrounding spheres whose size is comparable to r, the least distance to a fixed point, and whose bending becomes equal in all directions faster than 1/r. Precisely, max distance ≤ Cr, intrinsic diameter ≤ Cr, area ≤ Cr², and the trace-free shape operator B obeys r¹⁺ᵗ sup\|B\| + r²⁺ᵗ sup\|∇B\| ≤ C, for the end's decay exponent t and one constant C.

**Problem.** Assume a three-dimensional end approaches Euclidean space with two derivatives at decay rate t &gt; ½ and has integrable scalar curvature. Along nearly round spheres escaping to infinity, the Hawking mass calculated from area and mean curvature tends to the total mass at infinity.

**How the definition helps.** The bound on B makes the error in the Hawking mass vanish as the spheres grow (our own). Without it, dilated copies of a fixed nonspherical Euclidean ellipsoid keep ∫H² a fixed amount above 16π by Gauss–Bonnet, so their Hawking mass tends to −∞ although Euclidean space has zero total mass (our own). The nearly round surface convergence theorem identifies the limit with total mass.

**nLab:** [ADM mass](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/ADM+mass). It says: “a notion of total mass contained in asymptotically flat spacetimes.”

**Paper or page:** [On the behavior of quasi-local mass at the infinity along nearly round surfaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/0806.0678v1). It says: “\\lim<sub>r\\rightarrow \\infty </sub>m<sub>H</sub>(\\Sigma r)=m{ADM}(M).”

**Sources:**

- [Yuguang Shi, Guofang Wang, and Jie Wu (2009), On the behavior of quasi-local mass at the infinity along nearly round surfaces](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10455-009-9169-5)

### Rescaling makes horizon inversion isometric

**Remember:** Divide by radius squared to turn horizon inversion into an isometry.

*True by definition.* MSC 83C57 (Black holes). arXiv gr-qc. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In the extremal Reissner–Nordström exterior with mass M &gt; 0 and areal radius r &gt; M, in geometric units, inversion replaces r − M by M²/(r − M) and keeps time and angles. It multiplies the metric g by the square of new radius over old radius, so the rescaled metric g/r² is the natural one to compare (our own).

**Problem.** The inversion preserves the rescaled metric. On the extended exterior it exchanges the future horizon with the boundary reached by outgoing light, and similarly for the past.

**How the definition helps.** Dividing by r² cancels exactly the factor that inversion puts on g (our own). Since inversion sends r − M → 0 to r − M → ∞, it swaps the horizon with the region reached by outgoing light (our own). A separate boundary argument identifies where incoming and outgoing rays end.

**Paper or page:** [Peeling at extreme black hole horizons](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.14574v1). It says: “It fixes the photon sphere and exchanges the future event horizon ℋ⁺ and the future null infinity ℐ⁺”

**Sources:**

- [Jack Borthwick, Eric Gourgoulhon and Jean-Philippe Nicolas, Peeling at extreme black hole horizons](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.14574v1)

### A quadratic test detects type D

**Remember:** Type D means W solves (W − λ)(W + 2λ) = 0.

*True by definition.* MSC 83C60 (Spinor and twistor methods in general relativity and gravitational theory; Newman-Penrose formalism). arXiv gr-qc, math-ph. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** At a point of an oriented four-dimensional spacetime, let W be the trace-free part of curvature acting on the three-dimensional complex space of self-dual two-forms, those the Hodge star sends to i times themselves. Petrov type D means W is diagonalizable with eigenvalues λ, λ and −2λ for some λ ≠ 0, so (W − λI)(W + 2λI) = 0.

**Problem.** Suppose tr(W²) ≠ 0 and set λ = −tr(W³)/tr(W²). The curvature has Petrov type D exactly when W² + λW − 2λ²I = 0, where I is the identity.

**How the definition helps.** For type D, tr(W²) = 6λ² and tr(W³) = −6λ³ recover λ, and the identity is the factored quadratic (our own). Conversely, λ = 0 would make the identity W² = 0, against tr(W²) ≠ 0 (our own). The distinct roots λ and −2λ then give diagonalizability, and zero trace in dimension three forces multiplicities two and one (our own).

**Paper or page:** [An ideal conformally covariant characterization of the Kerr conformal structure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.04783). It says: “is of “genuine” Petrov type D (Petrov type D, but not any of its specializations) if and only if\\begin{equation}  \\tilde{a}\\neq 0\\; ,\\quad \\tilde{\\mathcal{D}}<sub>abcd</sub>=0\\; ,  \\end{equation}”

**Sources:**

- [An ideal conformally covariant characterization of the Kerr conformal structure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.04783)

### Curvature blocks twice differentiable extensions

**Remember:** Curvature can diverge where first derivatives still extend continuously.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 83C75 (Space-time singularities, cosmic censorship, etc.). arXiv gr-qc. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A C² extension identifies a spacetime with a proper open subset of a larger spacetime, keeping its metric, where the metric has continuous second derivatives in smooth coordinates. Then curvature is continuous in every smooth frame, while a C¹ extension, with only continuous first derivatives, allows curvature to blow up.

**Problem.** Each interior Lorentzian Hawking–Page metric in the cited family extends across its specified lightlike boundary with continuous first derivatives. No extension across that boundary has continuous second derivatives.

**How the definition helps.** A C² metric has continuous curvature in every smooth local frame, so curvature that blows up at the boundary rules out any C² extension (our own explanation). The cited paper proves that the sectional curvature blows up along the boundary for every extension. Constructing the C¹ extension and proving that blow-up are the substantive results.

**Paper or page:** [Extensions of Lorentzian Hawking--Page Solutions with Null Singularities, Spacelike Singularities, and Cauchy horizons of Taub--NUT type](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.06134), [Extensions of Lorentzian Hawking--Page Solutions with Null Singularities, Spacelike Singularities, and Cauchy horizons of Taub--NUT type](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.06134). It says: “For any extension of the Lorentzian Hawking–Page vacuum solution, the sectional curvature blows up along C₀⁻.”

**Sources:**

- [Extensions of Lorentzian Hawking--Page Solutions with Null Singularities, Spacelike Singularities, and Cauchy horizons of Taub--NUT type](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.06134)

### Strict trapping rules out flat cylinders

**Remember:** Strictly shrinking light fronts must focus; merely parallel ones need not.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 83C75 (Space-time singularities, cosmic censorship, etc.), 83C57. arXiv gr-qc, math.DG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In a spacelike Cauchy slice, take a smooth compact separating surface without boundary with a chosen outer side. It is outer trapped if its outgoing orthogonal light rays start with strictly shrinking area, that is, future outward null expansion θ⁺ &lt; 0 everywhere.

**Problem.** Assume a spacetime has a spacelike Cauchy surface and Ric(k,k) ≥ 0 for every lightlike k. If a connected outer trapped surface separates the slice and its outer side has noncompact closure, then some future light ray ends at finite affine parameter.

**How the definition helps.** Strict negativity excludes surfaces whose outgoing rays keep constant area (our own). An example is a fixed-time torus in flat spacetime with two directions made periodic: its expansion is zero and every ray extends forever (our own). The outer trapped surface singularity theorem turns strict focusing and the noncompact outside into null incompleteness.

**Paper or page:** [Rigidity aspects of Penrose's singularity theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.11315v3). It says: “outer trapped (i.e., θ⁺ &lt; 0)”

**Sources:**

- [Rigidity aspects of Penrose's singularity theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.11315v3)

## 85 Astronomy and astrophysics

### Distance modulus adds to magnitude

**Remember:** Logarithms turn inverse-square dimming into an added distance term.

*True by definition.* MSC 85A04 (General questions in astronomy and astrophysics). arXiv astro-ph.SR, astro-ph.GA. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** Luminosity distance D is the distance at which inverse-square dilution turns bolometric luminosity L into the observed flux F, so F = L/(4πD²). The distance modulus 5 log₁₀(D/(10 parsecs)) is the magnitude change from moving the source from 10 parsecs, where absolute magnitude is defined, out to D.

**Problem.** Sum the light over all wavelengths and assume transparent propagation. Apparent magnitude equals absolute magnitude plus the distance modulus.

**How the definition helps.** Magnitude is −2.5 log₁₀ of flux, and the flux falls by (D/(10 parsecs))² from 10 parsecs to D (our own). So the logarithm turns this dilution into the added term 5 log₁₀(D/(10 parsecs)) (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Distance modulus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distance_modulus). It says: “the observed brightness of a light source is related to its distance by the inverse square law”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.
