### Redshift factors multiply

**Remember:** Consecutive wavelength ratios multiply along a light path.

*True by definition.* MSC 85A40 (Astrophysical cosmology). arXiv astro-ph.CO. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** The redshift factor 1 + z is the received wavelength divided by the emitted wavelength, a ratio used instead of the fractional change z.

**Problem.** Along one light path, the total redshift factor equals the product of the factors on consecutive parts, when the same observer measures at each shared endpoint.

**How the definition helps.** Ratios multiply because the wavelength at each shared endpoint appears once above and once below and cancels (our own). Predicting each ratio from motion or cosmic expansion needs a separate physical calculation.

**Wikipedia:** [Redshift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redshift). It says: “corresponding to the fractional change in wavelength (positive for redshifts, negative for blueshifts), and by the wavelength ratio 1 + z”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Flat spectra have zero AB color

**Remember:** A flat flux density has the same AB magnitude in every filter.

*True by definition.* MSC 85A04 (General questions in astronomy and astrophysics). arXiv astro-ph.SR, astro-ph.GA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The AB magnitude in a filter is −2.5 log₁₀(F/F₀), where F &gt; 0 is the average flux density per unit frequency weighted by the normalized filter response. The reference F₀, about 3631 janskys, is the same for every filter (our own), and an AB color is the difference of two AB magnitudes.

**Problem.** A source with positive constant flux density per unit frequency has zero AB color between any two properly calibrated filters.

**How the definition helps.** A normalized average of a constant is that constant, so a flat source has the same F, and so the same AB magnitude, in every filter (our own). Their difference is zero. A reference star with a varying spectrum would instead give a different zero point in each filter.

**Wikipedia:** [AB magnitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AB_magnitude). It says: “The bandpass AB magnitude is defined so that the zero point corresponds to a bandpass-averaged spectral flux density”

**Sources:**

- [J. B. Oke and J. E. Gunn (1983), Secondary standard stars for absolute spectrophotometry](https://doi.org/10.1086/160817)

### Orbit constants give stellar equilibria

**Remember:** A function of orbit constants stays constant as stars move.

*True by definition.* MSC 85A05 (Galactic and stellar dynamics). arXiv astro-ph.GA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Write the distribution of stars in position and velocity as a function of orbit constants such as energy, quantities that keep the same value all along each star's orbit.

**Problem.** In a time-independent gravitational field, every smooth function of time-independent orbit constants solves the steady collisionless Boltzmann equation. This equation says the distribution stays constant along each star's orbit when encounters are negligible.

**How the definition helps.** Each orbit constant is unchanged along an orbit, so by the chain rule any function of them is too (our own). The work lies in finding the orbit constants, and if the stars make the field, their density must also reproduce it.

**Wikipedia:** [Jeans's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeans%27s_theorem). It says: “any function of the integrals is a steady-state solution”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Squared buoyancy frequency flags instability

**Remember:** Positive squared buoyancy frequency restores a displaced parcel.

*True by definition.* MSC 85A15 (Galactic and stellar structure). arXiv astro-ph.SR. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Move a small parcel of stellar gas vertically without heat exchange. The squared buoyancy frequency N² is the restoring acceleration per unit displacement at equilibrium, minus the derivative of buoyancy acceleration with respect to displacement. It keeps its sign, so N² &lt; 0 means buoyancy pushes the parcel further away.

**Problem.** With constant local coefficients, the linearized displacement oscillates if N² is positive. It has an exponentially growing mode if N² is negative.

**How the definition helps.** The linearized displacement obeys x″ = −N²x, which oscillates for N² &gt; 0 and grows like exp(√(−N²) t) for N² &lt; 0 (our own). The physical work compares the parcel's density after displacement with the surrounding density.

**Wikipedia:** [Brunt–Väisälä frequency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunt%E2%80%93V%C3%A4is%C3%A4l%C3%A4_frequency). It says: “If a gas parcel is pushed up and N² &gt; 0, the air parcel will move up and down”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Eddington ratios compare accelerations

**Remember:** The same luminosity ratio compares outward radiation and inward gravity.

*True by definition.* MSC 85A25 (Radiative transfer in astronomy and astrophysics). arXiv astro-ph.SR, astro-ph.HE. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a spherical source of mass M, the Eddington luminosity 4πGMc/κ is the radiated power at which light's outward push on gas balances gravity. Here κ is the opacity, the effective area per unit mass that light pushes on, and both push and pull fall as 1/r².

**Problem.** Outside a spherical source, use Newtonian gravity and assume constant luminosity and opacity. The ratio of radiation acceleration to gravity equals the ratio of luminosity to Eddington luminosity.

**How the definition helps.** Radiation acceleration κL/(4πr²c) divided by gravity GM/r² equals L divided by 4πGMc/κ, since the r² cancels (our own). The physical work establishes these two acceleration laws for the gas.

**Wikipedia:** [Eddington luminosity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddington_luminosity). It says: “The limit is obtained by setting the outward radiation pressure equal to the inward gravitational force.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Optical depths add along rays

**Remember:** Transmission multiplies, so optical depth adds.

*True by definition.* MSC 85A25 (Radiative transfer in astronomy and astrophysics). arXiv astro-ph.SR. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Optical depth is minus the natural logarithm of transmission, the fraction of a beam's intensity at one wavelength that survives a region, for positive transmission. The logarithm turns multiplied fractions into added depths (our own).

**Problem.** If successive regions only remove light from this beam, their optical depths add.

**How the definition helps.** When regions only remove light, the beam leaving one region is the input to the next, so transmissions multiply and their logarithms add (our own). With loss proportional to intensity, the optical depth is the integral of the local loss coefficient (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Optical depth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optical_depth). It says: “the transmitted flux decays exponentially with optical depth”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Comoving distances stay fixed

**Remember:** Divide out the stretch of space, and comoving galaxies stand still.

*True by definition.* MSC 85A40 (Astrophysical cosmology). arXiv astro-ph.CO. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Comoving distance is proper distance on a constant cosmic time slice divided by the scale factor, the common factor by which expansion stretches every length.

**Problem.** Suppose space looks the same at every point and in every direction at each cosmic time. Two observers following the common expansion stay at constant comoving distance.

**How the definition helps.** When space looks the same everywhere and in every direction, the spatial metric is a fixed metric times the square of the scale factor (our own). So the proper distance between observers following the expansion is the scale factor times a constant, and dividing leaves the constant (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Comoving and proper distances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comoving_and_proper_distances). It says: “Comoving distance factors out the expansion of the universe, giving a distance that does not change in time except due to local factors”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Lens Jacobians give signed magnification

**Remember:** The determinant gives the area change and tells whether orientation flips.

*True by definition.* MSC 85A40 (Astrophysical cosmology). arXiv astro-ph.CO. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A thin lens treats deflection as happening in one plane, and its lens map sends each observed image direction to the source direction without deflection. Signed magnification is the local ratio of image to source angular area, negative when orientation reverses, so it is the area factor of the inverse lens map.

**Problem.** Where the derivative of the lens map is invertible, signed magnification equals the reciprocal of its determinant in local angular area coordinates.

**How the definition helps.** The determinant of a derivative is its signed area factor, and the inverse derivative has reciprocal determinant (our own). Relating the absolute value to a flux ratio also needs conservation of surface brightness, the flux per unit solid angle.

**Wikipedia:** [Gravitational lensing formalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitational_lensing_formalism). It says: “The amplification is the inverse of the Jacobian”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Toomre’s ratio detects disk instability

**Remember:** Pressure and rotation must beat self-gravity: Q at least one.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 85A05 (Galactic and stellar dynamics). arXiv astro-ph.GA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a thin rotating gas disk, Toomre's ratio Q = cₛκ/(πGΣ) weighs the stabilizing effects of pressure and rotation against self-gravity. Here cₛ is sound speed, κ is the frequency of small radial oscillations about a circular orbit, and Σ is mass per unit area.

**Problem.** Consider small local disturbances that are the same at every angle around the disk. For positive κ, cₛ, and Σ, no radial wavelength grows exponentially exactly when Q ≥ 1.

**How the definition helps.** Waves with radial wave number k have squared frequency κ² − 2πGΣ\|k\| + cₛ²k² (our own). Its minimum over k is κ²(1 − 1/Q²), which is nonnegative exactly when Q ≥ 1 (our own). Deriving the wave equation from gas dynamics is the physical work.

**Wikipedia:** [Toomre's stability criterion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toomre%27s_stability_criterion). It says: “The stability criterion can then simply be stated as, Q ≥ 1 for a disk to be stable against collapse.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Interior mass matches exterior mass

**Remember:** Define the interior mass through the same metric coefficient as outside.

*True by definition.* MSC 85A15 (Galactic and stellar structure). arXiv astro-ph.SR, gr-qc. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a static spherical star with areal radius r, so that spheres have area 4πr², and G = c = 1, define the enclosed mass m(r) by writing the radial metric term as (dr)²/(1 − 2m(r)/r). This is the same form as the exterior Schwarzschild term (dr)²/(1 − 2M/r).

**Problem.** Match the stellar surface at radius R smoothly to the spherical vacuum solution without a surface layer. The mass inferred from the exterior gravitational field equals m(R).

**How the definition helps.** At the surface R, continuity of the metric equates 1/(1 − 2m(R)/R) with 1/(1 − 2M/R), so M = m(R) (our own). Computing the interior geometry and establishing the match still require the field equations.

**Wikipedia:** [Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tolman%E2%80%93Oppenheimer%E2%80%93Volkoff_equation). It says: “continuity of the metric and the definition of m(r) require that”

**Sources:**

- [J. R. Oppenheimer and G. M. Volkoff (1939), On Massive Neutron Cores](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.55.374)

### Polytropic stars share a scaled profile

**Remember:** Scale the center to one and let the pressure-law index set the shape.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 85A15 (Galactic and stellar structure). arXiv astro-ph.SR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a Newtonian polytrope P = Kρ⁽¹⁺¹⁄ⁿ⁾ with K, n &gt; 0 and central density d &gt; 0, measure density by θ = (ρ/d)¹⁄ⁿ and radius by ξ = r/a, where a &gt; 0 and a² = (n + 1)K d⁽¹⁄ⁿ⁻¹⁾/(4πG). This length unit removes K and d from the star's equation, leaving only n (our own).

**Problem.** In Newtonian gravity, these stars share one scaled density profile for each index n. For 0 &lt; n &lt; 5, the first zero of θ gives the radius in the chosen units.

**How the definition helps.** In these units, pressure balance and Newtonian gravity give the Lane–Emden equation for θ(ξ), which involves only n (our own). Regularity at the center gives θ(0) = 1 and θ′(0) = 0, so all stars of one index share one solution. The remaining work proves this solution is unique and, for n below five, has a first zero (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Lane–Emden equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lane%E2%80%93Emden_equation). It says: “The standard boundary conditions are θ(0) = 1 and θ′(0) = 0.”

**Sources:**

- [Jonathan Homer Lane, On the theoretical temperature of the Sun, under the hypothesis of a gaseous mass maintaining its volume by its internal heat, and depending on the laws of gases as known to terrestrial experiment (1870).](https://doi.org/10.2475/ajs.s2-50.148.57)

### Rosseland averaging preserves diffusive flux

**Remember:** Average transparency, not opacity, weighted by the Planck spectrum's temperature slope.

*True by definition.* MSC 85A25 (Radiative transfer in astronomy and astrophysics). arXiv astro-ph.SR, astro-ph.HE. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** At temperature T &gt; 0, the Rosseland mean opacity is the reciprocal of the weighted average of 1/κν, weighting each frequency ν by w = ∂Bν(T)/∂T, where Bν is the Planck spectrum. For positive κν and finite integrals, it is ∫w dν divided by ∫(w/κν) dν over positive frequencies.

**Problem.** Suppose photons travel only short distances between interactions and radiation is nearly in thermal equilibrium with nearby matter. In the diffusion approximation, the Rosseland mean gives the same total energy flux as the frequency-dependent law.

**How the definition helps.** In the diffusion approximation, frequency ν carries flux proportional to (w/κν) times the temperature gradient, so the total flux depends only on ∫(w/κν) dν (our own). The Rosseland mean is defined to give that same integral. The underlying transport equation supplies this diffusion law.

**Wikipedia:** [Opacity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opacity). It says: “The Rosseland opacity is derived in the diffusion approximation to the radiative transport equation.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Sky power depends on degree

**Remember:** Rotations shuffle each degree's modes, so they share one power.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 85A35 (Statistical astronomy), 85A40. arXiv astro-ph.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Expand a square-integrable random sky in orthonormal spherical harmonics, with coefficient aℓₘ for degree ℓ and order m. The angular power spectrum Cℓ = ∑ₘ 𝔼\[\|aℓₘ\|²\]/(2ℓ + 1), summing m from −ℓ through ℓ, is the average power of the 2ℓ + 1 modes of degree ℓ (our own).

**Problem.** For a rotationally invariant random sky with zero mean and finite variance, harmonic coefficients are uncorrelated across distinct modes. Their variance depends only on degree.

**How the definition helps.** Rotations mix modes only within each degree, and by Schur's lemma a rotation-invariant covariance is a scalar on each degree with no terms between degrees (our own). That scalar is Cℓ.

**Paper or page:** [Geometric Methods for Spherical Data, with Applications to Cosmology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.15278v1). It says: “there exists a family of orthogonal random coefficients”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Conformal time gives constant grid speed

**Remember:** Light crosses equal grid distances in equal conformal ticks.

*True by definition.* MSC 85A40 (Astrophysical cosmology). arXiv astro-ph.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Conformal time divides each tick of cosmic time by the current scale factor, and comoving coordinates divide expansion out of the spatial grid. Clocks and rulers then carry the same factor, so light's grid speed is constant (our own).

**Problem.** In a flat expanding universe that looks the same everywhere and in every direction, radial light crosses the comoving grid at constant speed c in conformal time. So the comoving particle horizon, the greatest distance light could have covered since the Big Bang, is c times the elapsed conformal time when finite.

**How the definition helps.** Light has ds = 0, and the metric a²(−c²dη² + dx²) then gives \|dx/dη\| = c (our own). Integrating gives the horizon distance (our own). The work lies in integrating the expansion history to find the elapsed conformal time (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Particle horizon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particle_horizon). It says: “the particle horizon is equal to the conformal time η that has passed since the Big Bang, times the speed of light c.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Critical density normalizes flatness

**Remember:** Measure density in critical units and flat space has density one.

*True by definition.* MSC 85A40 (Astrophysical cosmology). arXiv astro-ph.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** With Hubble rate H and light speed one, the critical density 3H²/(8πG) is the density at which the first Friedmann equation leaves no room for spatial curvature (our own). The density parameter Ω is total energy density, vacuum energy included, divided by critical density.

**Problem.** In a universe with uniform, direction-independent expansion governed by the Friedmann equations, assume H is nonzero. Spatial curvature vanishes exactly when Ω equals one.

**How the definition helps.** Dividing the first Friedmann equation by H² gives Ω = 1 + k/(a²H²), so Ω = 1 exactly when the curvature k is zero (our own). In ordinary density units the value giving flat space changes with the Hubble rate (our own).

**nLab:** [FRW model](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/FRW+model). It says: “Ω ≔ Ω<sub>R</sub> + Ω<sub>M</sub> + Ω\_Λ = 1 + k/(a²H²)”

**Sources:**

- [Alexander Friedmann, Über die Krümmung des Raumes (1922).](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01332580)

### Distance duality gives brightness dimming

**Remember:** Use one distance for flux and another for apparent area.

*True by definition.* MSC 85A40 (Astrophysical cosmology). arXiv astro-ph.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Luminosity distance Dₗ explains observed flux by inverse-square dilution of emitted power. Angular diameter distance Dₐ explains observed angular size: it is the square root of projected source area divided by observed solid angle.

**Problem.** Suppose photons follow light rays of the spacetime metric and their number is conserved. Then observed surface brightness summed over all frequencies equals emitted surface brightness divided by (1 + z)⁴, where 1 + z is received over emitted wavelength.

**How the definition helps.** For a small source patch, the two definitions make observed flux per solid angle equal emitted brightness times (Dₐ/Dₗ)² (our own). Etherington reciprocity with photon conservation gives Dₗ = (1 + z)²Dₐ, hence the factor (1 + z)⁻⁴ (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Etherington's reciprocity theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etherington%27s_reciprocity_theorem). It says: “The Etherington distance-duality equation is the relationship between the luminosity distance of standard candles and the angular diameter distance.”

**Sources:**

- [I. M. H. Etherington (1933), On the definition of distance in general relativity](https://doi.org/10.1080/14786443309462220)

### Redshift preserves blackbody spectra

**Remember:** A Planck spectrum keeps its shape when frequency and temperature fall together.

*True by definition.* MSC 85A40 (Astrophysical cosmology), 85A25. arXiv astro-ph.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Describe thermal radiation by the mean number of photons in a state of frequency ν, 1/(exp(hν/(kT)) − 1) at temperature T, with h and k Planck's and Boltzmann's constants. This number depends on ν and T only through ν/T.

**Problem.** Suppose thermal radiation travels freely through a uniformly expanding universe. If expansion divides every photon frequency by 1 + z, the radiation remains thermal with temperature divided by 1 + z.

**How the definition helps.** Free propagation keeps each photon's occupation number while dividing its frequency by 1 + z (our own). So the occupation at ν is the old value at (1 + z)ν, which is thermal with temperature T/(1 + z) (our own). Proving occupation conservation and the common frequency shift is the physical work.

**Wikipedia:** [Cosmic microwave background](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_microwave_background). It says: “expansion of the universe would cool blackbody radiation while maintaining a thermal spectrum.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Reduced shear hides a mass sheet

**Remember:** Rescale both parts of the shear ratio and its value stays put.

*True by definition.* MSC 85A40 (Astrophysical cosmology). arXiv astro-ph.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a gravitational lens, convergence κ measures local focusing and shear γ measures directional stretching of images. Reduced shear γ/(1 − κ), for κ ≠ 1, is the part of the distortion that image shapes reveal (our own).

**Problem.** For one thin lens and sources at a fixed distance, multiply the lens mass distribution by λ &gt; 0 and add a uniform sheet of convergence 1 − λ. This preserves reduced shear, so image shapes alone cannot distinguish the two models.

**How the definition helps.** Scaling the mass by λ multiplies γ by λ, and the uniform sheet adds no shear (our own). The new convergence is λκ + 1 − λ, so 1 − κ also gains the factor λ, which cancels in the ratio (our own). An independent magnification measurement can break the ambiguity.

**Wikipedia:** [Gravitational lensing formalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitational_lensing_formalism). It says: “this degeneracy can be broken if an independent measurement of the magnification is available”

**Sources:**

- [E. E. Falco, M. V. Gorenstein and I. I. Shapiro, On model-dependent bounds on H(0) from gravitational images: Application of Q0957 + 561A,B (1985).](https://doi.org/10.1086/184422)

## 86 Geophysics

### Buoyancy sign predicts oscillation

**Remember:** N² is buoyancy's restoring pull per unit of lift.

*True by definition.* MSC 86A10 (Meteorology and atmospheric physics), 86A05. arXiv physics.ao-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** In a resting fluid with density ρ(z) at height z, N² = −gρ′(z)/ρ₀ is the buoyant restoring acceleration per unit height on a parcel that is lifted while keeping its density (our own). Here g is gravitational acceleration and ρ₀ is a constant positive reference density for inertia.

**Problem.** For small vertical parcel displacements in this model, N² &gt; 0 gives oscillations. If N² &lt; 0, the linear equation has an exponentially growing solution.

**How the definition helps.** A parcel lifted by x keeps its density, so it differs from its surroundings by −ρ′x and accelerates by x″ = −N²x (our own). This equation oscillates for N² &gt; 0 and has an exponentially growing solution for N² &lt; 0 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Brunt–Väisälä frequency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunt%E2%80%93V%C3%A4is%C3%A4l%C3%A4_frequency). It says: “the displacement z′ has oscillating solutions (and N gives our angular frequency).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Geopotential height absorbs varying gravity

**Remember:** Measure altitude by lifting work so gravity drops out of the conversion.

*True by definition.* MSC 86A10 (Meteorology and atmospheric physics). arXiv physics.geo-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Geopotential height is the work per unit mass needed to lift air against gravity from a reference level, divided by a fixed standard gravity. Each step of it is the geometric step times local gravity over standard gravity (our own).

**Problem.** Suppose the vertical pressure force balances gravity at every height, a condition called hydrostatic balance. The derivative of pressure with respect to geopotential height then equals minus density times standard gravity, even when local gravity varies.

**How the definition helps.** Hydrostatic balance gives dp = −ρg dz, and each geopotential height step is (g/g₀) dz, so local gravity cancels and dp/dZ = −ρg₀ (our own). Recovering geometric height still requires the local gravity field (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Geopotential height](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geopotential_height). It says: “the simplification obtained by assuming a constant value of gravitational acceleration is the sole reason for defining the geopotential altitude.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Potential temperature survives adiabatic motion

**Remember:** Compare air parcels after bringing them to the same pressure without heating.

*True by definition.* MSC 86A10 (Meteorology and atmospheric physics). arXiv physics.geo-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Potential temperature is the temperature an air parcel would have if brought to a fixed reference pressure reversibly, with no heat exchange.

**Problem.** A dry ideal-gas parcel keeps its potential temperature during reversible motion with no heat exchange.

**How the definition helps.** A dry ideal gas that moves reversibly without heat exchange keeps its entropy, and at the reference pressure each entropy gives one temperature (our own). So the temperature the parcel would reach there never changes, even though its actual temperature does (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Potential temperature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potential_temperature). It says: “Potential temperature is conserved for all dry adiabatic processes”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Authalic latitude preserves ellipsoid area

**Remember:** Match the area of each latitude band before drawing the map.

*True by definition.* MSC 86A30 (Geodesy, mapping problems). arXiv physics.geo-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The authalic latitude of a point on an ellipsoid of revolution is the latitude, in the same hemisphere, on a sphere of equal total area whose band from the equator has the same area as the point's band on the ellipsoid. Longitude stays the same.

**Problem.** The authalic latitude map preserves area, so composing it with a spherical equal-area projection gives an equal-area ellipsoid map.

**How the definition helps.** Matching band areas from the equator matches every latitude band by subtraction, and rotational symmetry splits each band by longitude in proportion (our own). So all latitude-longitude rectangles keep their area, and those rectangles determine area (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Latitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latitude). It says: “gives an equal-area projection to a sphere.”

**Sources:**

- [J. P. Snyder, Map projections: A working manual (1987)](https://doi.org/10.3133/pp1395)

### Chord radius preserves mapped area

**Remember:** Use chord length as the map radius to keep areas unchanged.

*True by definition.* MSC 86A30 (Geodesy, mapping problems). arXiv physics.geo-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The spherical Lambert azimuthal equal-area map keeps each point's bearing from the center. It puts the point at map radius equal to the straight chord length to the center, not the distance along the surface.

**Problem.** The spherical Lambert azimuthal map preserves area away from the point opposite its center.

**How the definition helps.** A cap of angular radius θ on a sphere of radius R has area 2πR²(1 − cos θ), which is π times the squared chord, the area of its map disk (our own). Bearings keep sector fractions, so polar rectangles keep their area, and those rectangles determine area (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Lambert azimuthal equal-area projection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambert_azimuthal_equal-area_projection). It says: “It accurately represents area in all regions of the sphere, but it does not accurately represent angles.”

**Sources:**

- [J. P. Snyder, Map projections: A working manual (1987)](https://doi.org/10.3133/pp1395)

### Mercator straightens compass courses

**Remember:** Mercator stretches latitude until a steady compass bearing has a steady slope.

*True by definition.* MSC 86A30 (Geodesy, mapping problems). arXiv physics.geo-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The spherical Mercator map uses longitude as its horizontal coordinate and the integral of the secant of latitude from the equator as its vertical coordinate. This stretches north–south distances by the same factor, the secant of latitude, as east–west distances, so the map preserves angles (our own).

**Problem.** A course that keeps a constant angle to geographic north maps to a straight line when longitude runs continuously across the map edges.

**How the definition helps.** Since the map preserves angles, a course at a fixed angle to north crosses the vertical meridian lines at that same fixed angle (our own). A curve that meets parallel straight lines at a fixed angle is itself straight (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Mercator projection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercator_projection). It says: “representing rhumb lines as straight lines”

**Sources:**

- [J. P. Snyder, Map projections: A working manual (1987)](https://doi.org/10.3133/pp1395)

### The geoid follows local level

**Remember:** A level surface is one on which gravity can do no work.

*True by definition.* MSC 86A30 (Geodesy, mapping problems). arXiv physics.geo-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The geoid is the surface on which Earth's effective gravitational potential, including the effect of rotation, is constant, chosen to fit mean sea level.

**Problem.** In the reference gravity field, a plumb line meets the geoid at right angles wherever gravity is nonzero.

**How the definition helps.** The potential does not change along the surface, so its gradient, gravity, has no tangential part and is normal to the surface wherever it is nonzero (our own). A reference ellipsoid's normal need not point along real gravity (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Geoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoid). It says: “the geoid is, by definition, a surface upon which the force of gravity is perpendicular everywhere, apart from temporary tidal fluctuations.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Depth integration removes Ekman viscosity

**Remember:** Integrate the spiral and only the surface stress remains.

*True by definition.* MSC 86A05 (Hydrology, hydrography, oceanography). arXiv physics.ao-ph. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Ekman transport is the depth integral of the horizontal ocean current in excess of the interior current, which balances horizontal pressure forces against the effect of Earth's rotation. Integrating over depth replaces the unknown internal friction profile by the stresses at the top and bottom of the layer (our own).

**Problem.** Consider steady, horizontally uniform flow of constant density away from the equator, with zero stress at the layer base. The transport points perpendicular to nonzero surface wind stress, to its right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern Hemisphere.

**How the definition helps.** With zero stress at the base, the integrated balance says the rotation term, the transport turned by a right angle times the Coriolis parameter, equals surface stress over density (our own). So the transport is perpendicular to the stress, and the sign of the Coriolis parameter puts it to the right in the north and left in the south (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Ekman transport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ekman_transport). It says: “If all flow over the Ekman layer is integrated, the net transportation is at 90° to the right (left) of the surface wind”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Shallow-water potential vorticity follows parcels

**Remember:** Divide the total spin by layer depth to cancel stretching.

*True by definition.* MSC 86A05 (Hydrology, hydrography, oceanography). arXiv physics.geo-ph. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Shallow-water potential vorticity is absolute vorticity, the vertical curl of the horizontal velocity plus the planetary rotation term, divided by the water depth. Horizontal spreading lowers both by the same factor (our own).

**Problem.** In a smooth rotating shallow-water flow of positive depth, potential vorticity stays constant along each moving parcel. Assume no viscosity, external forcing or water sources.

**How the definition helps.** The momentum equation makes absolute vorticity change along a parcel at minus itself times the horizontal divergence, and water conservation gives the same law for depth (our own). The quotient rule then gives zero, even where vorticity vanishes (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Potential vorticity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potential_vorticity). It says: “The conserved quantity, in parentheses in equation (3), was later named the shallow water potential vorticity.”

**Sources:**

- [Carl-Gustaf Rossby, Relation between variations in the intensity of the zonal circulation of the atmosphere and the displacements of the semi-permanent centers of action (1939).](https://doi.org/10.1357/002224039806649023)

### Fixed rotation prevents geostrophic divergence

**Remember:** With fixed rotation, the divergence of a rotated gradient cancels.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 86A10 (Meteorology and atmospheric physics). arXiv physics.geo-ph. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Use a flat local model whose Coriolis parameter, the local strength of planetary rotation, is the same nonzero constant everywhere. Then the geostrophic wind is a fixed multiple of the geopotential gradient turned through a right angle (our own).

**Problem.** Assume the geopotential, the effective gravitational potential per unit mass, has continuous second derivatives on a constant-pressure surface. The horizontal wind that balances rotation against the pressure force then has zero horizontal divergence.

**How the definition helps.** A gradient turned through a right angle has divergence zero by equality of mixed partial derivatives (our own). If rotation strength varied northward, an eastward geopotential gradient would give a northward wind whose speed varies northward, so the divergence would not vanish (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [F-plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F-plane). It says: “the Coriolis parameter f, which measures the local effect of the planet's rotation, is a constant”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Layer thickness directs thermal wind

**Remember:** Wind shear runs along thickness contours, as wind runs along height contours.

*True by definition.* MSC 86A10 (Meteorology and atmospheric physics). arXiv physics.ao-ph. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Geopotential thickness between two fixed pressure surfaces is the upper geopotential minus the lower one, where geopotential is the lifting work per unit mass against gravity.

**Problem.** Assume gravity balances the vertical pressure force and Earth’s rotation balances the horizontal pressure force. Away from the equator, the upper wind minus the lower wind follows thickness contours wherever their gradient is nonzero.

**How the definition helps.** At each pressure level the balanced wind is the geopotential gradient turned through a right angle and divided by the Coriolis parameter, which is the same at both levels at one place (our own). Subtracting gives the turned thickness gradient over that parameter, which is tangent to the thickness contours (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Thermal wind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermal_wind). It says: “the thermal wind flows along thickness or temperature contours”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Fault-plane swaps preserve moment tensors

**Remember:** Switch the normal and slip direction and the tensor stays the same.

*True by definition.* MSC 86A15 (Seismology (including tsunami modeling), earthquakes), 74J15. arXiv physics.geo-ph. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Represent slip on one flat fault in an isotropic elastic solid by the symmetric matrix M = a(nsᵀ + snᵀ), where n is the unit fault normal, s the unit slip direction in the fault, and a the slip strength. The formula treats n and s the same way (our own).

**Problem.** Swapping the fault normal and slip direction leaves the source matrix unchanged. Thus the matrix alone cannot identify which of the two planes slipped.

**How the definition helps.** Swapping n and s exchanges the two terms, so their sum is unchanged (our own). The physical work lies in deriving this matrix from slip across an elastic fault (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Focal mechanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Focal_mechanism). It says: “It is impossible to determine solely from a focal mechanism which of the nodal planes is the fault plane.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### River order gaps survive pruning

**Remember:** Pruning lowers both surviving orders by one and leaves their gap alone.

*True by definition.* MSC 86A05 (Hydrology, hydrography, oceanography). arXiv physics.geo-ph. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In a binary river tree, headwaters have order one, and a junction takes the larger incoming order, adding one if the two orders match. For i &lt; j, T(i,j) is the expected number of order-i side branches entering order-j branches, per order-j branch.

**Problem.** Pruning removes headwaters and joins segments left with one input. If the ratios T(i,j) do not depend on the tree's maximum order whenever defined, pruning preserves them exactly when they depend only on j − i.

**How the definition helps.** Pruning lowers every surviving order by one, so the pruned ratio at (i,j) is the original ratio at (i+1, j+1) (our own). Since the ratios do not depend on maximum order, invariance means they are constant along each diagonal j − i (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Critical Tokunaga model for river networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.02991v1). It says: “the Toeplitz property Tᵢ,ᵢ₊ₖ = Tₖ and Horton prune-invariance”

**Sources:**

- [Yevgeniy Kovchegov, Ilya Zaliapin and Efi Foufoula-Georgiou, Critical Tokunaga model for river networks (2021).](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.02991v1)
- [Yevgeniy Kovchegov, Ilya Zaliapin and Efi Foufoula-Georgiou, Critical Tokunaga model for river networks (2022).](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevE.105.014301)

### Steady water keeps discharge and head

**Remember:** A steady current changes depth but keeps discharge and energy fixed.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 86A05 (Hydrology, hydrography, oceanography), 65M08. arXiv physics.ao-ph. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Describe the flow by its discharge q = hu, the water carried past a point per unit width, and its energy per unit mass E = u²/2 + g(h + b), where h is depth, u velocity, b bed height and g gravity. The scheme reconstructs the flow from q and E, so a steady flow whose depth varies still gives constant data.

**Problem.** In the paper's frictionless schemes for one-dimensional flow of positive depth, suppose q and E are constant across all cell and point data. Then every stored value has zero time derivative.

**How the definition helps.** Constant q and E give constant reconstructed data, so the discrete transport and bed-slope terms cancel in both update equations (our own). For smooth steady flow, q and E stay constant even where depth and velocity vary (our own).

**Paper or page:** [A New Approach for Designing Well-Balanced Schemes for the Shallow Water Equations: A Combination of Conservative and Primitive Formulations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.07809). It says: “qⱼ = qⱼ₊½ ≡ q̂ = Const, Eⱼ = Eⱼ₊½ ≡ Ê = Const, ∀j”

**Sources:**

- [A New Approach for Designing Well-Balanced Schemes for the Shallow Water Equations: A Combination of Conservative and Primitive Formulations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.07809)

### Convexity removes hidden mass alternatives

**Remember:** Known density and no hollows let outside gravity fix the shape.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 86A22 (Inverse problems in geophysics). arXiv physics.geo-ph. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The unknown body D is convex, so it has no hollows, has piecewise smooth boundary, and lies in a known bounded region Ω whose closure has connected exterior. Its density contrast f, the body's density minus the background density, is known, integrable and positive on Ω.

**Problem.** Enclose Ω in a convex domain with analytic boundary. Exact gravity measurements on any nonempty patch of that boundary determine D uniquely.

**How the definition helps.** Convexity rules out hollow bodies, which removes the basic ambiguity of exterior gravity (our own). By Newton’s shell theorem, a uniform ball and a concentric hollow shell of equal mass have the same exterior gravity (our own). The paper’s Theorem 0.1 proves uniqueness for the whole convex class.

**Paper or page:** [Learning on the correct class for domain inverse problems of gravimetry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07393v1). It says: “D is convex, f ∈ L₁(Ω), and 0 &lt; f on Ω.”

**Sources:**

- [Yihang Chen and Wenbin Li, Learning on the correct class for domain inverse problems of gravimetry (2024).](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07393v1)

## 90 Operations research, mathematical programming

### The segment definition makes every local convex minimum global

**Remember:** The chord to a lower point drags nearby values down.

*True by definition.* MSC 90C25 (Convex programming), 52A41. arXiv math.OC. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** A function on a convex domain is convex if, on every segment in the domain, its graph lies on or below the chord joining its end values. So moving from a point toward any point of lower value lowers the value at once.

**Problem.** If a convex function has its lowest nearby value at a point, it has its lowest value there on the entire convex domain.

**How the definition helps.** If some point had a lower value, the chord bound would make points near x on the segment toward it lower too (our own). This contradicts the local minimum. No smoothness or second derivative test is needed.

**nLab:** [convex function](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/convex+function). It says: “f(t x + (1−t) y) ≤ t f(x) + (1−t) f(y)”

**Wikipedia:** [Convex optimization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_optimization). It says: “every point that is local minimum is also a global minimum”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Generalized quantiles handle demand ties

**Remember:** Choose the first stock level where the demand probability reaches the cost ratio.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 90B05 (Inventory, storage, reservoirs). arXiv math.OC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For nonnegative demand D with distribution function F(x) = P(D ≤ x), the generalized quantile at level p in (0, 1) is the smallest x with F(x) ≥ p. It exists even where F jumps over p, so that no x has F(x) = p.

**Problem.** Choose a nonnegative stock level before demand with finite mean is known, paying a fixed positive cost per unit short and another per unit left over. The generalized quantile at p equal to the shortage cost divided by the sum of the two costs minimizes expected cost.

**How the definition helps.** Expected cost is convex, with left slope proportional to F just below x minus p, and right slope proportional to F(x) − p (our own). The generalized quantile is exactly where F reaches p, so zero lies between the two slopes (our own). If demand is 0 or 2 with equal probability, no x has F(x) = 1/4, yet the quantile 0 is optimal (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Newsvendor model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newsvendor_model). It says: “denotes the generalized inverse cumulative distribution function of D.”

**Sources:**

- [E. L. Porteus (2008), The Newsvendor Problem](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-387-73699-0_7)

### Customer time gives Little’s law

**Remember:** Count one block of customer time by customer or by clock.

*True by definition.* MSC 90B22 (Queues and service in operations research). arXiv math.PR. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Observed customer time is the total time customers spend inside the observation window: each customer's stay clipped to the window, summed. It is one block of customer–time pairs, which can be counted by customer or by clock time.

**Problem.** For finitely many visits, observed customer time equals the integral over the window of the number present. So if arrival rate and mean stay converge, and the time cut off at the window edges grows slower than the window, mean occupancy is their product.

**How the definition helps.** Summing the block by customer gives observed customer time, and summing it by clock time gives the occupancy integral (our own). Dividing by the window length gives arrivals per unit time times mean stay. The remaining work is controlling the visits that cross the window edges.

**Wikipedia:** [Little's law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little%27s_law). It says: “multiplied by the average time that a customer spends in the system (W).”

**Sources:**

- [J. D. C. Little (1961), A Proof for the Queuing Formula L = λW](https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.9.3.383)

### Reflected walks give waiting times

**Remember:** Waiting work is the walk minus its lowest point so far.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 90B22 (Queues and service in operations research). arXiv math.PR. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Start with an empty single-server queue served in arrival order. Form the walk that adds each customer's service time and subtracts the time to the next arrival, then subtract its lowest value so far, including the starting zero. This reflected walk is the work still waiting, which never goes below zero.

**Problem.** Just before each arrival, the reflected sum equals that customer’s waiting time. The next wait equals the current wait plus the increment, or zero if that sum is negative.

**How the definition helps.** Subtracting the running minimum gives exactly the waiting-time update: add the increment, or reset to zero when the walk reaches a new low (our own). A new low means the server has cleared all waiting work. Starting at zero, induction gives the waiting time at each arrival (our own).

**Paper or page:** [On fluctuation-theoretic decompositions via Lindley-type recursions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.01811v1). It says: “where Wₙ ∼ Sₙ − minₖ∈{0,…,n} Sₖ”

**Sources:**

- [Onno Boxma, Offer Kella, Michel Mandjes, On fluctuation-theoretic decompositions via Lindley-type recursions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.01811v1)

### Longest paths give project duration

**Remember:** Each event waits for its slowest chain of predecessors.

*True by definition.* MSC 90B35 (Deterministic scheduling theory in operations research). arXiv cs.DS. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Draw tasks as edges of a finite acyclic directed graph, weighted by duration, with every edge on a path from the single start to the single finish. Each event happens as soon as all its incoming tasks are done, and every ready task starts at once.

**Problem.** The earliest project finish equals the longest weighted path from the start to the finish event.

**How the definition helps.** Earliest event times obey the longest-path rule: each event takes the largest predecessor time plus task duration over its incoming tasks (our own). Applying this rule in dependency order from zero at the start gives both quantities (our own). The modelling work is encoding every precedence constraint.

**Wikipedia:** [Critical path method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critical_path_method). It says: “A critical path is determined by identifying the longest stretch of dependent activities”

**Sources:**

- [J. E. Kelley Jr. and M. R. Walker (1959), Critical-Path Planning and Scheduling](https://doi.org/10.1145/1460299.1460318)

### Preemption makes earliest deadlines optimal

**Remember:** With pause and resume, urgent work can always go first.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 90B35 (Deterministic scheduling theory in operations research). arXiv cs.DS. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Independent jobs, each with a release time and a deadline, run on one processor. Preemption lets a job pause and resume at no cost, and the earliest deadline rule always runs a ready job with the earliest deadline.

**Problem.** If any schedule meets all release times and deadlines, the preemptive earliest deadline rule does too.

**How the definition helps.** With pauses allowed, an exchange argument moves ready work with the earliest deadline forward without making the displaced work late (our own). Without pauses the rule fails: take a three-unit job released at 0 and due at 5, and a one-unit job released at 1 and due at 2 (our own). Starting the first job at once misses the second deadline, but idling until 1 meets both.

**Wikipedia:** [Earliest deadline first scheduling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earliest_deadline_first_scheduling). It says: “EDF is an optimal scheduling algorithm on preemptive uniprocessors”

**Sources:**

- [W. A. Horn (1974), Some Simple Scheduling Algorithms](https://doi.org/10.1002/nav.3800210113)

### Fractional assignments decompose into matchings

**Remember:** Fractional assignments are mixtures of whole assignments.

*True by definition.* MSC 90B80 (Discrete location and assignment). arXiv cs.DS. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A fractional assignment is a random whole assignment, which pairs each worker with a different job, recorded by the probability of each worker–job pair. Equivalently, it is a nonnegative square matrix whose rows and columns each sum to one.

**Problem.** The minimum linear cost over all fractional assignments equals the cheapest whole assignment’s cost.

**How the definition helps.** Its cost is an average of whole-assignment costs, which cannot beat the cheapest one, and probability one on that assignment attains it (our own). The work is showing that every matrix with unit row and column sums is such a mixture. This is the Birkhoff–von Neumann theorem.

**Wikipedia:** [Doubly stochastic matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doubly_stochastic_matrix). It says: “the vertices of Bₙ are precisely the permutation matrices.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Basic feasible solutions are vertices, so linear programs need finite search

**Remember:** Keep the positive variables on independent columns.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 90C05 (Linear programming), 90C49. arXiv math.OC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a linear program in standard form, minimize cᵀx subject to Ax = b and x ≥ 0, a feasible point is basic if the columns of A at its positive entries are linearly independent. Those entries are then fixed uniquely, so the point is not the average of two distinct feasible points (our own).

**Problem.** If a linear program in standard form has an optimal solution, then it has an optimal basic feasible solution. Each basic feasible solution is a vertex of the feasible polyhedron.

**How the definition helps.** Independent support columns fix the point uniquely, so it is a vertex (our own). At an optimum with dependent support columns, a dependence gives feasible moves both ways with zero change in cost, so move until a positive entry vanishes (our own). Repeating this gives an optimal basic solution (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Basic feasible solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basic_feasible_solution), [Linear programming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_programming). It says: “Geometrically, each BFS corresponds to a vertex of the polyhedron of feasible solutions. If there exists an optimal solution, then there exists an optimal BFS.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Basis prices turn simplex optimality into strong duality

**Remember:** Price the basic columns exactly and check the remaining columns.

*True by definition.* MSC 90C05 (Linear programming), 90C46. arXiv math.OC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For maximizing c·x under Ax = b and x ≥ 0, with redundant rows removed, a basis is a set of independent columns whose variables are solved for while the others are zero. Basis prices y match c exactly on the basic columns, so the reduced costs c − Aᵀy are all nonpositive exactly when y is dual feasible.

**Problem.** A feasible basis with no positive reduced costs supplies a primal optimum and a dual optimum of equal value. In particular, a feasible linear program with finite optimum has a dual optimum of the same value.

**How the definition helps.** No positive reduced cost means Aᵀy ≥ c, so y is dual feasible (our own). Only basic variables are nonzero and prices match c on them, so c·x = y·Ax = y·b, and weak duality makes both optimal. For a feasible program with finite optimum, the finite simplex theorem supplies such a basis.

**Paper or page:** [Zero-Sum Games and Linear Programming Duality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.11196v6). It says: “then there exist feasible x and y with cᵀx = yᵀb, which are therefore optimal solutions.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Dual prices give supporting bounds on the optimal value

**Remember:** The old prices still bound the new optimum.

*True by definition.* MSC 90C05 (Linear programming), 90C46. arXiv math.OC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For maximizing c·x under Ax ≤ b and x ≥ 0, a shadow price vector is an optimal dual solution: it minimizes b·y over y ≥ 0 with Aᵀy ≥ c. The dual constraints do not involve b, so the same prices stay feasible when the limits change.

**Problem.** Suppose the original linear program has finite optimum v(b) and an optimal dual vector y. If changed limits b′ give a feasible program, its optimum v(b′) is at most v(b) + y·(b′ − b).

**How the definition helps.** Changing b only changes the dual objective, so y stays dual feasible (our own). Weak duality gives v(b′) ≤ y·b′, and strong duality gives y·b = v(b). The bound holds even where v has no derivative.

**Wikipedia:** [Shadow price](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_price). It says: “the shadow price is the value of the Lagrange multiplier at the optimal solution”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Nonnegative artificial variables turn feasibility into a zero minimum

**Remember:** Every artificial variable disappears exactly when their sum is zero.

*True by definition.* MSC 90C05 (Linear programming). arXiv math.OC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** First make b ≥ 0 by multiplying each row with a negative right side by −1. Then add one artificial variable to each equation, Ax + a = b with a ≥ 0, and minimize the sum of the artificial variables, which is zero only when every one is zero.

**Problem.** The original system has a solution exactly when this auxiliary linear program has minimum zero.

**How the definition helps.** The sum is zero exactly when a = 0, that is, when x solves the original system. Conversely, any original solution extends by setting a = 0 (our own). The point x = 0, a = b gives a known feasible start.

**Wikipedia:** [Simplex algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplex_algorithm). It says: “where the artificial variables are all zero.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Nonnegative constraint weights make weak linear duality immediate

**Remember:** A weighted sum of valid upper bounds stays valid.

*True by definition.* MSC 90C05 (Linear programming). arXiv math.OC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The dual of maximizing c·x under Ax ≤ b and x ≥ 0 puts nonnegative weights y on the constraint rows, so y·Ax ≤ y·b is again a valid bound. It keeps only weights with Aᵀy ≥ c, so the combined row dominates the objective, and minimizes b·y.

**Problem.** Every feasible choice of dual weights gives an upper bound on the original maximization problem.

**How the definition helps.** For feasible x and y, c·x ≤ (Aᵀy)·x = y·Ax ≤ y·b, using x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0 (our own). That chain is the whole proof. Attaining the best primal value needs strong duality.

**Wikipedia:** [Dual linear program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_linear_program). It says: “upper bound on the objective.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Normalizing a nonnegative dependence gives Gordan’s alternative

**Remember:** Normalize the dependence, then separate zero from the hull.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 90C05 (Linear programming), 52A20. arXiv math.OC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The convex hull of finitely many vectors is the set of their weighted averages with nonnegative weights summing to one. Nonnegative weights, not all zero, with weighted sum zero become such an average after division by their sum, so they exist exactly when zero lies in the hull.

**Problem.** For a nonempty finite list of real vectors of equal length, exactly one of two alternatives holds. Either nonnegative weights, not all zero, give weighted sum zero, or some vector has positive dot product with every listed vector.

**How the definition helps.** So the first alternative says zero is in the hull. If it is not, the hull is compact and convex, and strict separation gives a vector with positive dot product with every listed vector (our own). If zero is in the hull, no such vector exists, because zero is not an average of positive numbers (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Polytopes, polyhedra, and the Farkas lemma](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.00221v2). It says: “There is a nonzero nonnegative vector x ∈ ℝⁿ such that A x = 0.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Paired columns make free variables yield dual equalities

**Remember:** Opposite columns impose opposite bounds.

*True by definition.* MSC 90C05 (Linear programming). arXiv math.OC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A free variable takes any real value, so write it as u − v with u, v ≥ 0; its column a and coefficient c then appear twice, once with each sign. In the dual of a maximization with upper-bound constraints, each nonnegative variable requires its column price to cover its coefficient.

**Problem.** A free variable in a maximization linear program gives an equality in its minimization dual. Variables restricted to be nonnegative still give inequalities.

**How the definition helps.** The two copies give a·y ≥ c and −a·y ≥ −c, hence a·y = c (our own). Every real value has such a split, and the program depends only on u − v.

**Wikipedia:** [Dual linear program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_linear_program). It says: “becomes a constraint in the dual LP”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Positive basic variables rule out simplex cycling

**Remember:** With no zero basic variables, an improving pivot actually moves.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 90C05 (Linear programming). arXiv math.OC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For Ax = b with m linearly independent rows, a basis is a set of m independent columns; setting the other variables to zero fixes the basic ones. A feasible basis is nondegenerate when every basic variable is strictly positive, so every improving pivot can take a positive step.

**Problem.** If every feasible basis is nondegenerate, primal simplex with improving entering variables cannot cycle.

**How the definition helps.** Each improving pivot then moves a positive distance and strictly raises the objective (our own). A basis cannot recur, because its objective value would repeat. With zero basic variables, the cited cycling examples show the argument fails.

**Wikipedia:** [Bland's rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bland%27s_rule). It says: “there are examples of degenerate linear programs, on which the original simplex algorithm cycles forever.”

**Sources:**

- [R. G. Bland, New Finite Pivoting Rules for the Simplex Method (1977).](https://doi.org/10.1287/moor.2.2.103)

### The simplex dictionary makes the next step a ratio test

**Remember:** Stop at the first basic variable to reach zero.

*True by definition.* MSC 90C05 (Linear programming). arXiv math.OC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A simplex dictionary solves the equality constraints for the basic variables, writing each as its current value minus fixed rates times the nonbasic variables. At the current solution the nonbasic variables are zero, and every variable must stay nonnegative.

**Problem.** From a feasible dictionary solution, raise one nonbasic variable and keep the others at zero. The largest feasible step is the smallest ratio of starting value to rate of decrease over the decreasing basic variables, and it is unlimited if none decreases.

**How the definition helps.** Each dictionary row shows directly when its basic variable reaches zero: starting at b and falling at rate a &gt; 0, it allows steps up to b/a (our own). The first variable to reach zero limits the step. The work lies in solving the original equations for the basic variables.

**Wikipedia:** [Simplex algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplex_algorithm). It says: “minimum ratio test”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Transposing the constraint matrix twice recovers the primal

**Remember:** Transpose twice and swap the roles twice.

*True by definition.* MSC 90C05 (Linear programming). arXiv math.OC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Use the symmetric dual rules for nonnegative variables: maximize c·x subject to Ax ≤ b becomes minimize b·y subject to Aᵀy ≥ c, and the reverse. Each rule transposes the matrix, swaps the objective vector with the bound vector, and flips max with min and ≤ with ≥.

**Problem.** The dual of the dual of a linear program in this form is the original program.

**How the definition helps.** Applying the rules twice flips each direction twice and swaps the vectors back, and transposing twice gives the original matrix (our own). Other sign conventions must first be converted to these forms.

**Wikipedia:** [Dual linear program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_linear_program). It says: “the dual of the dual is the primal.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Two nonnegative slack terms explain complementary slackness

**Remember:** A sum of nonnegative products vanishes only term by term.

*True by definition.* MSC 90C05 (Linear programming), 90C46. arXiv math.OC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For maximizing c·x with Ax ≤ b, x ≥ 0 and its dual, minimizing b·y with Aᵀy ≥ c, y ≥ 0, the slacks b − Ax and Aᵀy − c are the unused margins. For feasible x and y, the gap b·y − c·x equals y·(b − Ax) + x·(Aᵀy − c), a sum of nonnegative products (our own).

**Problem.** When both programs have optima, a feasible pair is optimal exactly when every slack times its corresponding variable in the other program is zero.

**How the definition helps.** A sum of nonnegative products is zero exactly when every product is zero (our own). Strong duality says a feasible pair is optimal exactly when the gap is zero.

**Wikipedia:** [Dual linear program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_linear_program). It says: “each primal variable corresponds to a dual slack variable, and each dual variable corresponds to a primal slack variable.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Total unimodularity makes every vertex of a linear program integral

**Remember:** Determinants ±1 make Cramer’s rule give integer vertices.

*True by definition.* MSC 90C10 (Integer programming), 90C57, 05B20. arXiv math.OC, math.CO. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A matrix is totally unimodular if every square submatrix has determinant 0, 1 or −1. So every invertible square submatrix has determinant ±1, and Cramer’s rule solves its systems with integer right sides in integers (our own).

**Problem.** If A is totally unimodular and b is an integer vector, every vertex of {x : Ax ≤ b} has integer entries. So the linear program 'maximize cᵀx subject to Ax ≤ b' has an integer optimum whenever it has an optimum, for every c.

**How the definition helps.** At a vertex, independent tight rows form a square system with determinant ±1 and integer right side, so Cramer’s rule gives integer coordinates (our own). For the optimum, add the integer bounds ⌊xᵢ⌋ ≤ xᵢ ≤ ⌈xᵢ⌉ around an attained optimum x; they keep total unimodularity by expansion along unit rows (our own). The bounded polyhedron has an optimal vertex, which is integral by the same argument (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Unimodular matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unimodular_matrix). It says: “Hence if A is totally unimodular and b is integral, every extreme point of the feasible region (e.g. {x \| Ax ≥ b}) is integral and thus the feasible region is an integral polyhedron.”

**Sources:**

- [A. J. Hoffman and J. B. Kruskal, Integral boundary points of convex polyhedra, in Linear Inequalities and Related Systems, Annals of Mathematics Studies 38 (1956), 223–246](https://doi.org/10.1515/9781400881987-014)

### Affine equalities keep the feasible set convex

**Remember:** A convex upper bound survives averaging, but a convex equality may not.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 90C25 (Convex programming), 52A41. arXiv math.OC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A convex program minimizes a convex function on a convex domain subject to constraints g(x) ≤ 0 with each g convex, and equalities a·x = b that are affine. Both kinds of constraint keep holding along the segment between two points that satisfy them.

**Problem.** The feasible set of a convex program is convex.

**How the definition helps.** A convex g that is at most zero at both ends stays at most zero along the segment, and an affine equality holds along the whole segment (our own). A nonaffine equality such as x² = 1 admits −1 and 1 but not their midpoint 0.

**Wikipedia:** [Convex optimization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_optimization). It says: “the equality constraints are all linear”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### An epigraph variable makes a convex objective linear

**Remember:** Move the curved objective into a constraint.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 90C25 (Convex programming), 52A41. arXiv math.OC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Add a height variable t with the constraint t ≥ f(x), which says (x, t) lies in the epigraph of f, and minimize t over the old constraints and this one. The smallest allowed t above any feasible x is exactly f(x).

**Problem.** Every convex minimization problem has an equivalent convex formulation with a linear objective and one extra variable.

**How the definition helps.** Minimizing t therefore gives the same infimum and the same minimizing x (our own). Convexity of f makes its epigraph convex, so the new constraint is convex.

**Wikipedia:** [Convex optimization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convex_optimization). It says: “adding a single variable t”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Normal directions make nearest point projection nonexpansive

**Remember:** From the nearest point, the whole set lies at an obtuse angle.

*True by definition.* MSC 90C25 (Convex programming), 52A20. arXiv math.OC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Projection onto a nonempty closed convex set C sends x to its nearest point p in C. Equivalently, x − p points away from C at p: (x − p)·(z − p) ≤ 0 for every z in C.

**Problem.** Nearest point projection onto a nonempty closed convex set in Euclidean space never increases distances.

**How the definition helps.** Use q as z in the inequality for p, and p as z in the inequality for q (our own). Adding them gives ‖p − q‖² ≤ (x − y)·(p − q), and Cauchy–Schwarz gives ‖p − q‖ ≤ ‖x − y‖. The projection theorem gives the equivalence with the nearest point.

**Paper or page:** [Metric Projection onto Closed Convex Set is 1-Lipschitz](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Metric_Projection_onto_Closed_Convex_Set_is_1-Lipschitz). It says: “is 1-Lipschitz.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions certify a convex minimum

**Remember:** A stationary convex Lagrangian is already minimized.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 90C25 (Convex programming), 90C46. arXiv math.OC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For minimizing f subject to g(x) ≤ 0 and h(x) = 0, the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions ask for a feasible x and weights, nonnegative on inequalities and zero on those holding strictly, such that the Lagrangian f + ∑λg + ∑μh has zero gradient at x. At feasible points this Lagrangian is at most f, and at x it equals f(x).

**Problem.** Assume a convex minimization on Euclidean space has differentiable objective and inequality functions, and affine equalities. Any point and multipliers satisfying the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions then give a global minimizer.

**How the definition helps.** With convex f and g and affine h, nonnegative weights keep the Lagrangian convex, so zero gradient makes x its global minimizer (our own). Hence f(x) equals the Lagrangian at x, which is at most the Lagrangian at any feasible z, which is at most f(z) (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karush%E2%80%93Kuhn%E2%80%93Tucker_conditions). It says: “the necessary conditions are also sufficient for optimality.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Strong quasiconvexity forbids tied minima

**Remember:** Two equal minima would make their midpoint lower than both.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 90C26 (Nonconvex programming, global optimization). arXiv math.OC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A function h on a convex set is strongly quasiconvex with modulus γ &gt; 0 if, at each point z = (1−t)x + ty of a segment, h(z) ≤ max(h(x), h(y)) − γt(1−t)‖x − y‖²/2. So between two distinct points the function dips strictly below the higher end value.

**Problem.** A real strongly quasiconvex function on a convex set has at most one minimizer.

**How the definition helps.** Two distinct minimizers would give a point between them strictly below the minimum value (our own). Ordinary quasiconvexity, without the gap term, allows ties: f(x) = max(0, \|x\| − 1) has a whole interval of minimizers (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Characterizations of Strongly Quasiconvex Functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.21580v1). It says: “If h is strongly quasiconvex with modulus γ &gt; 0”

**Sources:**

- [Characterizations of Strongly Quasiconvex Functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.21580v1)

### Diminishing returns bound greedy gains

**Remember:** The best single gain covers at least one share of the remaining gap.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 90C27 (Combinatorial optimization). arXiv cs.DS. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A nondecreasing set function has diminishing returns if adding an item outside B gains at least as much on A as on B whenever A ⊆ B. The greedy rule starts from the empty set and adds an item with the largest gain at each step.

**Problem.** Choose a budget k from one to the number of items. After k steps, the gain above the empty-set score is at least 1 − 1/e times the best gain with that budget.

**How the definition helps.** By diminishing returns, adding the k missing optimal items one at a time gains at most k times the best current single gain, so each greedy step closes at least 1/k of the gap (our own). After k steps at most (1 − 1/k)ᵏ ≤ 1/e of the gap remains (our own). Without diminishing returns, two items useful only together can lose to a small immediate gain (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Incremental space-filling design based on coverings and spacings: improving upon low discrepancy sequences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.05833v1). It says: “Let f be a non-decreasing submodular set function, then, for any given k, 1 ≤ k ≤ C, Algorithm 1 returns a set Xₖ with bounded optimality gap”

**Sources:**

- [Amaya Nogales Gómez, Luc Pronzato, Maria-João Rendas, Incremental space-filling design based on coverings and spacings: improving upon low discrepancy sequences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.05833v1)
- [G. L. Nemhauser, L. A. Wolsey and M. L. Fisher (1978), An Analysis of Approximations for Maximizing Submodular Set Functions I](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01588971)

### Touching objectives share envelope slopes

**Remember:** An envelope touching a curve from above shares its slope.

*True by definition.* MSC 90C31 (Sensitivity, stability, parametric optimization), 91B02. arXiv math.OC, econ.TH. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The value function, or upper envelope, gives at each parameter the supremum of the objective over a fixed set of feasible choices. So it lies on or above every choice's objective curve and touches the curve of any choice that attains it.

**Problem.** At an interior parameter where the value function and an attaining objective curve are differentiable, their derivatives agree.

**How the definition helps.** The envelope minus an attaining curve is nonnegative and zero at that parameter, so where both are differentiable the difference has zero derivative and the slopes agree (our own). No assumption about how the optimal choice moves is needed. The remaining work is proving attainment and differentiability.

**Wikipedia:** [Envelope theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envelope_theorem). It says: “the traditional envelope formula holds for optimization problems with arbitrary choice sets at any differentiability point of the value function”

**Sources:**

- [Milgrom and Segal, Envelope Theorems for Arbitrary Choice Sets (2002)](https://doi.org/10.1111/1468-0262.00296)

### Ratio minima become scalar zeros

**Remember:** Subtract the candidate times the denominator and look for zero.

*True by definition.* MSC 90C32 (Fractional programming). arXiv math.OC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a ratio A(x)/B(x) with B(x) &gt; 0, let F(q) be the minimum over x of A(x) − qB(x). Since B &gt; 0, each difference A(x) − qB(x) has the same sign as A(x)/B(x) − q.

**Problem.** If the ratio attains its minimum, and each defining minimum exists, F has exactly one zero. Its zero is the minimum ratio.

**How the definition helps.** Below the minimum ratio every difference is positive, so F(q) &gt; 0, and above it the ratio minimizer gives F(q) &lt; 0 (our own). At the minimum ratio all differences are nonnegative and the minimizer gives zero. The work moves to solving the difference minimizations.

**Paper or page:** [Fast Algorithms for Stackelberg Prediction Game with Least Squares Loss](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.05531v1). It says: “Then, the equation F(q) = 0 has a unique solution.”

**Sources:**

- [Werner Dinkelbach, On Nonlinear Fractional Programming (1967)](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.13.7.492)

### Scaling linearizes an affine ratio

**Remember:** Scale the denominator to one and optimize the scaled numerator.

*True by definition.* MSC 90C32 (Fractional programming). arXiv math.OC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** To optimize a ratio of affine expressions (c·x + α)/(d·x + β) with positive denominator, set t = 1/(d·x + β) and y = tx. Then the scaled denominator d·y + βt equals one, and the scaled numerator c·y + αt is linear in y and t.

**Problem.** On a nonempty bounded polyhedron where its denominator is positive, an affine ratio can be optimized by linear programming.

**How the definition helps.** Multiplying each constraint Gx ≤ h by t gives Gy ≤ ht, so optimizing c·y + αt subject to Gy ≤ ht, d·y + βt = 1 and t ≥ 0 is a linear program (our own). In reverse, t = 0 would give a nonzero direction along which the feasible region is unbounded, which boundedness excludes, so x = y/t recovers a solution (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Linear-fractional programming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear-fractional_programming). It says: “Any linear-fractional program can be transformed into a linear program, assuming that the feasible region is non-empty and bounded”

**Sources:**

- [A. Charnes and W. W. Cooper (1962), Programming with Linear Fractional Functionals](https://doi.org/10.1002/nav.3800090303)

### A fixed return edge turns a flow into a circulation

**Remember:** Send the required amount back on one fixed edge.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 90C35 (Programming involving graphs or networks), 90C05. arXiv math.OC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A circulation keeps each edge flow within its bounds and balances inflow and outflow at every vertex. A required flow d from s to t becomes a circulation once a zero-cost edge from t to s, with both bounds equal to d, sends that amount back.

**Problem.** A minimum-cost flow of fixed value has the same optimal cost as the resulting minimum-cost circulation. Feasible solutions correspond by adding or deleting the return edge.

**How the definition helps.** The return edge carries exactly d, balancing the net flow d out of s and into t (our own). Adding it turns a feasible flow into a circulation, and deleting it reverses this. Its zero cost leaves the objective unchanged.

**Wikipedia:** [Minimum-cost flow problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum-cost_flow_problem). It says: “forcing the total flow from s to t to also be d.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Consistent estimates settle vertices once

**Remember:** The estimate never drops by more than the edge cost.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 90C35 (Programming involving graphs or networks). arXiv cs.DS. Level 2: later undergraduate.
