**How the definition helps.** An average of nonnegative expected payoffs is nonnegative, so no distribution is both (our own). If p is not an average of the beliefs, a hyperplane separating p from their convex hull gives a bet that every belief accepts but p rejects (our own reading of the converse).

**Paper or page:** [Three Variations on Money Pump, Common Prior, and Trade](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.13132v1). It says: “In the single player setting we conclude that a probability distribution is a prior if it is disintegrable, because this definition excludes money pump.”

**Sources:**

- [Ziv Hellman, Miklos Pinter, Three Variations on Money Pump, Common Prior, and Trade, arXiv:2401.13132v1 (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.13132v1)

### Positional voting rules with shrinking score gaps cannot be obviously manipulated

**Remember:** Obvious lies improve the best case or the worst case.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 91B12 (Voting theory), 91B14, 91B03. arXiv econ.TH. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A voter manipulates obviously if some false ballot gives her a better best-case outcome, or a better worst-case outcome, than her true ballot, with cases ranging over all ballots of the other voters. A positional scoring rule gives each candidate points by its rank on each ballot.

**Problem.** A strict positional scoring rule whose gaps between the scores of consecutive ranks weakly shrink down the ballot cannot be obviously manipulated. By contrast, the Gibbard–Satterthwaite theorem says every unanimous, non-dictatorial rule with at least three candidates can be manipulated.

**How the definition helps.** The definition compares only the extremes, so manipulations that pay only at particular profiles of other ballots do not count. So the Gibbard–Satterthwaite theorem does not settle this weaker question. Theorem 4 proves that shrinking score gaps protect both extremes.

**Paper or page:** [Obvious Manipulability of Voting Rules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.01983v3). It says: “In contrast to the Gibbard-Satterthwaite theorem, many of the rules we examined are not obviously manipulable.”

**Sources:**

- [Haris Aziz, Alexander Lam, Obvious Manipulability of Voting Rules, arXiv:2111.01983v3 (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.01983v3)

### An allocation that is envy-free up to one item always exists

**Remember:** Envy is forgiven if removing one good from the other ends it.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 91B32 (Resource and cost allocation (including fair division, apportionment, etc.)), 91A68. arXiv cs.GT, econ.TH. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An allocation of indivisible goods is envy-free up to one item if each agent weakly prefers her own bundle to any other agent's bundle once at most one good is removed from that other bundle.

**Problem.** For indivisible goods and monotone utilities, an allocation of all items that is envy-free up to one item always exists, although an envy-free one need not.

**How the definition helps.** With one good and two agents who both want it, every allocation causes envy, but removing that good ends it (our own). The envy-cycle elimination algorithm keeps this one-good bound while it hands out the goods one at a time (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Envy-free item allocation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envy-free_item_allocation). It says: “An EF1 allocation always exists and can be found efficiently by various procedures”

**Sources:**

- [Lipton, R. J.; Markakis, E.; Mossel, E.; Saberi, A. (2004). On approximately fair allocations of indivisible goods. Proc. 5th ACM Conference on Electronic Commerce, 125–131.](https://doi.org/10.1145/988772.988792)
- [Budish, E. (2011). The combinatorial assignment problem: approximate competitive equilibrium from equal incomes. Journal of Political Economy 119(6), 1061–1103.](https://doi.org/10.1086/664613)

### Judging envy in expectation makes envy-free efficient lotteries always exist

**Remember:** Fairness before the draw can hold when fairness after the draw cannot.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 91B32 (Resource and cost allocation (including fair division, apportionment, etc.)), 91B15. arXiv econ.TH, cs.GT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An allocation lottery is a random allocation of indivisible items. It is ex-ante envy-free if each agent values her own random bundle, in expectation, at least as much as any other agent's random bundle.

**Problem.** In the finite fair-division model, with feasible allocations closed under exchanging agents' bundles, some allocation lottery is ex-ante envy-free and Pareto optimal in expected utility. A deterministic envy-free allocation need not exist.

**How the definition helps.** Judging envy in expectation lets a lottery share what no single allocation can: two people who both want one item each get it with probability one half (our own). Existence in general is the theorem of Cole and Tao. This paper shows that finding such a lottery lies in PPAD.

**Paper or page:** [On the complexity of Pareto-optimal and envy-free lotteries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.12605v1). It says: “Cole and Tao (2021) have proved that an ex-ante envy-free and Pareto-optimal allocation lottery is always guaranteed to exist.”

**Sources:**

- [Ioannis Caragiannis, Kristoffer Arnsfelt Hansen, Nidhi Rathi, On the complexity of Pareto-optimal and envy-free lotteries, arXiv:2307.12605v1 (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.12605v1)

### One allocation gives every agent half of any feasible fair share

**Remember:** A feasible share can be given to everyone at once.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 91B32 (Resource and cost allocation (including fair division, apportionment, etc.)), 91A68. arXiv econ.TH, cs.GT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Agents with entitlements, weights summing to one, divide indivisible goods. A share rule gives each agent a minimum value from her valuation and entitlement, and it is feasible if every instance has an allocation giving every agent her share.

**Problem.** Suppose agents value bundles additively and each picks her own feasible share rule. Then some allocation gives every agent at least half her chosen share, and one half cannot be improved in general.

**How the definition helps.** Feasibility bounds each rule's shares by what one allocation can give everyone at once (our own). The quoted theorem turns this into one allocation meeting half of each agent's own rule, even when the rules differ. A separate worst-case instance shows one half is best possible (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Share-Based Fairness for Arbitrary Entitlements](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14575v1). It says: “there is an allocation that gives every agent at least half her share value, regardless of which feasible share-based fairness notion the agent wishes to use.”

**Sources:**

- [Moshe Babaioff, Uriel Feige, Share-Based Fairness for Arbitrary Entitlements, arXiv:2405.14575v1 (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14575v1)

### Posterior messages preserve feasible beliefs

**Remember:** Tell each player the probability their old signal implied.

*True by definition.* MSC 91B44 (Economics of information), 91A27. arXiv econ.TH, cs.GT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Given a common prior and private signals, a player's posterior is the conditional probability of winning given their signal. A signal is direct if its value is that posterior, the winning probability it implies.

**Problem.** Any joint distribution of posterior winning probabilities obtainable from private signals is also obtainable from direct signals under the same prior.

**How the definition helps.** Replace each signal by the winning probability it implies; by the tower property, the probability of winning given this new report is the report itself (our own). So the joint law of posteriors is unchanged (our own).

**Paper or page:** [A Belief-Based Characterization of Reduced-Form Auctions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.04070v1). It says: “then there exists a direct information structure I such that ν is p₀-feasible for I.”

**Sources:**

- [A Belief-Based Characterization of Reduced-Form Auctions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.04070v1)

### Unbiased statistics elicit posterior means

**Remember:** Score the report against a signal with the right mean.

*True by definition.* MSC 91B44 (Economics of information). arXiv econ.TH. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A statistic h(Y) of the verifier's signal is unbiased for the target g(θ) if its conditional mean in each state θ equals g(θ). Since Y is independent of the analyst's information given θ, h(Y) then has conditional mean equal to the analyst's posterior mean of g(θ) (our own).

**Problem.** For finite states and signals, an unbiased statistic lets a verifier pay a risk-neutral analyst, who maximizes expected payment, so that reporting the posterior mean is optimal.

**How the definition helps.** Pay twice the report r times h(Y), minus r² (our own). Its expectation is 2rm − r², where m is the posterior mean, and this is uniquely maximized at r = m (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Elicitability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.00879v1). It says: “then the mean of g(θ) is elicitable with (Y, π).”

**Sources:**

- [Yaron Azrieli, Christopher Chambers, Paul Healy, Nicolas Lambert. Elicitability (2025).](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.00879v1)

### Saturated agent spaces make fractional and ordinary coalitions block the same allocations

**Remember:** Saturation lets some agents fully join in place of all partly joining.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 91B50 (General equilibrium theory), 91A12, 28B05. arXiv econ.TH. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An agent measure space is saturated if L¹ on every set of positive measure has no countable norm-dense subset, so Lyapunov's convexity theorem holds exactly, even in Banach spaces (our own). A fuzzy coalition joins a trade with measurable weights in \[0,1\], positive on a set of positive measure, and an ordinary coalition joins at full weight.

**Problem.** If the measure space of agents is saturated, the core equals the fuzzy core, the allocations that no fuzzy coalition can block. This holds with commodities in any Banach space and minimal assumptions on preferences.

**How the definition helps.** Exact Lyapunov convexity turns the integrals of a fuzzy block, with participation mass included, into those of an ordinary coalition of positive measure with the same totals (our own). Conversely, an ordinary coalition is a fuzzy one with weights 0 and 1 (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Fuzzy Core Equivalence in Large Economies: A Role for the Infinite-Dimensional Lyapunov Theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.15539v1). It says: “Due to the exact version of the Lyapunov convexity theorem in Banach spaces, we clarify that the additional structure of commodity spaces and preferences is unnecessary whenever the measure space of agents is "saturated".”

**Sources:**

- [M. Ali Khan, Nobusumi Sagara, Fuzzy Core Equivalence in Large Economies: A Role for the Infinite-Dimensional Lyapunov Theorem, arXiv:2112.15539v1 (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.15539v1)

### One blocking rule for pairs and coalitions equates strong core and stability

**Remember:** Allow ties in both tests, but always require someone to gain.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 91B68 (Matching models), 91A12. arXiv econ.TH. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A coalition strongly blocks a matching if a feasible rematching among its members makes all of them weakly better off and at least one strictly better off. The strong core excludes all such blocks, and strong stability requires individual rationality and excludes such blocks by worker–firm pairs.

**Problem.** For many-to-one matching with responsive preferences and possible ties, the strong core equals the set of strongly stable matchings.

**How the definition helps.** Pairs and coalitions use the same improvement test, so every matching in the strong core is strongly stable (our own). The paper's work is the reverse inclusion, which finds a blocking pair inside any blocking coalition.

**Paper or page:** [Core and stability notions in many-to-one matching markets with indifferences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.16293v1). It says: “the strong core coincides with the strongly stable set”

**Sources:**

- [Agustín G. Bonifacio, Noelia Juarez, Pablo Neme, Jorge Oviedo, Core and stability notions in many-to-one matching markets with indifferences, arXiv:2203.16293v1 (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.16293v1)

### Quasi-stability permits repair by iteration

**Remember:** Allow blocks from unemployed workers while the matching is being repaired.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 91B68 (Matching models). arXiv econ.TH. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A worker and firm block a matching if the worker prefers the firm and the firm would choose the worker from its staff plus that worker. A matching is worker-quasi-stable if all assignments are acceptable and every blocking pair has an unemployed worker. It is stable if all assignments are acceptable and there are no blocking pairs at all.

**Problem.** Assume finitely many workers and firms, strict preferences, and substitutable firm choices. The paper's repair round maps worker-quasi-stable matchings to worker-quasi-stable matchings, and its fixed points are exactly the stable matchings.

**How the definition helps.** Quasi-stability confines blocks to unemployed workers, so a repair round lets each apply to their favorite blocking firm while firms choose from applicants and staff (our own explanation). The hard step shows that no employed worker can block afterwards. A fixed point therefore has no unemployed blocker either, so it is stable; a stable matching has no applicants, so it is fixed.

**Paper or page:** [The lattice of worker-quasi-stable matchings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.16330v4). It says: “T(μ) = μ if and only if μ is stable.”

**Sources:**

- [Bonifacio, Guiñazú, Juarez, Neme and Oviedo, The lattice of worker-quasi-stable matchings (2022)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.geb.2022.06.004)

### Vote-margin edge weights turn popularity into one maximum-weight matching test

**Remember:** A rival matching's total weight is its vote margin against M.

*True by definition.* MSC 91B68 (Matching models), 05C70, 90C27. arXiv econ.TH, cs.GT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A matching M is popular if no rival matching wins more votes against it in a head-to-head vote. Weight each edge by the sum of its endpoints' votes, +1, 0 or −1 for preferring that partner to their partner in M, with unmatched ranked below acceptable partners. Give each vertex a self-loop weighted by its vote for being unmatched, so a rival's weight is its vote margin against M.

**Problem.** With strict preferences on both sides and incomplete lists, M is popular exactly when it is a maximum-weight matching for these weights, a test due to Biró, Irving and Manlove (2010). The paper derives the separate graph-structural tests for popularity from it, and back.

**How the definition helps.** A rival matching, completed with self-loops, counts each vertex's vote exactly once, so its weight is its vote margin against M, and M itself has weight zero (our own). So M is popular exactly when no matching has positive weight, that is, when M has maximum weight (our own).

**Paper or page:** [On the Equivalence of the Graph-Structural and Optimization-Based Characterizations of Popular Matchings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.00349v1). It says: “an optimization-based characterization described by maximum-weight matchings.”

**Sources:**

- [Yuga Kanaya, Kenjiro Takazawa, On the Equivalence of the Graph-Structural and Optimization-Based Characterizations of Popular Matchings, arXiv:2508.00349v1 (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.00349v1)
- [Péter Biró, Robert W. Irving, David F. Manlove, Popular Matchings in the Marriage and Roommates Problems, Algorithms and Complexity (CIAC 2010), Lecture Notes in Computer Science 6078 (2010), 97-108](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-13073-1_10)

### Linear portfolio rules make mean–variance optimization quadratic

**Remember:** Affine returns give linear means and quadratic variances.

*True by definition.* MSC 91G10 (Portfolio theory), 90C20. arXiv q-fin.PM, math.OC. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An affine portfolio rule chooses weights w₀(h) + ∑ⱼ θⱼwⱼ(h) at each observed history h, with baseline weights summing to one, adjustment vectors summing to zero, and coefficients θⱼ as the decision variables. The next return is then affine in the θⱼ, however nonlinearly the weights depend on h.

**Problem.** Assume the return terms have finite second moments. Minimizing return variance minus a nonnegative multiple of expected return gives a convex quadratic problem in the coefficients.

**How the definition helps.** An affine return has expectation affine in θ and variance quadratic in θ, with a positive semidefinite covariance matrix (our own). So variance minus a nonnegative multiple of the mean is a convex quadratic (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Signature Methods in Stochastic Portfolio Theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.02322v3). It says: “the following two optimization problems are convex quadratic optimization problems”

**Sources:**

- [Signature Methods in Stochastic Portfolio Theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.02322v3)

### Wealth-weighted portfolios add their wealth

**Remember:** Combine the accounts by current size, not by their starting shares.

*True by definition.* MSC 91G10 (Portfolio theory). arXiv q-fin.PM. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Split one unit of initial wealth into nonnegative shares summing to one, and let each account follow its own self-financing strategy. While total wealth is positive, the combined strategy weights each account's asset mix by that account's current share of total wealth, so it holds exactly the sum of the accounts' holdings (our own).

**Problem.** Under the paper’s continuous-time trading assumptions, this mix funds its own trades. On each price path its wealth equals the sum of the separately funded accounts.

**How the definition helps.** Since the combined holdings are the sum of the separate holdings, its gains are the sum of their gains (our own). Fixed starting weights would instead need money moved between accounts when returns differ (our own). The paper checks that this rule is a valid continuous-time trading strategy path by path.

**Paper or page:** [Model-free portfolio allocation in continuous-time](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.05470v3). It says: “then θ̂(b) ∈ Θ and W(θ̂(b)) = ∑ₖ₌₁ᵐ bₖ W(θ⁽ᵏ⁾)”

**Sources:**

- [Henry Chiu. Model-free portfolio allocation in continuous-time (2025).](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.05470v3)

### Closures catch vanishing-risk free lunches

**Remember:** Not even a limit of trades may give a riskless profit.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 91G15 (Financial markets). arXiv q-fin.MF. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** No free lunch with vanishing risk says that trades cannot even approach a riskless profit. Take the bounded payoffs no greater than the final gains of zero-cost trades whose wealth stays bounded below, and add all their limits in the essential supremum norm. The condition holds when zero is the only payoff in this closed set that is nonnegative apart from events of probability zero.

**Problem.** Let finitely many discounted prices over a finite horizon be locally bounded semimartingales. There is no free lunch with vanishing risk exactly when some probability with the same null events makes the prices local martingales.

**How the definition helps.** Closing the set in the uniform norm adds the limits of trades whose possible losses shrink to zero, so the condition rules these out too (our own). The Delbaen–Schachermayer fundamental theorem matches this closed condition with a probability that has the same null events and makes the prices local martingales (our own).

**Paper or page:** [The Golden Age of the Mathematical Finance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.06693v2). It says: “There are not free lunches with vanishing risk if and only if there is probability ℙ∗ ∼ ℙ under which S̃ is a local martingale.”

**Sources:**

- [Freddy Delbaen, Walter Schachermayer. A general version of the fundamental theorem of asset pricing (1994).](https://doi.org/10.1007/bf01450498)

### Comonotonic prices satisfy put–call parity

**Remember:** Payoffs that rise together are priced by adding.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 91G20 (Derivative securities (option pricing, hedging, etc.)). arXiv q-fin.PR. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Two payoffs X and Y are comonotonic when they rise and fall together: (X(s) − X(t))(Y(s) − Y(t)) ≥ 0 for every pair of states s, t. A pricing rule f is comonotonic additive when f(X + Y) = f(X) + f(Y) for every comonotonic pair.

**Problem.** For bounded measurable payoffs, a monotone pricing rule, one that never prices a pointwise smaller payoff higher, satisfies the paper’s put–call parity exactly when it is comonotonic additive.

**How the definition helps.** A call, a short put and a constant strike rise together and sum to the underlying payoff, so comonotonic additivity prices the underlying as the sum of their prices (our own). The paper’s parity characterization proves the converse for monotone rules on bounded measurable payoffs.

**Paper or page:** [Put-Call Parities, absence of arbitrage opportunities and non-linear pricing rules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.16292v1). It says: “satisfies PCP if and only if it is Comonotonic Additive.”

**Sources:**

- [Bastianello, Chateauneuf and Cornet, Put–Call Parities, absence of arbitrage opportunities, and nonlinear pricing rules (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1111/mafi.12433)

### One currency prices both markets

**Remember:** Measure euros and dollars in one shared unit.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 91G20 (Derivative securities (option pricing, hedging, etc.)). arXiv q-fin.PR. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Price both currencies in an intermediate unit in which they play symmetric roles: if one euro costs f dollars, one euro costs √f units and one dollar costs 1/√f units. A payoff has degree one if multiplying both its inputs by a positive factor multiplies the payoff by that factor.

**Problem.** In the paper’s euro–dollar model, consider options payable only at expiry with degree-one payoffs. The same pricing probability values options written on euros and options written on dollars.

**How the definition helps.** In the shared unit, options on euros and options on dollars are priced under one probability, and degree one lets the payoff be rescaled into that unit (our own). The paper constructs the intermediate interest rate and proves that this pricing probability exists.

**Paper or page:** [Pricing FX Options under Intermediate Currency](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.01387v2), [Pricing FX Options under Intermediate Currency](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.01387v2). It says: “Then the arbitrage price of a European option on EUR with a payoff g(x; K) being homogeneous function of order 1 and maturity time T is given by”

**Sources:**

- [S. Maurer, T. E. Sharp, M. V. Tretyakov. Pricing FX Options under Intermediate Currency (2021).](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.01387v2)

### Directional closure makes capital limits attainable

**Remember:** If every extra sliver suffices, nothing extra is needed.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 91G70 (Statistical methods; risk measures). arXiv q-fin.RM. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let A be an upward-closed set of acceptable positions and π a linear price on eligible trades, with an eligible U ≥ 0 of price one. Put B = A + ker π, the positions that some zero-price trade makes acceptable. Directional closure says that x lies in B whenever x + εU lies in B for every ε &gt; 0.

**Problem.** Required capital is the infimum price of trades making a position safe. Fix any real budget m. Directional closure holds exactly when every position requiring at most m admits a trade costing m that makes it safe.

**How the definition helps.** A trade costing m makes x safe exactly when x + mU lies in B, and capital at most m puts x + (m + ε)U in B for every ε &gt; 0 (our own). Closure then gives x + mU; conversely, budget attainment applied to y − mU puts y in B whenever every y + εU lies in B (our own). If only strictly positive balances are acceptable, every positive deposit works at the zero position but zero does not (our own).

**Paper or page:** [A new view on risk measures associated with acceptance sets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.12320v2). It says: “holds if and only if A + ker π is (−U)-directionally closed.”

**Sources:**

- [A new view on risk measures associated with acceptance sets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.12320v2)

### Logarithms turn risk products into sums

**Remember:** Logs turn dividing by a payoff into subtracting capital.

*True by definition.* MSC 91G70 (Statistical methods; risk measures). arXiv q-fin.RM. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a positive loss factor X, η(X) is the infimum price of a positive eligible payoff H that makes X/H acceptable, with positive prices. In logarithmic units, dividing by H becomes subtracting log H, at a cost equal to the logarithm of H's price. So log η(X) is the capital requirement for log X with these log payoffs and log costs (our own).

**Problem.** Assume products stay in the loss domain and the risks are positive and finite. Then η(XY) ≤ η(X)η(Y) exactly when the corresponding risk on log losses is subadditive, meaning the risk of a sum never exceeds the summed risks.

**How the definition helps.** Since log η(X) is the risk of log X, taking logarithms turns η(XY) ≤ η(X)η(Y) into subadditivity of the log risk (our own). The identity follows by translating every acceptable trade into log units and taking its infimum cost (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Multi-asset return risk measures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.08763v2). It says: “is subadditive if and only if ηℜ is submultiplicative, i.e., ∀ X,Y ∈ C: ηℜ(XY) ≤ ηℜ(X)ηℜ(Y).”

**Sources:**

- [Multi-asset return risk measures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.08763v2)

### Moment bounds control worst-case risk

**Remember:** Compare only means and covariances, and the ball can only grow.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 91G70 (Statistical methods; risk measures). arXiv q-fin.RM. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Quadratic transport distance is the least root mean square separation over all joint realizations of two finite-second-moment laws. The transport ball of radius ρ contains every such law within this distance ρ of the reference law. The Gelbrich set of radius ρ contains every such law whose mean and covariance lie within ρ of the reference’s, comparing moments by the transport distance between the matching Gaussian laws.

**Problem.** For the same reference law and radius, the supremum of risk over the Gelbrich set bounds the supremum over the transport ball from above.

**How the definition helps.** By the Gelbrich inequality, replacing two laws by Gaussians with the same means and covariances never increases their transport distance, so the transport ball lies inside the Gelbrich set (our own). A supremum over a larger set is larger, for each fixed loss function.

**Paper or page:** [Mean-Covariance Robust Risk Measurement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.09959v3), [Mean-Covariance Robust Risk Measurement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.09959v3). It says: “then we have 𝒲ᵨ(ℙ̂) ⊆ 𝒢ᵨ(μ̂, Σ̂).”

**Sources:**

- [Viet Anh Nguyen, Soroosh Shafiee, Damir Filipović, Daniel Kuhn. Mean-Covariance Robust Risk Measurement (2025).](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.09959v3)

## 92 Biology and other natural sciences

### Clock trees give ultrametric distances

**Remember:** Equal tip heights make the two largest triple distances tie.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 92B10 (Taxonomy, cladistics, statistics in mathematical biology). arXiv q-bio.PE. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A clock tree is a rooted tree with the same total length from the root to every tip, as under a strict evolutionary clock with tips sampled at one time. So the distance between two tips is twice the height of their most recent common ancestor above the tips (our own).

**Problem.** For any three tips of a clock tree with positive edge lengths, the largest two pair distances are equal. Its tip distances are therefore an ultrametric.

**How the definition helps.** Among three tips, two pairs share the oldest common ancestor, so their distances tie for largest (our own). This tie is the ultrametric inequality: each distance is at most the larger of the other two (our own). A three-tip star with edge lengths 1, 2 and 3 gives distances 3, 4 and 5 instead (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Hit and Run Sampling from Tropically Convex Sets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.15045v1). It says: “Then, u is an ultrametric if and only if T is an equidistant tree.”

**Sources:**

- [Peter Buneman, A note on the metric properties of trees (1974).](https://doi.org/10.1016/0095-8956(74)90047-1)

### Fitch sets count minimum changes

**Remember:** Keep every cheapest state, then intersect for free or unite for one.

*True by definition.* MSC 92B10 (Taxonomy, cladistics, statistics in mathematical biology). arXiv q-bio.PE, q-bio.QM. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** On a rooted binary tree with known leaf states, the Fitch set of a vertex holds every state it can take in an assignment with the fewest changes within its subtree. So a parent state in a child’s set adds nothing for that child, and any other parent state adds exactly one change, on the joining edge (our own).

**Problem.** Starting at the leaves, use the intersection of the two child sets whenever it contains a state. Otherwise use their union and count one change. The total count is the smallest possible number of changes on the tree.

**How the definition helps.** The parent’s cheapest states are those in both child sets, at no extra charge, if any exist; otherwise every state in either set costs exactly one change (our own). This is the intersection-or-union rule, applied from the leaves to the root (our own). Keeping a single minimizing state instead of the whole set can overcount (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Ancestral reconstruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancestral_reconstruction). It says: “if the intersection is the empty set, then it is the set union.”

**Sources:**

- [W. M. Fitch, Toward Defining the Course of Evolution: Minimum Change for a Specific Tree Topology (1971)](https://doi.org/10.2307/2412116)

### Split counts give a tree metric

**Remember:** Count the edge splits that only one tree has.

*True by definition.* MSC 92B10 (Taxonomy, cladistics, statistics in mathematical biology). arXiv q-bio.PE. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For two unrooted evolutionary trees on the same labeled tips, list each tree’s splits, the two-part partitions of the tips made by cutting one edge. The Robinson–Foulds distance is the number of splits that appear in exactly one list.

**Problem.** This distance is a metric on unweighted trees with the same labeled tips and no degree-two internal nodes. Identify trees when an isomorphism preserves their tip labels.

**How the definition helps.** Each tree becomes a 0–1 list over all possible splits, and the distance counts unequal entries, so the triangle inequality holds as for Hamming distance (our own). Distance zero identifies the trees by the theorem that a tree’s splits determine it (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Robinson–Foulds metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robinson%E2%80%93Foulds_metric). It says: “the number of splits that differ between a pair of trees”

**Sources:**

- [D. F. Robinson and L. R. Foulds, Comparison of phylogenetic trees (1981).](https://doi.org/10.1016/0025-5564(81)90043-2)

### Tree splits explain four-point ties

**Remember:** A tip distance adds up every edge that separates the tips.

*True by definition.* MSC 92B10 (Taxonomy, cladistics, statistics in mathematical biology). arXiv q-bio.PE. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The distance between two tips of an evolutionary tree is the total length of the edges on their path, that is, of the edges whose removal separates the two tips.

**Problem.** For four distinct tips, sum the two distances in each of the three possible pairings. The largest sum occurs at least twice in any tree with nonnegative edge lengths.

**How the definition helps.** Each pairing sum counts every edge once for each of its pairs that the edge separates (our own). An edge cutting off one tip adds its length to all three sums, and all edges splitting two tips from two induce the same split, since tree splits are compatible (our own). Those edges add twice their length to the two crossing pairings and nothing to the third, so the crossing sums tie for largest (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Tropical Grassmannian and Tropical Linear Varieties from phylogenetic trees](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.0752v2). It says: “the maximum of three number is achieved at least twice D({i,j}) + D({k,l}), D({i,k}) + D({j,l}) and D({i,l}) + D({j,k}).”

**Sources:**

- [Peter Buneman, A note on the metric properties of trees (1974).](https://doi.org/10.1016/0095-8956(74)90047-1)

### Single-neuron updates prevent Hopfield cycles

**Remember:** Move one neuron at a time, and every flip lowers energy.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 92B20 (Neural networks for/in biological studies, artificial life and related topics). arXiv q-bio.NC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** In a finite Hopfield network with states ±1, symmetric weights and no self-connections, update one neuron at a time to the sign of its weighted input, keeping its state at zero input, and visit every neuron infinitely often. Because weights are symmetric and only one neuron moves, each flip lowers the energy, minus the sum over pairs of weight times the product of states (our own).

**Problem.** Every such update run eventually reaches a fixed state.

**How the definition helps.** A flip changes the energy by minus the neuron’s input times its state change, which is negative, so only finitely many flips occur (our own). After the last flip, repeated visits show that every neuron agrees with its input, so the state is fixed (our own). Under simultaneous updates, two positively coupled neurons in opposite states swap forever (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Hopfield network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopfield_network). It says: “The constraint that weights are symmetric guarantees that the energy function decreases monotonically while following the activation rules.”

**Sources:**

- [J. J. Hopfield, Neural networks and physical systems with emergent collective computational abilities (1982)](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.79.8.2554)
- [J. Bruck, On the convergence properties of the Hopfield model (1990)](https://doi.org/10.1109/5.58341)

### Crossover distances add across intervals

**Remember:** Count every crossover, not just whether the markers switched.

*True by definition.* MSC 92D10 (Genetics and epigenetics). arXiv q-bio.GN, q-bio.PE. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Genetic distance in morgans is the expected number of crossovers, exchanges of segments between paired chromosomes, between two markers on a transmitted chromosome. It counts crossovers, not merely whether the two markers come from different parental chromosomes, which is the recombination fraction.

**Problem.** Genetic distances add across adjacent intervals. If the crossover count has a Poisson distribution with mean d, the recombination fraction equals (1 − exp(−2d))/2.

**How the definition helps.** Crossover counts on adjacent intervals add on each chromosome, so their expectations add without any independence assumption (our own). The markers switch parental chromosomes only for an odd count, and for a Poisson count N with mean d, E\[(−1)ᴺ\] = exp(−2d) equals one minus twice the odd-count probability (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Centimorgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centimorgan). It says: “the distance in centimorgans does not correspond exactly to the probability of genetic recombination.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Linkage excess decays geometrically

**Remember:** Subtract independent pairing first, then recombination scales only the excess.

*True by definition.* MSC 92D10 (Genetics and epigenetics). arXiv q-bio.PE. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Linkage disequilibrium D is the frequency of chromosomes carrying both chosen variants at two positions, minus the product of the two variants’ separate frequencies. It measures the excess over independent pairing.

**Problem.** In a deterministic random-mating model with no selection, mutation or migration, D becomes (1 − c)D each generation. Here c is the fixed fraction of reproductive cells in which recombination separates the two positions.

**How the definition helps.** Each generation, recombinant chromosomes carry both variants with the independent frequency pq, and the others keep the joint frequency J (our own). So J′ = (1 − c)J + cpq while p and q stay fixed, and subtracting pq gives D′ = (1 − c)D (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Linkage disequilibrium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linkage_disequilibrium). It says: “recombination is expected to decrease the value of D in each generation by a factor (1 - c)”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Relative fitness isolates selection

**Remember:** Divide each ancestor’s descendant count by the mean descendant count.

*True by definition.* MSC 92D15 (Problems related to evolution). arXiv q-bio.PE. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Assign each descendant to one ancestor, and assume at least one descendant exists. An ancestor’s relative fitness is its descendant count divided by the mean count per ancestor, so relative fitnesses average to one (our own).

**Problem.** The change in mean trait equals the covariance of relative fitness with ancestral trait, plus the average of relative fitness times the change from each ancestor’s trait to its descendants’ mean trait. Both averages weight ancestors equally, and childless ancestors add zero.

**How the definition helps.** Because relative fitness has mean one, the fitness-weighted ancestral mean differs from the plain mean by exactly the covariance (our own). Adding and subtracting this weighted mean splits the change into that covariance and the change within families (our own). Predicting either term still needs a model of reproduction and transmission (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Price equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Price_equation). It says: “The equation uses a covariance between a characteristic and fitness, to give a mathematical description of evolution and natural selection.”

**Sources:**

- [George R. Price, Selection and Covariance (1970).](https://doi.org/10.1038/227520a0)

### Log populations preserve volume

**Remember:** Use log sizes so each growth equation ignores its own coordinate.

*True by definition.* MSC 92D25 (Population dynamics (general)). arXiv math.DS, q-bio.PE. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Use the logarithm of each population size as its coordinate, where each species’ per capita growth rate is a constant plus multiples of the other species’ sizes, with no term in its own size. Then the velocity of each log coordinate is that growth rate, which does not depend on the coordinate itself (our own).

**Problem.** The flow preserves ordinary volume in log coordinates wherever the solutions exist and stay positive.

**How the definition helps.** Each velocity component ignores its own coordinate, so the divergence is zero and Liouville’s theorem gives preservation of volume in log coordinates (our own). In population coordinates, the same volume weights each region by the reciprocal product of the population sizes (our own).

**Paper or page:** [On a quadratic Poisson algebra and integrable Lotka-Volterra systems with solutions in terms of Lambert's W function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.14720v2). It says: “with aᵢᵢ = 0 are measure preserving with density M = (∏ᵢ₌₁ⁿ xᵢ)⁻¹.”

**Sources:**

- [Peter H. van der Kamp, D. I. McLaren and G. R. W. Quispel, On a quadratic Poisson algebra and integrable Lotka-Volterra systems with solutions in terms of Lambert's W function (2024).](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.14720v2)

### Reproductive value gives exact growth

**Remember:** Weight each age by its future offspring, and growth becomes exact.

*True by definition.* MSC 92D25 (Population dynamics (general)). arXiv q-bio.PE, math.DS. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The reproductive values of an age projection matrix A are the entries of a positive left eigenvector w for its dominant eigenvalue λ, so wA = λw (our own). The weighted population total adds each age count times its reproductive value.

**Problem.** For a primitive age projection matrix, the weighted total grows by its dominant eigenvalue every step, from any starting age distribution. Primitive means that some power of the matrix has strictly positive entries.

**How the definition helps.** Since wA = λw, one step multiplies the weighted total by exactly λ, from any starting age counts (our own). The Perron–Frobenius theorem supplies the positive w for a primitive matrix, and the age model ties it to discounted future offspring (our own). The plain head count’s growth factor generally approaches λ only in the limit (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Reproductive value (population genetics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reproductive_value_%28population_genetics%29). It says: “he proposed that future offspring be discounted at the rate of growth of the population”

**Sources:**

- [Ronald A. Fisher, The Genetical Theory of Natural Selection (1930).](https://doi.org/10.5962/bhl.title.27468)
- [P. H. Leslie, On the use of matrices in certain population mathematics (1945).](https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/33.3.183)

### Effective reproduction locates infection peaks

**Remember:** Infections grow exactly while each case causes more than one.

*True by definition.* MSC 92D30 (Epidemiology). arXiv q-bio.PE. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** In the closed SIR model S′ = −βSI, I′ = βSI − γI with constants β, γ &gt; 0, the effective reproduction number R = βS/γ compares the per-infected transmission rate with the recovery rate. So I′ = γI(R − 1), and infections grow exactly while R &gt; 1 (our own).

**Problem.** If I starts positive and R starts above one, I has a unique peak when R reaches one.

**How the definition helps.** S only decreases, so R falls through one at most once, and I′ changes sign there from positive to negative (our own). While R ≥ 1, I stays above its positive start, so S decreases at least at the fixed rate γI(0) and reaches γ/β in finite time (our own).

**Paper or page:** [The SIR model of an epidemic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.12029). It says: “The peak infection takes place when the effective reproduction number r₀ S = 1.”

**Sources:**

- [The SIR model of an epidemic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.12029)

### Effective diversity scales with replication

**Remember:** Exponentiating entropy makes doubling equal, disjoint samples double their diversity.

*True by definition.* MSC 92D40 (Ecology). arXiv q-bio.QM. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For each species with positive frequency p, form −p ln p and sum over species to obtain Shannon entropy H. Define order-one Hill diversity as exp(H), the number of equally common species that would give the same entropy.

**Problem.** Pool equally weighted communities with disjoint species and the same species frequency pattern. The pooled order-one Hill diversity equals the diversity of one community times the number of communities.

**How the definition helps.** Exponentiation turns the additive entropy increase into a multiplicative change in diversity (our own). Pooling m equal communities replaces each frequency p with m copies of p/m because the species sets are disjoint (our own). Substitution in the entropy sum adds ln m, so the effective number of species grows by a factor of m (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Diversity index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diversity_index). It says: “Hill numbers of order q or effective number of species”

**Sources:**

- [Lou Jost, Entropy and diversity (2006).](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2006.0030-1299.14714.x)

### Weighted contrasts give independent comparisons

**Remember:** Take the child difference and pass up the weighted mean.

*True by definition.* MSC 92B10 (Taxonomy, cladistics, statistics in mathematical biology), 92B15. arXiv q-bio.QM. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Starting at the tips, with each observed trait’s variance given by its branch, standardize each sister difference and pass the pair’s inverse-variance weighted mean upward. For child estimates x, y with variances a, b, record (x − y)/√(a + b), pass up (bx + ay)/(a + b), and give it variance ab/(a + b) plus the variance of the branch above. These weights make each passed-up mean uncorrelated with the difference just recorded (our own).

**Problem.** Suppose changes on separate branches are independent centered Gaussian variables with variance proportional to positive branch length. The standardized differences are independent centered Gaussian variables with variance one.

**How the definition helps.** Each difference cancels the common ancestral value and has zero covariance with the mean passed up, and jointly Gaussian variables with zero covariance are independent (our own). An unweighted mean lacks this property when the variances differ (our own). The updated variance lets the same argument repeat at each parent (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Phylogenetic comparative methods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phylogenetic_comparative_methods). It says: “transform the original tip data (mean values for a set of species) into values that are statistically independent and identically distributed.”

**Sources:**

- [J. Felsenstein, Phylogenies and the Comparative Method (1985)](https://doi.org/10.1086/284325)

### Spike edit costs vary continuously

**Remember:** Minimize unpaired spikes plus movement price times total paired displacement.

*True by definition.* MSC 92C20 (Neural biology). arXiv q-bio.NC, q-bio.QM. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For two finite spike trains, pair any subsets of their spikes one-to-one in chronological order. The Victor–Purpura distance at q ≥ 0 minimizes the number of unpaired spikes plus q times total absolute timing displacement over all such pairings.

**Problem.** For trains with at most one spike at each integer time from 0 to T, the distance is Lipschitz in q ≥ 0. Its change is at most T(T + 1) ÷ 2 times the absolute change in q.

**How the definition helps.** Each pairing’s cost is affine in q with slope equal to its total displacement, and a minimum of such functions is Lipschitz with the largest slope (our own). With k pairs matched in order, the two times in each pair differ by at most T + 1 − k (our own). So the total displacement is at most k(T + 1 − k) ≤ T(T + 1)/2 (our own).

**Paper or page:** [A Persistent Homology Pipeline for the Analysis of Neural Spike Train Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.08637). It says: “Let 𝖲 and 𝖲′ be two spike trains over the time domain X = {0, 1, 2, …, T}. For any q,q′ ≥ 0, we have \|VP<sub>q</sub>(𝖲, 𝖲′) − VP<sub>q</sub>′(𝖲, 𝖲′)\| ≤ T(T+1)/2 \|q−q′\|”

**Sources:**

- [A Persistent Homology Pipeline for the Analysis of Neural Spike Train Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.08637)

### Harmonic normalization removes sample-size bias

**Remember:** Divide the variable-site count by the harmonic sum for the sample.

*True by definition.* MSC 92D10 (Genetics and epigenetics), 92B15. arXiv q-bio.PE, q-bio.GN. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Sample n ≥ 2 gene copies from one randomly mating population of constant size, and count the sites where at least two copies differ. Watterson’s estimator divides this count by H = 1 + 1/2 + ⋯ + 1/(n − 1), which adds 1/(k − 1) for each stage of the ancestry with k lines (our own).

**Problem.** Assume the standard neutral coalescent without recombination, with mutations at a constant rate, each at a new site. Then the estimator has expectation θ, the population-scaled mutation rate for the sequence.

**How the definition helps.** The expected count is θ/2 times the expected total tree length, measured in units where each pair of lines merges at rate one (our own). A stage with k lines lasts 2/\[k(k − 1)\] on average and so adds 2/(k − 1) to that length (our own). Summing gives θH, so dividing by H leaves θ (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Watterson estimator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watterson_estimator). It says: “When its assumptions are met, the estimator is unbiased”

**Sources:**

- [G. A. Watterson, On the number of segregating sites in genetical models without recombination (1975)](https://doi.org/10.1016/0040-5809(75)90020-9)

### Evolutionary stability rejects neutral ties

**Remember:** When payoffs against residents tie, compare both strategies against the mutant.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 92D15 (Problems related to evolution). arXiv q-bio.PE, math.DS. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A strategy of a symmetric game is evolutionarily stable if it earns more than each alternative in a population with a small enough positive share of that alternative. Equivalently, it does at least as well against itself as any alternative does, and in a tie it does strictly better against the alternative.

**Problem.** Under replicator dynamics, each strategy’s share grows at its payoff minus the mean payoff. Every evolutionarily stable strategy of a finite symmetric two-player game is then locally asymptotically stable.

**How the definition helps.** Evolutionary stability gives the resident a strict payoff advantage over every nearby population mix (our own). Under replicator dynamics, relative entropy from the resident to the population then strictly decreases, a local Lyapunov function that proves attraction and stability (our own). If only mutual B earns one, all-A is a Nash equilibrium but a rare B grows (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Evolutionarily stable strategy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evolutionarily_stable_strategy). It says: “the population of players who continue to play strategy S has an advantage when playing against T.”

**Sources:**

- [John Maynard Smith and George R. Price, The Logic of Animal Conflict (1973).](https://doi.org/10.1038/246015a0)
- [Peter D. Taylor and Leo B. Jonker, Evolutionary stable strategies and game dynamics (1978).](https://doi.org/10.1016/0025-5564(78)90077-9)

### Weak reversibility excludes one-way sinks

**Remember:** Every reaction needs a return path, not necessarily a reverse edge.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 92E20 (Classical flows, reactions, etc. in chemistry), 92C42. arXiv q-bio.MN. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A reaction network is weakly reversible if every reaction can be undone by a chain of reactions, that is, every arrow between complexes lies on a directed cycle. Its deficiency is the number of complexes, minus the number of connected components of the reaction graph, minus the dimension spanned by the reaction change vectors.

**Problem.** Suppose each reaction rate equals a positive constant times the product of reactant concentrations raised to their reaction coefficients. Every weakly reversible network of deficiency zero then has a positive equilibrium where incoming and outgoing rates balance at each complex.

**How the definition helps.** A return path excludes complexes that can only lose material through a one-way reaction (our own). For example, A → B has deficiency zero but no equilibrium with A positive (our own). The deficiency-zero theorem proves existence for every choice of positive rate constants (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Advancing Mathematical Epidemiology and Chemical Reaction Network Theory via Synergies Between Them](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00488). It says: “𝒩 admits a “complex-balanced” equilibrium, and all its equilibria are complex-balanced.”

**Sources:**

- [Advancing Mathematical Epidemiology and Chemical Reaction Network Theory via Synergies Between Them](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00488)

### Any orchard cherry reduction works

**Remember:** Pick cherries until one leaf remains.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 92B10 (Taxonomy, cladistics, statistics in mathematical biology). arXiv q-bio.PE. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A rooted binary network is orchard if some sequence of cherry reductions, suppressing unary vertices including a unary root after each step, shrinks it to one leaf. A reduction either deletes one of two leaves sharing a parent, or cuts the edge from one leaf’s branching parent to the other leaf’s two-parent vertex.

**Problem.** Every maximal sequence of cherry reductions in an orchard network ends at one leaf.

**How the definition helps.** The key step proves that any legal reduction of an orchard network leaves an orchard network (our own). Each move shrinks the network, and every nontrivial orchard network has another move, so no maximal sequence gets stuck (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Defining phylogenetic networks using ancestral profiles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.00109). It says: “Let 𝒩 be an orchard network, and let 𝒩 = 𝒩₀, 𝒩₁, …, 𝒩ₗ be a maximal cherry-reduction sequence. Then this sequence is complete.”

**Sources:**

- [Defining phylogenetic networks using ancestral profiles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.00109)

### Child labels identify tree-child networks

**Remember:** A child with one parent appears in exactly one child set.

*True by definition.* MSC 92B10 (Taxonomy, cladistics, statistics in mathematical biology). arXiv q-bio.PE. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A network is tree-child if every vertex with children has a child with exactly one parent. In the paper’s encoding, each such vertex becomes the set of its children’s labels, so a label occurs in the cover once for each parent of its vertex (our own).

**Problem.** For networks admitting this encoding, the network is tree-child exactly when every set contains a label occurring only once in the cover.

**How the definition helps.** A child with one parent is a label that occurs once, so tree-child asks for such a label in every set (our own). The work lies in the paper’s bijection between these covers and the networks that admit the labeling (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Phylogenetic network classes through the lens of expanding covers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.06519v2). It says: “Tree-child networks are in bijection with expanding covers for which each set contains an integer that appears exactly once in the cover.”

**Sources:**

- [Andrew Francis, Daniele Marchei and Mike Steel, Phylogenetic network classes through the lens of expanding covers (2024).](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.06519v2)

### Leaf correlations contract forest space

**Remember:** Stretch every leaf edge, and all correlations shrink to zero.

*True by definition.* MSC 92B10 (Taxonomy, cladistics, statistics in mathematical biology). arXiv q-bio.PE, q-bio.QM. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Wald space records each labeled forest with positive edge lengths by its correlation matrix: connected labels get exp(−d), where d is their path distance, and disconnected labels get zero. The forests have distinct labels on distinct vertices, and every vertex of degree at most two carries a label.

**Problem.** Wald space can shrink continuously to the matrix for isolated labels.

**How the definition helps.** Because correlation is exp(−distance), moving each label onto a new pendant edge of length −ln(t)/2 multiplies every off-diagonal correlation by t, for 0 &lt; t &lt; 1 (our own). Pruning unlabeled dead ends and suppressing unlabeled degree-two vertices keeps label distances and returns a forest of the allowed kind (our own). Letting t run from 1 to 0 contracts the space continuously to the matrix of isolated labels (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Foundations of the Wald Space for Phylogenetic Trees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.05332). It says: “Conveyed by the homeomorphism φ, 𝒲 is star shaped as a subset ℝᴺˣᴺ with respect to F∞ and hence contractible.”

**Sources:**

- [Foundations of the Wald Space for Phylogenetic Trees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.05332)

### Stack-free networks have unique profiles

**Remember:** Without stacks, ancestral path counts pin down the network.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 92B10 (Taxonomy, cladistics, statistics in mathematical biology), 92D15. arXiv q-bio.PE. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A network is stack-free if no edge joins two vertices that both have several parents. Its ancestral profile lists, for each leaf label, the numbers of paths to that leaf from all internal vertices, in a common vertex order.

**Problem.** Among rooted phylogenetic networks on the same leaf labels, the ancestral profile determines a stack-free orchard network, one that cherry reductions shrink to one leaf, up to relabeling internal vertices.

**How the definition helps.** Stacked reticulations can give different orchard networks the same path counts, and stack-freeness removes these counterexamples (our own). The proof reads a legal cherry reduction from the profile and shows that it can be reversed in only one way (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Defining phylogenetic networks using ancestral profiles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.00109). It says: “Then, up to isomorphism, 𝒩 is the unique phylogenetic network on X realising Σ𝒩.”

**Sources:**

- [A. Bai, P. L. Erdős, C. Semple and M. Steel, Defining phylogenetic networks using ancestral profiles (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mbs.2021.108537)

### Finite phase shifts test synchrony

**Remember:** Compose the two pulse responses before testing whether the phase gap shrinks.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 92B25 (Biological rhythms and synchronization), 92C20. arXiv q-bio.NC. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Two identical oscillators advance uniformly in phase; when one reaches phase one, it fires, resets to zero and moves the other’s phase from x to F(x) = x + g(x). Assume F increases, fixes 0 and 1, and is differentiable on \[0, 1\], one-sided at the ends. So each firing sends the phase gap x to 1 − F(x) (our own).

**Problem.** For two such oscillators that advance uniformly between pulses, simultaneous firing attracts nearby phases if \|F′(0)F′(1)\| &lt; 1. It repels nearby phases if this product has absolute value above one.

**How the definition helps.** Two firings give the map x ↦ 1 − F(1 − F(x)), whose derivative at zero is F′(1)F′(0) by the chain rule (our own). A derivative of absolute value below one attracts nearby gaps, and above one repels them (our own). A first-order approximation in pulse strength can give the wrong stability prediction.

**Paper or page:** [Infinitesimal phase response functions can be misleading](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.08392). It says: “Synchrony is g-attracting if \|(1 + ∂g/∂φ(0, ε))(1 + ∂g/∂φ(1, ε))\| &lt; 1,”

**Sources:**

- [Infinitesimal phase response functions can be misleading](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.08392)

### Subsamples inherit the same genealogy

**Remember:** Trace one pedigree; dropping labels just deletes them.

*True by definition.* MSC 92D10 (Genetics and epigenetics), 60J10. arXiv q-bio.PE. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Trace each sampled label back through one realized population pedigree, recording at each past generation which samples share an ancestor and that ancestor’s type. Since all labels follow the same pedigree, not separately simulated ones, dropping a label just deletes it from its block (our own).

**Problem.** Suppose each type has fixed population size and relabeling parents within types leaves the joint offspring law unchanged. Keeping the first m of n sampled labels gives the same ancestry law as sampling those m labels directly.

**How the definition helps.** Because the labels share one pedigree, the history of a subsample is the full history with the other labels deleted (our own). The probabilistic work shows that this restricted history has the law of a directly sampled one, using the relabeling assumption (our own).

**Paper or page:** [On the genealogy of multi-type Cannings models and their limiting exchangeable coalescents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10744). It says: “has the same distribution as the multi-type ancestral process”

**Sources:**

- [On the genealogy of multi-type Cannings models and their limiting exchangeable coalescents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10744)

## 93 Systems theory; control

### Transposition swaps controllability and observability

**Remember:** Transpose the dynamics and swap the input and output.

*True by definition.* MSC 93B05 (Controllability), 93B07. arXiv eess.SY, math.OC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The dual of a continuous-time linear system x′ = Ax + Bu, y = Cx with constant real matrices transposes and swaps roles: it uses Aᵀ for dynamics, Cᵀ for input and Bᵀ for output.

**Problem.** A finite-dimensional continuous-time linear system can reach every state from rest exactly when its dual can distinguish all initial states from their outputs.

**How the definition helps.** The dual’s observability matrix, with rows Bᵀ, BᵀAᵀ, …, is the transpose of the original’s controllability matrix \[B, AB, …\], and transposition preserves rank (our own). The Kalman rank tests say that full rank means every state is reachable, or every initial state is distinguishable (our own).

**nLab:** [controllability and observability](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/controllability+and+observability). It says: “Now controllability of the original system corresponds to observability of the dual, and vice versa.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Gramians detect unobservable states

**Remember:** Zero output energy means the state left no trace.

*True by definition.* MSC 93B07 (Observability), 93C05. arXiv math.OC, eess.SY. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** On a fixed interval of positive length, the observability Gramian W is the matrix for which xᵀWx is the integral of the squared output norm from initial state x with zero input. So xᵀWx = 0 exactly when the state x leaves no trace in the output (our own).

**Problem.** For a real finite-dimensional linear system, the observed output determines the initial state exactly when W is nonsingular.

**How the definition helps.** W is positive semidefinite, so it is singular exactly when some nonzero state has zero output energy (our own). By continuity, zero energy means zero output on the whole interval, and by linearity such a state looks like zero (our own). This replaces comparing whole output curves with checking one matrix (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Controllability and observability of tempered fractional differential systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.05349v1). It says: “if, and only if, the observability Gramian matrix”

**Sources:**

- [Controllability and observability of tempered fractional differential systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.05349v1)

### Error coordinates separate stability tests

**Remember:** Track the error and the two designs separate.

*True by definition.* MSC 93B52 (Feedback control), 93B53. arXiv eess.SY, cs.SY. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Describe the closed loop by the state x and the estimation error e = x − x̂, instead of x and the estimate x̂. In these coordinates the error obeys its own equation, free of x.

**Problem.** For x′ = Ax + Bu with output Cx, use feedback u = −Kx̂ from an observer that corrects its model by L(Cx − Cx̂). The closed loop’s eigenvalues are those of A − BK and A − LC, counted with multiplicity.

**How the definition helps.** Subtraction gives e′ = (A − LC)e, and substitution gives x′ = (A − BK)x + BKe (our own). The resulting matrix is block triangular, so its eigenvalues are those of its two diagonal blocks. The change of coordinates is invertible, so it keeps the eigenvalues (our own).

**nLab:** [controllability and observability](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/controllability+and+observability). It says: “the design of a feedback controller and of a state observer are mutually independent.”

**Wikipedia:** [Separation principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Separation_principle). It says: “the eigenvalues are just those of A − BK together with those of A − LC.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Strict properness prevents algebraic loops

**Remember:** One missing direct term breaks the instantaneous loop.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 93B52 (Feedback control), 93C05. arXiv eess.SY, cs.SY. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A scalar rational transfer function is strictly proper if it is zero or its numerator has smaller degree than its denominator. Equivalently, it tends to zero at high frequency, so its realizations have no direct term and the output depends only on the current state (our own).

**Problem.** Connect two proper finite-dimensional scalar linear time-invariant systems in feedback. If either transfer function is strictly proper, the current states and external inputs uniquely determine both current inputs.

**How the definition helps.** The strictly proper system’s output comes from its state alone, so it can be computed first and then fed to the other system (our own). If both systems have direct terms, the loop equation can fail: a static gain of −1 in negative feedback gives y = −(r − y), impossible for nonzero r (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Proper transfer function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proper_transfer_function). It says: “A strictly proper transfer function will approach zero as the frequency approaches infinity”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The bilinear transform preserves stability

**Remember:** The left half-plane goes inside the unit circle.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 93C57 (Sampled-data control/observation systems), 93C80. arXiv eess.SY, cs.SY. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For step size h &gt; 0, the bilinear transform sends a continuous rate s ≠ 2/h to the discrete multiplier z = (1 + hs/2)/(1 − hs/2). Its modulus \|z\| is the ratio of the distances from s to −2/h and to 2/h (our own).

**Problem.** If every eigenvalue of a state matrix has negative real part, every transformed eigenvalue has magnitude below one for every positive step size.

**How the definition helps.** A rate with negative real part is closer to −2/h than to 2/h, so its multiplier has modulus below one (our own). A rational function of a matrix maps each eigenvalue to its value there (our own). Forward Euler instead sends the stable rate −3 to the unstable multiplier −2 at step size 1 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Bilinear transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bilinear_transform). It says: “The bilinear transform maps the left half of the complex s-plane to the interior of the unit circle in the z-plane.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Minimum-phase systems compose reversibly

**Remember:** Both the system and its inverse must be causal and stable.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 93C80 (Frequency-response methods in control theory), 93D25. arXiv eess.SY, cs.SY. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A discrete-time linear time-invariant system is minimum-phase if both it and its inverse are causal, using only current and past inputs, and stable, mapping bounded inputs to bounded outputs.

**Problem.** A series connection of discrete-time minimum-phase systems is minimum-phase. Its inverse is the series of their inverses in reverse order.

**How the definition helps.** The inverse of a series connection is the series of the inverses in reverse order, and a series of causal stable systems is causal and stable (our own). By contrast, (z − 2)/(z − ½) is stable, but its causal inverse has a pole at 2, outside the unit circle, so bounded inputs can give unbounded outputs (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Minimum phase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_phase). It says: “a linear, time-invariant system is said to be minimum-phase if the system and its inverse are causal and stable.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Independent readings add information

**Remember:** Multiply Gaussian likelihoods by adding their information.

*True by definition.* MSC 93E11 (Filtering in stochastic control theory), 93E10. arXiv eess.SY, cs.SY. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The information form of a Gaussian with nonsingular covariance stores the precision matrix, the inverse covariance, and the information vector, the precision matrix times the mean. These are the coefficients of the quadratic and linear terms in the log density (our own).

**Problem.** Start from a Gaussian prior and take linear measurements with centered Gaussian errors, independent of each other and of the state, all covariances nonsingular. Each measurement then adds its own term to the precision matrix and to the information vector.

**How the definition helps.** Multiplying independent likelihoods adds log densities, so it adds these coefficients (our own). A measurement y = Hx plus noise with covariance R contributes HᵀR⁻¹H to the precision matrix and HᵀR⁻¹y to the information vector (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Kalman filter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalman_filter). It says: “measurements can be filtered at each time step simply by summing their information matrices and vectors.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Chain-reachable sets are closed

**Remember:** Leave room for a last small jump, and limits stay reachable.

*True by definition.* MSC 93B03 (Attainable sets, reachability), 93B24. arXiv math.OC. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In a metric state space, y is chain reachable from x if every ε,T &gt; 0 admit a finite chain from x to y. Each link follows an admissible trajectory for at least T, then jumps a distance less than ε.

**Problem.** The set of chain-reachable states from any fixed state is closed.

**How the definition helps.** A nearby chain endpoint can use its last jump to reach the limit point (our own). Choose an endpoint within ε/2 and reach it with jumps smaller than ε/2 and durations at least T (our own). The triangle inequality keeps the modified last jump below ε (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Chain controllability of linear control systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.14595v1). It says: “The chain controllable sets Cᶜ(x) and the chain reachable sets Rᶜ(x) are closed.”

**Sources:**

- [Chain controllability of linear control systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.14595v1)

### Detectability permits a convergent observer

**Remember:** An invisible error is harmless only if it dies out.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 93B07 (Observability), 93B53. arXiv eess.SY, cs.SY. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A finite-dimensional continuous-time linear system with constant coefficients is detectable if every zero-input motion with identically zero output tends to zero. In words, whatever the output cannot see dies out by itself.

**Problem.** A linear observer estimates the state from the known input and measured output. An observer whose estimation error decays exponentially for every initial error exists exactly when the system is detectable.

**How the definition helps.** An error that the output never shows gets no correction, so it must decay on its own (our own). In the observability decomposition, detectability makes the unobservable block stable, and pole placement stabilizes the observable block, so the triangular error system decays exponentially (our own). For example, x′ = x with zero output hides a growing error that no observer can correct (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Observability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Observability). It says: “A system is detectable if all the unobservable states are stable.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Flat outputs generate trajectories

**Remember:** Choose a flat output path and differentiate to recover the motion.

*True by definition.* MSC 93B18 (Linearizations), 93C10. arXiv eess.SY, math.OC. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A flat output is a signal computed locally from the state, the input and finitely many input derivatives. It can be chosen freely within its domain, and it and finitely many of its derivatives determine the state and input by explicit formulas.

**Problem.** Every sufficiently smooth choice of flat output gives a system trajectory, provided its derivatives stay in the domain of the reconstruction formulas.

**How the definition helps.** The reconstruction formulas turn any sufficiently smooth flat output curve into a state and input that satisfy the system equations (our own). So planning a trajectory needs no integration, while an ordinary measured output need not determine the motion this way (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Optimal Control for Kinematic Bicycle Model with Continuous-time Safety Guarantees: A Sequential Second-order Cone Programming Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.08980v1). It says: “obtained by passing the parameterized flat outputs”

**Sources:**

- [M. Fliess, J. Lévine, P. Martin and P. Rouchon, Flatness and defect of non-linear systems: introductory theory and examples (1995)](https://doi.org/10.1080/00207179508921959)

### Hankel rank gives minimal dimension

**Remember:** Count the independent futures that past inputs can produce.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 93B20 (Minimal systems representations), 93B15. arXiv eess.SY, cs.SY. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Start a discrete-time linear system at zero and apply a finite input history. The Hankel map sends that history to all subsequent outputs when every subsequent input is zero. Its rank counts the independent future output sequences the past can produce.

**Problem.** For a finite-dimensional time-invariant linear system, the Hankel rank equals the smallest state dimension that reproduces its input-output behavior.

**How the definition helps.** Every past input affects future outputs through the current state, so the Hankel rank bounds every realization’s dimension from below (our own). The Ho–Kalman realization theorem attains that bound with a state space of independent future responses (our own).

**nLab:** [controllability and observability](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/controllability+and+observability). It says: “a system may be seen as giving rise to a map from an initial algebra to a terminal coalgebra which factors through it”

**Sources:**

- [B. L. Ho and R. E. Kalman, Effective construction of linear state-variable models from input/output functions (1966)](https://doi.org/10.1524/auto.1966.14.112.545)

### Minimality rules out hidden poles

**Remember:** In a minimal model, no internal mode can hide from the transfer function.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 93B20 (Minimal systems representations), 93D25. arXiv eess.SY, cs.SY. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A realization of a transfer function is a state-space model with that input-output behavior. It is minimal if its input can reach every state and its output can distinguish all starting states, so no internal mode hides from the transfer function (our own).

**Problem.** Consider a minimal finite-dimensional continuous-time linear realization with constant coefficients. Bounded inputs give bounded outputs from rest exactly when every zero-input state tends exponentially to zero.

**How the definition helps.** In a minimal realization, every eigenvalue of the state matrix is a pole of the transfer function, by the realization theorem (our own). Bounded inputs give bounded outputs exactly when every pole has negative real part, so this matches exponential decay of the state. Without minimality, ẋ = x with output equal to input gives a bounded response from rest while hiding a growing state (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Minimal realization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_realization), [BIBO stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BIBO_stability). It says: “model that is both controllable and observable and has the same input-output behaviour as the transfer function”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Tangent cones reject false tangency

**Remember:** Test the set’s directions, not just its equation.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 93B27 (Geometric methods), 93C10. arXiv math.OC, eess.SY. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The tangent cone of a closed set at a point x holds the directions in which one can leave x and stay in the set to first order. Exactly, it contains the limits of (y − x)/t over points y of the set and times t &gt; 0 tending to zero.

**Problem.** Let a continuous vector field on ℝⁿ have unique global solutions. A closed set is forward invariant exactly when the field lies in its tangent cone at every boundary point.

**How the definition helps.** Invariance needs the field to point along feasible directions of the set, not merely to pass a derivative test on a boundary equation (our own). For the set x³ ≤ 0, the derivative of x³ vanishes at zero, so that test accepts x′ = 1, but the tangent cone x ≤ 0 rejects it (our own). The Nagumo tangency theorem uses uniqueness to turn these local directions into whole trajectories that stay inside (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Safe Control Synthesis via Input Constrained Control Barrier Functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.01704v1). It says: “a closed set S ⊆ X is forward invariant for the system, if and only if”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Rich input windows span trajectories

**Remember:** Enough independent windows turn one experiment into many trajectories.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 93B30 (System identification), 93C55. arXiv eess.SY, math.OC. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An input record is persistently exciting of order q if its overlapping windows of q consecutive inputs span all input sequences of length q.

**Problem.** Take a discrete-time linear time-invariant system with n states that can be steered between any two states, recorded without noise. If its input is persistently exciting of order L + n, the paired state and input windows span exactly the trajectories of length L.

**How the definition helps.** By linearity, combinations of recorded windows are trajectories, so the windows span only trajectories (our own). Willems’ fundamental lemma uses the n extra steps of excitation and controllability to show that they span all of them (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Fast and memory-efficient optimization for large-scale data-driven predictive control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.13090v1). It says: “is persistently exciting of order L + n.”

**Sources:**

- [J. C. Willems, P. Rapisarda, I. Markovsky and B. L. M. De Moor, A note on persistency of excitation (2005)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sysconle.2004.09.003)

### Invariant endpoints preserve plan feasibility
